We owe this information to Gabriel Gerberon, an outstanding hero of the faction, who, as a most bitter enemy of all simulation in the business of Religion, attacked these most shameful frauds with both voice and pen, foretelling from these the ruin of the sect, or the fall of Jansenism, as is read in his process. Hence he fearlessly resisted Quesnel, who did not hesitate to approve such deceitful subscriptions. Indeed, he dared to brand Arnauld himself with the mark of shameful subterfuge, because he, in a certain writing, "The Notion of Liberty," inserted into the Arnauldian cause, admitted that the love of the Blessed in heaven is not free. This man, I say, in a book against the Protestant Leydecker, while he explains the Christian doctrine concerning the Predestination and Grace of Jesus Christ, at the same time tore the mask from the prevaricators, which he had for a long time fruitlessly exhorted them to put off.

There were, however, a few who, offended by this very shameful way of acting by others, and moved by the fierce obstinacy of others, having perceived the truth, returned to a sounder mind, and having made the subscription, submitted themselves from their heart to the judgment of the Bull, the Pope, and the Church.

## §. 4.
### Obsequious Silence and the Peace of Clement.

That the fruit did not lie open more widely was caused by the negligence of many Bishops, who did not immediately at the beginning make fruitful the wishes and commands of the King, and did not urge the subscription of the formula proposed by the Clergy among their own, or not at all, or certainly more slowly than was proper.
pages.35:
But a matter of a far worse example occurred after the promulgation of the formula of Alexander: this was the act of four Bishops: Nicolas Pavillon of Alet, François-Étienne de Caulet of Pamiers, Nicolas Choart de Buzanval of Beauvais, and Henri Arnauld of Angers, the brother of Antoine. For these men, in their letters and pastoral mandates, explicitly absolved their own from the subscription of the formula in clear words, and contended with many arguments that nothing was owed to the pontifical commands in this business beyond an obsequious silence, and that nothing more could be required.

These letters were suppressed by the King as soon as possible, and later also condemned at Rome in the year 1667. The Bishops themselves were summoned to plead their cause, and Commissioners were sent by the Pope, as was requested, who would be present to examine the cause. But in the midst of these movements, Alexander died: Clement IX succeeded him. Nineteen Bishops of France gave letters to him, in which they much excused those four colleagues of theirs, and in order to show that it was a legitimate excuse, they openly denied that the Church is infallible in questions of fact, even though a far greater part of the same had previously subscribed to the sentence of the Clergy issued in 1656.

Made bolder by this patronage, those four did not hesitate to urge them, in new encyclicals sent to all the Bishops, to reject the pontifical Bull entirely. However, when they were more sharply pressed by their colleagues and by the Pope himself, and finally feared more for themselves from the King, they eventually agreed that they would subscribe on this condition: that they would be exempted from the infamy of revoking their mandates. The condition was accepted by the Pope—if you consult the outcome, not well; worse
pages.36:
was the faith liberated by them. For having made, about the whole business of the formula, and secretly indeed, a verbal process, as they call it, they subscribed to this very thing, and made it be subscribed to by their own, without, however, adding themselves, or demanding anything more from others regarding the internal assent provided and the sincere acceptance of the apostolic Constitutions. Indeed, when the Pope asked for testimony of the subscription made, signed with their own hand, they gave that in a most authentic form, which nevertheless contained in by no means ambiguous terms the distinction again between law and fact. And thus the whole business rested.

And this was the so-called *Peace of Clement IX*, which some in the year 1668 attempted to render more famous to the memory of posterity with a newly minted coin. The front side had the image of the King: on the other was seen on the altar a book of the Gospels with the keys and a scepter, with the Holy Spirit shining above, and a certain hand extended. In the margin was read: *Grace and Peace from God*: at the base of the altar: *For the peace of the Church restored*. Many indeed write that the coin pleased the King when he had seen it: however, Dumafius, a Doctor of the Sorbonne and a Clerical Councilor of the Parliament of Paris, in his History of the five propositions, testifies that the King, when the coin had been shown to him by the apostolic Nuncio, inquired into its author, and when there was no one from the inner council of state who confessed that he had dictated it, or that it had been minted with his foreknowledge or assent, having broken the press, forbade all faculty of minting it in the future.

## The Progress of the Jansenist Phantasm.

### §. I.
### The Beginnings of Quesnel.

By this peace, quiet was not at all restored to the Church, but rather troubles were increased. For a new hero arose to be seconded by his Arnauld in his own time, Paschasius Quesnel, born in Paris in 1634 and later admitted into the Oratory of Bérulle. His first short work, *Four Gospels with the briefest notes*, did not appear until the year 1672, after having been approved by Vialart, Bishop of Châlons, with corrections made in very many places. The other emerged less happily: *Works of St. Leo the Great with dissertations, notes, etc.*, prohibited at Rome in the year 1676, the second year after its edition; indeed, it sufficiently showed with what spirit he was driven, being most hostile to the authority of the Roman See. Finally, he put off his mask entirely, when the Fathers of the Oratory in the year 1678, in order to expel the Jansenist pestilence already admitted into their vitals, celebrated general assemblies, and in them proscribed the condemned doctrine of Jansenius for all their schools and colleges, with a formula proposed to all for subscribing; for Quesnel, bent neither by the warnings of his Superiors nor by threats, stubbornly resisted continuously, and having despised the commands of the King and the Archbishop, leaving Paris, he hid himself in secret places, until, having returned to Paris from time to time, he escaped into Belgium.

First, there was huge trepidation, then cries: on one side the torments and mournful laments of those deploring the persecution of truth and innocence; on the other side, curses of those condemning whatever there was of sacred and profane dignity: finally, there was tumult among the very parts of the faction, and it was contested for many years of the present century. X.text: and by the severe command of the King, the rigid Morality of many suffered no small stain; they subscribed, without laying aside the error in their mind, they perjured themselves, so that they might be allowed to retain their own for themselves, or aspire to new things. Those who were, or wished to seem, of a more tender conscience, looked around for subterfuges and means by which they might mitigate the horror of perjury, and took refuge in equivocations and mental restrictions, which even the most lax Morality might shudder at. Thus they condemned the first proposition, and said that grace is given to all the just, by which the commands of God become possible for them, if they ask it from God, as they ought: but in their mind they held that the grace to pray, as they ought, is not given to all the just. They condemned the second, because the small grace of Jansenius, which excites in us a desire for good that is only weak, is at the same time inferior to earthly delight, (understand) to the overcoming of which it is not sufficient, it can certainly be resisted: because, they add among themselves, it is always resisted. In the third, they condemned and rejected from their mind natural, or physical, necessity, which makes one act not through choice, but through impulse. Regarding the fourth and fifth, they argued according to the document of the three columns, and said that undoubtedly any prevenient grace can be resisted, if the human will wished, and the grace itself (this in silence) did not make it so that it wished. Thus likewise they granted that certain graces come to the reprobate from the merits of the death of Christ, but not those without which they could not be saved. Behold the vanity of men!

Furthermore, Lord Pascal, that famous author of the *Provincial Letters* <note>original: "litterarum provincialium"</note>, which he had written under the direction of Arnauld, having turned away from these entanglements, solved the knot more expeditiously. He contended that the Bull of Alexander was subreptitious and obreptitious <note>legal terms meaning obtained through concealment or misrepresentation of facts</note> on several counts and of no authority. For he says first that any solecism invalidates any Bull, and in the original document itself, "imprimantur" <gloss>let them be printed</gloss> is read instead of "imprimatur" <gloss>let it be printed</gloss>. Next, everything is commanded under penalties to be incurred *ipso facto* <gloss>by the very fact of the action</gloss>, but it is not for the Pope to threaten the subjects of the King of France with penalties. Thirdly, since the Pope says: "We, who have sufficiently and attentively examined all that has been done in this matter, as one who, by the order of the same Innocent while we were still in minor orders and performing the duties of Cardinal, participated in all those gatherings where the same cause was discussed by apostolic authority with that diligence which greater could not be desired" — he wants nothing more to be required beyond the decision of Innocent and his own, although dogmas are received in the Gallican Church <note>original: "Ecclesia Gallicana"</note> only when defined by the authority of Councils. Furthermore, he speaks too abjectly and vilely of the Episcopal Order; since Chisius, now Pope, says of himself that he was a Cardinal Bishop even then, when he was in minor orders. But finally, even if these were absent, since the Pope declared everything by his own motion <note>original: "motu proprio"</note>, from the duty of the Pastoral Office—that is, as is commented, without the counsel and vote of the Cardinals—the authority and all force of the Bull collapses by itself.
pages.31:
Thus Pascal, I say, wrote no less learnedly and theologically, if you please; unless you prefer to say ironically, by which he mocked his own colleagues who did not cease to declaim and write against the Bulls of Innocent and Alexander and other decrees concerning various nullities. For this writer seemed too inconsistent to the Jansenists themselves, and indeed sometimes of doubtful faith, never fearing to contradict himself when it pleased him, of which he also gave a sample in his *Provincial Letters*, where he ridicules the doctrine of the Thomistic school at the beginning, but later commends it as his own.

But neither could the King's authority do anything against these men at that time; although he ordered the mandate for the acceptance of the Bull and its subscription to be entered into the registers of the Parliament. This was an entirely new act, and the first of all, by which a declaration of the King of that kind was sent to the Parliament, by which the Papal Bull was commanded to be received as dogmatic by royal power. The King, therefore, in order to cut off all excuses by which they might exempt themselves from the formula of subscription, sought that a formula be prescribed by the Pope himself; that which the Clergy also demanded together with the highest prayers.

The deed that was sought was done, and Alexander sent the Bull *Regiminis Apostolici* <gloss>of the Apostolic Government</gloss> in the year 1664, in which he proposed the following formula to be subscribed to by all ecclesiastical men of both Clergy, Bishops, and Archbishops: "I, N. N., submit myself to the Apostolic Constitution of Innocent X given on May 31, 1653, and to the Constitution of Alexander VII given on October 16, 1656, of the Supreme Pontiffs, and I reject and condemn with a sincere heart the five

pages.34:
We owe this notice to Gabriel Gerberon, a notable hero of the faction, who, as a very sharp enemy of all simulation in the matter of Religion, attacked these most shameful frauds both with his voice and his pen, foretelling from these the ruin of the sect, or the sunset of Jansenism, as is read in his process. Hence he fearlessly resisted Quesnel, who did not hesitate to approve of such deceitful subscriptions; indeed, he dared to brand Arnauld himself with the mark of a shameful refuge, because he confessed in a certain writing, *The Notion of Liberty*, inserted into the Arnauldian cause, that the love of the Blessed in heaven is not free. This man, I say, in a book against the Protestant Leydecker, while he explains the Christian doctrine concerning the Predestination and Grace of Jesus Christ, at the same time tore the mask from the prevaricators, which he had long exhorted them in vain to remove.

There were, however, a few who, offended by this very shameful manner of acting of others, and moved by the fierce obstinacy of others, with the truth perceived, returned to a saner mind, and having made the subscription, submitted themselves from their heart to the Bull, the Pope, and the judgment of the Church.

---

## §. 4.
### Obedient Silence, and the Peace of Clement.

The fact that the fruit did not spread as widely was due to the negligence of many Bishops, who did not immediately at the beginning make the wishes and orders of the King fruitful, and who did not urge the subscription of the formula proposed by the Clergy among their own
pages.35:
either at all or certainly more slowly than was fitting. But a matter of the worst example occurred after the publication of Alexander's formula, which was the action of four Bishops: Nicolas Pavillon of Alet, François-Étienne de Caulet of Pamiers, Nicolas Choart of Beauvais, and Henri Arnauld, brother of Antoine, of Angers. For these men, in their letters and pastoral mandates, absolved their own people in express words from the subscription of the formula, and contended with many arguments that nothing was owed to the pontifical commands in this matter beyond an obedient silence, and that nothing more could be demanded.

These letters, as soon as they were suppressed by the King, were later condemned at Rome also in the year 1667; the Bishops themselves were summoned to plead their cause, and Commissioners were sent by the Pope, as was requested, to participate in the examination of the cause. But during these movements, Alexander died: Clement IX succeeded him. Nineteen Bishops of France sent letters to him, in which they excused those four colleagues of their own much, and in order to show that it was a legitimate excuse, they openly denied that the Church is infallible in questions of fact; even though by far the greater part of the same had subscribed to the sentence of the Clergy once passed in 1656.

By this patronage, those four were made more audacious, and having sent new encyclicals to all the Bishops, they did not hesitate to exhort them to reject the papal Bull entirely. But when they were urged more sharply by their colleagues and by the Pontiff himself, and finally feared more for themselves from the King, they promised at last that they would subscribe on this condition: that they would be exempted from the infamy of having to revoke their mandates. The condition was accepted by the Pontiff, if you look at the result, not well:
pages.36:
the faith was broken even worse by them. For after the whole business of the formula was transacted, and indeed privately, by a *processus verbalis* <gloss>verbal proceeding</gloss>, as they call it, they subscribed to this very thing, and made their own people subscribe, without however adding themselves, or demanding further from others, anything regarding the internal assent given and the sincere acceptance of the apostolic Constitutions. Indeed, when the Pope requested a testimony of the subscription made, signed by their own hand, they gave that in a most authentic form, which however, in terms that were by no means ambiguous, contained again the distinction between law and fact. And so the whole business rested.

And this was called the *Peace of Clement IX*, which in the year 1668 some attempted to render more famous to the memory of posterity with a newly minted coin. The front side had an image of the King: on the reverse was seen the book of the Gospels upon an altar with keys and a scepter, with the Holy Spirit radiating above, and a certain hand extended. In the margin was read: *Grace, and Peace from God*; at the base of the altar: *For the Restored Concord of the Church*. Many indeed write that the coin pleased the King when he had seen it: Dumafius, however, Doctor of the Sorbonne and Clerical Councilor of the Parisian Parliament, in his History of the five propositions, testifies that the King, when the coin had been exhibited to him by the Apostolic Nuncio, inquired into its author, and when there was no one from the inner council of state who confessed to having dictated it, or that it was minted with his foreknowledge or assent, he broke the press and forbade all power of minting it in the future.

## Progress of the Jansenist Phantasm.

### §. I.
### Beginnings of Quesnel.

By this peace, rest was by no means restored to the Church; rather, the troubles were increased. For a new hero arose to be a successor to his Arnauld in his own time, Paschasius Quesnel, born in Paris in 1634 and later admitted into the Oratory of Bérulle. His first short work, *Four Gospels with very brief notes*, appeared in the year 1672, approved by Vialart, Bishop of Châlons, only after corrections had been made in many places. For Quesnel, bent neither by the warnings of his Superiors nor by threats, stubbornly resisted continuously, and having spurned the mandates of the King and the Archbishop, departing Paris, he hid himself in secret places, until, having returned to Paris from time to time, he escaped into Belgium.

These studies were the precursors of a larger work on which he was already laboring at that time, and for the completion of which he was accustomed to use the New Testament of Mons <note>the "New Testament of Mons," a French translation associated with Jansenist circles</note> here and there, as it was rumored, though in reality it was published in Holland. Pontanus, a Doctor of Louvain and an Apostolic Censor of books—and no obscure supporter of the Jansenists—approved this French version. Although he was little skilled in either the Greek or French languages, he highly recommended it as most faithful, to such an extent that the Bishops of Cambrai and Namur, relying on the testimony of the censor, affixed their own approval without further examination. But at Rome, the version was found to be too unfaithful, with exotic and not infrequently perverse meanings, and by no means in accord with the Vulgate, as it had nevertheless claimed. Already in 1668 it was condemned and prohibited by Clement IX, and again in 1679 by Innocent XI, and Pontanus was removed from his censorship office. Furthermore, when this edition from Mons was also prohibited by the Archbishop in Paris, and its copies were seized from booksellers by mandate of the royal Council, they did not refrain from new complaints and clamors, perhaps fearing for the nascent work; and Arnauld, in particular, raged against those he believed were the informants and the authors of the condemnation and prohibition with such ferocity and bitterness that he offended even his own followers, among whom he then began to be lashed for his foul language hardly less than others. And indeed, he finally deemed it necessary to write a defense in a geometric method for those who, in certain circumstances, use a rather harsh style or mode of writing, as it appears to men.

->Flee<-
pages.39:
Arnauld had fled Brussels in that same year, 1679, after having hidden for a long time in Paris. For they were terrified by the most severe royal edicts, against which the spirit of the novel Church had not yet sufficiently gathered the courage to oppose them openly. Content, therefore, to fight from a distance, one after another departed from France to show their ferocity from afar. Thus Gerberon, a degenerate alumnus of the Benedictine family from the Abbey of Corbie of the Congregation of Saint Maur, about to escape the hostile hands of the Professor of Theology, sought Holland not long after. In 1682, having been received into the company of Arnauld—who was then staying at Delft for the sake of changing his hiding place—and having subsequently proceeded to Rotterdam, he obtained citizenship and, assuming the name of *Augustinus Kergré*, was called by Quesnel a hooded citizen of Rotterdam. A writer of an intemperate mind and pen, he published many small works filled with taunts even against the highest dignities and with pestiferous doctrines. Not a few similar things were found unpublished when he was captured; he prefixed to them the names of Florus of Saint Faith, Rigberius, Pressignius, Abbot Richard, etc.

Quesnel himself followed him three years later, in 1685, the very year in which Louis XIV, having revoked the Edict of Nantes, expelled the Huguenots from France. Brought to Brussels, he found Arnauld, who had returned from Delft, with whom, hidden in a small house in a secluded village for almost five years, he was intent on completing his work and on writing and disseminating other pestiferous papers. For besides the Belgian and Batavian printing houses, they also had other secret ones in France, one of which was very well equipped in Toulouse in the house of the noble woman Juliarde de Mondoville,
pages.40:
which provided an asylum for the fleeing Jansenists and a safe exit from the kingdom, and she founded an entire congregation called the Virgins of the Infancy of Christ, to be imbued with the new dogmas. But this nest also was disturbed in the year following the hegira <note>exile</note> of Quesnel by order of the King, and the whole congregation was dissolved in 1686, with the author of the book *Innocentia oppressa* <gloss>Oppressed Innocence</gloss> providing a lavish funeral oration.

But neither could these turbulent spirits hide for long in Belgium. In 1690, they were detected by Castanaga, the Governor of Belgium, and were ordered to depart from Brussels. They complied without delay and went to Leiden in the month of April. However, having changed their plan shortly after, they departed into the territory of Liège and settled near a certain castle. There, soon considering themselves less safe, they entered the city itself and kept themselves there until the end of August with very few aware of their presence. When they grew weary of wandering, they disregarded the danger and furtively returned to Brussels after a six-month interval, seeking their old hiding places, from which, according to Quesnel himself in some of his letters, they did not step foot for the entire four years that Arnauld survived. At this time, Quesnel polished his work, and Arnauld, with him assisting, wished to exert his remaining strength against the Bulls of the Pontiffs and against the recent Decree of Alexander VIII—by which 31 propositions and several of Arnauld’s were condemned—in a book written as *Difficulties proposed against Steyaert, a Doctor of Louvain*. Having finished this labor, the 82-year-old man, deprived of his censorship, expired on August 8, 1694, having received the viaticum <note>the Eucharist administered to the dying</note> from the hands of Quesnel.
pages.41:
The anonymous continuator of Briet, in his Appendix, adds a full five years to his life; from what source, I do not know. And he weaves a distinguished eulogy, which it will not be irrelevant to append, illustrated with added notes; it reads thus:

> In the year 1699, on the 17th day before the Calends of September, Antoine Arnauld, a French Doctor of the Sorbonne, died in a village of Liège, a man borne along by an ambiguous reputation (a) among many because with an upright spirit (b) he extolled in many writings (c) the grace of God effective by itself (d) against its impugners, with the errors condemned in Cornelius Jansen being imputed to him (e), which he professed to condemn with a sincere judgment together with the Catholic Church until his last breath (f)—a man of moral probity not unequal to his learning (g), which he showed while enduring—with equal zeal and patience (h)—slanders and exiles (i) with a spirit always unconquered and docile (k). He wrote many books filled with sacred erudition (l), especially in defense of the Most Holy Eucharist, the faith and reverence of which he vigorously defended against the heterodox (m) and the nibblers at the sacred table (n). Yet he experienced the minds of some as no more placated toward him (o); to withdraw himself from their harassment, he diverted himself into a secret solitude, and there he grew old amidst meditations and writing: in the judgment of Innocent XI (check your laughter) he was once to be co-opted among the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, had not human reason persuaded (suppress your anger) that this sacrifice be taken as a precaution to be redeemed from his harassers for the sake of the Church’s peace (p).

The anonymous author writes these things in the Appendix of a Jesuit book—he pursues Nicole, Codde, the Bishop of Sebaste, and others like them with a similar eulogy. You will know a bird by its song.

(a) Read—all those less fond of novelties and more addicted to the Apostolic See.

(b) Impatient of all contradiction.

(c) Both captious and bilious.

(d) The Jansenist [grace]; which, however, he did not wish to appear as, pretending it was Thomist, as in the Treatise on the true doctrine of St. Thomas regarding sufficient and efficacious grace.

(e) And deservedly; for did he not wish the case of the first proposition to be held in the threefold denial of Peter in his letter to Parem? I pass over other things.

(g) Read—with impropriety and asperity; with this he exercised even the patience of Quesnel, which was barely tolerable in the last four years. He gave a specimen of this in the recitation of the Breviary, in the case of the little woman Perette des Lyons, etc.

(h) And indeed demonstrated by the geometric method. Seek the testimonies from the writings against Habert, etc.

(i) It is little short of calling him a Martyr: the cause is missing.

(k) With an unconquered spirit, or inflexible against any power: correctly,—and docile—this is too much. The anonymous author perhaps read the letter of Arnauld which he sent to Rome in 1644, where his book on frequent communion—which he greatly feared—was being ventilated. In it, he invokes God as a witness of his docility, reverence, and submission toward the Pontiff and his Archbishop. But how contrary was his protestation to his deeds and writings afterward?

(l) Consult the Apologies for Jansen, the book on frequent communion concerning ancient Church discipline; add the monuments of Barcos.

<margin>(m)</margin> *(m)* Arnauld wrote an excellent treatise on the Perpetuity of the faith of the Catholic Church concerning the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, and why? The anonymous author seems to hint at the cause, subjoining: "Yet he experienced the minds of some as no more placated toward him," etc. Namely, he desired the Roman censorship to be milder toward him. But with what fruit he undertook this labor among the heterodox, Jurieu has these things to say about the spirit of Arnauld: "All those things (which he had previously mentioned regarding the acts and writings of Arnauld) lead me to this opinion, that Arnauld, however much he wrote to defend transubstantiation and the true presence of Christ, nevertheless himself derogated all faith from them."

<margin>(n)</margin> (n) By this most modest name are noted those who approach communion more frequently and, in the Arnaldist spirit, do not wish to abstain from the sacred table even at Easter, or for many years, or even until the end of life as an act of penance.

<margin>(o)</margin> (o) Such as the King with his most severe edicts, and the Archbishop with his impending inquisitions, etc.

<margin>(p)</margin> (p) Indeed, because of his merits and signal reverence and submission toward the Apostolic See, ineptly—Cardinal Cibo, in letters given in the name of the Pope to Arnauld, mentions nothing at all about this mind of Innocent XI, besides the congratulations and praises deservedly earned by the aforementioned study on the Perpetuity of the faith. Did the Continuator write about sacrifice, peace, human reason, etc., for children?

In the same year, 1694, already on February 6, when everything was resounding both in Belgium and in France against the formula of Alexander VII, and various interpretations were being tossed about again, it was provided by a new decree of Innocent XII that everything should be taken only in the obvious sense of the words, "namely, the one which the words immediately offer to each person in that signification which they have from human institution,
pages.44:
"nor is it almost predominant, and it immediately offers itself to the readers—which also often appears even more evidently from the preceding and following [text], from the genius and intention of the Author—etc." What counsel? Hence the mild Quesnel indeed tolerated the subscription; he consoled the trembling. On the other hand, Gerberon cried out most bitterly. But they quickly extricated themselves, they triumphed: crying out that the formula of Alexander VII had been explained, reformed, and corrected by Innocent XII. Nor could the Pope wonder enough, who, having been petitioned on this matter by the Belgian Bishops of Mechelen, Bruges, Roermond, Ghent, and Antwerp, wrote back to them on November 24, 1696, that he had indeed confirmed both the constitution and the formula of Alexander in his Brief with express words, and had intended, and still intended, to adhere to them, and in no way to allow anything to be added or subtracted; but it was a fable to deaf ears.

The Moral Reflections on the New Testament of Quesnel are published: the same is included with Gerberon.

Meanwhile, the work of Quesnel, of twenty years as they say, appeared in 1693 with the title *Moral Reflections on the New Testament*, and again the following year, 1694, under another: *Compendium of moral doctrine from the Gospels, Acts of the Apostles, Canonical Epistles, and Apocalypse, or Christian thoughts, etc.*, published in Paris. Fraud was not absent: to this edition
pages.45:
they prefixed that approval which Vialart had once given to the first Quesnellian work, as was related above, in 1672, so that they might prevent any suspicion of erroneous doctrine from the very beginning, and so that in the future, even those ignorant of the facts might be persuaded that this work had been worn by the hands of men for a long time, even while Vialart was still living, and afterward dead, without any scourge, without any suspicion of error. And indeed, they bore fruit: they prophesied; for sworn witnesses cry out against this approval. Let Fromegovius, Doctor of the Sorbonne, come forth, who in that same year, 1694, proposed to the sacred Faculty 199 propositions worthy of censure in his Critical extract of the Quesnellian work. Let the very History of the work of Quesnel testify that it was brought to the Holy Office shortly after its edition. Nevertheless, there will be an anonymous continuator of Briet who dares to write that in the year 1713, by the Bull *Unigenitus*, the book of Quesnel—which had been read for many years (elsewhere he says it was already published 40 years ago) without suspicion of error—was condemned.

But what was the head of the matter, and subsequently provided a large harvest of disturbances, was that they brought it about that Louis Antoine de Noailles, the successor of Vialart, would commend this work of Quesnel to the Clergy of his diocese with verbose praise in 1695. Therefore, when he was translated from the See of Châlons to the Archbishopric of Paris in 1696 the following year, Quesnel did not hesitate to implore the same as the Protector of his offspring for a new approval. Noailles hesitated at first; for he immediately noticed that he was being marked by the oblique eyes of many as a supporter of error,

N.text:
which provided an asylum for the fleeing Jansenists and a safe exit from the kingdom, and she founded an entire congregation called the Virgins of the Infancy of Christ, to be imbued with the new dogmas. But this nest also was disturbed in the year following the hegira <note>exile</note> of Quesnel by order of the King, and the whole congregation was dissolved in 1686, with the author of the book *Innocentia oppressa* <gloss>Oppressed Innocence</gloss> providing a lavish funeral oration.

But neither could these turbulent spirits hide for long in Belgium. In 1690, they were detected by Castanaga, the Governor of Belgium, and were ordered to depart from Brussels. They complied without delay and went to Leiden in the month of April. However, having changed their plan shortly after, they departed into the territory of Liège and settled near a certain castle. There, soon considering themselves less safe, they entered the city itself and kept themselves there until the end of August with very few aware of their presence. When they grew weary of wandering, they disregarded the danger and furtively returned to Brussels after a six-month interval, seeking their old hiding places, from which, according to Quesnel himself in some of his letters, they did not step foot for the entire four years that Arnauld survived. At this time, Quesnel polished his work, and Arnauld, with him assisting, wished to exert his remaining strength against the Bulls of the Pontiffs and against the recent Decree of Alexander VIII—by which 31 propositions and several of Arnauld’s were condemned—in a book written as *Difficulties proposed against Steyaert, a Doctor of Louvain*. Having finished this labor, the 82-year-old man, deprived of his censorship, expired on August 8, 1694, having received the viaticum <note>the Eucharist administered to the dying</note> from the hands of Quesnel.

The anonymous continuator of Briet, in his Appendix, adds a full five years to his life; from what source, I do not know. And he weaves a distinguished eulogy, which it will not be irrelevant to append, illustrated with added notes; it reads thus:

> In the year 1699, on the 17th day before the Calends of September, Antoine Arnauld, a French Doctor of the Sorbonne, died in a village of Liège, a man borne along by an ambiguous reputation (a) among many because with an upright spirit (b) he extolled in many writings (c) the grace of God effective by itself (d) against its impugners, with the errors condemned in Cornelius Jansen being imputed to him (e), which he professed to condemn with a sincere judgment together with the Catholic Church until his last breath (f)—a man of moral probity not unequal to his learning (g), which he showed while enduring—with equal zeal and patience (h)—slanders and exiles (i) with a spirit always unconquered and docile (k). He wrote many books filled with sacred erudition (l), especially in defense of the Most Holy Eucharist, the faith and reverence of which he vigorously defended against the heterodox (m) and the nibblers at the sacred table (n). Yet he experienced the minds of some as no more placated toward him (o); to withdraw himself from their harassment, he diverted himself into a secret solitude, and there he grew old amidst meditations and writing: in the judgment of Innocent XI (check your laughter) he was once to be co-opted among the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, had not human reason persuaded (suppress your anger) that this sacrifice be taken as a precaution to be redeemed from his harassers for the sake of the Church’s peace (p).

The anonymous author writes these things in the Appendix of a Jesuit book—he pursues Nicole, Codde, the Bishop of Sebaste, and others like them with a similar eulogy. You will know a bird by its song.

These lucubrations were the precursors of a larger work upon which he was already laboring at that time, and for the completion of which he was accustomed to use the New Testament of Mons, as it was rumored, though in reality it was published in Holland. Pontanus, a Doctor of Louvain and an Apostolic Censor of books—and no obscure supporter of the Jansenists—approved this French version. Although he was little skilled in either Greek or French, he commended it highly as being most faithful, to such an extent that the Bishops of Cambrai and Namur, trusting the censor's testimony, added their own approval without further examination. But at Rome, the version was found to be overly unfaithful, containing exotic and often perverse meanings, and by no means in agreement with the Vulgate, as it had nevertheless claimed. Already in 1668, and again in 1679 by Innocent XI, it was condemned and prohibited, and Pontanus was removed from his censorial office. Furthermore, when this Mons edition was also prohibited at Paris by the Archbishop, and its copies were seized from the booksellers by the mandate of the royal Senate, they did not refrain from new complaints and clamors, fearing perhaps for the work already being born. Arnauld, in particular, raged against the informers—whom he believed to be the authors of the condemnation and prohibition—with such ferocity and bitterness that he offended even his own supporters, among whom he began to be beaten back with no less mildness than he treated others, owing to his abusive language. Indeed, he finally deemed it necessary to write a defense using a geometric method for those who, in certain circumstances, employ a rather harsh style or mode of writing, as it appears to men.

Finally, he did indeed grant approval to Quesnel’s work, but not without a prior examination and the correction of discovered errors: and in order to consult further for his own reputation, he condemned the book *Exposition of the Faith* <note>original: "Expositio fidei"</note>, recently edited in defense of the doctrine. At first, Quesnel easily conceded to Noailles, and promised that he would submit himself, together with his book, to censure, while meanwhile confirming his spirit, as he had sacredly asserted to his own followers by letter, to reject every correction that would corrupt the integrity of his doctrine. Nor was there anything to fear; for the Prelate had named revisers of the work who had long served in the camp of the faction, whom Quesnel could also recognize. But truly, when in his mandate, in which he had condemned the *Exposition of the Faith*, he had on one hand highly extolled the doctrine of Augustine, and at the same time by another ordinance had forbidden anyone to accuse another of Jansenism based on light suspicion: but on the other hand had condemned the very doctrine of Augustine, as they boasted it to be, he exacerbated the spirits of both parties not a little.

Among other things, for which they reproached him for inconsistency of mind, was the *Ecclesiastical Problem — Whether one ought to believe Noailles of Chalon in 1695, or Noailles of Paris in 1696?* <note>original: "Problema ecclesiasticum — Utrum Noaillio Cabilonenfi 1695. an Parifino 1696. credendum fit?"</note> in which, after a comparison was made between the *Moral Reflections* <note>original: "Reflexiones morales"</note> and the *Exposition of the Faith*, the Author contended that Noailles had condemned in Paris what he had approved in Chalon. The book paid for its crime on an infamous pyre. The author was said to be a certain Jesuit by the name of P. Soiiatre. But Gerberon, who certainly knew the matter more accurately, testified in his defenses and in his true resolution of the Problem that the work was of one of the disciples of Augustine, with notes added to the mandate to the great offense of the Prelate, upon whom he most crudely cast the mark of Jansenism. Quesnel also praised Gerberon, criticizing nothing in the letters to Boileau, a confidant of the Prelate, save that the book was edited too hastily and at an inopportune time, namely, when Noailles, at the request of the King, was called to the Purple <note>meaning the cardinalate</note> by Innocent XII.

Shortly after the Problem, there followed the *Case of Conscience* <note>original: "Casus Conscientiæ"</note>. It was asked whether a confessor had rightly absolved a cleric who confesses that he does not internally submit to the judgment of the Church regarding the text of the Authors, yet nevertheless shows it external submission and reverence by his silence. The response, subscribed to by 40 Theologian Doctors, held that this opinion of the Cleric was neither new, nor singular, nor condemned by the Church: such a one also ought not to be urged further, nor held in suspicion. Cardinal Noailles also condemned this response, and at the same time took care that nothing sinister or injurious be published against the subscribed Doctors, all of whom, save two, later excused their action.

In the meantime, while the Quesnellians were planning a new edition of the work, and seeing well that condemnation could not be averted by a softer censure, thinking that they should consult otherwise, they offered it to be examined equally by the celebrated Bossuet, Bishop of Meaux. Since he could not favor error, yet wished to safeguard the authority of the Cardinal, who was very close to him, he noted that very many propositions, which admitted no excuse, were to be cut out, others he castigated, or mi-
pages.48:
tigated, and furthermore added many annotations, so that by this correction of the book he might save the Cardinal's reputation entire, if he were to approve it. But nothing fair was to be expected from this sort of men, who looked to nothing else than to provide protection for the work with great names and to prepare an obstinate defense of their errors by any arts whatsoever. The correction could in no way please: therefore, the edition is deferred until the death of Bossuet, after which, in the year 1699, it appeared immediately under the title: *New Testament in French with Moral Reflections upon each verse. Paris.* Nothing in it was deleted, nothing corrected; only Bossuet's annotations were prefixed to the work like a shield.

All good men were stunned, until Saint-André, Bossuet's Vicar, who as witness and arbiter knew everything that had been done by the Bishop in this affair, exposed the most shameful frauds. Then indeed the indignation of all erupted, the work was referred to the sacred tribunals, and antidotes were sought against the plague. Meanwhile, Quesnel, having been established as the head of the faction after Arnauld, and Gerberon, having scattered seditious pamphlets through Belgium and France, as was related above, having taken the opportunity especially from the aforementioned case of conscience, threw everything into confusion; and now the unbridled license of these men seemed as if it could only be curbed by the application of force. But this was the labor. Quesnel, frequently changing his hiding places and clothing, and using fictitious names, now called P. Prior, or Provincial of the Augustinians, now Monsieur de Fresne, Frekerberg, Baron de Rebeck, du Puis, etc., had until then eluded the industry of the most sagacious men.

But at last, the Archbishop of Mechlin, Humbert William de Precipiano, after he had subjected to canonical penalties in the year 1700 another priest of the Oratory, Van Hame, who was spreading lower principles of faith despite repeated warnings, and in the year 1702 instituted an action against Quesnel in Rome, having been provided in the following year with surer clues of his hiding places, first captured Gerberon in 1703, extracted from the extreme corner of the city of Brussels. Quesnel then himself, with his inseparable companion Brigodeus—who, although warned by Roman letters to depart the city, had merely moved his lodging to the house called *Refuge de Forest*—was discovered there; by the help of his associate, he had already evaded the hands of the imminent bailiffs, but being recalled by the memory of papers which it was of the greatest importance to keep from the eyes of men, he was intercepted by the hidden guards in the month of May, on the Wednesday after Pentecost, and led likewise into the Palace of the Prelate.

Quesnel remained there for no more than three months. For his fellow-partisans, since they were exploring all the chinks by which they might bring aid, finally, having removed the lead from the windows, by a note inscribed to Ernest, Canon of Saint Gudula, were warned of the place, location, and condition of his custody, and through labor continued for two nights, they perforated the wall, and thus on September 13th, after midnight, restored their precious head to liberty, who soon rushed off into Holland. All the papers of that man, having been intercepted, showed what he had prepared to disturb the peace of the Church. Among other things, a voluminous work was found: *Dogmas, discipline, and moral doctrine of the Church* <note>original: "Dogmata, disciplina, & doctrina moralis Ecclesiæ"</note>, in which he Church-
pages.50:

Then Quesnel himself, with his constant companion Brigode—who, although warned by Roman letters to depart the city, had merely changed his residence and taken refuge in a house called the *Refuge de Forest*—was discovered in the same place. Through the help of his associate, he had already escaped the hands of the imminent bailiffs, but being recalled by the memory of papers which it was of the greatest importance to conceal from the eyes of men, he was intercepted by hidden guards in the month of May and was led on the Wednesday after Pentecost into the Palace of the Prelate.

Quesnel remained there for no more than three months. For his fellow members, since they tried every chink to offer help, finally, by means of a note written on lead pulled from the windows, alerted Ernest, a Canon of St. Gudula, about the location, situation, and condition of his custody. They perforated the wall with work continued over two nights, and thus on September 13th, after midnight, they restored their precious head to liberty, and he immediately rushed off into Holland. All of his papers, which were intercepted, showed what he had prepared to disturb the peace of the Church. Among other things, a voluminous work was found: *Dogmas, discipline, and moral doctrine of the Church*, in which
pages.50:
he asserts a two-headed Church and defends the proposition of Barcos, which he has in his preface to the book on frequent communion, namely, that Peter and Paul are the two heads of the Church, who constitute nothing but one, and in such a way that Paul is equal, and by no means subject to Peter in the Primacy and Government of the universal Church. Furthermore, an action having been brought against him, he was accused and cited; since he would not appear, in his absence he was convicted of Bajanism, Jansenism, and of inciting a tumult. He was declared to have incurred excommunication by public sentence, with added penalties, until he should satisfy the Pontiff.

Gerberon, however, who wished to be called Augustine Kergré, just as Quesnel attributed to himself the name of Baron de Rebeck, after a six-month imprisonment, was likewise convicted. Since he would not acquiesce to the sentence passed upon him, he was sought and extradited by the King of the French as his subject, and first had to move to Amiens, then to Vincennes for custody, where after six years, now an octogenarian, having finally recognized the truth, he solemnly abjured his errors on April 16, 1710, before the Vicar of the Archbishop of Paris. Having been released, he died ten days after the feast of the conversion of St. Paul, in the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, having confirmed his retraction of errors for a second time.

# §. 3.
## The Clementine Bulls against the Obsequious Silence and the Work of Quesnel.

At the request of the Prelates of France that every path be closed to those erring, Pope Clement XI, on July 16, 1705, issued the Bull *Vineam Domini Sabaoth* (The Vineyard of the Lord of Hosts), in which, having confirmed once again the bulls of Innocent X and Alexander VII, he condemns the Resolution of the famous *Case of Conscience* and those who assent to it. He declares that the obedience owed to the said constitutions is by no means satisfied by that *obsequious silence*, but that the condemned sense of the propositions, which the words themselves express, must be rejected and condemned by all as heretical, not only with the mouth, but also with the heart; nor can the aforementioned formula (of Alexander) be subscribed to with any other mind, intention, or belief.

This Bull was immediately accepted by the Clergy, and the decree of acceptance was sent to Rome. To this was inserted the proposition: that the Constitutions of the Supreme Pontiffs, after solemn acceptance made by the body of Pastors, ought to be regarded as an edict and law of the Church. This greatly offended the Pope, who wrote back swiftly that the Prelates should not flatter themselves, but learn to obey, to execute, and not presume to judge; and he added another form of acceptance. But this was too much for the French. However, to cut off this untimely dispute, it was agreed that another form of acceptance should be conceived, with the opinions on both sides mitigated. But behold! When Noailles had taken upon himself the task of writing this in the name of the Prelates, he sent it to the Pontiff with changes in several
pages.52:
places. New complaints returned from this: the Prelates were astonished. Noailles testified that he had fulfilled what was enjoined upon him. Finally, a copy of the Cardinal’s letter transmitted by the Pontiff exposed the fraud, and he was forced by the King himself to send to Rome a genuine testimony of the acceptance, up to the final version, as it had been drawn up in the second assembly of the Clergy, subscribed by himself and eleven other Bishops, with severe silence imposed on everyone regarding this matter. This testimony was an explanation of the first decree of acceptance, made, as was written, first in the year 1710, which Noailles, in letters given in his own name besides to the Pope, comprehended in four articles. He says that he testifies that, first, the Clergy intended to accept the constitution of the Pope with the same obedience as they had accepted others issued against Jansen. Second, that the acceptance of the Bishops was not reputed by him as necessary for those constitutions to be held by Catholics as rules of believing and speaking; yet it was useful, where error had arisen, to close off evasions, and therefore, etc. Third, that he had not arrogated an examination to himself or judged, but that, as the Gallican Bishops once wrote to Leo the Great, he rejoiced because of the recognized consensus of their faith. Fourth, finally, that nothing was lacking in the Pontifical decrees against Jansen to oblige the whole Church, and that regarding them, neither an appeal could be admitted, nor could a change be expected, etc.

This weighed heavily upon the Cardinal, but much more did the intervening Bull *Universi Dominici Gregis* (Of the whole flock of the Lord), by which the work of Quesnel was condemned on July 13, 1708;

which condemnation, that he might prevent it by a prior retraction of his approval, he could be led to do by no force of reason, by no counsel of friends, nor by the indignation of the King himself, which he had felt not obscurely; although he had otherwise proclaimed that he would be the first to subscribe if the book were condemned by some Bull. The Bull arrived, and Noailles openly complained that the Pope had attempted such things without consulting him, that he was not so much attacking Quesnel as he was attacking him, the approver, with these condemnations. And thus, whatever sinister things had happened to the Jansenians, he allowed himself to be persuaded by the dregs of men with whom he was besieged that all of it was done out of hatred for him; whence also, in order to do evil to those whom he thought were hostile to him, he condemned for I know not what pretext, in the year 1711, the censure of the two Bishops of Luçon and La Rochelle, which they had brought against Quesnel’s book.

Truly, this Bull did not please even the French themselves very much; both because the book was condemned by a simple condemnation alone, and because the delicate temperament of those men, who were no less tenacious of their own liberties than of their opinions, seemed to be wounded by the customary formulas of the bulls, even from the fact that all copies of the condemned book, which nevertheless bore royal permission for the press, were ordered to be burned. Wherefore King Louis, in order to impose an end to a cause so sad and so pernicious to the kingdom and the Church, although he would have preferred that it be done by a shorter path, gave orders to his Legate at Rome, Cardinal de la Trémoille, to insist to the Pontiff for another Bull, in which certain propositions, and those specifically excerpted from the work of Quesnel, would be condemned, and whatever [concerns] morals and li-ber-

N.text:
, and in addition he added many annotations so that, by this correction of the book, he might save the entire reputation of the Cardinal, if he were to approve it. But nothing fair was to be expected from this kind of men, who looked to nothing other than to provide cover for the work with great names and to prepare, by any arts whatsoever, a stubborn defense of their errors. The correction could in no way please them; therefore, the edition was delayed until the death of Bossuet, after which, in the year 1699, it immediately appeared under the title: *New Testament in French with Moral Reflections on each verse. Paris.* Nothing was deleted in it, nothing corrected; only Bossuet’s annotations were prefixed to the work like a shield.

All good men were stunned until Saint-Andrè, Bossuet’s Vicar, who knew as a witness and arbiter everything that had been done by the Bishop in this matter, exposed the most shameful frauds. Then indeed the indignation of all erupted; the work was denounced to the sacred tribunals, and antidotes against the plague were sought. Meanwhile, Quesnel, having been established as the head of the faction after Arnauld, and Gerberon, by spreading seditious pamphlets through Belgium and France, as was related above—especially taking the opportunity from the aforementioned *Case of Conscience*—confounded everything. And now the unbridled license of those men seemed to need curbing by nothing less than the application of force. But this was the labor. Quesnel, by frequently changing his hiding places, clothes, and assumed names—now called Father Prior, or Provincial of the Augustinians, now Monsieur de Fresne, Frekerberg, Baron de Rebeck, du Puis, etc.—had hitherto eluded the industry of the most sagacious men.

pages.38: These lucubrations were the precursors of a larger work, upon which he was already toiling at that time, and for the completion of which he was accustomed to use, as was rumored, a New Testament <note>translated in</note> the Mons <note>a city in the Southern Netherlands</note> version, but which in truth was published in Holland. Pontanus, a Doctor of Louvain and an Apostolic Censor of books—and no obscure supporter of the Jansenists—approved this French version. He recommended it highly as being most faithful, however little he was skilled in either the Greek or French language, to such an extent that the Bishops of Cambrai and Namur, trusting the testimony of the censor, also appended their own approval without further examination. But at Rome, this version was found to be excessively unfaithful, with exotic and not rarely perverse meanings, and by no means in agreement with the Vulgate, as it nevertheless pretended. Already in 1668, it was condemned and prohibited by Clement IX, and again in 1679 by Innocent XI, and Pontanus was removed from his censorial office. Furthermore, when this edition from Mons was also prohibited at Paris by the Archbishop, and its copies were seized from booksellers by mandate of the Royal Council, they did not refrain from new complaints and clamors, perhaps already fearing for the work being born. Arnauld, in particular, raged with such ferocity and bitterness against the informers—whom he believed to be the authors of the condemnation and prohibition—that he offended even his own supporters, among whom he began to be thrashed for his scurrility scarcely less mildly than others. And truly, he himself finally deemed it necessary to write justifications using a "geometric method" for those who, in certain circumstances, use a style—or manner of writing—that seems rather harsh to men.
pages.39:
Arnauld had fled Brussels in that same year, 1679, after having hidden for a long time in Paris. For they were terrified by the most severe royal edicts, by which the spirit of the new Church had not yet had enough courage to oppose them openly. Content, therefore, to fight from a distance, one after another left France to show their ferocity from afar. Thus, Gerberon, a degenerate alumnus of the Benedictine family from the Abbey of Corbie of the Congregation of Saint Maur, about to escape similar hostile hands, sought Holland not long after. In 1682, having been received into the company of Arnauld—who was then staying at Delft for the sake of changing his hiding place—he subsequently set out for Rotterdam; having obtained citizenship and assumed the name of *Augustine Kergré*, he was called by Quesnel the hooded citizen of Rotterdam. A writer of an intemperate spirit and pen, he published many booklets filled with gibes even against the highest dignities and with pestiferous doctrines. Not a few similar works were found, while he was being captured, that were unpublished: he prefixed the names of Florus of Saint Faith, Rigberius, Pressignius, Abbot Richard, etc.

Three years later, Quesnel himself followed him in the year 1685, the very year in which Louis XIV, having revoked the Edict of Nantes, expelled the Huguenots from France. Having been brought to Brussels, he found Arnauld, who had returned from Delft, with whom he stayed in a humble little house in a secluded village for nearly five years, intent on completing his work and on writing and disseminating other pestiferous papers. For besides the Belgian and Dutch printing houses, they also had other clandestine ones in France, one of which was very well equipped in Toulouse in the house of the noble woman Juliarda de Mondoville,
pages.40:
who provided an asylum and a safe exit from the kingdom for the fugitive Jansenists, and who founded an entire congregation of virgins called of the Infancy of Christ to be imbued with new dogmas. But this nest, too, was disturbed by the King's order shortly after the Hegira of Quesnel in the year 1686, and the entire congregation was dissolved, while the author of the book *Innocentia oppressa* <gloss>Oppressed Innocence</gloss> sang dirges abundantly.

But these turbulent spirits could not remain hidden for long even in Belgium; they were detected in 1690 by Castanage, the Governor of Belgium, and were ordered to depart from Brussels. They complied without delay and went to Leiden in the month of April. However, having soon changed their plan, they departed into the territory of Liège and settled near a certain castle, where, soon thinking themselves less safe, they entered the city itself and kept themselves there until the end of August with very few aware of it. When they grew weary of the wandering, and having scorned the danger, they returned stealthily to Brussels after a six-month interval and sought their old hiding places, from which, by the testimony of Quesnel himself in some of his letters, they did not stir a foot for the whole four years that Arnauld survived. During this time, Quesnel polished his work, and Arnauld, with him assisting, wished to test his final strengths against the Bulls of the Pontiffs and against the recent Decree of Alexander VIII—by which 31 propositions, and many more of Arnauld's, were condemned—in the book written as *Difficulties proposed against Steyaert, a Doctor of Louvain*. Having finished this labor, the old man, aged 82, having received the viaticum from the hands of Quesnel, expired on the 8th of August, 1694.

An anonymous continuator of Brietius adds an entire five years to his life in an Appendix, from which source I know not, and he composes a notable eulogy which it will not be irrelevant to append, illustrated with added notes. It reads thus:

> To the year 1699, 17th of the Kalends of September, died in the territory of Liège, Antoine Arnauld, a Frenchman and Sorbonne Doctor, brought into disrepute by ambiguous fame among many (a), because with an integral spirit (b) he exalted in many writings (c) the grace of God that is efficacious by itself (d) against its impugners, with the errors condemned in Cornelius Jansenius imputed to him (e), which he professed up to his final breath to condemn with sincere judgment along with the Catholic Church (f), a man of probity of morals not unequal to his learning (g), which he showed by equal zeal, and enduring obloquies and exiles with patience (h), always with an unconquered and docile mind (i). He composed many books filled with sacred erudition (k), especially in defense of the Most Holy Eucharist, the faith and reverence of which he defended forcefully against heterodoxies (l) and the despoilers of the sacred table (m). Yet he experienced no less placated spirits of some against him (o), so that, to withdraw himself from their persecution, he turned aside into a secret solitude, there aging among meditations and writing: according to the judgment of Innocent XI (restrain your laughter), he was at one time to be co-opted among the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, had not human reason persuaded that this sacrifice be provided for by its persecutors for the sake of the peace of the Church (restrain your anger) (p).

These things the anonymous author says in the Appendix of a Jesuit book—he pursues Nicole, Codde, the Bishop of Sebaste, and similar ones with a similar eulogy. You will recognize the bird by its song.

(a) Read—all those less fond of novelties and more addicted to the Apostolic See.

(b) Impatient of all contradiction.

(c) As much captious as bilious.

(d) The Jansenist <gloss>grace</gloss>; which, however, he did not want to appear, pretending it was Thomistic, as in his Treatise on the true doctrine of St. Thomas concerning sufficient and efficacious grace.

(e) And deservedly; for did he not want the case of the first proposition to be held in the triple denial of Peter in his letter to Parem? I pass over other things.

(f) Namely, with a distinction of law and fact, and a denied subscription to the formulas. His last work, *Difficulties proposed to Mons. Steyaert*, provides a clear testimony, in which he almost died in the arms of Quesnel.

(g) Read—improbity and asperity; with this he exercised even Quesnel's patience, which was scarcely tolerable in the last four years: a specimen of the former he gave in reciting the Breviary, in the case of the little woman Perette des Lyons, etc.

(h) And indeed demonstrated by a geometric method. Seek the testimonies from his writings against Habert, etc.

(i) It lacks little for him to call him a Martyr: the cause is missing.

(k) With an unconquered mind, or inflexible against any power: correctly—and docile—this is too much. Perhaps the anonymous author read the letter of Arnauld which he sent to Rome in 1644, where his book on frequent communion, which he feared greatly, was then being ventilated. In it, he invokes God as a witness of his docility, reverence, and submission toward the Pontiff and his Archbishop. But how contrary was this protestation to his subsequent deeds and writings!

(l) Consult his Apologies for Jansenius, the book on frequent communion concerning the ancient discipline of the Church; add the monuments of Barcos.

He wrote

<margin>(m)</margin> *()* Arnauld wrote an excellent treatise on the Perpetuity of the faith of the Catholic Church concerning the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, and why? The anonymous author seems to hint at the cause, subjoining: "Yet he experienced no less placated spirits, etc." Namely, he was hoping for a milder Roman censure against himself. But with what fruit he undertook this labor among the heterodox, Jurieu has these things to say concerning the spirit of Arnauld: "All those things (which he had mentioned before regarding the acts and writings of Arnauld) lead me to the opinion that Arnauld, however much he wrote to defend transubstantiation and the true presence of Christ, nevertheless detracts from all faith in them himself."

<margin>(n)</margin> (n) By this most modest name are noted those who approach communion more often, and, out of the Arnauldian spirit of penance, do not want to abstain from the sacred table even at Easter, or for many years, or even until the end of life.

<margin>(o)</margin> (o) Such as the King with most severe edicts, and the Archbishop with impending inquisitions, etc.

<margin>(p)</margin> (p) By all means on account of his merits and notable reverence and submission toward the Apostolic See—ineptly—Cardinal Cibo, in letters sent in the name of the Pope to Arnauld, mentions nothing at all of this mind of Innocent XI, beyond congratulations and praises deservedly earned through the aforementioned lucubration on the Perpetuity of the faith. Concerning the sacrifice, peace, human reason, etc., did the Continuator write to children?

In the same year, 1694, already on the 6th of February, when everything was resounding in Belgium as well as in France against the formula of Alexander VII, and various interpretations were again being bandied about, it was provided by a new decree of Innocent XII that all things be taken not otherwise than in the obvious sense of the words: "namely, that which the words immediately offer to everyone in that signification which they have from the institution of men,
pages.44:
and which is, as it were, predominant, and immediately presents itself to the readers—which also often appears even more evidently from the preceding and following, from the genius and intention of the Author—etc." What counsel? Hence, Quesnel, indeed soft, tolerated the subscription; he consoled the trembling: on the other hand, Gerberon cried out most bitterly. But they extricated themselves quickly; they triumphed: crying out that the formula of Alexander VII had been explained, reformed, and corrected by Innocent XII. Nor could the Pope wonder enough, who, having been interrogated on that matter by the Bishops of the Belgians—Malines, Bruges, Roermond, Ghent, and Antwerp—wrote back to them on the 24th of November, 1696, that he had indeed confirmed both the constitution and the formula of Alexander in his Brief with express words, and had intended, and still intended, that they should be adhered to, and by no means allowed that anything be added or subtracted; but it was a fable to the deaf.

*Moral Reflections* on the N. T. of Quesnel are published: he is likewise comprehended with Gerberon.

Meanwhile, the work of Quesnel of twenty years equally, as they say, appeared in 1693 with the title *Moral Reflections on the New Testament*, and again in the following year, 1694, under another: *Compendium of moral doctrine from the Gospels, Acts of the Apostles, Canonical Epistles, and Apocalypse, or Christian thoughts, etc.*, published in Paris. Fraud was not absent: to this edition
pages.45:
they prefixed that approval which Vialart had once given to the first Quesnellian work, as was narrated above, in the year 1672, so that, namely, they might immediately prevent every suspicion of erroneous doctrine from the beginning, and so that, for the future as well, it might be persuaded to those ignorant of the facts that this work had for a long time, while Vialart was still alive and after his death, been worn by the hands of men without any scourge, without any suspicion of error. And indeed, they bore fruit: they divined; for sworn witnesses clamor against this approval. Let Fromegovius, a Doctor of the Sorbonne, come forth, who in the same year, 1694, proposed to the sacred Faculty 199 propositions worthy of censure in his Critical extract of the Quesnellian work; let the History of the work of Quesnel itself testify that it was brought to the sacred office shortly after its edition. Yet there will be a certain anonymous continuator of Brietius, who dares to write that in the year 1713, through the bull *Unigenitus*, the book of Quesnel—which had been read for many years without suspicion of error (elsewhere he says, published 40 years ago)—was condemned.

But that which was the head of the matter, and subsequently provided an ample harvest of disturbances, was that they accomplished that Louis Antoine de Noailles, the successor of Vialart, in 1695, recommended this work of Quesnel with prolix encomium to the Clergy of his diocese. Wherefore, when in the following year he was translated from the See of Chalon to the Archbishopric of Paris in 1696, Quesnel did not hesitate to implore the same man, as the Protector of his offspring, for a new approval. Noailles hesitated at first; for he immediately noticed that he was being marked by the oblique eyes of many as a supporter of error,

liberties of the Gallican Church <note>original: "libertates Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ"</note> might be maintained, while formulas born from the fullness of power, by his own motion, and similar things customary at Rome would be omitted: so that in this way all quibbles and excuses for accepting the Bull might be forestalled. To this excellent intention of the Most Christian King and his zeal for restoring peace, as the prayers and exhortations of very many Bishops were added, the Pontiff at last granted everything, and as soon as possible the examination of the entire work was resumed by two Cardinals and several theologians.

When Noailles saw these things being prepared, moved both by the example of the King, who had revoked the license to print Quesnel's books, and by fear of the coming Bull, he had already decided with himself to condemn the book which he had once approved: but then, two men undermined the whole thing. The General of the Minims, <term>Rollet</term>, and the so-called Expeditionary, <term>Chauffeur</term>, wrote to the Cardinal that everything being done to elaborate the Bull was merely a shadow-play meant to terrify the Cardinal, and having perceived this, he gave no further place to sounder counsel or more certain reports. Furthermore, the faction spread the rumor in Rome and in France that there was no hope of receiving the Bull: that the Dauphin favored Quesnel, that the Parliament was hostile to the Roman Curia, and that the Sorbonne was not so inimical to the new doctrine; which they confirmed with recent documents. For when the Jesuit <term>Juvency</term> had written certain things in the History of his Society regarding acts during the time of Henry IV that were not at all approved by the Parliament, the Superiors of the three Colleges that were in Paris were summoned to declare what they thought about the four most well-known articles out of 82,

namely concerning the power of the Pope in the Kingdoms of Princes and in the Church, and finally they were ordered to bind themselves by oath to hold the doctrine of those articles. Then the Abbot of <term>Saint-Aignan</term>, when he had sought letters of confirmation from Rome for his Bishopric, was persuaded, lest he succumb to the envy and deceitful arts of the Jansenists at Rome as the worst advisors suggested, to defend the fourth proposition of Jansenius in the Sorbonne itself.

However, these terrors soon vanished; for when neither the acts of the Parliament nor the error of the abbot seemed of such importance that they could raise a prudent suspicion that the acceptance would be refused: and the Dauphin had even given a public testimony in writing of the Catholic faith and his firm adherence to it, after the two-year labors of examinations and collation of texts were finally exhausted, the famous Bull <term>Unigenitus</term> <gloss>The Only-Begotten</gloss> was subscribed to by Clement XI on September 8, 1713, after all points had been previously examined and revised by <term>Trémoille</term>, and published two days later, on September 10. In it, one hundred and one propositions excerpted from Quesnel's work are condemned in a lump, as they say, that is, as false, impious, heretical, etc., with these and other censures attached to be applied respectively to each: it is added that many others similar to these and akin to them are contained therein, worthy of condemnation, and that the very text of Scripture was corrupted by the reprobated <term>Montenfi</term> edition; wherefore the whole book, in whatever language published or to be published, is prohibited and condemned.

<summary>This page covers the failed attempts to sabotage the papal examination and details the publication of the Bull Unigenitus in 1713, which condemned Quesnel's work.</summary>
<keywords>Clement XI, Bull Unigenitus, Jansenism, Quesnel, Sorbonne, Montenfi edition</keywords>
pages.56:
<note>A decorative horizontal rule appears at the top of the page.</note>

Having understood this, Noailles, without delay, issued a mandate on the 28th of the same month, in which he says that he could not bear his name to be prefixed to a book condemned by the Pope, and therefore, as he had promised, he revoked the approval he had previously given to the book in another diocese, condemned the book, and prohibited its reading and retention, etc. Then the Clergy was convened and Commissioners were elected, the chief of whom was Cardinal Rohan; Noailles was named President of the Council. By October 18, seven of the 18 Archbishops and thirty-three of the 112 Bishops had gathered. Noailles prefaced the meeting with remarks about his previously given preface to the book and the mandate issued shortly before, and soon began to discourse on the obscurity of the Bull and the doubts that would arise from it, to the astonishment of the others, to whom everything in it seemed clear and plain. Rohan demonstrated that there was not one of the 101 propositions to which one of the censures did not apply; yet Noailles contended as much as he could that the Bull could not be accepted otherwise than with a prefixed instruction and added explanations and restrictions. This proposal was rejected by almost everyone, and four articles were opposed to it by Cardinal Rohan: 1. It is manifestly certain from the Bull, and must be held, that Quesnel's book is heretical: 2. That those 101 propositions are deservedly condemned and worthy of one of the applied censures: therefore 3. The Bull must be accepted before any further explanation, as it is neither ambiguous nor obscure regarding the aforementioned matters. 4. There is no need for any other previous instruction, except one by which the faithful would be protected against false interpretations of the Bull. These points pleased the Assembly, but not Noailles; who, since he could obtain nothing...

pages.57:
he could obtain nothing, withdrew with nine other Bishops and abstained from the sessions until he was forced by the King's authority to revisit them. In these, the decree of acceptance was finally made and subscribed by all except Noailles and a few of his followers: after this, a pastoral instruction was proposed, which Noailles himself praised with no less artifice and eloquence than if it were his own; the Acts of the Assembly were sent to the absent Bishops: finally, a letter was sent to the Pope on February 5, 1714, with an attached instruction, by which they signify the acceptance of the Bull, congratulate the repression of the errors by his constitution, and pledge obedience and prompt fidelity in executing it: all of which were approved by the Pontiff. And when the responses of many absent Bishops had arrived, in which they also approved the acts and, by giving their consent, signified the acceptance of the Bull, the King issued an edict or letters patent on February 14, by which he commanded the Bull to be accepted, published, and observed by all, and to be entered into the public records by all Parliaments throughout the Kingdom. Soon the Bull was promulgated in 113 dioceses: the Parliaments also complied, but not well; for although the Bishops publicly protested that nothing was derogated from the Gallican liberties by the Bull, nevertheless, formulas of cautions were added by them, such as "saving the liberties, etc.," omitting the Bishops' protests, which would cause new disturbances in their own time.

Noailles, to excuse himself to the King, protested in a letter sent to him on January 14 that he and his adherents in no way disagreed with the others regarding the faith, and together with them condemned not only the famous five propositions of Jansenius, but all other errors which they believed were condemned by the Pope through his constitution: and that he had always sincerely intended to proscribe the book of Reflections throughout his dioceses, all the more so the more certainly they thereby confirmed themselves to the Pope on the principal point of the constitution.

<summary>This page details the official acceptance of the Bull Unigenitus by the French Clergy and the King, despite the resistance and subsequent protests of Cardinal Noailles and the Parliaments.</summary>
