pages.58:
Meanwhile, they spread the rumor that the acceptance of the Bull was neither necessary nor could it be done without explanation, nor indeed had it been done by the Clergy except in relation to the aforementioned instruction: which was certainly most false; since the other Bishops, for that very reason, in order to remove every suspicion of ambiguity found in the Bull, studiously held off from bringing the instruction to be approved by the whole Assembly until a few days after the acceptance had been made. In their mandates, however, they most fiercely attacked both the Bull, the explanation of which they claimed to be awaiting from the Pope, and the instruction itself.

The King, greatly moved by these actions, forbids Noailles access to the royal court and orders the Bishops affected by his views to return to their dioceses; he commands the Sorbonne, under the most severe penalties, to accept the Bull and record it in their annals, which was done notwithstanding the suspension threatened against the Clergy by the mandate of Noailles, if anyone should decide anything regarding the acceptance of the Bull without his authority. The remaining Universities throughout France followed the Sorbonne. But the Pontiff, rightfully foreseeing even greater damage to Religion from this resistance of the Bishops and the superfluous caution of the Parliaments, and having condemned their mandates, one of which by the Bishop of <term>Châlons</term> was branded as if it were heretical...

<summary>This page describes the escalating conflict between the King and the dissenting Bishops led by Noailles, highlighting the King's decisive measures to enforce the acceptance of the Bull.</summary>
<keywords>Cardinal Noailles, Bishops, Sorbonne, Bull Unigenitus, King Louis XIV, Bishop of Châlons</keywords>
pages.59:
heretical, he insisted vehemently to the King that the formulas of those exceptions be removed from the Acts of the Parliaments, and that he himself should send the Cardinal to Rome to plead his case.

Now the King, when he thought that the stubbornness of Noailles, who was promising the acceptance of the Bull one moment and retracting his promises under various pretexts the next, could not be bent in any other way, decided to send him to the Pope. However, having later changed his mind, he sent <term>Amelot</term> to Rome, who was to ask the Pontiff for a new Bull by which the constitution <term>Unigenitus</term> would be declared a universal law of the Church and a finished cause, and at the same time ask for legates to be sent to convene a national Council. Clement resisted for a long time, claiming that the rebels were being indulged too much and that the matter was being drawn out too long: however, he sent two Briefs, one grave with paternal warnings, the other with threats, to be shown to Noailles if he would not be bent by the first. But when the King did not desist from his purpose, and had already named the same Commissioners who had been at the last Assembly of the Clergy, he himself finally consented. Thus the commissioners meet to prepare what is necessary for a future Synod, and above all they seek and obtain a decree from the King, by which the constitution <term>Unigenitus</term> is ordered to be promulgated as the law of the Kingdom and the rule of faith. The Parliament refused to enter this into the records, pretending that it must be waited for until it was confirmed that the Bull was received in other Kingdoms as well; and when Louis was preparing to compel the Parliament to obedience by his supreme power, he was struck by a sudden illness, to the great grief of orthodox France and no less of Rome, and at Versailles...

<summary>This page outlines the King's failed attempt to resolve the Jansenist crisis by sending Noailles to Rome, the subsequent request for a new Bull, and the final moments of the King's life during the conflict.</summary>
<keywords>King Louis XIV, Cardinal Noailles, Amelot, Bull Unigenitus, Parliament, Clement XI</keywords>
pages.60:
September 1715, aged 77, he dies, with the most joyous hope of restored peace carried with him to the grave. Shortly before his death, with Cardinals Rohan and Bissy present, he protested that he was dying in the union and Catholic faith, and that he had aimed at only one thing: that union between the Prelates, peace, and concord might be restored in the Kingdom and the Church.

The faction, liberated from great fear, was openly triumphant, believing the Duke of <term>Orléans</term>, the administrator of the Kingdom, to be favorable to Noailles. Indeed, the Duke tried to obtain from the Cardinal, by gentleness and extraordinary signs of benevolence, what the King could not obtain by his authority, and with this hope of moving him to the acceptance of the Bull, he vainly filled himself and the Pontiff. Meanwhile, countless pamphlets are spread, and among these two most pestiferous ones: the *Hexapla* and the *Testimony of Truth*, in which not only was Catholic doctrine attacked in general, but the people themselves were pronounced to be the sole rule and judge of faith. These books were indeed condemned by the Clergy, while the author, who was <term>Basnage</term>, a Protestant minister, was still hiding: yet since many from the Sorbonne especially fostered these offspring, it was effected by their fraudulent arts that the publication of the decree of condemnation was hindered by <term>Orléans</term>, and the decree itself was suppressed for seven years, never to be brought to light, to the great disgrace of the Clergy even after the author was recognized, unless copies had been conveniently preserved by most of the Bishops. Furthermore, with the most disgraceful declamations of the Sorbonnists against the Bull persisting—who called it nothing but a monstrous decree, a work breathing nothing but laxity...

<summary>This page covers the death of Louis XIV and the rise of the Duke of Orléans, whose leniency allowed Jansenist factions to circulate subversive materials like the Hexapla and the Testimony of Truth.</summary>
<keywords>King Louis XIV, Cardinal Rohan, Cardinal Bissy, Duke of Orléans, Hexapla, Testimony of Truth, Basnage, Sorbonne</keywords>

laxity, infidelity, one of the gates of hell that will not prevail—they even shamelessly denied that it had ever been accepted by the Sorbonne, against <term>Basnage</term> himself testifying in the *Hexapla* that it was done by 525 votes against 22. Finally, <term>Orléans</term> prohibited the entire Assembly of the Sorbonne; he excluded from Holy Orders several Prelates who had studied in the Sorbonne; the Pope also decided that confirmation would be granted to no one presented by the King for a Bishopric unless the Bull had been accepted first.

Hitherto, the Bishops who opposed the acceptance of the Bull were in idleness. They turned to new arts and composed letters to the Pontiff, seeking an explanation of the Bull according to which they would be willing to accept it. They showed these to their colleagues, and persuaded ten of those who had already performed the simple acceptance to subscribe to these letters, even though they had been changed significantly. Then, having suppressed these letters, the opponents spread the rumor that thirty Bishops in total had sought an explanation of the Bull. But those ten immediately protested publicly against the fraud and the abuse of their subscription, one of whom, the Bishop of <term>Agde</term>, dissipated these smokes most effectively by a simple account of the entire trick. Once this machine was overturned, Noailles dealt with the Duke so that he might send <term>Cavalier</term>, the so-called Great Vicar, to Rome in his name (for the Cardinal distrusted himself), to treat with the Pope regarding the composition of the controversies. The Duke sent the man; although Cardinal <term>Bissy</term> had confessed to him that <term>Cavalier</term> was suspect of Jansenism:

pages.62:
He obeyed the warning, however, so that Religion might not suffer detriment from this negotiation, and he submitted the necessary instruction and notification about all matters to Rome at the same time.

The arrival of <term>Cavalier</term> was little accepted at Rome, also because he had brought with him P. Laborde from the Oratory, a well-known supporter of Quesnell. Soon after the second day of his arrival, Clement XI summoned all the Cardinals early in the morning. In a brilliant speech, he exposed the deplorable state of the Gallican Church, the obstinacy of many, and the frauds of some of the Bishops themselves, and while he argued the cause of the Bull with most weighty words, having finally fallen into the point that those opposing the acceptance of the Bull were accustomed to use for their defense—namely, that the liberty of the Gallican Church would be overturned by this very obstinacy of theirs—he demonstrated it invincibly. "This," he said, "turns on two main heads as if on as many hinges: first, that it is for the Bishops to judge on a matter of faith in the first instance; second, that they hold as legitimate that they can even interpret the Bulls of the Pontiffs." Indeed, the first had been done, and without his opposition, in that numerous Convent of the Clergy and Bishops held in the year 1714; the second had been performed no less completely by them through the instruction added to the acceptance, which was likewise approved by him. If these things did not suffice, there would be no authority of the Episcopal Order henceforth, no legitimate power of judging or interpreting, that is, one easily eluded by anyone, and there would be no Bull, no law of the Church, which they would be bound to accept if they did not wish to. Therefore, since
pages.63:
they were concluding, through the path of leniency tried until now, nothing had been accomplished, he would use his own authority against Noailles and the other opponents. Everyone agreed everywhere: Cavalier was prohibited from the Pope's audience: two Briefs were sent to the Apostolic Nuncio, one to be delivered to the Duke, the other to the opponents.

Terrified at first by these, the opponents nevertheless soon breathed again; for the papal letters, since the royal Nuncio did not wish to present them to the Ministers, were not admitted, and Cavalier, with the support of Tremoille, first obtained the faculty of speaking to the sacred College of Cardinals, then also of explaining his business to the two Cardinals assigned by the Pope, Ferrari and Ptolemeo. He fulfilled the wishes of the faction: now he proposed various explanations of the Bull, now other and different forms of acceptance: sometimes he defended certain propositions as innocent, sometimes he twisted them into various meanings; and in order to deceive the orthodox, and disturb and animate his own, and at the same time to place a price on his industry, he did not blush to boast in frequent letters sent to Paris that Cardinal Ptolemeo, having been drawn to his opinion, already confessed that the entire matter of the Bull touched on nothing but discipline, nor was any dogma of the faith injured if it were not received. Meanwhile, he held frequent meetings in the garden of the Minims, of the French of the Trinità dei Monti <note>original: "de la Trinité du Mont"</note>, in which the Bull was treated most insultingly, and no more mildly than by heretics: upon discovering this, the Pope prohibited such conventicles under the gravest penalties, and henceforth forbade the Cardinals any meeting with Cavalier. Wherefore he
pages.64:
through the Legate Tremoille insisted with Clement that, following the example of the forty Bishops, it might be allowed to propose a certain formula of acceptance related to a previous explanation: the Pope replied that he would be content if the Opponents accepted the Bull in relation to the instruction of those 40 Bishops; but Cavalier demanded not this, but another, namely with various restrictions and distinctions of meanings. In the end, having laid aside all shame, various demands were exposed by the opponents to the Pope through Tremoille, and among these a national Council, upon which they dared to establish as a foundation so that an appeal to a General Council could be made. Indeed, Clement, to put an end to these trickeries and frauds, replied in a few words: there remained two ways of finishing the composition, spontaneous submission or Canonical force. And thus was finished the negotiation of Cavalier.

§. 4.
*Appeal to the General Council.*

The thunders of the Vatican were now being prepared: Noailles was deemed unworthy of the purple by the College of Cardinals itself. Nevertheless, time was still given to repent, from the hope that the Opponents had shown by a certain draft of doctrine having been prepared, which, since it was not approved by the acceptors, they offered them a document of three columns, similar to that Jansenist one from before, in the middle of which were read the very propositions of Quesnell, on one side the obvious meaning, on the other some other Catholic one, or at least one patient of excuse
pages.65: patient. But even this could not please, and glosses were added by the acceptors, by which they showed that both the obvious meaning of the propositions was rightly condemned, and that they could not have another unless by violent distortion. However, so that all hope might not perish again along with this business, Cardinal Rohan moved the Bishop of Orléans to call a convent of Bishops on November 20, 1716, in which the Acceptors might propose some explanation of the Bull. The Pontiff took this very badly, and attempting in every way to hinder this plan, he sent two Briefs, one to the Duke, signaling what he was preparing for Noailles, the other to the Sorbonne, whose faculties and all privileges he suspended for a time: and when Tremoille wished to persuade the Cardinals, who had otherwise given letters with most friendly exhortations to Noailles, and the Pope himself, that something should be added regarding the giving or admitting of some explanation; he added a third Brief to the accepting Bishops, by which he exhorted them not to allow themselves to be deceived by the Opponents, and neither to expect any explanation of the Bull from him, nor to give or admit one themselves. But the Bishop of Orléans did not show the Cardinals' letters to Noailles, who meanwhile spoke solemn thanks to the Parliament of Douai, which had suppressed certain Theses favoring the Constitution; and the other Parliaments forbade the Apostolic letters to be received unless fortified by royal letters; for the decree of the Parliament of Brittany held that this custom had flourished from the very beginning of the Monarchy: truly falsely; since both King Philip the Fair and Louis XI, although they forbade various Roman letters to be received by name, were entirely silent regarding Rescripts, Briefs, and Bulls: and we have the example of letters patent only from Louis XIV. But by these indications, truly, the poison sprinkled into the innermost bowels of France betrayed itself. Nor did the evil stop here.
pages.66:
However, to give the Pope's leader something, he suspended the Convent of Bishops already called. But since Rohan did not cease to urge it, and had also accomplished at Rome that even the Pontiff himself, from some hope of fruit, was already less contrary, he permitted again that a meeting be convened in which the Bishops might confer among themselves about the controversy. Having therefore communicated this plan with Noailles, eighteen Bishops gathered at Rohan's, and the business was begun, with, indeed, very bad and truly deplorable success. Mailly, the Archbishop of Reims, invited, could not be absent from his diocese, which twelve Canons with three Parish Priests had so disturbed that it, which at the beginning had embraced the Bull with singular zeal following the example of its Pastor, then became the first of those opposing themselves: nor did those excommunicated by the Prelate cease to celebrate sacred mysteries. But when, from the remaining Bishops also, after they had understood what was being agitated in Paris, thirty in all had flocked together; the Bishop of Orléans, lest a crowd hinder the proceedings, wanted only six or five of the acceptors, and as many of the opponents, to confer before him.

The first thing was that they should agree on certain conditions, and the accepting Bishops indeed proposed five main ones: 1st. All instructions and explanations regarding the Bull would not be from the fact that the Bull is obscure, but they would be given by them to the opponents to facilitate acceptance. 2nd. A certain schema of doctrine was to be crafted. 3rd. A formula of acceptance was to be shown to the acceptors, and it, as they judged would please the Pope, was to be held and published. 4th. If anything had been omitted in the opponents' schema of doctrine, it should be allowed for the acceptors to supply it, yet to cut nothing else away. 5th. If, all these being observed, acceptance did not follow, all acts would be void and null. The third condition alone displeased the opponents; which, however, seemed entirely necessary to the others, having so often experienced the bad faith of the faction. But lest the exacerbation of spirits in such discussions at the threshold should complicate the business more, it had to be yielded, the Bishop of Orléans wishing it so, and that condition was no longer urged; since Noailles had solemnly promised that, harmony having been established regarding the doctrine itself, everything would finally be smooth, and acceptance would follow as desired. Otherwise, the opponents demanded that in the exposition of doctrine, the liberty of opinion of other schools being excluded, the sole and rigorous doctrine of the Thomists should be maintained. They finally gather: the Opponents, according to custom, repeatedly ventilate various meanings of the propositions and their censures: the acceptors respond patiently, and at last bring forth a schema of doctrine, in which reverence toward the Apostolic see was mainly commended. Nor was there anything in it that the opponents could criticize. Therefore, the others, happy and relying on the promises of Noailles, were already waiting for nothing else but the unanimous acceptance of the constitution,
pages.67: and they were asking for its formula to be shown to them: they do indeed bring forth a formula, but they do not want it changed: Noailles furthermore lists 26 Quesnellian propositions as having been unjustly condemned, about which the Pope must necessarily explain his mind more. Here the acceptors call upon their faith, protest, complain that they have been deceived and mocked, and resist. But in vain: Four Bishops from the opponents, of Mirepoix, Montpellier, Boulogne, and Senez, on March 1, 1717, sign the instrument of Appeal from the Bull Unigenitus to a General Council, and propose it to the Sorbonne to be subscribed on March 5, which was done, two other Theological faculties in France following this example. Noailles also signed an appeal separately but secretly, with the condition: if the Pope should deny or not admit an explanation of the Bull. This was the end of the conferences, as it usually almost is, this was the fruit.

pages.54:
of the Gallican Church could be constrained, might be omitted, suppressing in this way the formulas of “from the fullness of power,” “of his own accord,” and similar ones customary at Rome, so that in this manner all complications and excuses in accepting the Bull might be forestalled. To this excellent disposition of the Most Christian King and his zeal for restoring peace, with the added strong prayers and exhortations of many Bishops, the Pontiff at last granted everything, and as soon as possible the examination of the whole work was resumed by two Cardinals and several Theologians.

When Noailles saw these things being prepared, moved by the example of the King, who had revoked the license for printing the books of Quesnel, as well as by the fear of the coming Bull, he had already decided with himself to condemn the book which he had once approved. But then two men frustrated the whole matter. The General of the Minims, Rollet, and the “Expeditionary,” as they call him, Chauffe, wrote to the Cardinal that everything being done for the drafting of the Bull was merely a shadow play to frighten the Cardinal, to which, once he had heard it, he gave room for no further sounder counsel, no more certain report. Furthermore, the faction spread in Rome and in France that there was no hope of the Bull being received: that the Dauphin favored Quesnel, that the Parliament was hostile to the Roman Curia, and that the Sorbonne was not so unfriendly to the new doctrine; which they confirmed with recent documents. For when the Jesuit Juvencius had written certain things in the History of his Society regarding the acts of the time of Henry IV that were not at all approved by the Parliament, the Superiors of the three Colleges which were in Paris were summoned, and they were ordered to speak out regarding the four most well-known articles out of the 82, regarding the Power of the Pope in the Realms of Princes and in the Church, what they thought, and finally, they were ordered to bind themselves by oath to hold the doctrine of those articles for themselves and their own.
pages.55:
concerning the Pope's Power in the Realms of Princes, and in the Church, what they thought, and finally, they were ordered to bind themselves by oath to maintain the doctrine of those articles for themselves and their own. Then Abbot Saint-Aignan, when he had requested letters of confirmation from Rome for the Episcopacy, lest he succumb to the envy and deceitful arts of the Jansenists even in Rome, as his worst advisors suggested, he allowed himself to be persuaded to defend the fourth proposition of Jansenius in the Sorbonne itself.

In truth, these terrors soon vanished; for when neither the acts of the Parliament nor the error of the abbot seemed of such moment that they could move a prudent suspicion of the acceptance being denied; and indeed the Dauphin had even given a public testimony in writing of the Catholic faith and of his own firm adhesion to it, after the two-year labors of examinations and comparisons of texts were finally exhausted, the famous Bull *Unigenitus* was subscribed to by Clement XI on September 8, 1713, after all things had first been examined and revised by de la Trémoille, and published two days later, on September 10. In it, one hundred and one propositions excerpted from the work of Quesnel are condemned in a lump sum, as they say, that is, as false, impious, heretical, etc., with these and other censures subjoined to be applied to each respectively: it is added that many other propositions similar to these and akin to them are contained therein, worthy of condemnation, and that moreover the very text of scripture itself was corrupted from the reprobated Montenfi edition; wherefore the entire book, edited in any language or to be edited, is prohibited and condemned.
pages.56:
<note>A decorative horizontal rule appears at the top of the page.</note>

Having understood this, Noailles, without delay, issued a mandate on the 28th of that same month, in which he stated that he could no longer bear his name prefixed to a book condemned by the Pope, and therefore, as he had promised, he revoked the approval he had given in another diocese to a book already approved previously by his predecessor, condemned the book, and prohibited its reading and retention, etc. The Clergy were then convened, and Commissioners were elected, the head of whom was Cardinal Rohan; Noailles was named President of the Council. Of the 18 Archbishops, seven arrived by October 18; of the 112 Bishops, thirty-three. Noailles, having prefaced his remarks with his own previously given preface to the book and the mandate issued a short while before, soon began to preach about the obscurity of the Bull and the doubts that would arise from it, to the astonishment of the others, to whom everything in it seemed clear and plain. Rohan demonstrated that there was not one of the 101 propositions to which one of the censures did not apply: Noailles, however, contended as much as he could that the Bull could not be accepted otherwise than with a prefixed instruction and the addition of certain explanations and restrictions. This proposal was rejected by almost everyone, and four articles were opposed to it by Cardinal Rohan: 1. It is manifestly clear from the Bull, and it must be held, that the book of Quesnel is heretical: 2. That those 101 propositions were rightly condemned and each is worthy of one of the applied censures: therefore 3. The Bull ought to be accepted before any further explanation; since it is neither ambiguous nor obscure regarding the aforementioned matters. 4. That no other previous instruction is needed, except that which would guard the faithful against false interpretations of the Bull. These things pleased the Assembly, but not Noailles; who, since nothing

<note>A decorative printer's ornament appears at the bottom of the page.</note>
pages.57:
could be obtained, made a secession and refrained from the congresses with nine other Bishops, until he was compelled by the authority of the King to visit them again. In these meetings, the decree of acceptance was finally made and signed by everyone except Noailles and a few of his followers: after this, a pastoral instruction was proposed, which Noailles himself praised as if it were his own with no less artifice and eloquence; the Acts of the Convent were sent to the absent Bishops: finally, on February 5, 1714, a letter was given to the Pope with an attached instruction, by which they signify the acceptance of the Bull, congratulate him on the errors overcome by his constitution, and pledge obedience and prompt faithfulness in executing it: all of which were approved by the Pontiff. And when the responses of many absent Bishops arrived, by which they also approved the acts and signified their acceptance of the Bull by their given consent, the King issued an edict, or letters patent, on February 14, by which he commanded the Bull to be accepted, published, and observed by all, and to be registered in the public records by all Parliaments throughout the Kingdom. Soon the Bull was promulgated in 113 dioceses: the Parliaments also complied, but not well enough; for although the Bishops publicly protested that nothing was derogated from the Gallican liberties by the Bull, nevertheless, formulas of caution “saving the liberties, etc.” were added by them, omitting the protests of the Bishops, which would cause new troubles in their own time.

Noailles, in order to excuse himself before the King, protested in a letter sent to him on January 14 that he and his adherents in no way disagreed with the others regarding the faith,
pages.58:
and that they condemned along with these not only the famous five propositions of Jansenius, but also all other errors which they believed were condemned by the Pope through his constitution: and that he had always sincerely intended to proscribe the book of Reflections throughout his dioceses, all the more so, the more certainly he would thereby confirm himself to the Pope on the principal point of the constitution. Meanwhile, they spread the word that the acceptance of the Bull was neither necessary nor could it be done without explanation, and that it was not even done by the Clergy except in relation to the aforementioned instruction: which was certainly most false; since the other Bishops, for that very reason, in order to remove every suspicion of ambiguity found in the Bull, had studiously delayed producing the instruction until a few days after the acceptance had been made, to be approved by the whole Assembly. In their mandates, however, they very sharply attacked both the Bull, for which they were awaiting an explanation from the Pope, and the instruction itself.

Moved greatly by these things, the King forbade Noailles access to the royal Court, and ordered the Bishops affected by his views to return to their own dioceses: he commanded the Sorbonne, under the most severe penalties, to accept the Bull and record it in their registers, which was done notwithstanding the suspension threatened against the Clergy by the mandate of Noailles, if anyone should decree anything concerning the acceptance of the Bull without his authority. The remaining Universities throughout France followed the Sorbonne. But the Pontiff, also foreseeing, from this resistance of the Bishops and the superfluous caution of the Parliaments, even greater harms to Religion, condemned their mandates, one of which—the Bishop of Châlons—as if it were
pages.59:
heresy, was being confessed, and he pressed the King vehemently that both the formulas of those exceptions be removed from the Acts of the Parliaments, and that he himself send the Cardinal to Rome to plead his cause.

And now the King, when he thought the stubbornness of Noailles—now promising the acceptance of the Bull, now retracting his promises under various pretexts—could not be bent in any other way, decided to send him back to the Pope. However, having changed his counsel afterwards, he sent Amelot to Rome, who sought from the Pontiff a new Bull, by which the constitution *Unigenitus* would be declared as the universal law of the Church and as a finished case, and at the same time he asked for legates to be sent to convene a national Council. Clement resisted for a long time, claiming that the refractory were being indulged too much and that the matter was being drawn out too long: yet he submitted two Briefs, one grave with paternal admonitions, the other grave with threats, to be presented to Noailles if he were not bent by the first. But since the King did not desist from his purpose, and had already named the same Commissioners who had been in the last Convent of the Clergy, he himself finally consented. The commissioners therefore convene to prepare what is necessary for the future Synod, and before all else, they seek and obtain a decree from the King, by which the constitution *Unigenitus* is ordered to be promulgated as the law of the Realm and the rule of faith. The Parliament refused to record this in the acts, pretending that it was necessary to wait until it was established that the Bull had been received in foreign Realms also; and when Louis was preparing to compel the Parliament to obedience by his supreme power, he was struck by a sudden illness, to the great grief of orthodox France, and no less in Rome and Versailles
pages.60:
he died in September 1715, at the age of 77, with the most joyous hope of restoring peace buried with him in the tomb. A little before his death, in the presence of Cardinals Rohan and Bissy, he protested that he was dying in the union and Catholic faith, and that he had aimed at this one thing, that union among the Prelates, peace, and concord might be restored in the Kingdom and the Church.

The faction, liberated from great fear, since it believed the Duke of Orléans, the administrator of the Kingdom, favored Noailles, openly triumphed. Indeed, the Duke strove to obtain from the Cardinal what the King could not by his authority, through leniency and exceptional signs of benevolence, and with this hope of moving him toward the acceptance of the Bull, he vainly filled himself and the Pontiff himself. Meanwhile, countless pamphlets are spread, and among these, two that are most pestiferous: the *Hexapla*, indeed, and the *Testimony of the Truth*, in which not only was the Catholic doctrine impugned in general, but furthermore the people themselves were pronounced to be the sole rule and judge of the faith. These books were indeed condemned by the Clergy, while the author remained hidden, who was Basnage, a Protestant minister: when, however, very many, especially in the Sorbonne, cherished these fruits greatly, it was brought about by their fraudulent arts that the publication of the decree of condemnation was hindered by Orléans, and the decree itself was suppressed for seven years, never to be brought to light, to the great disgrace of the Clergy even after the author was known, had not copies of it been conveniently preserved by most of the Bishops. Furthermore, as the most shameful declamations of the Sorbonnists against the Bull grew loud, who called it nothing but a monstrous decree, a work breathing nothing but laxity
pages.61:
<note>A decorative horizontal rule appears at the top of the page.</note>

infidelity, one of the gates of hell which shall not prevail, and finally they impudently denied altogether that it had ever been accepted by the Sorbonne, against Basnage himself, who testified in the *Hexapla* that it was done by 525 votes against 22. The Duke of Orléans finally prohibited the entire Assembly of the Sorbonne; he excluded from sacred Orders several Prelates who had studied in the Sorbonne: the Pope also decided to grant confirmation to no one presented by the King to a Bishopric, unless the Bull had been accepted first.

The Bishops who opposed themselves to the acceptance of the Bull had been idle up to this point. They turned to new arts and drafted letters to the Pontiff, seeking an explanation of the Bull, according to which they would be willing to accept it. They showed these to their colleagues and persuaded ten of those who had already rendered a simple acceptance to subscribe to these letters as well, even though they had been changed in many respects. Then, indeed, having suppressed these letters, the opponents spread the claim that thirty Bishops in total had sought an explanation of the Bull. But those ten immediately publicly protested against the fraud and the abuse of their subscription; one of them, the Bishop of Agde, having made a simple report of the whole intrigue, dissipated these clouds of theirs better than anyone. But this machine having been overturned, Noailles worked upon the Duke so that he, in his own name (for the Cardinal distrusted himself), might send Cavalier, the grand Vicar, as they call him, to Rome, to treat with the Pope face-to-face regarding the settlement of the controversies. The Duke sent the man; although Cardinal Bissy had confessed to him that Cavalier was suspicious of Jansenism.

pages.62:
He obeyed the warning, however, so that Religion might not suffer detriment from this negotiation, and he submitted the necessary instruction and notification about all matters to Rome at the same time.

The arrival of Cavalier was little accepted at Rome, also because he had brought with him P. Laborde from the Oratory, a well-known supporter of Quesnell. Soon after the second day of his arrival, Clement XI summoned all the Cardinals early in the morning. In a brilliant speech, he exposed the deplorable state of the Gallican Church, the obstinacy of many, and the frauds of some of the Bishops themselves, and while he argued the cause of the Bull with most weighty words, having finally fallen into the point that those opposing the acceptance of the Bull were accustomed to use for their defense—namely, that the liberty of the Gallican Church would be overturned by this very obstinacy of theirs—he demonstrated it invincibly. "This," he said, "turns on two main heads as if on as many hinges: first, that it is for the Bishops to judge on a matter of faith in the first instance; second, that they hold as legitimate that they can even interpret the Bulls of the Pontiffs." Indeed, the first had been done, and without his opposition, in that numerous Convent of the Clergy and Bishops held in the year 1714; the second had been performed no less completely by them through the instruction added to the acceptance, which was likewise approved by him. If these things did not suffice, there would be no authority of the Episcopal Order henceforth, no legitimate power of judging or interpreting, that is, one easily eluded by anyone, and there would be no Bull, no law of the Church, which they would be bound to accept if they did not wish to. Therefore, since
pages.63:
concluding, he said that since nothing had been gained through the path of leniency attempted until now, he would use his authority against Noailles and the other opponents. Everyone agreed everywhere: Cavalier was prohibited from speaking with the Pope: two Briefs were sent to the Apostolic Nuncio, one to be delivered to the Duke, the other to the opponents.

Terrified by these at first, the opponents nonetheless soon recovered; for the pontifical letters, since the royal Nuncio did not wish to show them to the Ministers, were not admitted, and Cavalier, with the support of Trémoille, obtained the opportunity first of speaking to the sacred College of Cardinals, and then also of explaining his business to the two Cardinals assigned by the Pope, Ferrari and Tolomei. He fulfilled the wishes of the faction: now he proposed various explanations of the Bull, now other and different forms of acceptance: at times he defended certain propositions as innocent, at others he twisted them into various meanings: and in order to deceive the orthodox, and to disturb and animate his own, and at the same time to put a price on his industry, he did not blush to boast in frequent letters given at Paris that Cardinal Tolomei had already been won over to his opinion, confessing that the whole matter of the Bull touched only on discipline, and that no dogma of faith would be injured if it were not received. Meanwhile, he held frequent assemblies in the garden of the Minims, the French of the Trinity on the Mount <note>original: "de la Trinité du Mont"</note>, in which the Bull was criticized most contumeliously, and no more mildly than by heretics: upon discovering this, the Pope prohibited such conventicles under the gravest penalties, and henceforth forbade the Cardinals from any meeting with Cavalier. Wherefore he
pages.64:
insisted through the Legate Trémoille before Clement that, following the example of the forty Bishops, it should be permitted to propose a certain formula of acceptance related to a previous explanation: the Pope replied that he would be content if the Opponents accepted the Bull in relation to the instruction of those 40 Bishops; but Cavalier demanded not this, but another, with various restrictions, indeed, and distinctions of meanings. In the end, all modesty being laid aside, the various demands of the opponents were exposed to the Pope through Trémoille, and among these a national Council, from which they dared to establish as a foundation that an appeal to a General Council could be made. Truly Clement, to put an end to these tricks and frauds, answered in a few words: two paths remained for ending the composition, spontaneous submission or Canonical force. And thus the negotiation of Cavalier was terminated.

§. 4.
*Appeal to a General Council.*

The bolts of the Vatican were already being prepared: Noailles was judged unworthy of the purple by the College of Cardinals itself. Nevertheless, time was still given to repent, from the hope that the Opponents had shown by having finished a certain draft of doctrine, which, when it was not approved by the acceptors, they offered them a document of three columns, similar to that Jansenist one of old, in the middle column of which the propositions of Quesnell were read, on one side the obvious meaning, on the other some other Catholic [meaning], or at least one patient of excuse
pages.65: patient of excuse. But neither could that please, and glosses were added by the acceptors, by which they showed that the obvious meaning of the propositions was rightly condemned, and that they could not have another, except through a violent distortion. Lest, however, all hope perish again together with this business, Cardinal Rohan persuaded the Orléanais to indicate a convention of Bishops for November 20, 1716, in which the Acceptors might propose some explanation of the Bull. The Pontiff took this very badly, and, having attempted in every way to impede this counsel, he sent two Briefs, one to the Duke, signaling what he was preparing for Noailles, the other to the Sorbonne, whose faculties and all privileges he suspended for a time: and when Trémoille wanted to persuade the Cardinals, who had already given other letters with most friendly exhortations to Noailles, and the Pope himself, that something should be added concerning the giving or admitting of some explanation; he added a third Brief to the accepting Bishops, by which he exhorted them not to allow themselves to be deceived by the Opponents, and neither to expect any explanation of the Bull from him, nor to give or admit one themselves. But the Orléanais did not exhibit the letters of the Cardinals to Noailles, who meanwhile spoke solemn thanks to the Douai Parliament, which had suppressed certain Theses favoring the Constitution; and the other Parliaments forbade the Apostolic letters from being received unless fortified by royal letters; for the decree of the Parliament of Brittany held that this custom had flourished from the very beginning of the Monarchy: certainly mendaciously; since both King Philip the Fair, and Louis XI, although they forbade various Roman letters from being received by name, were entirely silent, however, about Rescripts,
pages.66:
Briefs, and Bulls: and indeed we have the first example of letters patent from Louis XIV. But by these signs, surely, the poison sprinkled into the innermost vitals of Gaul betrayed itself. Nor did the evil stop here.

However, in order to give some favor to the Pope, he suspended the Convention of Bishops already indicted. But since Rohan did not cease to urge it, and had also brought it about at Rome that the Pontiff himself, from whatever hope of fruit, was now less opposed, he permitted again that an assembly be gathered, in which the Bishops might confer among themselves about the controversy. Having thus communicated this plan with Noailles, eighteen Bishops gathered at Rohan, and the business was begun with very poor success, and indeed a deplorable one. Mailly, Archbishop of Reims, invited, could not be absent from his diocese, which twelve Canons with three Parish Priests had so disturbed that it, which at the beginning had embraced the Bull with singular zeal following the example of its Pastor, then became the first of those opposing itself: nor did those excommunicated by the Prelate cease to celebrate the sacred mysteries. But when, after they had understood what was being agitated at Paris, thirty in total had flowed together from the remaining Bishops; the Orléanais, lest the crowd hinder the proceedings, wanted only six or five of the acceptors, and as many from the opponents, to confer before him.

The first [point] was that they should agree on certain conditions, and the Accepting Bishops indeed proposed five main [conditions]: 1st. That all instruc-
pages.67: tions and explanations concerning the Bull would not be from the fact that the Bull is obscure, but they would be given by them to the opponents to facilitate acceptance. 2nd. That a certain scheme of doctrine should be composed. 3rd. That a formula of acceptance should be exhibited to the acceptors, and that it, just as they should judge it pleasing to the Pope, should be held and published. 4th. If anything had been omitted in the scheme of doctrine of the opponents, it should be permitted for the acceptors to supply it, yet to prune nothing else. 5th. If, after all these were observed, acceptance did not follow, all acts would be void and null. Only the third condition displeased the opponents; which, however, seemed entirely necessary to the others, having so often experienced the bad faith of the faction. But lest the exacerbation of spirits in such arguments at the threshold implicate the business more, it had to be yielded, the Orléanais so wishing, and that condition was no longer urged; since Noailles had holily promised that, with harmony established concerning the doctrine itself, everything would finally be plain, and acceptance would follow according to wishes. Furthermore, the opponents demanded that, in the exposition of doctrine, the freedom of opinion of other schools being excluded, the sole and rigorous doctrine of the Thomists should be preserved. They assemble at last: the Opponents, according to custom, repeatedly ventilate various meanings of the propositions and their censures: the acceptors respond patiently, and finally bring forth a scheme of doctrine, in which reverence toward the Apostolic See was especially commended. Nor was there anything in it that the opponents could criticize. Therefore, the others, joyful and relying on the promises of Noailles, were already expecting nothing other than the unanimous acceptance of the constitution,
pages.68:
and were seeking for its formula to be exhibited to them: they indeed bring forth a formula, but they do not wish for it to be changed: Noailles furthermore reviews 26 Quesnellian propositions as undeservedly condemned, concerning which the Pope must necessarily explain his mind more. Here the acceptors shout against their faith, attest that they are deceived and played for fools, and push back. But in vain: Four Bishops from the opponents, of Mirepoix, Montpellier, Boulogne, and Senez, on March 1, 1717, sign the instrument of Appeal from the Bull Unigenitus to a General Council, and propose the same to the Sorbonne to be subscribed on March 5, which was done, with two other Theological faculties in France following this example. Noailles also, but secretly, subscribed to another separate appeal, with the condition: if the Pope denied or did not admit an explanation of the Bull. This was the end of the conferences, as is almost always the case, this was the fruit.

The Orléanais, offended by this most shameful manner of acting, and grieving too late that he too had been deceived, orders the Bishops to leave Paris soon, and the Notary who had written the instrument of Appeal to go to prison. Meanwhile, a very large crowd of appellants of all orders was being received, nay, was being sought with tireless zeal and no small amount of money, the very dregs of the people not excluded, with many hundreds of thousands of French pounds spent for that purpose in not so much time, which, as they said, the Secretary of Noailles, Cardinal Delort, in the name of the Cardinal, and Servien, similarly from the letters of the Brother of Noailles, the Bishop of Châlons,
pages.69:
had scraped together to complete the grave business of Religion. But the matter being revealed by the Creditors, the former was punished with exile, Servien was relegated to the galleys, from which he was later exempted when, before the Vicar General of the diocese of Verdun on Feb. 10, 1724, he had revoked the appeal, and at the same time confessed his own huckstering. But a little later he returned to the fold. Nevertheless, the multitude of appellants, even if increased beyond the truth by the factious (they counted two thousand themselves), was not so great that it could come into comparison with those thinking well. Of the twenty-three theological faculties that are in France, only the Nantes and Reims faculties besides the Sorbonne adhered to the appeal, of which not one outside France dreamed: and while the Prelate of Reims was urging his own to obedience with futile labor, in Montpellier they did not wish the sheep to hear the voice of the Shepherd who would not hear the voice of the Church.

The conferences finished, Trémoille labored that, with silence imposed on the parties, the disputes concerning the Bull should be removed: which the Orléanais also sanctioned by Decree on Oct. 17, 1717. Noailles, however, consigned to the same a certain exposition of doctrine made in the assembly of Bishops, as he said, to be approved by the Pontiff at Rome. The Legate did everything zealously, as he had been ordered. The response: the exposition was not entirely devoid of all error, and it was asked: was it the same composed by the acceptors, or conformable to it? Finally, it was requested that the formula of acceptance also be exhibited. Meanwhile, the Instrument of Appeal solemnly published by the 4 Bishops appears, with the appeal of Noailles prefixed to it, different in this, that

"This," he said, "turns on two main heads as if on as many hinges: first, that it is for the Bishops to judge on a matter of faith in the first instance; second, that they hold as legitimate that they can even interpret the Bulls of the Pontiffs." Indeed, the first had been done, and without his opposition, in that numerous Convent of the Clergy and Bishops held in the year 1714; the second had been performed no less completely by them through the instruction added to the acceptance, which was likewise approved by him. If these things did not suffice, there would be no authority of the Episcopal Order henceforth, no legitimate power of judging or interpreting, that is, one easily eluded by anyone, and there would be no Bull, no law of the Church, which they would be bound to accept if they did not wish to. Therefore, since
pages.63:
it was concluded that, since nothing had been achieved through the path of leniency attempted until now, he would use his own authority against Noailles and the other opponents. All agreed everywhere: Cavalier was prohibited from speaking to the Pope: two Briefs were sent to the Apostolic Nuncio, one to be delivered to the Duke, the other to the opponents.

Terrified by these at first, the opponents nonetheless soon recovered; for the papal letters, since the Nuncio would not show them to the royal ministers, were not admitted, and Cavalier, with the support of La Trémoille, first obtained the faculty of speaking to the sacred College of Cardinals, and then also of explaining his business to the two Cardinals assigned by the Pope, Ferrari and Tolomei. He fulfilled the wishes of his faction: he proposed now various explanations of the Bull, now one form of acceptance after another; at one moment he defended certain propositions as innocuous, at another he twisted them into various meanings: and in order to deceive the orthodox, disturb them, and encourage his own, while simultaneously placing a price on his own industry, he did not blush to boast in frequent letters given at Paris that Cardinal Tolomei had already been drawn to his opinion and confessed that the whole business of the Bull touched on nothing but discipline, and that no dogma of faith would be injured if it were not received. Meanwhile, he held frequent meetings in the garden of the Minims, of the French of Trinità dei Monti (de la Trinité du Mont), in which the Bull was treated most contumeliously, and no less than by heretics: when this was discovered, the Pope prohibited conventicles of this kind under the most severe penalties, and subsequently forbade the Cardinals all meeting with Cavalier. Wherefore he
pages.64:
insisted through the Legate La Trémoille to Clement that, following the example of the forty Bishops, it might be allowed to propose a certain formula of acceptance in relation to a prior explanation: the Pope replied that he would be content if the Opponents accepted the Bull in relation to the instruction of those 40 Bishops; but Cavalier demanded not this, but another, with various restrictions, of course, and distinctions of meanings. Finally, with all shame cast aside, various demands of the Pope were exposed by the opponents through La Trémoille, and among these a national Council, upon which they dared to establish as a foundation so that an appeal to a General one could be made. But Clement, in order to put an end to these trickeries and frauds, replied in few words: two paths remained for finishing the composition, spontaneous submission or Canonical force. And thus the negotiation of Cavalier was terminated.

§. 4.
*Appeal to a General Council.*

Vatican thunderbolts were now being prepared: Noailles was deemed unworthy of the purple by the College of Cardinals itself. Nevertheless, time was still given for repentance, from the hope that the Opponents had shown by having prepared a certain scheme of doctrine, which, when it was not approved by those accepting, they offered them a document of three columns, similar to that Jansenist one of old, in the middle of which were the very propositions of Quesnell, on one side the obvious meaning, on the other some other Catholic one, or at least one patient of excuse.
pages.65: was read. But not even that could please, and glosses were added by those accepting, by which they showed that both the obvious meaning of the propositions was rightly condemned, and that they could not have another, except through violent distortion. However, so that all hope might not perish again together with this business, Cardinal Rohan persuaded the Orléanais to appoint a meeting of Bishops on November 20, 1716, in which the Acceptants might propose some explanation of the Bull. The Pontiff bore this very badly, and, having set out to impede this counsel in every way, he sent two Briefs, one to the Duke, signifying what he was preparing for Noailles, another to the Sorbonne, whose faculties and all privileges he suspended for a time: and when La Trémoille wanted to persuade the Cardinals, who had otherwise given letters with most friendly exhortations to Noailles, and the Pope himself, that something should be added about giving or admitting some explanation; he added a third Brief to the accepting Bishops, by which he exhorted them not to allow themselves to be deceived by the Opponents, and neither to wait for any explanation of the Bull from him, nor to give or admit one themselves. But the Orléanais did not show the letters of the Cardinals to Noailles, who meanwhile spoke solemn thanks to the Douai Parliament, which had suppressed certain Theses favoring the Constitution; and the other Parliaments forbade the Apostolic letters to be received unless fortified by royal letters; for the decree of the Parliament of Brittany held that this custom had flourished from the very beginning of the Monarchy: truly falsely; since both King Philip the Fair, and Louis XI, however much they prohibited various Roman letters from being received by name, were nevertheless silent about Rescripts,
pages.66:
Briefs, and Bulls entirely: and we have an example of letters patent indeed first from Louis XIV. But by these signs, surely, the poison sprinkled into the innermost vitals of France betrayed itself. Nor did the evil stop here.

However, to give the Pope something, he suspended the meeting of Bishops already appointed. But when Rohan did not cease to urge it, and had also achieved at Rome that the Pontiff himself, from some hope of fruit, was now less contrary, he permitted again that the meeting be held, in which the Bishops might confer among themselves about the controversy. Having therefore communicated this plan with Noailles, eighteen Bishops gathered at Rohan, and the business was begun with very poor success indeed, and truly deplorable. Mailly, the Archbishop of Reims, invited, could not be absent from his diocese, which twelve Canons with three Parish priests had so disturbed that it, which at the beginning had embraced the Bull with singular zeal following the example of its Shepherd, then became the first of those opposing itself: nor did those excommunicated by the Prelate cease to celebrate the holy mysteries. But when, after they had learned what was being agitated in Paris, thirty had gathered in total from the remaining Bishops too; the Orléanais, so that a crowd might not hinder the proceedings, wanted that no more than six or five from the acceptants, and as many from the opponents, should confer before him.

The first was that they should agree on certain conditions, and the accepting Bishops indeed proposed five main ones: 1st. All instructions
pages.67: and explanations concerning the Bull would not be from the fact that the Bull is obscure, but that they would be given by them to the opponents to facilitate acceptance. 2nd. A certain scheme of doctrine must be prepared. 3rd. A formula of acceptance must be exhibited to the acceptants, and it must be held and published as they judge would please the Pope. 4th. If anything was omitted in the opponents' scheme of doctrine, it may be permitted to the acceptants to supply it, but to cut nothing else. 5th. If, all these being observed, acceptance did not follow, all acts would be void and null. The third condition alone displeased the opponents; which, however, seemed altogether necessary to the others, who had so often experienced the bad faith of the faction. But so that exacerbation of spirits would not implicate the business more in such preliminary discussions, it had to be yielded, the Orléanais so wishing, and that condition was no longer urged; since Noailles had solemnly promised that, harmony being established concerning the doctrine itself, everything would finally be plain, and acceptance would follow according to wishes. Otherwise, the opponents demanded that in the exposition of doctrine, the liberty of sentiment of other schools being excluded, the sole and rigorous doctrine of the Thomists should be preserved. They finally meet: the Opponents, according to custom, repeatedly ventilate various meanings of the propositions and their censures: the acceptants respond patiently, and finally bring forward a scheme of doctrine, in which reverence toward the Apostolic See was especially commended. Nor was there anything in it that the opponents could carp at. Therefore the others, glad and relying on the promises of Noailles, were now expecting nothing else than the unanimous acceptance of the constitution,
pages.68:
and were asking that a formula of the same be shown to them: they indeed bring forward a formula, but they do not wish it to be changed: Noailles further enumerates 26 Quesnellian propositions as having been undeservedly condemned, concerning which the Pope must necessarily explain his mind more. Here the acceptants cry out at their bad faith, protest, complain that they were deceived and mocked, and resist. But in vain: Four Bishops from the opponents, of Mirepoix, Montpellier, Boulogne, and Senez, on March 1, 1717, sign an instrument of Appeal from the Bull Unigenitus to a General Council, and on March 5 propose it to the Sorbonne to be subscribed, which was also done, with two other Theological faculties in France following this example. Noailles also, but secretly, signed another appeal separately, with the condition: if the Pope denied an explanation of the Bull, or did not admit it. This was the end of the conferences, as usually happens, this was the fruit.

The Orléanais, offended by this most shameful manner of acting, and grieving that he too had been deluded far too late, orders the Bishops to leave Paris soon, and the Notary who had written the instrument of Appeal to go to prison. Meanwhile, a very large crowd of appellants of all orders was being received, nay, was being searched for with tireless zeal and not a little silver, the very dregs of the people not excluded, with many hundreds of thousands of French pounds spent on this in not so much time, which to complete the grave business of Religion, as they said, the Secretary of Noailles, Cardinal Delort by name, and Servien, similarly from the letters of the brother of Noailles, the Bishop of Châlons,
pages.69:
had scraped together. But the matter being revealed by the Creditors, the former was punished with exile, Servien was relegated to the galleys, later exempted from these when he had revoked his appeal before the Vicar General of the diocese of Verdun on Feb. 10, 1724, and confessed his own trafficking at the same time. But a little later he returned to the same sty. Nevertheless, the multitude of appellants, even increased by the factionists beyond the truth (they themselves counted two thousand), was not so great that it could come into comparison with those thinking well. Of the twenty-three Theological faculties that are in France, only the Nantes and Reims ones, besides the Sorbonne, adhered to the appeal, of which, out of 70 and more Academies outside France, not one dreamed: and while the Prelate of Reims was urging his own to obedience with vain labor, in Montpellier the sheep did not want to hear the voice of the Pastor, who would not hear the voice of the Church.

The conferences finished, La Trémoille was working that, silence being imposed on the parties, the disputes concerning the Bull might be removed: which the Orléanais also sanctioned by Decree on Oct. 17, 1717. Noailles, however, consigned to the same a certain exposition of doctrine made, as he said, in the meeting of Bishops, to be approved by the Pontiff at Rome. The Legate did everything zealously, as he had been ordered. The response: the exposition was not entirely free from all error, and it was asked: was it the same one prepared by the acceptants, or conformable to it? finally, that the formula of acceptance also be exhibited, it was requested. In the midst of this, the Instrument of Appeal solemnly published by the 4 Bishops appears, with the appeal of Noailles prefixed to it, different in this, that

pages.54:
the liberties of the Gallican Church <note>original: "libertates Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ"</note> might be preserved, omitting the formulas of "the fullness of power," "of his own accord," and similar terms customary in Rome; so that in this way all traps and excuses for accepting the Bull might be averted. To this excellent disposition of the Most Christian King, and to his zeal for restoring peace, as the pleas and exhortations of very many Bishops were added, the Pontiff at last granted everything, and as soon as possible the examination of the whole work was resumed by two Cardinals and several Theologians.

When Noailles saw these things being prepared, moved both by the example of the King, who had revoked the license to print Quesnel's books, and by fear of the coming Bull, he had already decided with himself to condemn the book he had once approved. But behold, two men undermined the whole affair. The General of the Minims, Rollet, and the "Expeditionary," as they call him, Chauffeur, wrote to the Cardinal that everything being done to elaborate the Bull was merely a shadow-play meant to terrify the Cardinal; having perceived this, he gave no place to any saner counsel, nor to any more certain news. Furthermore, the faction spread in Rome and in France that there was no hope of the Bull being accepted: that the Dauphin favored Quesnel, that the Parliament was hostile to the Roman Curia, and that the Sorbonne was not so unfriendly to the new doctrine, which they confirmed with recent documents. For when the Jesuit Juvencius had written certain things in the History of his Society regarding the acts of the time of Henry IV that were not at all approved by the Parliament, the Superiors of the three Colleges that were in Paris were summoned and ordered to declare what they felt regarding the four most well-known articles out of the 82,
pages.55:
namely, regarding the Power of the Pope in the Kingdoms of Princes and in the Church, and finally, they were ordered to bind themselves by oath to hold the doctrine of those articles for themselves and their own. Then Abbot Sanctagnanus, when he had sought letters of confirmation from Rome for his Bishopric, let himself be persuaded to defend the fourth proposition of Jansenius in the Sorbonne itself, lest he succumb even at Rome to the envy and deceitful arts of the Jansenists, as the worst counselors were suggesting.

Truly, these scare tactics vanished shortly; for since neither the acts of the Parliament nor the error of the abbot seemed of such importance that they could stir a prudent suspicion of the refusal of acceptance, and since the Dauphin had even given a public written testimony of the Catholic faith and of his own firm adhesion, after the two-year labors of examinations and collation of texts were finally exhausted, the famous Bull *Unigenitus* <note>original: "Bulla Unigenitus"</note> was subscribed by Clement XI on September 8, 1713, after all had been examined and reviewed by Trémoille, and was published two days later, on September 10. In it, one hundred and one propositions excerpted from the work of Quesnel are condemned in a lump, as they say, namely, as false, impious, heretical, etc., with these and other censures attached to be applied respectively to each; it is added that many other things similar and akin to these are contained therein that are worthy of condemnation, and that the text of the scripture itself, from the reprobated Montenfi edition, is corrupted; wherefore the whole book, published or to be published in any language, is prohibited and condemned.
pages.56:
<note>A decorative horizontal rule appears at the top of the page.</note>

Upon understanding this, Noailles, without delay, issued a mandate on the 28th of that same month, in which he stated that he could no longer bear his name prefixed to a book condemned by the Pope, and therefore, as he had promised, he revoked the approval he had given to the book in another diocese, a book previously approved by his predecessor, condemned the book, and prohibited its reading and retention, etc. Then the Clergy was convened, and Commissioners were elected, the leader of whom was Cardinal Rohan; Noailles was called the President of the Council. Of 18 Archbishops, seven gathered by October 18, and thirty-three of 112 Bishops. Noailles spoke first regarding his own formerly given preface to the book and the mandate promulgated a little earlier, and soon he began to discourse on the obscurity of the Bull and the doubts that would arise from it, to the wonder of the others, to whom everything in it seemed clear and plain. Rohan demonstrated that there was not one of the 101 propositions to which one of the censures did not apply. Noailles, however, contended as much as he could that the Bull could not be accepted otherwise than with a prefixed instruction and added explanations and restrictions. This proposal was rejected by almost everyone, and four articles were opposed to it by Cardinal Rohan: 1. It is manifest from the Bull, and must be held, that Quesnel's book is heretical: 2. That those 101 propositions are deservedly condemned and worthy of one of the applied censures: therefore 3. The Bull ought to be accepted before any further explanation, since regarding the aforementioned it is neither ambiguous nor obscure. 4. There is no need for any other previous instruction, except one that would fortify the faithful against false interpretations of the Bull. These things pleased the Assembly, but not Noailles; who, when he could obtain nothing,
<note>A decorative printer's ornament appears at the bottom of the page.</note>
pages.57:
having seceded with nine other Bishops, he abstained from the meetings until he was compelled by the authority of the King to revisit them again. In these, the decree of acceptance was finally made and signed by all except Noailles and a few of his followers. After these, the pastoral instruction was proposed, which Noailles himself, as if it were his own, praised with no less artifice and eloquence; the Acts of the Convention were written out for the absent Bishops; finally, a letter was given to the Pope on February 5, 1714, with an attached instruction, by which they signified the acceptance of the Bull that had been made, congratulated the Pope on the errors put to flight by his constitution, and pledged obedience and prompt fidelity in executing it; all of which were approved by the Pontiff. And when the responses of many absent Bishops arrived, in which they also approved the acts and, having given their consent, signified their acceptance of the Bull, the King issued an edict or letters patent on February 14, by which he ordered the Bull to be accepted, published, and observed by all, and to be entered into the public records by all Parliaments in the whole Kingdom. Soon the Bull was promulgated in 113 dioceses; obedience was also rendered by the Parliaments, but not sufficiently well; for although the Bishops publicly protested that the Gallican liberties <note>original: "libertatibus gallicanis"</note> were in no way derogated by the Bull, nevertheless, the formulas of caveats "saving the liberties," etc., were added by them, omitting the protests of the Bishops, which would give rise to new troubles in their own time.

Noailles, in order to excuse himself before the King, in a letter given to him on January 14, testified indeed that he, and those adhering to him, in no way dissented from the others regarding the faith,
pages.58:
and that with them he condemned not only the famous five propositions of Jansenius, but all other errors which they believed were condemned by the Pope through his constitution: and that it had always been his sincere intention to proscribe the book of Reflections throughout his dioceses, all the more so the more certainly he confirmed himself to the Pope through this in the chief point of the constitution. Meanwhile, they spread the word that the acceptance of the Bull was neither necessary, nor could be done without explanation, nor indeed had it been made by the Clergy except in relation to the aforementioned instruction: which was certainly most false; since the other Bishops, for that very reason, in order to remove every suspicion of ambiguity found in the Bull, had studiously delayed the instruction until only a few days after the acceptance was made, to be approved by the whole Assembly. In his mandates, however, he attacked most fiercely both the Bull, for which they expected an explanation from the Pope, and the instruction itself.

The King, greatly moved by these things, forbade Noailles from accessing the royal Court, and ordered the Bishops affected by his cause to return to their own dioceses. To the Sorbonne, however, under the gravest penalties, he ordered the acceptance of the Bull and its entry into the records, which was done notwithstanding the suspension intended for the Clergy by the mandate of Noailles, if anyone should decree anything about accepting the Bull without his authority. The remaining Universities throughout France followed the Sorbonne. But the Pontiff, rightfully foreseeing even greater damage to Religion from this resistance of the Bishops and the superfluous caution of the Parliaments, having condemned their mandates, one of which—that of the Bishop of Châlons—was branded as if heretical,
pages.59:
urged the King vehemently that both the formulas of those exceptions be removed from the Acts of the Parliaments, and that he himself should dismiss the Cardinal to Rome to plead his case.

Now the King, since he thought the obstinacy of Noailles—who was now promising acceptance of the Bull, now retracting his promises under various pretexts—could not be bent otherwise, decided to send him back to the Pope. Having later changed his plan, however, he sent Amelot to Rome, who was to seek from the Pontiff a new Bull, by which the constitution *Unigenitus* would be declared a universal law of the Church and a finished case, and at the same time to seek legates for convening a national Council. Clement resisted for a long time, claiming that too much indulgence was being shown to the refractory and that the matter was being dragged out: nevertheless, he submitted two Briefs, one grave with paternal admonitions, the other with threats, to be presented to Noailles if he were not bent by the first. But since the King did not desist from his purpose, and had already named the same Commissioners who had been in the last Convention of the Clergy, he himself at last consented. And so the commissioners met to prepare what was necessary for the future Synod, and above all they sought and obtained a decree from the King, by which the constitution *Unigenitus* was ordered to be promulgated as the law of the Kingdom and the rule of faith. The Parliament refused to enter this into the acts, using as a pretext that one must wait until it was established that the Bull had been received in foreign Kingdoms as well; and when Louis was preparing to compel the Parliament to obedience by his supreme authority, struck by a sudden illness, to the greatest grief of orthodox France and no less at Rome and Versailles,
pages.60:
died in September 1715, at 77 years of age, with the most joyful hope of restoring peace carried with him to the grave. Shortly before his death, in the presence of Cardinals Rohan and Bissy, he protested that he was dying in the union and Catholic faith, and that he had aimed at only one thing: that union among the Prelates, peace, and concord should be restored in the Kingdom and the Church.

The faction, liberated from great fear, since it believed the Duke of Orléans, the administrator of the Kingdom, favored Noailles, openly triumphed. Indeed, the Duke strove to obtain from the Cardinal, by gentleness and outstanding signs of benevolence, what the King could not obtain by his authority, and in this hope of moving him toward the acceptance of the Bull, he vainly satisfied himself and the Pontiff. Meanwhile, countless pamphlets were spread, and among these two most pestiferous ones: namely, the *Hexapla* <note>original: "Hexapla"</note> and the *Testimonium veritatis* <note>original: "Testimonium veritatis"</note>, in which not only was Catholic doctrine attacked in a general way, but furthermore the people themselves were proclaimed to be the sole rule and judge of faith. These books were indeed condemned by the Clergy, while the author, who was Basnage, a Protestant minister, remained hidden; since, however, very many from the Sorbonne especially fostered these births, through their fraudulent arts it was brought about that the publication of the decree of condemnation was hindered by the Duke of Orléans, and the decree itself was suppressed for seven years, never to be brought to light, to the greatest disgrace of the Clergy even after the author was recognized, unless copies of it had been conveniently preserved by most Bishops. Furthermore, with the most shameful declamations of the Sorbonnists against the Bull resounding, who called it nothing but a monstrous decree, a work breathing nothing but laxity,
pages.61:
infidelity, and one of the gates of hell that will not prevail, until they finally impudently denied that it had ever been accepted by the Sorbonne, against Basnage himself, who testified in the *Hexapla* that it had been done by 525 votes against 22. Finally, the Duke of Orléans prohibited the entire Assembly of the Sorbonne; he excluded from sacred Orders several Prelates who had studied in the Sorbonne; the Pope also decided to grant confirmation to no one presented by the King for a Bishopric unless the Bull had been accepted first.

Hitherto, the Bishops who opposed the acceptance of the Bull had been idle. These turned to new arts and composed letters to the Pontiff, seeking an explanation of the Bull, according to which they would be willing to accept it. They showed these to their colleagues and persuaded ten of those who had already performed simple acceptance to subscribe to these letters, even though they had been changed for the most part. Then, indeed, having suppressed these letters, the opponents spread the rumor that thirty Bishops in all had sought an explanation of the Bull. But those ten immediately protested publicly against the fraud and abuse of their subscription, one of whom, the Bishop of Agde, having given a simple account of the whole plot, dissipated these smokes most excellently. But once this machine was overthrown, Noailles acted before the Duke so that he would send (for the Cardinal distrusted himself) Cavalier, a great Vicar, as they call him, to Rome, who would treat with the Pope regarding the composition of the controversies face-to-face. The Duke sent the man, although Cardinal Bissy had confessed to him that Cavalier was suspect to him regarding Jansenism.
