the Cardinal criticized the obscurity of the Bull and appealed only conditionally, should the explanation be denied; they, however, absolutely accused and rejected the Bull as contrary to Catholic dogma and to the Decalogue itself. Nor was there delay; by order of the Duke, this writing was condemned and suppressed by the Parliament as having been published against the law of silence. Noailles indeed protested that the publication of his appeal had been done without his knowledge, yet he rejoiced to see it received by almost his entire diocese; indeed, having become bolder, when the Pope initially kept everything concealed, awaiting the formula of acceptance to be sent by the Cardinal, he dared to demand not only an explanation of the Bull conformable to the submitted scheme of doctrine, but besides this, also a Brief to all the faithful, by which the Constitution *Unigenitus* would be derogated: nor was this enough; instead of the formula of acceptance, he finally sends an <term>apostilla</term> <gloss>marginal note/appendix</gloss>, as they call it, to Rome, by which he declares that he neither seeks an explanation nor a Brief, nor cares for it, unless in addition silence were imposed on everyone concerning the question of fact. Then indeed the Pontiff, moved by this insolent temerity and obstinacy, when he had simultaneously understood that the scheme of doctrine proposed by the acceptors had been changed in 25 articles and 48 propositions, the beginning and end altered, mutilated, and full of deceitful substitutions of phrases (as, when it was being read, "the Bull condemns, the Pope condemns," it was replaced by the opponents with "the Bull wishes to condemn, the intention of the Pope was to condemn"), had been offered to him, he orders that instrument of appeal to be condemned by the Holy Office <note>original: "S. Officio"</note>, and the decree was posted in the Campo dei Fiori on February 8, 1718, nor did he permit the apostolic letters of confirmation to be dispatched for the three nominated by the King for the mitres,

<note>A small symbol, likely a printer's mark, appears at the bottom of the page.</note>
pages.71:
nor did he permit the apostolic letters of confirmation to be dispatched, until La Trémoille <note>original: "Tremoillius"</note> had exhibited a writing from the same persons as a testimony of their submission in accepting the Bull, even though the Court was unwilling.

There was subsequent contention through writings from each side, and through condemnations and suppressions by the Parliaments under the law of silence, though not with equal fairness. Mailly, the Archbishop of Reims <note>original: "Maillyus Rhemenfis"</note>, had published a letter to the Duke Regent, in which he complained of the silence imposed, which only the acceptors observe, while the opposing faction stirs up everything with impunity through its clamors and libels. The Parliament of Paris condemned this letter to the infamous fire on March 19, and its decree, sent to the Archbishop of Reims, ends with this truly memorable exhortation: *Cease, Prelate, to support the arrogance and avarice of the Roman Court, which has given cause for the separation of half of Europe from the Roman Church.* Having received the message, Mailly, intending to give thanks to God, founded a perpetual sacrifice in the Episcopal Palace; the Pope granted him the Purple, and in that same year 1718, and on the same day on which he had issued the Constitution *Unigenitus* five years prior—namely, September 8—he promulgated the Bull *Pastoralis officii* <gloss>Of the Pastoral Office</gloss>, directed to all the faithful, in which he excludes from the Communion of the faithful all who do not accept the Constitution *Unigenitus*, though without expressing any name. And since Noailles himself had issued his appeal from the Bull *Unigenitus* on September 24, and shortly thereafter another on October 3 from the Bull *Pastoralis officii*, along with a Pastoral Instruction, this too was condemned in Rome, and two hundred propositions worthy of censure were noted in it. Conversely, the Parliament of Paris also resisted the reception of the last-

<note>A decorative headpiece ornament appears at the top of the page.</note>
pages.72:
last Bull on the same day, October 3, by a decree; furthermore, more than 47 Bishops declared in their Mandates, Instructions, and letters given to their own people that all Appellants were schismatics. And with these, finally, all the plans that the Duke had conceived in his mind to bring the Cardinal back to the path were overturned.

Meanwhile, the Appellants triumphed, though not without grief at the death of Quesnel, their leader—most esteemed after Arnauld—from whom this whole present cause was derived. It is not my pleasure to weave the history of this man's life here, but it is helpful to add two things to what has already been said about him that are worth noting. The first is a certain writing sent by Quesnel himself to a certain priest, who, having finally wiped away the mist of errors and being returned to himself and to the Church, produced it. They were rules comprised in 12 articles, which his followers were to use in conversation among themselves and with various kinds of men. The sum of it was almost this: Union and concord; fidelity to the secret; circumspection in speech according to the various conditions of men; ambiguity in various chapters of Religion; he wanted it to be said that Christ is present in the Eucharist, not only by faith or figure, as the heterodox say, but neither by transubstantiation, nor substantially or really, as the Catholics say: how then? in an imperceptible way. In the Sacrament of Penance, they would urge the insufficiency of attrition and the necessity of perfect contrition. They would openly attack sufficient grace, the liberty of indifference, and merits, sometimes directly and sometimes through the maze of words, so that an exit might be open for the pressured: let them exalt only victorious grace: and so many other things.
pages.73:
The second is a notable testimony of truth given by the man himself. Quesnel, asked by his nephew Pinfon, a sculptor, to which party of those then litigating about matters of Religion he should adhere, responded by letter: "He should hold himself to the greater part of the faithful, or firmly adhere to the trunk of the tree of the Church; for he himself had not been provoked and compelled to foster these disputes so pertinaciously except by the injuries of the Jesuits." Pinfon asserted that he had heard the same from Quesnel's own mouth not only once, with the Bishop of Angers, Poncet de la Rivière, as witness in his *Reflexions consolatoires* <gloss>Consolatory Reflections</gloss>. But from the time when madness swept the man away, in the year 1719, at the very end of his old age in Amsterdam and brought to the borders of death, four days before his passing, he renewed his appeal, having summoned two witnesses, and thus, having received viaticum <gloss>the Eucharist given to the dying</gloss> from his Pastor, the old man lived on until December 2.

The fruits of these disturbances were, moreover, very sad. To say nothing of the countless writings of fanatical men, by which they labored to destroy human and divine laws, it suffices to bring forward one or another fact to understand the nature of the heresy. Dupin, a Doctor of the Sorbonne, had a frequent commerce of letters with the Archbishop of Canterbury, which, having begun for the sake of erudition and courtesy, was at first believed to have been continued, but eventually became suspect. Therefore, once Dupin's papers were seized unexpectedly, it was clear that he had been plotting nothing less than to betray the Catholic Religion and to attempt to reconcile a union and communion between the Gallican Church and the Anglican. The conditions were fa-

<note>A decorative printer's ornament appears at the bottom of the page.</note>
pages.74:
liberal: Transubstantiation must be denied: auricular confession must be abolished: fasts and monastic vows must be removed: the yoke of the Pope must be cast off. Let these suffice. Petitpied, one of the 40 Doctors who had subscribed to the famous Case of Conscience in the year 1703, when he was almost the only one who did not want to retract, was relegated to Bauné and deprived of his office; yet, permitted to return, he was received with honor into the Sorbonne and restored to his rights, and even moved to govern the church of Asnières, which is hardly a mile from Paris. He rendered remarkable service to the faction, especially by introducing a new Liturgy, in which the people offered not only bread and wine, but also produce appropriate to the season, for the sacrifice—to be celebrated only on Sundays and more solemn feasts—upon an altar excavated in the shape of a tomb and covered with a simple linen cloth. He himself, with the cross raised and accompanied by a deacon, would approach, then sitting at the corner of the Epistle side, he would intone the first words of the *Gloria* and *Credo*—the people would continue the chant—blessings would be performed, and crosses made over all the produce—various prayers would be recited, and always one for the preservation and growth of the new Church. In turn, the Sorbonne exerted its own zeal and removed Tamponnet from the rank of Doctor. He opposed the appeal and did not want to subscribe to a thesis, even one accepted by the Academy of Cayenne: *that it is erroneous to defend the infallibility of the Pontiff*—this was the crime. And these and similar things were done with the knowledge, inspection, and silence of Noailles.

It ought to seem strange to one who is ignorant of the power of blind passion, fed by the smoke of the most disgraceful adulation, that such things could have no
pages.75: power against the Cardinal, which would strike horror into any good man who has not completely cast off the Roman faith. Other things followed, which could do even less. In the year 1720, the Bishop of Orléans <note>original: "Aurelianenfis"</note> renews the law of silence. To Mailly, whose other letter the Parliament of Paris had burned, the King sends the doctoral cap on March 19, which he obtained as Red <note>meaning the Cardinal's hat</note> from Rome on the same day. The Pope denies confirmation to two men presented by the King for Bishoprics who hesitated to accept the Bull, and he considers abolishing the Congregation of Saint Maur, from which it was said that very many had joined the appellants; he was barely turned from this plan by the prayers and promises of Father Conrad, the Procurator General of the same. La Trémoille proposes a new idea for reconciling peace and dies while refining it; Clement himself spoke a notable eulogy of his sincerity. Yet the business of La Trémoille was not neglected. A Decree is issued by the King by which every impugnation of the Pontifical Constitution and the Instruction of the 40 Bishops is prohibited: a new, somewhat tolerable formula of acceptance is put forward again: a rumor is spread that Noailles is yielding: the matter is sold as almost concluded; in the end, his circular letter to his Curates appears, in which he warns them not to be disturbed by his acceptance; that it will never be anything other than in relation to appropriate explanations: this is soon followed by two completely pestilential libels: *Mémoire sur la Paix de l’Église* <gloss>Memoir on the Peace of the Church</gloss> and *Notes sur les explications* <gloss>Notes on the explanations</gloss>, published with the knowledge and connivance of the Cardinal; the formula is sent to Rome but basely deformed, interpolated with indecent words and restrictions, of which Noailles denies being aware. But when the examination and correction of the formula
pages.76:
is underway, Clement XI dies on March 19, 1721, at the age of 82, in the 21st year of his Pontificate, truly called the Father of the poor, by whose money six hundred poor families were secretly fed, and who, in time of famine, provided daily food for eight thousand and more starving people.

Nor were the opposing and appealing Bishops lacking, seven of whom—François Caillebot, formerly of Tournai, J. B. de Verthamont of Pamiers, Jean Soanen of Senez, Charles Colbert of Montpellier, Pierre Langle of Boulogne, Charles Caylus of Auxerre, and Michel Cassagnet of Mâcon—gave a letter in their common name to his successor, Innocent XIII, formerly Cardinal Conti, full of complaints against Clement and his constitutions. Innocent, as soon as possible, orders this to be condemned by the Holy Office on January 8, 1722, as a satire most injurious to Clement XI; and when the faction openly boasted with incredible temerity through the *Nouvelles Ecclésiastiques* <note>original: "Notitias Batavicas"</note> that the new Pontiff favored them and disapproved of the acts of his predecessors, he sends a Brief to the King, in which he wipes away the calumny by the very confirmation of all the acts; the King immediately had it published, and at the same time had the same letter of the Bishops to the Pope condemned by his Royal Council of State as injurious, temerarious, and seditious to the Apostolic See and to the Bishops of France. And when the same Bishops complained again in other letters given to the King, now about the decree of the Royal Senate, now about the new condemnation issued by order of the King of their Response opposed to the pastoral Instruction of Cardinal Bissy, in which the Constitution *Unigenitus* was most fiercely defended, and all the right
pages.77:
of judging about it, which the Parliament had rashly arrogated to itself, was vindicated for the Pastors of the Church; all writings of this kind were rejected and condemned again and again by both Royal and Apostolic authority: terrified by this, they remained quiet for a time, and until the death of the Duke of Orléans, whom the Pontiff followed shortly thereafter on March 7, 1724.

§. 5.
The Last Retreat of the Jansenists.

It has long since passed into the custom of any faction rebellious to the Church to boast of great names as authors, followers, or defenders of their doctrine. Thus, the Jansenists from the beginning wanted to appear not only disciples of Augustine, but also friends of Aquinas and the Thomistic School, which supported them, and even its followers. I name one witness, the Abbot La Lane, a writer of iron strength, who, among 40 various minor works composed by himself in defense of Jansen and the 5 Propositions, also wrote one on the Conformity of the Jansenists with the Thomists. Thus, the appealing Bishops likewise labored to protect their Quesnel by means of the Thomistic School: others accompanied them, and other most inept scribblers followed, whose vain labor should draw no follower unless he is blind or willing to go insane, if perchance he attempted the five propositions of Jansen or the first forty or so of Quesnel from the one hundred and one condemned, with these following five indubitable ones, no less received in the Thomistic school than in any other school addicted to the Roman faith

Noailles was further terrified by the Council of Embrun and by the King's authority in defending its acts. At that very time, the letters of the famous monk who had fled to the Dutch, Dom Thierry—or Theodoric, a man of thoroughly fanatical character—were fortuitously intercepted, by which his worst machinations, the impious councils of the faction, and also the dissensions familiar to heresy, were laid bare. One part urged a free ecumenical council, as they speak with the Pelagians and Lutherans, to which he, in the name of all Thomists, Augustinians, and their brethren the Benedictines, etc., impudently denounced all the Bulls of the Pontiffs issued against Jansen and Quesnel, and whatever else exists written against Jansenism. Now, for this free council, some wanted only bishops; others wanted the clergy of the second order to have equal authority with the bishops; still others wanted laymen to be judges in it with the same rights as the former. One part rejected every council, having assumed the private spirit as the rule of faith after the fashion of other heretics. Indeed, there were those who dreamed of the coming of Elias. Added to these were no light disputes about usury, so frequent in Holland, which the highly moderated rigor of some (for the subsidy of the Corbona, namely the new church) wished to be overlooked, while the purer zeal of others wanted it entirely removed. When these things were finally understood, Noailles, as if his eyes were suddenly opened while on the very edge of the precipice toward which the deceitful and perfidious tongues of sycophants had led him, was seized with horror at the pit; he abandoned his 24 years of stubbornness, yielded to the truth, and [renounced] whatever writings [had been produced] by him, or in his name-

they refused, having disregarded the punishments even of excommunication established by the Order. The King inhibited the decision of the Parliament and recalled the case to the Royal Council. There were two primary acts of the council: the condemnation of Father Courrayer of the monastery of Saint Genevieve, together with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, who, intending to carry out the system of <term>Dupin</term> <gloss>Louis Ellies Dupin, a French ecclesiastical historian</gloss>, crossed into England and extolled himself there with other writings concerning the ordinations of Anglican bishops; the second was the sentence passed on September 20 against Soanen, the Bishop of Senez. A certain pastoral instruction had appeared under his name, teeming with infamous errors of every kind, in which the work of <term>Quesnel</term> <gloss>Pasquier Quesnel, a prominent Jansenist theologian</gloss> was commended as much as the Bull condemning it was prostituted as being worthy of all execration. Soanen initially prevaricated, naming thirteen bishops before whom he would plead his case, and against whom he himself had nothing to object, but eventually, he traveled to Embrun, not without a profane retinue, nor one that was unarmed. But before he entered the city, he ordered it to be announced to those gathered that he would never recognize them as judges. When he was subsequently asked by the Council whether that was indeed his Instruction, he denied that it was composed by him; nevertheless, he openly professed that he adopted it entirely as his own, held it, and approved of it until he should be convinced of the errors the bishops had condemned in it. Therefore, by the sentence of the Council, he was forbidden from every function, both Episcopal and Priestly, and a Vicar General was appointed for his diocese. Fifty advocates of the Parisian Court signed a consultation on the nullity of the sentence and the acts of the Council of Embrun. until Trémoille had exhibited a writing from the same persons as a testimony of their submission in accepting the Bull, although against the wish of the Court.

Contention followed thereafter with writings from both sides, and by the condemnations and suppressions of the Parliaments under the law of silence, though not with equal fairness. Mailly of Reims had published a letter to the Duke Regent, in which he complained about the silence imposed, which only the acceptors observe, while the opposing faction disturbs everything with impunity by its clamors and libels. The Parliament of Paris condemned this letter to the infamous fire on March 19, and concluded its decree sent to Reims with this truly memorable exhortation: "Cease, Prelate! to bolster the arrogance and avarice of the Roman Court, which has given cause for the separation of half of Europe from the Roman Church." Having received the news, Mailly, about to give thanks to God, founded a perpetual sacrifice in the Episcopal Palace; the Pope decreed the Purple to him, and in that same year of 1718, and on the same day on which he had issued the Constitution *Unigenitus* five years prior, namely September 8, he promulgated the Bull *Pastoralis officii* directed to all the faithful, in which he excludes from the Communion of the faithful all those who do not accept the Constitution *Unigenitus*, though without naming anyone explicitly. And when Noailles himself had published his appeal from the Bull *Unig.* on September 24, and soon again another on October 3 from the Bull *Pastoralis off.* together with a Pastoral Instruction, this too was condemned in Rome, and two hundred propositions therein were marked as worthy of censure. Conversely, the Parliament of Paris also resisted the reception of the last Bull with a decree on the same day, October 3, by which, moreover, more than 47 Bishops declared in their Mandates, Instructions, and letters given to their own that all Appellants were schismatics. And with these, finally, all the Duke's plans conceived in his mind to bring the Cardinal back to the path were overturned.

It does not please me to weave the history of this man's life here, but it is useful to add two things worthy of memory to what has already been said about him. The first is a certain writing sent by Quesnel himself to a certain Priest, who, having at last wiped away the darkness of errors, was restored to himself and to the Church and produced it. They were Rules comprised in 12 articles, which his followers were to use in conversation among themselves and with various kinds of men. The sum of it was nearly this: Union and concord: faith in the secret: circumspection in speech according to the varying condition of men: amphibology <note>equivocation</note> in various chapters of Religion: for instance, he wished it to be said that Christ is present in the Eucharist, neither only through faith or figure, as the heterodox say, nor through transubstantiation, or substantially or really, as the Catholics say: how then? in an imperceptible manner. In the Sacrament of penance, they were to urge the insufficiency of attrition and the necessity of perfect contrition. They were to attack sufficient grace, the liberty of indifference, and merits, sometimes openly, sometimes through the vagaries of words, so that a path might be open for those hard-pressed: they were to extol only triumphant grace: and so on for many other things. The other is
pages.73:
an outstanding testimony of the truth given by himself. Quesnel, when asked by his nephew Pinfon, a sculptor, to which party of those then litigating about matters of Religion he should adhere, replied by letter: "He should hold himself to the greater part of the faithful, or firmly adhere to the trunk of the tree of the Church; for he had not been compelled to foster these litigations so pertinaciously except by the injuries of the Jesuits." Pinfon asserted that he had heard the same thing also in person, and not just once, from the mouth of Quesnel himself, as witnessed by the Bishop of Angers, Poncet de la Rivière, in his *Reflexions consolatoires* <gloss>Consolatory Reflections</gloss>. But since the time when madness carried the man away, in the year 1719, at Amsterdam, brought to the borders of death in extreme old age, four days before his passing, he renewed his appeal before two summoned witnesses, and thus, having received the viaticum from his Pastor, the old man lived until December 2.

Furthermore, the fruits of those disturbances were the most sorrowful by far. To say nothing of the innumerable writings of fanatical men, by which they labored to overturn human and divine laws, it may suffice to bring forward one or two facts for understanding the genius of the heresy. Dupin, a Doctor of the Sorbonne, had frequent commerce of letters with the Archbishop of Canterbury, which, begun for the sake of erudition and courtesy, and believed to be continued as such, finally became suspicious. Therefore, once Dupin's papers were seized unexpectedly, it became clear that he had aimed at nothing less than to betray the Catholic Religion and to attempt to reconcile the union and communion of the Gallican Church with the Anglican. The conditions were

pages.74:
liberal: Transubstantiation was to be denied: auricular confession was to be abolished: fasts and the vows of Monks were to be removed: the yoke of the Pope was to be cast off. Let these suffice. Petitpied, one of the 40 Doctors who had subscribed to the famous Case of Conscience in the year 1703, when he was almost the only one who did not want to retract, was relegated to Baunay and stripped of his office; yet permitted to return later, he was received into the Sorbonne with honor and restored to his rights; indeed, having been moved to govern the church of Anien, which is scarcely a mile distant from Paris, he rendered notable service to the faction, especially by introducing a new Liturgy, in which the people offered not only bread and wine, but also produce appropriate to the season, for the sacrifice—to be celebrated only on Sundays and more solemn feast days—upon an altar excavated in the shape of a tomb and covered with a simple linen cloth. He himself, with the cross raised, approaching with a deacon, then sitting at the corner of the Epistle, intoned the first words of the *Gloria* and *Credo*—the people continued the chant—blessings were made, and crosses were traced over all the produce—various prayers were recited, and always one for preserving and increasing the new Church. Conversely, the Sorbonne exerted its zeal and stripped Tamponnet of the rank of Doctor. He had opposed himself to the appeal, nor did he want to subscribe to a thesis, even one received by the Cayenne Academy: *that it is erroneous to defend the infallibility of the Pontiff*—this was the crime. And these things and similar ones were done while Noailles knew, watched, and kept silent.

It ought to seem strange to one who is ignorant of the power of blind passion, fed by the smoke of most base adulation, that such things could have no
pages.75: power against the Cardinal, which might strike horror into any good man who has not utterly cast away the Roman faith. Other things followed, which were even less able to do so. In the year 1720, the Bishop of Orléans renews the law of silence. The King sends the doctoral cap to Mailly—whose other letter the Parliament of Paris had burned—on March 19, which he obtained as Red in Rome on the same day. The Pope denies confirmation to two presented by the King for the Episcopate who were delaying to accept the bull, and he considers abolishing the Congregation of Saint Maur, from which many were said to have joined the appellants; he was barely turned from this plan by the prayers and promises of Father Conrad, the Procurator General of the same. Trémoille proposes a new idea for reconciling peace and dies while refining it; Clement himself spoke an outstanding eulogy for his sincerity. Yet the business of Trémoille was not neglected. A Decree is issued by the King, by which every impugnation of the Pontifical Constitution and the Instruction of the 40 Bishops is prohibited: a new formula of acceptance is put forth again, however tolerable: a rumor is spread that Noailles is yielding: the matter is sold as already nearly completed; at the end, his circular letter to his Curés is produced, whom he warns not to be disturbed by his acceptance; that it would never be anything other than in relation to appropriate explanations: this is soon followed by two altogether pestilential libels: *Mémoire sur la Paix de l’Eglise* <gloss>Memoir on the Peace of the Church</gloss> and *Notes sur les explications* <gloss>Notes on the explanations</gloss>, published with the knowledge and connivance of the Cardinal; the formula is sent to Rome but shamefully deformed, interpolated with indecent words and restrictions, of which Noailles denies he was aware. But when it comes to the examination and correction of the formula
pages.76:
Clement XI dies on March 19, 1721, in the 82nd year of his life, the 21st of his Pontificate, truly called the Father of the poor, by whose wealth six hundred poor families were secretly fed, and who in times of famine provided daily meals to eight thousand and more starving people.

Nor were there lacking Bishops opposing and appealing, seven of whom—François Caillebot, formerly of Tournai; J. B. de Verthamont of Pamiers; Jean Soanen of Senez; Charles Colbert of Montpellier; Pierre Langle of Boulogne; Charles Caylus of Auxerre; and Michel Cassagnet of Mâcon—gave a letter in their common name to his successor, Innocent XIII, formerly Cardinal Conti, full of complaints against Clement and his constitutions. Innocent, as soon as possible, orders this to be condemned by the Holy Office on January 8, 1722, as a satire most injurious to Clement XI; and when the faction openly boasted with incredible temerity through the *Notitiae Batavicae* <gloss>Batavian News</gloss> that the new Pontiff favored them and disapproved of the acts of his Predecessors, he sends a Brief to the King in which he wipes away the calumny by the very confirmation of all his acts; which the King immediately caused to be published, and at the same time caused that same letter of the Bishops to the Pope to be condemned by his Royal Council of State as injurious, temerarious, and seditious to the Apostolic See and to the Bishops of France. And when the same Bishops complained again in other letters given to the King, now about the decree of the Royal Senate, now about the new condemnation issued by the King's order of their Response opposed to the pastoral Instruction of Cardinal Bissy, in which the Constitution *Unigenitus* was most fiercely defended, and every right
pages.77:
of judging concerning it, which the Parliament had temerariously arrogated to itself, was vindicated for the Pastors of the Church; all writings of this kind were again and again rejected and condemned by the authority of both King and Apostle: terrified by which, they remained quiet for a time, and until the death of the Duke of Orléans, whom the Pontiff followed shortly after on March 7, 1724.

§. 5.
The Last Retreats of the Jansenists.

It has long since passed into the custom of every faction rebellious to the Church to boast of great names as authors, followers, or defenders of its doctrine. Thus, the Jansenists from the beginning wished to appear not only disciples of Augustine, but also of Aquinas and friends of the Thomistic School supporting them, and even its followers. I name one witness, the Abbé La Lane, a writer of iron resolve, who among 40 various minor works composed by him in defense of Jansenius and the 5 Propositions, also wrote one on the Conformity of the Jansenists with the Thomists. Thus, the appealing Bishops similarly labored to protect their Quesnel by means of the Thomistic School: accompanied and followed by others, and other most inept scribblers, whose empty labor should drag no follower unless he is blind or willing to go insane, if perchance he were to attempt to reconcile the five propositions of Jansenius, or the first forty or so of Quesnel's propositions out of the one hundred and one condemned, with these five following, which are undoubted and no less received in the Thomistic School than in any other school addicted to the Roman faith.

Having received the message, Mailly, about to offer thanks to God, founded a perpetual sacrifice in the Episcopal Palace; the Pope granted him the Purple, and in that same year of 1718, on the very same day on which he had issued the Constitution <term>Unigenitus</term> five years earlier, namely September 8, he promulgated the Bull <term>Pastoralis officii</term> <gloss>Pastoral Office</gloss>, directed to all the faithful, in which he excludes from the communion of the faithful all those not accepting the constitution <term>Unigenitus</term>, though without expressing the name of anyone. And when Noailles himself had edited his own appeal from the Bull <term>Unigenitus</term> on September 24, and soon again another on October 3 from the Bull <term>Pastoralis officii</term> together with a Pastoral Instruction, this too was condemned in Rome, and two hundred propositions worthy of censure were noted in it. Conversely, the Parliament of Paris also resisted the reception
pages.72:
of the last Bull on the same day, October 3, by a decree with which, furthermore, the Bishops, beyond 47 in number, declared all the Appellants to be schismatics in their Mandates, Instructions, and letters given to their own. And with these, finally, all the Duke's plans conceived in his mind for bringing the Cardinal back to the path were overturned.

The Appellants were triumphant in the meantime, though not without grief due to the death of Quesnel, their leader, most esteemed after Arnaldus, from whom all this present cause was derived. It is not pleasing here to weave the history of this man's life; it is enough to add two things worthy of memory to those which have already been said about him. The first is a certain writing sent by Quesnel himself to a certain priest, who, having at last wiped away the darkness of errors, having been restored to himself and to the Church, produced it. They were rules comprised in 12 articles, which his followers were to use in their conversation among themselves and with various kinds of men. The summary of these was almost as follows: Union and concord: faith in the secret: circumspection in speech according to the varying condition of men: amphibology <note>equivocal language</note> in various heads of Religion: how he wanted Christ to be said to be present in the Eucharist, not only through faith or figure, as the heterodox do, but also not through transubstantiation, or substantially, or really, as the Catholics say: how, therefore? in an imperceptible manner. In the Sacrament of penance, they would urge the insufficiency of attrition and the necessity of perfect contrition. They would openly attack sufficient grace, the liberty of indifference, and merits, and sometimes attack them through the ambages <note>roundabout ways</note> of words, so that an exit might be open for the hard-pressed: they would uniquely extol victorious grace: and so many other things.
pages.73:
The second is a notable testimony of the truth given by himself. When Quesnel was asked by his nephew Pinfon, a sculptor, to which party of those then litigating about matters of Religion he should adhere, he replied by letter: "He should hold himself to the greater part of the faithful, or firmly adhere to the trunk of the tree of the Church; for he himself had not been provoked and compelled to foster these litigations so stubbornly except by the injuries of the Jesuits." Pinfon asserted that he had also heard the same thing in person, and not just once, from the mouth of Quesnel himself, as attested by the Bishop of Angers, Poncet de la Rivière, in his <term>Reflexiones consolatoriæ</term> <gloss>Consolatory Reflections</gloss>. But from the time that madness seized the man, in the year 1719, having been brought to the confines of death at an extreme old age in Amsterdam, on the fourth day before his passing he renewed his appeal, and thus, having received viaticum from his pastor, the old man lived on December 2.

Furthermore, the fruits of those disturbances were the saddest by far. To say nothing of the innumerable writings of fanatical men, by which they labored to destroy human and divine laws, it may suffice to bring forward one or two facts to understand the nature of the heresy. Dupin, a Doctor of the Sorbonne, had frequent commerce of letters with the Archbishop of Canterbury, which was believed at first to have been begun and continued for the sake of erudition and courtesy, [but] it finally became suspect. Therefore, when Dupin’s papers were unexpectedly seized, it was clear that he had aimed at nothing less than to betray the Catholic Religion and to attempt to reconcile the union and communion of the Gallican Church with the Anglican one. The conditions were
pages.74:
quite liberal: Transubstantiation must be denied: auricular confession must be abolished: fasts and the vows of Monks must be taken away: the yoke of the Pope must be cast off. Let these suffice. Petitpied, one of the 40 Doctors who had subscribed to the famous Case of Conscience in the year 1703, when he was almost alone in refusing to retract, was banished to Baun and stripped of his authority, yet permitted to return again; having been received into the Sorbonne with honor and restored to his rights, and even moved to govern the church of Asnières, which is scarcely a mile from Paris, he rendered significant service to the faction, especially by introducing a new Liturgy, in which the people, for the sacrifice to be celebrated only on Sundays and more solemn feasts, offered upon the altar excavated in the form of a tomb and covered with a simple linen cloth, besides bread and wine, also fruits convenient to the season. He himself, with a cross carried before him, coming with a deacon accompanying, then sitting at the corner of the Epistle, intones the first words of the <term>Gloria</term> and <term>Credo</term>—the people continue the chant—blessings are made, and all crosses are led over the fruits—various prayers are recited, and always one for preserving and increasing the new Church. Conversely, the Sorbonne exercised its own zeal and cast Tamponnet out of his Doctor's degree. He opposed himself to the appeal and did not want to subscribe to a thesis, even one accepted by the Cayenne Academy: "it is erroneous to defend the infallibility of the Pontiff"—this was the crime. And these things and similar ones were done with the knowledge, inspection, and silence of Noailles.

It ought to seem wondrous to one who is ignorant of the force of blind passion, fed by the smoke of the most disgraceful adulation, that such things
pages.75: could have nothing to do with the Cardinal, which would strike horror into any good [person] who has not completely cast off the Roman faith. Other things followed which could do even less. In the year 1720, the Bishop of Orléans renews the law of silence. On March 19, the King sends the doctoral cap to Mailly, whose other letter the Parliament of Paris had burned, for which he obtained the Red [hat] from Rome on the same day. The Pope denies confirmation to two presented by the King for the Episcopate who were hesitant to accept the Bull, and he thinks of abolishing the Congregation of S. Maur, from which it was said that very many had joined the appellants, but was barely turned away from this plan by the prayers and promises of Father Conrad, the Procurator General of the same. Tremoillius proposes a new idea for reconciling peace, and dies while working it out, for whose sincerity Clement himself spoke a notable eulogy. Nor, however, was Tremoillius's business neglected. A Decree is issued by the King, by which every impugnation of the Pontifical Constitution and the Instruction of the 40 Bishops is prohibited: a new formula of acceptance, however tolerable, is again put forward: a rumor is spread that Noailles is giving himself up: the matter is sold as already nearly completed; at the end, his circular letter to his Curés emerges, whom he warns not to be disturbed by his acceptance; that it would never be anything other than in relation to fitting explanations: this is soon followed by two pamphlets that are completely pestiferous: <term>Memoire sur la Paix de l'Eglise</term> <gloss>Memorandum on the Peace of the Church</gloss> and <term>Notes sur les explications</term> <gloss>Notes on the explanations</gloss>, published with the knowledge and connivance of the Cardinal; the formula is sent to Rome but shamefully deformed, interpolated with indecent words and restrictions, of which Noailles denies being aware. But when the examination and correction of the formula
pages.76:
was being discussed, Clement XI died on March 19, 1721, in the 82nd year of his age and the 21st of his Pontificate, truly called the Father of the poor, by whose wealth six hundred poor families were secretly maintained, and who in the time of famine provided daily food to eight thousand starving people and more.

Nor were the opposing and appealing Bishops lacking for themselves, seven of whom—Franc. Caillebot, formerly of Tournai; J. B. de Verthamont of Pamiers; Jo. Soanen of Senez; Charles Colbert of Montpellier; Petr. Langle of Boulogne; Carol. Caylus of Auxerre; and Mich. Cassagnet of Mâcon—gave a letter in their common name to the Successor Innocent XIII, formerly Cardinal Conti, full of complaints against Clement and his constitutions. Innocent orders this to be condemned by the Holy Office on Jan. 8, 1722, as a satire most injurious to Clement XI; and when the faction openly boasted with incredible temerity through the <term>Notitiae Batavicae</term> <gloss>Batavian News</gloss> that the new Pontiff favored them and disapproved of the acts of his Predecessors, he sends a Brief to the King in which he washes away the calumny with a confirmation of all the acts themselves; which the King caused to be published immediately, and at the same time caused that same letter of the Bishops to the Pope to be condemned by his Royal Council of State as injurious to the Apostolic See and to the Bishops of France, rash, and seditious. And when the same Bishops complained again in other letters given to the King, now about the decree of the Royal Senate, now about the new condemnation issued by the order of the King of their Response opposed to the Pastoral Instruction of Cardinal Bissy, in which the constitution <term>Unigenitus</term> was most fiercely defended, and the right
pages.77:
of judging about it, which the Parliament had rashly arrogated to itself, was vindicated for the Pastors of the Church; all writings of this kind were rejected and condemned again and again by the authority of both the King and the Apostolic See: terrified by this, they remained quiet for a time, and until the death of the Duke of Orléans, whom the Pontiff followed shortly after on March 7, 1724.

§. 5.
The Last Retreats of the Jansenists.

It has long since passed into the custom of any faction rebellious to the Church to boast of great names as authors, followers, or defenders of their doctrine. Thus, the Jansenists from the beginning wanted to be seen not only as disciples of Augustine, but also as friends of Aquinas and the Thomistic School that supported them, and even as followers. I name one witness, Abbot La Lane, a writer of iron-willed stubbornness, who, among 40 various minor works composed by him in defense of Jansenius and the 5 Propositions, also wrote one on the Conformity of the Jansenists with the Thomists. Thus, the appealing Bishops likewise labored to protect their Quesnel by means of the Thomistic School: accompanied and followed by others, and other most inept scribblers, whose empty labor should draw no follower unless a blind man, or one wishing to go insane, if by chance he were to try [to reconcile] the five propositions of Jansenius, or the first forty or so of Quesnel, out of the one hundred and one condemned [propositions], with these following five undoubted [propositions], and no less received in the Thomistic School than in any other school addicted to the Roman faith

But at that time Moses himself, both husband and spouse of Zipporah, was present. He was not only staying in the same lodging, but in the same bedroom, so much so that Zipporah, in her anger, threw the foreskin of her sons, having been cut off, at the feet of Moses. Furthermore, Zipporah did not circumcise strangers, but only her own. And yet, Osiander allows this to women as if they were midwives (as appears from their custom and practice), so that they may even baptize the children of others. What then does Zipporah's example contribute to Osiander's opinion, when the contrary is rather gathered from it? Namely, even if a husband is present, a woman is able to baptize not just anyone, but only her own children. This, therefore, is our first response to this example of Zipporah. The second, however, is that he gathers a general principle from a particular case, and establishes a perpetual rule from an extraordinary act, when nowhere else do we read that women in the people of God, and under the Law, circumcised their own or others' children. Furthermore, this was even to the disgrace and reproach of Moses himself. For the Lord, by that action, argued to Moses through his wife that he had been guilty of too much negligence, because he had not circumcised his sons and had neglected that most holy covenant of God with his family by omitting circumcision. Finally, who does not see that in this matter the nature of Baptism and Circumcision was different? For we never read that the duty of circumcising was once specifically commanded by God to the Priests, since circumcision was both instituted by God and practiced by the people for more than four hundred years before the Priests were set apart from the rest of the people. Moreover, did Christ delegate the ministry of baptizing to anyone except those to whom...

<margin>Gen. 17.</margin>
<margin>Matt. 28.</margin>

<sig>D</sig>

...to whom He gave the duty of preaching the Gospel word? From which it follows that Osiander ineptly concludes a similar mode of acting from that dissimilarity. And yet these are the things which, because they are not taught by us in the French Churches (because they are false), he reproaches us for and accuses us of a very serious error, as if we were impostors and teachers of lies. Furthermore, Osiander also has other things in that same disputation on Baptism, in which we desire either clarity or truth of doctrine from him. As when he interprets that saying of John and Christ, *Amen, Amen, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven*, he neither distinguishes whether Christ was speaking only about adult men or also about infants, who was then addressing Nicodemus; nor does he teach whether the Spirit itself is always joined with water, that is, with the external sign of Baptism, given that he takes *Water* to mean Baptism according to the opinion of Chrysostom, as if everyone who is baptized with water were regenerated. Therefore, let him speak more clearly so that he may be understood. But that, too, is also ambiguous, which the same man wrote later about infants in these words: *For although in adults the Lord, when He wishes to grant faith to someone, uses the preaching of the Gospel about Christ as an instrument or medium, yet there is no doubt that the Lord grants faith to an infant when either pious parents or other pious men intercede for the infant before the Lord with their prayers.*

<margin>John 3:5.</margin>
<margin>Osiand. page 59.</margin>
<margin>Page 63.</margin>

For first, he ought to have explained whether he wants this to be true of all the infants of the faithful who are baptized, as if whoever is baptized...
pages.53:
<header>EPISTLE</header>

...with water, they also receive the Holy Spirit, and have faith even without the word of God, that is, outside the ordinary way: or whether he understands this only of those infants who are predestined by God to eternal salvation. Then, indeed, it should also have been said whether he himself thinks that infants have actual or habitual faith after the prayers of the Church of this kind, or whether they have faith only <term>δυνάμει</term> <gloss>potentially</gloss>. For although Augustine, in his letter to Dardanus, says thus: We say that the Holy Spirit dwells in baptized infants, although they do not know it; yet the same man, interpreting himself in his letter to Boniface, writes thus about faith in infants and how they possess it: The sacrament of faith is faith in a certain manner. But to believe is nothing else than to have faith. And through this, when it is answered that infants believe (who do not yet have the affection of faith), it is answered that they have faith on account of the sacrament of faith, and that they turn themselves to God on account of the sacrament of conversion. Concerning this very matter, the same Augustine treats more copiously in book 3 of *On Free Will*, chapter 23. Therefore, Osiander ought to have explained himself, my dearest brothers, if he wished either to speak the truth or to speak intelligently among you. For he who teaches obscurely teaches nothing; or rather, according to the advice of Jerome, he ought to have spent a long time learning what he wished to teach others.

### ON PREDESTINATION.

But what he writes regarding Predestination is of such a kind that, on that subject too, we are forced to desire many things, whether he prudently passed over...

# EPISTOLA
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Osiander is rather an enemy of your salvation, while he tries to lead you away from the Gospel and the doctrine that you already have as most certain from the word of God, to another. Furthermore, as to the peace of the Gallic Churches with the German Churches of God, who is a Christian—I do not say so devoid of all Christian mind, but so alien to all humanity—that he would not himself desire it above all things, and beg for it from God the Best and Greatest with every prayer and tear of his heart? To me, certainly, this sentiment of Augustine has always seemed golden: *Such is the good of peace, that even in earthly and mortal affairs nothing is heard more gladly, nothing desired more longingly, and finally, nothing found better.* I would call him a beast, and indeed a savage one, a most cruel <term>alastor</term> <gloss>avenging demon</gloss> of the human race, a public enemy of his own country, and a most hostile persecutor of the Church of God, who would either refuse or hate peace between the Churches of God. Especially between the Gallic and German [Churches], since those peoples have the same origin, a most ancient kinship, and even the highest consensus in other matters, with the greatest benevolence always between them, and many benefits of the German nation existing toward ours. The great bonds of friendship themselves sufficiently exhort both Churches to enter into that sweetest peace, or rather to preserve what was long ago begun and confirmed. Who is this, therefore, who so falsely divines that there are, or are being prepared, enmities, hatred, or wars between pious Gauls and Germans? This, certainly, we have never believed before, as you know, brothers, nor do we persuade ourselves of it even now. For even if there are some controversies between us regarding matters not of the least moment, we have decided to treat them with Christian moderation of spirit, and not to break the peace on that account; and if any consensus regarding these cannot yet exist between us (as our sins so burden us), we have learned, we wish, and we are able to tolerate those who differ from us with kindness and brotherly love, according to the precept of Paul.
pages.9:
# AD ECCLES. GALLICAS.

Gregory the Great <note>Refers to the Regula Pastoralis</note> says famously, based on the same Paul, *He who does not care to keep the peace, refuses to bear the fruit of the spirit. For whoever desires to be an heir of the heavenly Father, let him keep the peace.* And would that, Osiander, it were permitted for us to see and experience, through you, that sweetest and most desired time, concerning which Luke writes in Acts: *The Churches had peace, and were built up, and walking in the fear of the Lord and the consolation of the Holy Spirit, were multiplied.* For blessed, indeed most blessed, Osiander, are the <term>eirēnopoioi</term> <gloss>peacemakers</gloss>, as our Lord Jesus Christ says. Those are they, however, who are not only themselves ready with the most prepared mind to accept a pious peace (whom Bernard calls "placid"), but also those who, by any means, conciliate and foster the peace and concord of God among others. Everyone knows that you are by no means of the kind or number of those (whatever you may feign or dissimulate here) who have read those virulent earlier *Antisturmian* writings of yours published against us, and your savage condemnations of us. And so, the adornments are for the public; I know you from within and under the skin <note>A classic idiom for knowing someone's true nature.</note>. But you should remember, Dearest ones, what Jerome writes about John, Bishop of Jerusalem (who, while he was in fact sowing most grievous errors in the Church of God, nevertheless offered peace to the Churches with his words): *It is nothing great to profess peace with one's voice and destroy the work of peace; to sound concord with words, and demand servitude in reality. We also want peace, and we not only want it, but we ask for it: but the peace of Christ.*
pages.10: *For that is the foundation and guardian of all peace. Now that peace of Christ is that which, acknowledging him as true God and true man, and thus our only Mediator before the Father, tastes all things from his word in faith, and hopes for all its salvation from his perfect obedience. This is the peace which we desire, which we offer to all men. But you must also take care, again and again, that you are not deceived in the name of an insidious peace. For the rest, I consider that I owe this to you, brothers, and to the Gallic Churches. For the Belgic Churches themselves have, by the grace of God, their own who will undertake their protection, and defend their doctrine, and will not let this man leave without an answer. But since it has pleased God the Father of mercies that I, a Gaul in Gaul, should fulfill the sacrosanct office of an Evangelical Pastor, and should announce to you from the word of God that doctrine which Osiander [treats] as not sufficiently sincere, and others—his associates—even anathematize as erroneous, I cannot, Brothers, unless I wish to be deemed a plain impostor and <term>pseudoprophetēs</term> <gloss>false prophet</gloss>, fail to defend with all my might that for which I am prepared to pour out my life itself, if the Lord so wills. When, therefore, we see that an account of our faith is demanded, it must certainly be rendered according to the precept of Peter. For he conducts this cause so astutely that, while attributing great praises—both of singular piety toward God and of patience—to you (that is, the flock and little sheep, as he calls them), he ascribes the whole blame for the errors (in which, if it pleases God, he wishes the Gallic and reformed Churches of Christ to be entangled) to us, the Pastors. Thus he tries to tear us Pastors away from you, the sheep, and you, the sheep, away from us, the Pastors—that is, the most closely joined members of the same body—so that, just as he scattered those fatal discords in the midst of Germany, he might also be able to disseminate the same dissensions in the Gallic Churches on account of Ubiquity.*
pages.11:
# AD ECCLES. GALLIC.

Osiander, so that you may know the man, is the <term>diapyros</term> <gloss>fire-bearer</gloss> and carrier of a certain new Pandora, manufactured by—I know not whom—Vulcan, which he has undertaken to carry off to other shores and provinces of the world, such as Gaul and Belgium. But he either thinks you are logs and stumps, to tolerate such bitter [charges] for so long, concerning a doctrine unknown to you and never weighed against the standard of the Divine word as a just scale; or, if he thinks you are pious and prudent, he ought surely to have thought well of you, and to have assumed that you had done what is written of the Beroeans and Thessalonians, namely, that you would search the scriptures and diligently compare our doctrine with them. That, however, brothers, you have done and are doing, by the grace of God, and because of this you are confirmed more and more each day by the spirit of God in that doctrine which you have received from us. Furthermore, when this man so proudly condemns all the Pastors of the Gallic Churches together in one judgment, as if they were whitewashed walls, how many and how great—immortal God—men does he condemn? How many faithful servants of God, how many holy martyrs of Christ does he condemn? For there is one voice, doctrine, and confession of faith for all Gallic Pastors; this is known to all who have heard us. Therefore, he who pronounces the doctrine of our Churches not sincere, not true, and not consenting to the word of God, calumniously calls all those lights of the world heretics, impostors, and false teachers.
pages.12:
# 10 EPISTOLA

Therefore, will you hold as heretics Theodore Beza (to pass over that great John Calvin, by whose counsel our Churches were begun to be built, rather than by his living voice) and Pierre Viret, those chosen organs of God, who themselves taught our Churches by living voice? Indeed, I will mention a few (for I could not, nor is it necessary to name them all), so that when your Pastors are condemned by this most unlearned and most obscure man—either for fraud, if they have not taught sincerely, or for ignorance, if they have not known—either he may be ashamed of such great impudence, if only he is able, or you may bear true witness against him, as he calumniously judges such great men, who are so well known to you. Behold, therefore, brothers, a few out of an infinite number whom the Lord has raised up for you as Doctors of the Gospel, in addition to those three whom I have already named (Calvin, Beza, Viret): Augustin Marlorat, Daniel Toussain, Antoine de la Roche Chandieu, Jean de Serres, Jean de l'Espine, Nicolas des Gallars, Villiers, Palmerius, Borgonius, whose singular piety and excellent erudition have testimony that is not obscure, both from their lives and their writings. Some of them still survive, by the grace of God, and shine in the Churches; others, however, have already most constantly poured out their blood for the name of Christ. If these lights of the world are unknown to this young man and new Mercury of Pandora, Osiander, what wonder is it, since such men are accustomed to read only their own, lest they be forced to learn better things; and the varied wandering of this robust youth for the sake of carrying about his Pandora, and thereby procuring for himself some position in the German Churches, does not permit him to know or read many things?
pages.13:
# AD ECCLES. GALLIC.

And yet, this one man has been found out of all, who, because of his own obscurity, does not know those [men], yet most proudly condemns them, since, as Jerome rightly says from an old Proverb: <term>Amathia tharros, episteme d’ oknon poiei</term> <gloss>Ignorance breeds boldness, but knowledge breeds caution</gloss>. But the world itself is not ignorant of how excellent those men were, and the honest testimonies of most illustrious men—Melanchthon, Bucer, and even Brentius himself—bear witness to them. Wherefore, since from those things which I have said, the extent of this man's temerity can be sufficiently understood by you, I proceed to the examination of his doctrine and his writing.

First, therefore, so that he, who is German, might glory over you as if he were another corrupter of the Galatians, he says that *the doctrine of the Gospel, purified and the legitimate worship of God, reached you from the Germans*, certainly so that he might later pronounce that you ought by no means to have departed from the judgment of those [Germans], as if they were Metropolitans. For in this same way, the Roman Pontiffs formerly usurped the right and tyranny over the remaining Churches of God, so that the other Churches might have the rules of magisterium and doctrine from where they had received the beginnings of honor and consecration. As if Christians should swear to the words of anyone other than Christ himself, or acknowledge anyone other than God himself, acting in their hearts by the power and efficacy of his Spirit, as the true and first author of their faith. Although, if the first beginnings of the restored true religion are also considered in Germany itself, those proceeded from the Waldensian brothers, from whose fountains even Luther himself (which he does not deny) emerged. Now, the Waldenses originated from the Gauls, who were driven out from the borders of the French kingdom by the monks before the year 400.
pages.14:
# EPISTOLA

Furthermore, in the year of the Lord 1417, in the town of Montpellier, Catharina Sorbea, a most constant woman, died for asserting the kingdom and empire of Christ against the Antichrist, having been consumed by most savage flames. But yet, brothers, just as we acknowledge God as the author of that doctrine of the purified Gospel which we have learned, so we ingenuously proclaim his excellent organs, who existed in Germany, Switzerland, and other nations, and who excited our own people by their example and their constancy to seek the truth and reject idolatry; to them, while they lived, we gave thanks, and we piously and holily cultivate the memory of the dead. And we ingenuously profess that we owe much to the Germans and other nations in this (for we do not wish to be ungrateful to any mortal), because some men existed among them who shone forth to us with their virtue for the sake of embracing the true Christ. *But that he praises from among ours those who preferred to tolerate the most extreme things for the love of Christ the redeemer, rather than to reject the truth they had acknowledged, and calls them pious and holy Martyrs of Christ, and writes that they enjoy eternal happiness*, in that he thinks rightly, indeed, if only he were consistent with himself and agreed with some of his own associates. For those whom he calls pious and holy here, out of a desire to flatter you, and Martyrs of Christ, both he and certain associates in the public pulpit most insultingly call *Martyrs of the Devil*. And he even praises them in such a way that he nevertheless attributes more insult and reproach to them than praise, while he writes that they suffered for that doctrine, the fuller (*he even wished to say "purer"*) instruction of which they had not yet attained.
pages.15:
# AD ECCLES. GALLIC.

As if, Osiander, they were foolishly and rashly dying for an unknown God and a doctrine unknown to them. For Cyprian rightly says, *The penalty does not make the martyrs, but the cause:* nor can anyone truly be called a martyr and witness of Christ who is ignorant of the doctrine of Christ for which he dies. For it is first to be believed with the heart unto justice, before confession is made unto salvation.

Truly, this smooth monitor excuses them. For he teaches that the blame for their error is to be attributed not to the little sheep themselves, but entirely to their Pastors, who did not hand down a sufficiently sincere doctrine to that flock, so pious and so ardent in the love of God. But whether we, the Pastors, taught thus prudently and knowingly, or whether, ignorant of that purer doctrine, we were not able to hand down a better one, this subtle persuader does not explain. For if he were to say that we taught otherwise, prudently and knowingly, he would clearly, and impudently, usurp for himself what belongs to God, so as to judge our consciences; but if he were to write that we, being ignorant, were not able [to teach otherwise], he would certainly render us excusable by that very fact, or he would himself diminish our crime itself, which he nevertheless wishes to appear most grievous. Perhaps, moved by that charity with which he denies that he is delighted by our miseries and punishments, he wished to spare us, of course. For the charity of these men toward us and toward you yourselves is of such a kind (whatever he may dissimulate)—which they are not ashamed to testify to even in public writings—namely, that they [describe] us as Atheists, worse than the Turks themselves, seditious, despisers of magistrates, deceivers, <term>Schwärmer</term> <gloss>enthusiasts/fanatics</gloss>, executioners, most foul heretics, and sacramentarians, and what not? publicly.

N.text: *For that is the foundation and guardian of all peace. Now that peace of Christ is that which, acknowledging him as true God and true man, and thus our only Mediator before the Father, tastes all things from his word in faith, and hopes for all its salvation from his perfect obedience. This is the peace which we desire, which we offer to all men. But you must also take care, again and again, that you are not deceived in the name of an insidious peace. For the rest, I consider that I owe this to you, brothers, and to the Gallic Churches. For the Belgic Churches themselves have, by the grace of God, their own who will undertake their protection, and defend their doctrine, and will not let this man leave without an answer. But since it has pleased God the Father of mercies that I, a Gaul in Gaul, should fulfill the sacrosanct office of an Evangelical Pastor, and should announce to you from the word of God that doctrine which Osiander [treats] as not sufficiently sincere, and others—his associates—even anathematize as erroneous, I cannot, Brothers, unless I wish to be deemed a plain impostor and <term>pseudoprophetēs</term> <gloss>false prophet</gloss>, fail to defend with all my might that for which I am prepared to pour out my life itself, if the Lord so wills. When, therefore, we see that an account of our faith is demanded, it must certainly be rendered according to the precept of Peter. For he conducts this cause so astutely that, while attributing great praises—both of singular piety toward God and of patience—to you (that is, the flock and little sheep, as he calls them), he ascribes the whole blame for the errors (in which, if it pleases God, he wishes the Gallic and reformed Churches of Christ to be entangled) to us, the Pastors. Thus he tries to tear us Pastors away from you, the sheep, and you, the sheep, away from us, the Pastors—that is, the most closely joined members of the same body—so that, just as he scattered those fatal discords in the midst of Germany, he might also be able to disseminate the same dissensions in the Gallic Churches on account of Ubiquity.*

X.text:
# AD ECCLES. GALLIC.

Osiander, so that you may know the man, is the <term>diapyros</term> <gloss>fire-bearer</gloss> and carrier of a certain new Pandora, manufactured by—I know not whom—Vulcan, which he has undertaken to carry off to other shores and provinces of the world, such as Gaul and Belgium. But he either thinks you are logs and stumps, to tolerate such bitter [charges] for so long, concerning a doctrine unknown to you and never weighed against the standard of the Divine word as a just scale; or, if he thinks you are pious and prudent, he ought surely to have thought well of you, and to have assumed that you had done what is written of the Beroeans and Thessalonians, namely, that you would search the scriptures and diligently compare our doctrine with them. That, however, brothers, you have done and are doing, by the grace of God, and because of this you are confirmed more and more each day by the spirit of God in that doctrine which you have received from us. Furthermore, when this man so proudly condemns all the Pastors of the Gallic Churches together in one judgment, as if they were whitewashed walls, how many and how great—immortal God—men does he condemn? How many faithful servants of God, how many holy martyrs of Christ does he condemn? For there is one voice, doctrine, and confession of faith for all Gallic Pastors; this is known to all who have heard us. Therefore, he who pronounces the doctrine of our Churches not sincere, not true, and not consenting to the word of God, calumniously calls all those lights of the world heretics, impostors, and false teachers.

# EPISTOLA
<meta>continues from previous page: Osiander is rather an enemy of your salvation, while he tries to lead you away from the Gospel and the doctrine that you already have as most certain from the word of God, to another. Furthermore, as to the peace of the Gallic Churches with the German Churches of God, who is a Christian—I do not say so devoid of all Christian mind, but so alien to all humanity—that he would not himself desire it above all things, and beg for it from God the Best and Greatest with every prayer and tear of his heart? To me, certainly, this sentiment of</meta> Augustine has always seemed golden: *Such is the good of peace, that even in earthly and mortal affairs nothing is usually heard with more pleasure, nothing desired more wishfully, and finally, nothing better found.* I would truly call that man a beast, and indeed a savage monster, a most cruel <term>alastor</term> <gloss>avenging spirit/destroyer</gloss> of the human race, a public enemy of his own fatherland, and a most spiteful persecutor of the Church of God, who either does not want or hates peace between the Churches of God. Especially between the Gallic and German Churches, since the origin of those peoples is the same, as is their most ancient kinship, their highest consensus in other matters, their mutual benevolence which has always been supreme, and the many benefits of the German nation that exist toward our own. These such great bonds of friendship themselves sufficiently exhort both Churches to enter into that sweetest peace, or rather to preserve it, having been initiated and confirmed long ago. Who is this, therefore, who so falsely divines that enmities, hatreds, and wars either exist or are being prepared between the pious Gauls and Germans? We certainly have never believed this before, as you know, Brothers, nor do we persuade ourselves of it even now. For although there are certain controversies between us of no small moment, we have decided to treat them with Christian moderation of character, and not to break the peace on account of them; and if any consensus concerning them cannot yet exist between us (as our sins so burden us), we have learned, wish, and are able to tolerate those who disagree with us kindly and fraternally.

# AD ECCLES. GALLICAS.

<margin>Gal. 6.</margin> according to Paul's precept. For Gregory the Great, speaking excellently from the same Paul, says: *Whoever does not care to keep peace, refuses to bear the fruit of the spirit. For whoever desires to be an heir of the heavenly Father, let him guard the peace.* And would that, Osiander, through you, it were finally granted to us to see and experience that sweetest and most longed-for time, about which Luke writes in Acts, when it could truly be said of the Churches of God: <margin>Act. 9.</margin> *The Churches had peace, and were built up, and walking in the fear of the Lord and the consolation of the Holy Spirit, were multiplied.* <margin>Matth. 5.</margin> For blessed, indeed most blessed, Osiander, are the <term>eirēnopoioi</term> <gloss>peacemakers</gloss>, as our Lord Jesus Christ says. Those are they, however, who are not only themselves ready with the most prepared mind to accept a pious peace (whom <margin>Bernardus.</margin> Bernard calls "placid"), but also those who, by any means, conciliate and foster the peace and concord of God among others. Everyone knows that you are by no means of the kind or number of those (whatever you may feign or dissimulate here) who have read those virulent earlier *Antisturmian* writings of yours published against us, and your savage condemnations of us. And so, the adornments are for the public; I know you from within and under the skin. We also want peace, and we not only want it, but we ask for it: but the peace of Christ.*

<header>EPISTLE</header>

But at that time Moses himself was present, the husband and spouse of Zipporah, and he was not only in the same lodging, but in the same room, to such an extent that Zipporah, in her anger, threw the foreskin of her sons at the feet of Moses. Furthermore, Zipporah did not circumcise strangers, but only her own children. And yet Osiander permits this to women as if they were midwives (as is apparent from their custom and practice), so that they may also baptize the children of others. What, therefore, does the example of Zipporah have to do with Osiander's opinion, when the opposite is gathered from it? Namely, that even if a husband is present, a woman is able to baptize not just anyone, but only her own children. This, therefore, is our first response to this example of Zipporah. The second, however, is that he gathers a general rule from a particular instance, and establishes a perpetual regulation from an extraordinary act, when we read nowhere else that women among the people of God, and under the law, circumcised their own or others' children. Furthermore, this was also to the reproach and rebuke of Moses himself. For the Lord, by that reason, argued that Moses was guilty of too much negligence through his wife, because he had not circumcised his sons, and had neglected that most holy covenant of God with his family by omitting circumcision. Finally, who does not see that the nature of Baptism and Circumcision was different in that matter? For we nowhere read that the duty of Circumcision was once specifically commanded by God to the Priests, since Circumcision was both instituted by God and practiced by the people more than four hundred years before the Priests were set apart from the rest of the people. Moreover, did not Christ delegate the ministry of baptizing to those alone to whom...

<margin>Matt. 28.</margin>

Regarding this very thing, the same Augustine treats more copiously in book 3 of On Free Will, chapter 23. Therefore, Osiander should have explained himself, dearest brothers, if he wished either to tell the truth or to speak intelligently among you. But at that time Moses himself was present, the husband and spouse of Zipporah, and he was not only in the same lodging, but in the same room, to such an extent that Zipporah, in her anger, threw the foreskin of her sons at the feet of Moses. Furthermore, Zipporah did not circumcise strangers, but only her own children. And yet Osiander permits this to women as if they were midwives (as is apparent from their custom and practice), so that they may also baptize the children of others. What, therefore, does the example of Zipporah have to do with Osiander's opinion, when the opposite is gathered from it? Namely, that even if a husband is present, a woman is able to baptize not just anyone, but only her own children. This, therefore, is our first response to this example of Zipporah. The second, however, is that he gathers a general rule from a particular instance, and establishes a perpetual regulation from an extraordinary act, when we read nowhere else that women among the people of God, and under the law, circumcised their own or others' children. Furthermore, this was also to the reproach and rebuke of Moses himself. For the Lord, by that reason, argued that Moses was guilty of too much negligence through his wife, because he had not circumcised his sons, and had neglected that most holy covenant of God with his family by omitting circumcision. Finally, who does not see that the nature of Baptism and Circumcision was different in that matter? For we nowhere read that the duty of Circumcision was once specifically commanded by God to the Priests, since Circumcision was both instituted by God and practiced by the people more than four hundred years before the Priests were set apart from the rest of the people. Osiander is rather an enemy of your salvation, while he tries to lead you away from the Gospel and the doctrine that you already have as most certain from the word of God, to another. Furthermore, as to the peace of the Gallic Churches with the German Churches of God, who is a Christian—I do not say so devoid of all Christian mind, but so alien to all humanity—that he would not himself desire it above all things, and beg for it from God the Best and Greatest with every prayer and tear of his heart? To me, certainly, this sentiment of Augustine has always seemed golden: *The benefit of peace is so great that even in earthly and mortal affairs nothing is usually heard with more pleasure, nothing is desired with more longing, and finally, nothing is found to be better.* I would say, Brothers, that he is truly a beast, and indeed a savage one, a most cruel <term>alastor</term> <gloss>avenging spirit</gloss> of the human race, a public enemy of his own country, and a most troublesome persecutor of the Church of God, who either does not want, or hates, peace to exist between the Churches of God. This is especially true between the Gallic and German [Churches], since those peoples share the same origin, a most ancient kinship, and the highest consensus in other matters, as well as the greatest mutual benevolence; furthermore, many benefits of the German people toward our own abound. These great bonds of friendship themselves sufficiently exhort both Churches to enter into that sweetest peace, or rather to preserve the peace already entered into and confirmed long ago. Who is this person, therefore, who so falsely predicts that enmities, hatred, and wars either exist or are being prepared between pious Gauls and Germans? We have certainly never believed this, as you know, Brothers, nor are we persuading ourselves of it even now. For although there are certain controversies between us on matters not of the least importance, we have decided to treat them with Christian moderation of our spirits
pages.9:
# TO THE GALLIC CHURCHES.

and not to break the peace because of them. If, due to our sins pressing upon us, there cannot yet be agreement between us regarding these things, we have learned, we wish, and we are able to tolerate those who differ from us, kindly and fraternally, according to the precept of Paul. <margin>Gal. 6.</margin> For Gregory the Great, speaking excellently from the same Paul, says: *He who does not care to preserve peace refuses to bear the fruit of the spirit. For whoever desires to be an heir of the heavenly Father must guard peace.* And would that, Osiander, through you, it might finally be allowed for us to see and experience that sweetest and most longed-for time, when it may truly be said of the Churches of God what Luke writes in the Acts: <margin>Act. 9.</margin> *The Churches had peace, and were built up, and walking in the fear of the Lord and the consolation of the Holy Spirit, were multiplied.* For blessed, indeed most blessed, Osiander, are the <term>eirēnopoioi</term> <gloss>peacemakers</gloss>, as our Lord Jesus Christ says. Those are they, however, who are not only themselves ready with the most prepared mind to accept a pious peace (whom Bernard calls "placid"), but also those who, by any means, conciliate and foster the peace and concord of God among others. Everyone knows that you are by no means of the kind or number of those—whatever you may feign or dissimulate here—who have read those virulent earlier *Antisturmian* writings of yours published against us, and your savage condemnations of us. And so, the adornments are for the public; I know you from within and under the skin. But you should remember, Dearest ones, what Jerome writes about John, Bishop of Jerusalem (who, while he was in fact sowing most grievous errors in the Church of God, nevertheless offered peace to the Churches with his words): *It is nothing great to profess peace with one's voice and destroy the work of peace; to sound concord with words, and demand servitude in reality. We also want peace, and we not only want it, but we ask for it: but the peace of Christ.*
