*For that is the foundation and guardian of all peace. And that is the peace of Christ, which, recognizing Him as true God and true man, and thus our only Mediator before the Father, understands all things from His word in faith, and hopes for all its salvation from His perfect obedience. This is the peace which we desire, which we offer to all men. But lest you be deceived by the name of an insidious peace, you must also be careful again and again. For the rest, I consider that I owe this to you, brothers, and to the Gallic Churches. For the Belgic Churches themselves have, by the grace of God, their own men who will undertake their patronage and defend their doctrine, and will not allow this man to depart without a response. But since it has pleased God the Father of mercies that I should fulfill the holy office of Evangelical Pastor in Gaul, and should announce to you from the word of God that doctrine which Osiander treats as not sufficiently sincere, while others—his associates—even anathematize it as erroneous, I cannot, Brothers, unless I wish to be deemed a plain impostor and <term>pseudoprophetēs</term> <gloss>false prophet</gloss>, fail to defend it with all my might, for which I am prepared to pour out my life itself, if the Lord should so will. Since, therefore, we see that an account of our faith is demanded, it must certainly be rendered according to the precept of Peter. For he maneuvers this cause astutely, in such a way that by attributing to you (that is, the flock and little sheep, as he calls them) both singular piety toward God and praises of patience, he ascribes the entire blame for the errors (in which, if it pleases God, he wishes the Gallic and reformed Churches of Christ to be entangled) to us, the Pastors. Thus he tries to tear us, the Pastors, from you, the sheep, and you, the sheep, from us, the pastors—that is, the most joined members of the same body—so that just as he sowed those fatal discords in the middle of Germany, he may also be able to disseminate the same dissensions in the Gallic Churches because of Ubiquity.*

and not to break the peace. Osiander is, as you might know the man, a <term>diapyros</term> <gloss>a carrier of fire</gloss> and a bearer of a certain new Pandora, manufactured by—I know not what—Vulcan, which he has undertaken to transport to other regions and provinces of the world, such as Gaul and Belgium. But he either thinks you are trunks and blocks, that you would endure such bitter things for so long for a doctrine unknown to you, and not at all weighed according to the norm of the Divine Word as a just balance; or if he judges you to be pious and prudent, he should certainly have thought well of you, and believed that you had done what is written of the Bereans and Thessalonians, <margin>Act. 17. Ioan. 5.</margin> namely, that you would search the scriptures and diligently compare our doctrine with them. That, however, brothers, you have done and are doing by the grace of God, and for that reason you are being confirmed more and more each day by the Spirit of God in the doctrine you have received from us. Furthermore, when this man so proudly condemns all the Pastors of the Gallic Churches together in one judgment, like someone whitewashing a wall, how many, and how great, O immortal God, what men, how many faithful servants of God, how many holy martyrs of Christ does he condemn? For there is one voice and doctrine, and one confession of faith, of all the Gallic Pastors: this is known to all who have heard us. Therefore, he who pronounces the doctrine of our Churches not to be sincere, not true, not consenting to the word of God, slanderously calls all those lights of the world heretics, and impostors, and false teachers
pages.12:
# 10 LETTER

and calls them such. Will you therefore hold as heretics both *Theodore Beza* (to pass over that great *John Calvin*, by whose counsel rather than by his living voice our Churches began to be built up) and *Pierre Viret*, those chosen organs of God who themselves taught our Churches with their living voice? I will mention a few indeed (for I could not, nor is it necessary to list all), so that when your Pastors are condemned by this most unlearned and most obscure man for fraud, if they have not taught sincerely, or for ignorance, if they have not known—either he should be ashamed of this great impudence, if he is at all capable, or you should bear true witness against him for judging slanderously of such great men, and men so well known to you. See, therefore, brothers, a few from the infinite number whom the Lord has raised up for you as Doctors of the Gospel in addition to those three whom I have already named (*Calvin*, *Beza*, *Viret*): *Augustin Marlorat*, *Daniel Toussain*, *Antoine de la Roche Chandieu*, *Jean de Serres*, *Jean de l'Espine*, *Nicolas Des Gallars*, *Villierius*, *Palmerius*, *Borgonius*, whose singular piety and excellent erudition bear clear testimony, both from their lives and their writings. Some of these, by the grace of God, still survive and shine in the Churches; others have already most constantly poured out their blood for the name of Christ. If these lights of the world are unknown to this young man and new Mercury of Pandora, *Osiander*, how is it a wonder, when such men are accustomed to read only their own, lest they be forced to learn better things, and the various roamings of this robust young man for carrying around his Pandora, and for the sake of obtaining for himself some Provostship in the German Churches, do not allow him to know or read many things?

# TO THE GALLIC CHURCHES.

and yet this one was found among all who would most proudly condemn those whom he does not know because of his own obscurity, because, as Jerome rightly says from the old Proverb, "Ignorance breeds boldness, while knowledge creates caution." But that those men were excellent, the world itself does not ignore, and the honest testimonies of most distinguished men, *Melanchthon*, *Bucer*, and even *Brentius* himself, provide assurance. Therefore, since from what I have said it can be sufficiently understood by you how great this man's temerity is, I proceed to the examination of his doctrine and his writing.

<margin>Pag. 1.</margin> <margin>Gelaſi epiſt. 1. cap. 11.</margin> <margin>Toleta. 11. cap. 3.</margin> First, therefore, so that he himself, who is German, may boast about you like another corrupter of the Galatians, he says *that the doctrine of the Gospel purified, and the legitimate worship of God, arrived to you from the Germans*, namely, so that he may later pronounce that you should in no way depart from their judgment, as if they were your Metropolitans. For by this same reasoning the Roman Pontiffs once usurped rights and tyranny over the remaining Churches of God, so that the other Churches would have rules of magisterium and doctrine from the same source from which they had received the beginnings of honor and consecration. As if Christians should swear by the words of anyone other than Christ himself, or acknowledge any other than God himself, working by the power and efficacy of His Spirit in their hearts, as the true and first author of their faith. Although, if the first beginnings of the restored true religion are also looked at in Germany itself, those proceeded from the Waldensian brethren, from whose fountains even Luther himself (which he does not deny) emerged. The Waldenses, however, originated from the Gauls who were expelled by the monks from the borders of the Gallic kingdom
pages.14:
# LETTER

before the year 400. Furthermore, in the year of our Lord 1417, in the town of Montpellier, *Catharina Sorbea*, a most constant woman, died, burned by most cruel flames, for asserting the kingdom and empire of Christ against the Antichrist. But yet, brothers, just as we acknowledge God as the author of that doctrine of the purified Gospel which we have learned, so we ingenuously proclaim His distinguished organs who have existed in *Germany*, *Switzerland*, and other nations, and who stirred up our men by their example and their constancy to seek the truth and reject idolatry. To these, while they lived, we gave thanks, and we piously and holily cultivate the memory of the dead. And in this we ingenuously profess that we owe much to the Germans and other nations (for we do not wish to be ungrateful to any mortal) because there existed among them some men who shone before us with their virtue for embracing the true Christ. <margin>Pag. 8.</margin> *But that he praises from among our number those who, out of love for Christ the redeemer, preferred to endure every extreme rather than reject the truth they had acknowledged, and calls them pious and holy Martyrs of Christ, and writes that they enjoy eternal happiness*, in that he indeed feels correctly, if only he were consistent with himself and agreed with some of his other associates. For those whom he here calls pious and holy and Martyrs of Christ out of a desire to flatter you, he himself, and certain of his associates, most insultingly call *Martyrs of the Devil* in the public pulpit. And he even praises them in such a way that he nevertheless attributes more insult and abuse to them than praise, while he writes that they suffered for that doctrine of which a more full (*he also wanted to say purer*) institution

they had not yet attained, as if, Osiander, they were dying foolishly and rashly for a God unknown to them and a doctrine unknown to them. For Cyprian says excellently: *The penalty does not make the martyr, but the cause:* nor can anyone truly be called a martyr and witness of Christ who is ignorant of the doctrine of Christ for which he dies. For one must first believe with the heart unto justice before confession is made unto salvation.

<margin>Pa. 3. & 4.</margin> But this smooth monitor excuses them. For he teaches that the blame for their error should be laid not on the little sheep themselves, but entirely upon their Pastors, who did not hand down a sufficiently sincere doctrine to that flock, which was so pious and so burning in the love of God. But whether we Pastors taught thus prudently and knowingly, or whether, ignorant of that purer doctrine, we could not hand down a better one, this wily persuader does not explain. For if he were to say that we taught otherwise prudently and knowingly, he would plainly and impudently usurp to himself what belongs to God, in order to judge our consciences; but if he were to write that we were ignorant and could not, he would certainly render us excusable by that very fact, or he himself would diminish our own crime, which he nevertheless wants to appear most grievous. <margin>Pag. 4.</margin> Perhaps, moved by that charity with which he denies that he is delighted by our miseries and punishments, he wanted to spare us, forsooth. But at that time, Moses himself was present, both as a man and as Sephora’s husband, nor was he merely in the same inn, but in the same room, so much so that Sephora, in her anger, threw the foreskin of her circumcised son at the feet of Moses. Furthermore, Sephora did not circumcise strangers, but only her own children. And yet Osiander permits this to women as if they were midwives (as appears from their custom and practice), so that they may even baptize the children of others. What, therefore, does the example of Sephora have to do with Osiander’s opinion, when the contrary is rather gathered from it? Namely, that even if the husband is present, a woman may baptize not just anyone, but only her own children. This, therefore, is our first response to this example of Sephora. The other point is that he draws a general rule from a particular instance, and establishes a perpetual law from an extraordinary act, when we read nowhere else that women among the people of God, and under the Law, circumcised their own or others' children. Furthermore, this was also to the disgrace and rebuke of Moses himself. For the Lord, by that action, argued that Moses was guilty of excessive negligence through his wife, because he had not circumcised his sons, and had neglected that most holy covenant of God with his family by omitting circumcision. Finally, who does not see that the nature of Baptism and Circumcision was different in this regard? For we never read that the task of circumcising was once specially mandated to the priests by God, since circumcision was instituted by God and practiced by the people for more than four hundred years, even before the priests were separated from the rest of the people. Moreover, Christ delegated the ministry of baptizing only to those

to whom He gave the duty of preaching the Evangelical word? From which it follows that Osiander foolishly concludes a similar mode of action from that dissimilarity. And yet these are the things which, because they are not taught by us in the Gallican Churches (as they are false), he reprimands us and charges us with a most grave error, as if we were impostors and teachers of falsehood. But Osiander also has other things in that same discussion about Baptism in which we desire either clarity from him or the truth of doctrine. For example, when he interprets that saying of John and Christ, *Amen, amen, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven*, he does not distinguish whether Christ, who was addressing Nicodemus at the time, was speaking only of adult men or also of infants; nor does he teach whether the spirit itself is always joined with water, that is, with the external sign of Baptism, since he takes *Water* to mean Baptism according to the opinion of Chrysostom, as if everyone who is baptized with water is regenerated. Therefore, let him speak more clearly so that he may be understood. But that, too, is ambiguous, which he later writes about infants in these words: *For although the Lord, when He wishes to grant faith to someone among adults, uses the preaching of the Gospel about Christ as an instrument or means, yet there is no doubt that the Lord grants faith to an infant when either pious parents or other pious men intercede for the infant before the Lord with their prayers.*

This very thing he also explains with this comparison. As if, indeed, there were no action and operation of God, who justly punishes one sin with another sin, and thus acts in the heart of Pharaoh itself, which is already evil in itself. But in truth, Osiander, God truly both roused Pharaoh and hardened him, and sends the spirit of error, not by mere permission, as you think: not by mere foreknowledge: not by mere intuition: not by mere patience, or <term>ἐνεργείᾳ</term> <gloss>activity</gloss>, or <term>συν</term> <gloss>together</gloss>: but by the very thing itself,
<margin>2 Thess. 2.11</margin>
as Paul himself speaks and interprets it, <term>ἐνεργείᾳ</term> <gloss>activity</gloss>, that is, by operation and efficacy. But the man is afraid, namely out of imitation of that most impure Father, the pious Osiander, lest, according to the dogma of the Manichaeans, he should constitute God as the author of evil and sin. Truly, one should have been afraid that, if God did not have such an eloquent patron for his cause, he would be condemned. As if, indeed, before this youth was born, God had lost his case, and had truly been convicted by the Manichaeans as the author and culprit of sin. The truth of God needs none of your lies (such as appear in this interpretation of yours) to defend itself. Therefore,
<margin>Exod. 4.9</margin>
God hardened Pharaoh, and yet Pharaoh hardened himself, because in one and the same work God and men act in different ways. God indeed acts justly, because God is most just: but man acts most unjustly, because he looks to and follows the movement of his own mind, and his own wicked goal and end. For example. The Scribes and Pharisees wanted Christ to die: God, that heavenly Father, also wanted this very same thing, and Christ himself also wanted to die. Is the will of God the Father, and of Christ himself, therefore unjust in the same death of Christ, because it was most unjust for the Scribes and Pharisees? By no means, Osiander. Wherefore,
<margin>Act. 4.28</margin>
to conclude this place...

->ON IDOLS.<-

IT remains, therefore, that we also discuss very briefly the chapter that he added last. It is, however, about Idols. Which was mentioned by Osiander not so much out of any necessity of time or idolatry (which remains among you, by the grace of God the Best and Greatest), as so that he might publicly slander you all, seizing upon however untimely an occasion, and bring you into envy and hatred before all Magistrates. For what other scope does that tail of yours have, Osiander, than that you might vomit forth your poison against us under that honeyed oratory, written most exquisitely with the <term>θεοφρονήσει</term> <gloss>wisdom of God</gloss> <note>often used ironically here to mean 'false pretense of divine wisdom'</note> from the correction of all your colleagues, and wish that we be held guilty? Therefore, in this entire writing of yours, the voice indeed was the voice of Jacob, but the hands were the hands of Esau, that is, your own. Therefore you accuse us verbosely, because in these civil wars of ours certain idols were—against the will of the Magistrate (who, as you say, still follows the Pontifical religion)—in some places removed and violently cast down by our people.
pages.61:
<header>EPISTOLA</header>
<meta>continues from previous page: a few, and removed, and violently cast down.</meta> This is that grave cause of complaint against us. What then? Has the blood and cry of those idols reached you, Osiander, or is it so dear and precious to you that you would wish to accuse us (whom you so often—but falsely—call most dear and most beloved) before all mortals in a public writing? For that reason do you call our actions, and those of our most illustrious Princes, the King of Navarre, Condé, and others, turbulent? Do you tell the Pastors of the Gallican Churches to bid their listeners to make an assault upon the revenues and temples of the mass-priests? Finally, do you—expecting some wretched pension of money from our Pontifical enemies—slander us, I say, with those most shameless insults for this reason? Therefore, you knave, do you so slanderously, so impudently, so falsely call our most illustrious Princes, under whose leadership we fought those wars for the liberty of the Fatherland—in accordance with royal Edicts approved by the assembly of the Gallic Estates—turbulent, and robbers and invaders of other men's property? Do you, who accuse us of contempt for the Magistrate, condemn him with the most savage criminations? Here, certainly, you now show what your intent was in promulgating this entire sycophantic writing. You hide nothing from us. We know these frauds of yours: and we smell this new Popish Charity of yours. But if we were to wish to speak about your Parent, a most impure man; if about yourself, a wicked, erroneous, and wandering man, what abundance of material, I ask, would we not now have to speak and to write? Learn therefore now, Censor and Cretan, you who [accuse] us of neglected authority—
<margin>Pag. 96.</margin>
<margin>Pag. 94.</margin>

<header>AD ECCLES. GALLIC.</header>
<sig>E.j.</sig>
<meta>continues from previous page: of the Magistrate so harshly lash us, learn, I say, not only to think well of our Magistrates and Princes: but also not to judge rashly about those things which you do not understand in their actions (for those things exceed the grasp of your intellect).</meta> But yet, so that everyone may understand how undeservedly we, the Pastors of the Gallican Churches, are accused by him, we answer this, with God himself as our witness: that we indeed rejoice that those idols, which had been erected for so long in contempt of God, and which held so many thousands of men in vain superstition, have been taken away from the eyes of men. For, says Paul, whether out of occasion, or out of a true spirit, if Christ is announced, we rejoice in this. But the mode itself and the manner of acting, through which those idols were removed, neither our most Illustrious Princes, who were also faithful Magistrates, nor we Pastors ever approved. Evidence for this is provided by the letters written by the Pastors of the Gallican Churches themselves (who had gathered at the Council of Poissy) in the name and with the common consent of all to the Aquitanian brothers and churches, and the edicts and most grave warnings of the most Illustrious Prince of Condé and the most Illustrious Admiral Coligny (whose most holy and most happy memory flourishes and will always flourish among all the pious), even publicly proposed against those who perpetrated these things. I will say more: In the very heat and danger of our wars, (although the Pontifical [forces] raged against our people with every kind of cruelty) when the ruin and dejection of those idols had begun to happen at Orléans, a most noble city on the Loire, the most Illustrious Admiral immediately hastened from the very camps to Orléans, and even with instruments of war drove away those who dared to do this.
pages.63:
<header>EPISTOLA</header>
<meta>continues from previous page: But who does not know how many things happen in war, especially civil war, beyond the wishes of the leaders and good men themselves? These things are by no means defended by us. "For all things," as he said, "are miserable in civil wars."</meta> Therefore, when the spirits of men had grown hot: when our leaders were absent: when some had been moved by a zeal that was good, but not according to knowledge: the idols were cast down not out of a spirit of greed or plunder, but out of a single zeal for overthrowing idolatry, which could not be retained without danger in the Church of God and even among the Pontifical people themselves. But what do idols have to do with the cause of the Lord's Supper, which is the one thing you most urge here and wished to argue? Whither does that complaint and accusation of yours for the sake of idols tend toward your goal? This is the sum of it: Osiander wished to curse you, brothers. And so he sought an opportunity: but since he did not dare to gnaw [at the truth] immediately, he finally ejected his pus, like a serpent [ejecting] its poison in a final hiss. For which manifest and grave insults against you, most beloved brothers, and against us Pastors, we pray for a better mind from God for this man. But you, brothers, by the bowels of the mercy of God, who redeemed you with the most precious blood of his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, who snatched you from the very thickest darkness of idolatry, who called you to the most true light of his doctrine regarding the Supper, Baptism, Predestination, and also other articles, who so many times placed you, when oppressed, into safety beyond all hope, I beseech you to persevere in that truth of holy doctrine which you learned from us;
pages.64:
<header>AD ECCLES. GALLIC.</header>
<sig>E.ij.</sig>
<meta>continues from previous page: mindful of those by whom you were called to the Gospel, and how our doctrine—that is, the doctrine of the pure Gospel preached by us—has now been confirmed among you in so many ways.</meta> Indeed, I wish that you would even recall both him and those like him from their error, and that you would by no means agree with him. For he usually ceases to err to whom no one agrees. Finally, beloved, we have persuaded ourselves of better things regarding you, and things joined with your salvation. But we desire that each one of you may show the same [diligence] for the full persuasion of hope unto the end: That you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience obtain the promised inheritance. Be mindful of your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you, whose faith you imitate. I myself, most beloved brothers, although I am absent from you in body, yet I am present in spirit, and I daily pray and ask God the most merciful Father, through our Lord Jesus Christ our only mediator, for all the best things both for the salvation of your souls and for the stability of your peace. We will easily tolerate all the other insults: but we could not be mute regarding the suspicion of heresy which this man fastens upon us. "I do not want anyone," says Jerome, "to be patient under the suspicion of heresy." Finally, let it be permitted for me to close this Epistle of mine with that speech, and to address you, brothers, with which Father Ignatius, the disciple of John the Evangelist, once addressed the most beloved Philippians, when he was fortifying them against the sowers of tares: <italic>Farewell, brothers, in flesh and soul,</italic>
<margin>Ignatius in Epist. ad Philippenses.</margin>
<italic>Perfectly wise in Spirit, turning away from the workers of iniquity and the corruptors of the word of truth, strengthened in</italic>
pages.65:
<header>AD ECCLES. GALLIC.</header>

the Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

All the brothers who are with me greet you with duty. Farewell again, and help us with your prayers before God. Calends of September, in the year of the Lord 1580.

->*Most addicted to you,*<-
->*L. DANEAU.*<-

Do you tell the Pastors of the Gallican Churches to order their listeners to make an assault on the incomes and temples of the priests? Finally, do you, (you who, expecting some pension of money from our Pontifical side, lie in wait for us,) do you, I say, tear us to pieces with those most impudent insults for that reason? Do you, a trifler, call our most illustrious Princes—under whose leadership we waged those wars for the liberty of the Fatherland, approved by the very Royal Edicts and the assembly of the Gallican Orders—so slanderously, so impudently, and so falsely turbulent, and invaders and plunderers of other people's faculties? You who accuse us of contempt for the Magistrate, do you condemn him with the most savage accusations? Here, indeed, you show what your intention was in promulgating this entire sycophantic writing. You conceal nothing from us; we know these frauds of yours, and we smell this new charity of yours. But if we wanted to speak about your Parent, a most impure man, or about yourself, a worthless, erroneous, and wandering man, what abundance of material, I pray, would we have now to speak and to write? Learn then, Censor and Cretan, you who [attack] us regarding neglected authority
<margin>Pag. 96.</margin>
<margin>Pag. 94.</margin>

of the Magistrate so harshly, learn, I say, not only to think well of our Magistrates and Princes yourself, but also never to judge rashly about those things which you do not understand in their actions (for they exceed the capacity of your wit). But nevertheless, so that all may understand how undeservedly we, the Pastors of the Gallican Churches, are accused by him, we respond, with God himself as our witness: that we indeed rejoice that those idols, which had been erected for so long in contempt of God and were keeping so many thousands of men in vain superstition, have been removed from the eyes of men. For whether, says Paul, Christ is proclaimed out of opportunity or out of a true mind, we rejoice in this. However, we have never approved the mode and method of acting by which those idols were removed, neither our most illustrious Princes, who were also faithful Magistrates, nor we, the Pastors. Evidence for this fact is provided by the letters written by the Pastors of the Gallican Churches themselves (who had gathered at the Colloquy of Poissy) in the common name and consent of all to the brothers and churches of Aquitaine, and the most grave edicts and threats of the most illustrious Prince of Condé and the most illustrious Admiral Coligny (whose most holy and most happy memory flourishes and will always flourish among all the pious) which were even publicly proposed against those who perpetrated these things. I will say more: In the very heat and danger of our wars, (although the Pontificals were raging against our people with every kind of cruelty) when that ruin and destruction of idols began to happen at Orléans, a most noble city on the Loire, the most illustrious Admiral himself rushed immediately from the camps to Orléans and drove out with weapons of war those who dared to do this.

To cut off all litigation with outsiders, to preserve ecclesiastical immunity, and for greater conformity and concord in the chapter, all our predecessors unanimously concluded and ordained on July 7, 1684, with the subsequent confirmation of the Most Reverend Ordinary of Konstanz, that if any Confrere should decide to draw up a testament in our chapter concerning his acquired goods, he shall not choose or appoint any executor of his last will other than one from the fold of the chapter. This is the very thing that this man also explains through this analogy. As if there were no action and operation of God, who justly punishes one sin with another sin, and thus acts in the heart of Pharaoh, which is already evil in itself. But truly, Osiander, God did indeed rouse Pharaoh, and hardened him, and sent a spirit of error, not by mere permission, as you suppose; not by mere foreknowledge; not by mere intuition; not by mere patience; or by <term>ἐνεργείᾳ</term> <gloss>operation/energy</gloss>, or by <term>συν</term> <gloss>with/cooperation</gloss>: but by that very thing, 

<margin>2 Thess. 2.11</margin> as Paul himself speaks and interprets, <term>ἐνεργείᾳ</term> <gloss>operation</gloss>, namely, effectiveness and efficacy. But the man fears, perhaps from the imitation of that most impure Father, the pious Osiander, lest, by the dogma of the Manichaeans, he establish God as the author of evil and sin. Truly, it would have been something to fear, so that if God did not have such an eloquent patron for his cause, he would be condemned. As if, indeed, before this youth was born, God had already lost the case and been truly found guilty and the author of sin by the Manichaeans. The truth of God needs none of your lies (such as appear in this interpretation of yours) to defend itself. Therefore, 

<margin>Exod. 4.9</margin> God hardened Pharaoh, and yet Pharaoh hardened himself, because in one and the same act, God and men act in different ways. God indeed acts justly, because God is most just; but man acts most unjustly, because he looks to and follows the movement of his own soul, and his own wicked goal and end. For example: The Scribes and Pharisees wanted Christ to die; God the Heavenly Father also wanted this very thing, and Christ himself also wished to die. Is then the will of God the Father, and of Christ himself, in the same death of Christ, unjust because that of the Scribes and Pharisees was most unjust? By no means, Osiander. Therefore 

<margin>Act. 4.28</margin> to conclude this point,
pages.60:
<header>TO THE GALLICAN CHURCHES.</header>

to conclude this point, even if the works and judgments of God are hidden and unknown to us, they are nevertheless always most just. Nor does it follow that if he is involved in the same work as we men, he works viciously as we do. But because you are very often and very correctly instructed about these things by your pastors, and the goal of this entire dispute is only to demonstrate that the doctrine of this monitor is both false and neither full nor sincere, I think it unnecessary to add more about this subject, even though it is a very serious one.

->OF IDOLS.<-

IT remains, therefore, that we also briefly discuss the chapter that he added last. It is concerning Idols. Which was mentioned by Osiander not so much out of any necessity of the time or of idolatry (which, by the grace of God the Best and Greatest, rests among you), as to publicly defame you all, seizing upon however untimely an occasion, and to bring you into ill will and hatred before all Magistrates. For what other goal does this tail of yours have, Osiander, than to vomit forth your poison against us under that sugared speech and <term>θεοφρονήσει</term> <gloss>wise-thinking/thoughtful piety</gloss> written most exquisitely from the emendations of all your colleagues, and to wish that we be found guilty? Thus, in that entire writing of yours, the voice indeed was the voice of Jacob, but the hands were the hands of Esau, that is, your hands. Therefore you accuse us verbosely, because in these civil wars of ours, certain idols were, against the will of the Magistrate (who, as you say, still follows the Pontifical religion), cast down in some places by some of our people
pages.61:
<header>EPISTLE</header>

and removed, and violently cast down. This is that so grave cause of complaint against us. What then? Has the blood and cry of those idols reached you, Osiander, or is it so dear and precious to you that you would wish to accuse us (whom you so often call dearest and most beloved, though falsely) before all mortals in a public writing? And because of this, to call the actions of our most illustrious Princes, the King of Navarre, Condé, and others, turbulent? To say that the pastors of the Gallican Churches told their listeners to make an assault upon the incomes and temples of the priests? And finally, to tear us apart (whom you, expecting some pension of money from our Pontifical enemies, miserably lay in wait for) with those most shameless insults? Therefore, you knave, do you so slanderously, so impudently, so falsely call our most illustrious Princes—under whose leadership we waged those wars for the liberty of the Fatherland, approved by the very royal Edicts and the assembly of the Gallican Orders—turbulent, and rapers and invaders of other men's faculties? You who accuse us of contempt for the Magistrate, do you condemn him with the most savage accusations? Here, indeed, you show what your intent was in publishing this entire sycophantic writing. You hide nothing from us. We know these frauds of yours; and we smell this new charity of yours, this "Papal Charity." But if we wished to speak of your parent, a most impure man; if we wished to speak of yourself, a wicked, erroneous, and wandering man, what abundance of material would we not now have, I ask you, to say and to write? Therefore learn now, Censor and "Cretan," <note>Referring to the proverb "Cretans are always liars," implying the accuser is a liar.</note> you who accuse us of neglected authority
<margin>Pag. 96.</margin>
<margin>Pag. 94.</margin>
pages.62:
<header>TO THE GALLICAN CHURCHES.</header>

of the Magistrate, and lash out so harshly, learn, I say, not only to think well of our Magistrates and Princes, but also not to judge rashly about those things in their actions that you do not understand (for those things surpass the grasp of your wit). But nevertheless, so that all may understand how undeservedly we, the Pastors of the Gallican Churches, are accused by this man, we respond, with God himself as our witness: that we indeed rejoice that those idols, which had been erected for so long in contempt of God, and were holding so many thousands of men in vain superstition, have been removed from the eyes of men. For whether, says Paul, Christ is proclaimed out of occasion or out of true spirit, we rejoice in this. But the manner itself and the method of acting by which those idols were removed, neither our most illustrious Princes, who were also faithful Magistrates, nor we, the Pastors, ever approved. This is testified to by the letters written in the name and with the common consent of all by the Pastors of the Gallican Churches (who had gathered at the Council of Poissy) to our brothers and the Aquitanian Churches, and by the most grave edicts and threats publicly proposed by the most illustrious Prince Condé and the most illustrious Admiral Coligny (whose most holy and most happy memory flourishes and will always flourish among all the pious) against those who committed these things. I will say more: in the very heat and danger of our wars (although the Pontificals raged against our people with every kind of cruelty), when that ruin and destruction of idols had begun to happen at the most noble town of Orléans on the Loire, the most illustrious Admiral immediately rushed from the very
<margin>Pag. 96.</margin>
<margin>Pag. 94.</margin>
pages.63:
<header>EPISTLE</header>

camps to Orléans, and even with siege engines drove off those who dared this. But who does not know how much occurs in war, especially in civil war, beyond the wishes of the leaders and good men themselves? Which are by no means defended by us. *For all things, as he says, are wretched in civil wars.* Therefore, when the minds of men had grown hot; when our leaders were absent; when some had been moved by a zeal that was good, but not according to knowledge, the idols were cast down, not in a spirit of greed or plunder, but only with the desire of overturning the idolatry that could not be retained without danger in the Church of God and among the Pontifical people themselves. But what do idols have to do with the case of the Lord's Supper, which you especially press here, and wanted to argue? To what purpose is this complaint and accusation of yours concerning idols to your "rhombus"? <note>A term possibly used here to mean a circular, wandering, or misguided argument.</note> This is the sum of it: Osiander wanted to curse you, brothers. And so he seized the opportunity; but when he did not dare to nibble immediately, at the end he spat out his pus, like a serpent hissing its poison at the very last. For which manifest and grave insults against you, dearest brothers, and against us, Pastors, let us pray for a better mind for this man from God. But you, brothers, through the bowels of the mercy of God, who redeemed you with the most precious blood of his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, who snatched you from the very thickest darkness of idolatry, who called you to the truest light of his doctrine concerning the Supper, Baptism, Predestination, and other articles, who so often placed you in safety beyond all hope when you were oppressed, I implore you to persevere in that truth of the holy doctrine which you have learned from us
pages.64:
<header>TO THE GALLICAN CHURCHES.</header>

mindful of those by whom you were called to the Gospel, and how our doctrine—that is, the pure Gospel preached by us—has now been confirmed among you in so many ways. Nay, indeed, so that you may also recall both this man and those like him from their error, and in no way agree with him. For he who no one agrees with generally learns to cease erring. Finally, beloved, we are persuaded of better things concerning you, and things joined with your salvation. We desire, however, that each one of you show the same <margin>Heb. 6.</margin> zeal for the full assurance of hope until the end: that you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience obtain the promised inheritance. Be mindful of your leaders who spoke the word of God to you, whose faith you imitate. I indeed, dearest brothers, although I am absent from you in body, am nevertheless present in spirit, and I daily pray and ask of God the most merciful Father, through our Lord Jesus Christ our only mediator, for all things that are best for both the salvation of your souls and the stability of your peace. We will easily tolerate all the other insults; but in the suspicion of heresy, which this man fastens upon us, we could not be silent. I do not want anyone, says Jerome, to be patient when under suspicion of heresy. Finally, let it be permitted to me to close this my Epistle with that speech with which Father Ignatius, the disciple of John the Evangelist, once addressed the Philippians, who were most dear to him, when he was fortifying them against the sowers of tares: <italic>Farewell, brothers, in flesh and soul,</italic> <margin>Ignatius in Epistle to the Philippians.</margin> <italic>perfectly wise in Spirit, turning away from the workers of iniquity and the corrupters of the word of truth, strengthened in</italic>
pages.65:
<header>TO THE GALLICAN CHURCHES.</header>

the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

All the brothers who are with me greet you dutifully. Farewell again, and help us with your prayers before God. Calends of September, in the year of the Lord 1580.

-><italic>Most devoted to you,</italic><-
-><italic>L. DANEAU.</italic><-

But nevertheless, so that all may understand how undeservedly we, the Pastors of the Gallican Churches, are accused by this man, we respond, with God himself as our witness: that we indeed rejoice that those idols, which had been erected for so long in contempt of God, and were holding so many thousands of men in vain superstition, have been removed from the eyes of men. For whether, says Paul, Christ is proclaimed out of occasion or out of true spirit, we rejoice in this. But the manner itself and the method of acting by which those idols were removed, neither our most illustrious Princes, who were also faithful Magistrates, nor we, the Pastors, ever approved. This is testified to by the letters written in the name and with the common consent of all by the Pastors of the Gallican Churches (who had gathered at the Council of Poissy) to our brothers and the Aquitanian Churches, and by the most grave edicts and threats publicly proposed by the most illustrious Prince Condé and the most illustrious Admiral Coligny (whose most holy and most happy memory flourishes and will always flourish among all the pious) against those who committed these things. When, however, the pestiferous Zwinglian plague, namely heresy, crept into even our formerly [pure] Chapter and, alas, infected seven parishes with irreparable damage. Such are: Neukirch, Wil, Beringen, Glattfelden, Löningen, Buchberg, Eglisau, and thus the number of Confratres was greatly diminished, namely to 13 Parishes: Kaiserstuhl, Lostetten, Jestetten, Baltersweil, Büel, Erzingen, Rheinheim near Zurzach, Ober-Eggingen, Tegernau, Schwerzen, Grießen, Lienheim, and lastly added in the year 1622, the Parish of Oberlauchringen. With two chaplaincies joined, namely Grießen and Dangstetten.

Therefore, the manner of celebrating chapters or convocations as often as our ancient Statutes require has been restricted to spare expenses and prescribed by the Most Reverend Ordinary, such that at a minimum a chapter shall be celebrated in two years, and in the second year a local visitation shall be held, unless a pressing and extraordinary cause prevails.

A local visitation must be carried out, as follows below by
pages.28:
the Dean, Chamberlain, or a deputy or Secretary of the chapter at the expense of the aforementioned chapter. However, the Dean must choose a convenient time, yet first he shall present himself to the Reverend Constantian Office, to see what they have in their mandates. He shall diligently prepare a roll of the visitation from place to place, so that he may more easily find errors that have been corrected and improved, or those not improved.

Meanwhile, it is to be observed: if a Chapter is not celebrated in one year, nevertheless every Confrater and Chaplain must in that year say one holy Mass around Pentecost for the deceased Confratres and Chaplains, if a chapter is announced to be celebrated by the beadle <note>original: "Pedellum"</note> <gloss>an official usher</gloss> at the order of the Dean, just as our predecessors observed around the feast of Pentecost. All and singular, unless truly canonically impeded, under the penalty already taxed or to be taxed by the Dean and Chamberlain, shall appear in the Chapter wearing a surplice <note>original: "subpelliciati"</note> <gloss>wearing a white vestment</gloss> or induciatus, that is, cloaked, as is for decency. (For craftsmen do not frequent their guilds without cloaks). They shall strictly observe everything that is given to us in these statutes and by our predecessors, to the letter.

Let no one speak unless asked or called, and let him respond not noisily but discreetly.

Let them not chatter in the Church during divine services, but rather edify those present.

In elections, votes are no longer given orally but are deposited in folded slips into a chalice prepared for this purpose to avert future passions.

*Number VIII.*

Item, if anyone molests any Confrater by words or deeds, or inflicts any injury upon him, and the one injured or molested makes a complaint about this in the chapter, the Dean and the other Confratres of the said deanery ought to punish or correct the injurer according to the magnitude of his excesses; if, however, he is rebellious and disobedient to the Chapter, they ought to denounce him to the Lord Bishop existing for the time being, through the Dean or other Confratres, at the expense of the Chapter.

OBSERVATION EIGHTH, REGARDING
Number Eight.

"At the expense of the chapter" is understood thus, and it is observed that the Chapter may later have recourse for expenses against the rebellious and disobedient. However, no Confrater shall report a Confrater to Constance without the prior knowledge of the Dean, so that the first instance may be observed in its own place.

*Number IX.*

Item, if it should happen that a Confrater passes from this world, his family or his nearest Confrater is bound to announce it to
pages.30: the Dean or Chamberlain, so that he may be present at the burial with the four nearest Confratres to celebrate the burial of the aforementioned deceased, and a meal is provided for the aforementioned Priests from the goods and things left behind by the heirs. If it should happen that a Confrater chooses to be buried elsewhere than in the Church he presided over, they are not bound to leave the chapter, nor for the Burial, nor for the Seventh-day [Mass], nor for the Thirtieth-day [Mass], but only in the place where he died while presiding, unless at the discretion of the Dean or Chamberlain. And on the Seventh day, the Dean or Chamberlain with six nearest Confratres shall celebrate the Seventh [Mass] in the Church he presided over while dying. Item, on the Thirtieth day, all Confratres shall be summoned to celebrate the Thirtieth [Mass], and all prepared for Masses and wearing surplices, as is contained in all manners as above in the general [rules]. Item, that whenever the Confratres are gathered, whether it is in general [meetings] or thirtieth-day [Masses], for any of the deceased, they are bound to have Vigils with notation or without, just as it pleased the Dean or Chamberlain at that time, and each of the Confratres is bound to have a memory of the one who departed every Sunday in the chancel for a year, and to have three Masses with three Vigils for the salvation of the soul of the departed.

OBSERVATION NINTH, REGARDING NUMBER
Nine.

To cut off all litigation with outsiders, to preserve Ecclesiastical immunity, and for greater conformity and concord in the chapter, all our predecessors unanimously concluded and ordained on July 7, 1684, with the subsequent confirmation of the Most Reverend Ordinary of Constance, that if any of the Confratres decides to make a will in our chapter regarding his acquired goods, he shall not choose or appoint any executor of his last will other than one from the membership of the chapter. And this statute was renewed and confirmed by decree of the Ordinary on October 31, 1713; therefore, each Confrater will dispose of his affairs in the best way to spare expenses if he chooses one from the Chapter as executor, who otherwise should be present by office at the sealing, inventory, and division. He may, however, employ even laymen, provided they are honest, to sign his Testament as witnesses.

OBSERVATION XIX. ON LOCAL VISITATION.

*On the Visitation of Ecclesiastical Persons.*

**F**irst, let every Parish Priest and Beneficiary be questioned regarding his name, surname, parents, and place of birth. Next, let him be asked for his letters of investiture and admission to the charge, if he holds a benefice with care of souls.
Thirdly, let him be asked how often he confesses in a year, and to whom.
Fourthly, let his books be inspected: Whether, besides others, he has the <term>Breviarium Constantiense</term> <gloss>Constance Breviary</gloss> with the Directory, the Roman Catechism, the Council of Trent, and the Synodical Statutes of this Diocese: Likewise a book on cases of conscience, and also some approved <term>Postillae</term> <gloss>sermon collections</gloss>, as they are called, along with the Bible, and whether he reads these diligently.
Fifthly, let the Visitors sometimes make an experiment with the simpler and suspicious ones, by questioning them on various matters pertaining to the Canonical hours, the ceremonies of the Church, and the administration of the Sacraments, whether they are trained in these or not.

And since, by force of the often-alleged Holy Council of Trent, Bishops have the right and power in all those things which pertain to visitation and the correction of morals, not only over those subject to their own ordinary jurisdiction, but also as delegates of the Apostolic See over those who are exempt. Therefore, our Visitors, under whose Deaneries monasteries and colleges both of men and women are situated, in nearby places at least (otherwise, in the monasteries or colleges themselves, they shall institute no visitation without our special mandate), shall also make a diligent inquiry among trustworthy persons regarding the following.

Whether the monasteries of regular men and women or the colleges of secular canons are administered correctly, both in spiritual and temporal matters.

Whether in the monasteries of men the Constitution of Pius V is observed, that women may not enter their cloisters, and in the monasteries of women, whether perpetual enclosure is kept.

Whether the Abbot, Abbess, Commendator, Provost, or other superior has committed and entrusted the care of souls to anyone without the license of the Bishop or his Vicar.

Finally, whether they know anything regarding secular or regular clerics, of whatever order, status, or condition they may be, even of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem, and other military orders, which in any way generates scandal, and whose reputation is at stake, or which can be proven.

OBSERVATION XX.
ON THE VISITATION OF LAYPEOPLE.

REGARDING the life and morals of the laypeople of any place, let the Parish Priests and Priests, and if necessity demands it, also some laymen, men of honor and proven faith and good testimony, be examined by means of an oath, according to the interrogatories which follow.

First, whether there is any heretic in the parish, or anyone suspected of heresy, who sends his own to the schools of heretics with the knowledge and permission of the local magistrate.

Whether anyone has at home and reads the books of heretics.

Whether there are in the parish any excommunicated persons, fortune-tellers, enchanters, those curing diseases superstitiously, blasphemers, usurers, murderers, those who have struck clerics or parents, married persons separated from each other by their own authority, or those persisting in capital enmities:

Whether
pages.56:
Whether anyone eats meat on days of fast or abstinence without license and a reasonable cause.

Whether all and singular of the parishioners having sufficient age confess and communicate at least once a year, and that around the feast of Easter.

Whether the secular magistrate compels clerics to his tribunal, oppresses, punishes, or harasses them: and whether he takes cognizance of and judges in spiritual causes and purely ecclesiastical crimes.

Whether the Parish Priest or beneficiary knows of any other defect which he desires to be amended.

### ON THE VISITATION OF CHURCHES, Benefices, and their revenues.

Therefore, above all, let them survey the places with the vessels in which the Holy Eucharist and the holy oils are accustomed to be kept.

But when the pestiferous Zwinglian contagion, namely the heresy, crept even into our formerly [entire] Chapter, and alas, infected seven parishes with irreparable damage. These are: Neukirch, Wil, Beringen, Glattfelden, Löningen, Buchberg, Eglisau, and thus the number of Con-Fratres was greatly reduced, namely to 13 parishes: Kaiserstuhl, Lostetten, Jestetten, Balterschwil, Büel, Erzingen, Rheinheim near Zurzach, Obereggingen, Tegernauw, Schwerzen, Grießen, Lienheim, and finally added in the year 1622, the parish of Oberlauchringen. With two chaplaincies united, namely Grießen and Dangstetten.

Therefore, the manner of celebrating chapters or convocations, as our ancient statutes require, has been restricted to spare expenses and prescribed by the Most Reverend Ordinary, such that at minimum, a chapter be celebrated in one of 2 years, but in the second year a local visitation be held, unless a pressing and extraordinary cause prevails.

A local visitation must be done, as is held below by

However, the convenience of time must be chosen by the Dean, having first insinuated himself before the Reverend Office of Constance, to await what it gives in mandates. He diligently compiles the roll of the visitation from place to place, so that he may more easily find errors corrected and improved, or not improved.

Meanwhile, it is to be observed: if a Chapter is not celebrated in one year, nevertheless every Con-Fratre and Chaplain ought, in that year, to say one holy Mass around Pentecost for the deceased Con-Fratres and Chaplains. If a chapter is ordered to be celebrated by the beadle by command of the Dean, as our predecessors observed around the feast of Pentecost, all and singular—unless truly canonically impeded—under the penalty already taxed or to be taxed by the Dean and Chamberlain, shall appear in the Chapter <term>subpelliciati</term> <gloss>wearing a surplice</gloss>, or <term>induciati</term> <gloss>wearing the habit</gloss>, that is, cloaked, as is for decency. (For mechanics do not frequent their guilds without cloaks). They shall strictly observe everything which is given to us in these statutes and by our predecessors, to a hair.

Let no one speak unless asked or called, and let him answer not clamorously, but discreetly.

Let them not chatter in the church during divine services, but rather edify those present.

In elections, votes are no longer given orally, but they cast them in folded slips into a chalice prepared for that purpose, to avert future passions.

*Number VIII.*

Item, if anyone has troubled some Con-Fratre with words or deeds, or has brought some injury upon him, and the one injured or troubled has made a complaint about this in the chapter, the Dean and the other Con-Fratres of the deanery must punish or correct the injurer according to the magnitude of his excesses. If, however, he is rebellious and disobedient to the Chapter, they must denounce him to the Lord Bishop existing at the time, through the Dean or through other Con-Fratres, at the expense of the Chapter.

Number Eight.

"At the expense of the chapter": this is understood, and it is observed, that the Chapter afterward has recourse regarding expenses against the rebellious and disobedient. However, no Con-Fratre shall bring a Con-Fratre to Constance without the foreknowledge of the Dean, so that the first instance is observed in his own place.

*Number IX.*

Item, if it happens that a Con-Fratre migrates from this life, his family or his nearest Con-Fratre is bound to announce [this] to the

If it happens that some Con-Fratre chooses a burial elsewhere than in the church over which he presided, they are not bound to leave the chapter, neither for the burial, nor for the Seventh Day [Mass], nor for the Thirtieth Day [Mass], but only in the place where the dying man presided, unless by the judgment of the Dean or Chamberlain. And on the Seventh Day, the Dean or Chamberlain with six of the nearest Con-Fratres shall celebrate the Seventh Day in the church over which the dying man presided. Item, on the Thirtieth Day, all Con-Fratres shall be summoned to celebrate the Thirtieth Day, and all prepared for Masses and wearing surplices as is contained in all ways, as above in the general [statutes]. Item, that whenever the Con-Fratres are gathered, whether it be in general meetings or thirtieth days, for any of the dying, they are bound to have Vigils with notation or without, as it then pleased the Dean or Chamberlain. And each of the Con-Fratres is bound to have a memory of the departed every Sunday in the chancel for a year, and to have three Masses with three Vigils for the salvation of the soul of the departed.

To cut off all litigation with outsiders, to preserve ecclesiastical immunity, and for greater conformity and concord in the chapter, all our predecessors unanimously concluded and ordained on the 7th of July, 1684, with the accession of confirmation by the Most Reverend Ordinary of Constance, that if any of the Con-Fratres in our chapter decides to make a testament regarding his acquired goods, he shall not choose and appoint any executor for his last will other than one from the bosom of the chapter. And this statute was renewed and confirmed by a decree of the Ordinary on the 31st of October, 1713. Wherefore, every Con-Fratre shall dispose of his things in the best way, to spare expenses, if he chooses one from the Chapter as executor, who otherwise by office ought to be present at the sealing, inventory, and division. He will be able to employ even laymen, provided they are honest, to subscribe as witnesses to his Testament.

OBSERVATION XIX.
ON THE LOCAL VISITATION.

*On the Visitation of Ecclesiastical Persons.*

**F**irst, let every <term>Parochus</term> <gloss>parish priest</gloss> and <term>Beneficiatus</term> <gloss>benefice holder</gloss> be questioned regarding his Name, Surname, Parents, and Birth. Thirdly, let him be asked how often he confesses in a year, and to whom.
Fourthly, let his Books be inspected: whether, besides others, he has the <term>Breviarium Constantiense</term> <gloss>Constance Breviary</gloss> with the Directory, the Roman Catechism, the Council of Trent, and the Synodical Statutes of this Diocese: Likewise a Book on cases of conscience, as well as some approved <term>Postillæ</term> <gloss>collections of sermons</gloss>, as they are called, and that he diligently reads the Bibles.
Fifthly, let the Visitors sometimes conduct an experiment with the simpler and suspected ones, by questioning them regarding various matters pertaining to the Canonical hours, the Ceremonies of the Church, and the administration of the Sacraments, to see whether they are trained in them or not.

REGARDING the life and morals of laypeople of any place, the Parish Priests and Priests, and if necessity demands it, also some laymen, men who are honest and of proven faith and good testimony, shall be examined by means of an oath, according to the interrogatories that follow.

Whether there are in the Parish excommunicated persons, sorcerers, enchanters, those who superstitiously cure diseases, blasphemers, usurers, murderers, those who strike clerics or parents, married persons separated from each other by their own authority, or those persisting in capital enmities:

These things having been accomplished, the Visitors, having called before them three, four, five, or seven men from each parish—those who are more mature, honorable, and truthful, and especially church wardens, prefects, and other laymen—shall bind each of them (where this can conveniently be done) by oath, or otherwise at least under good faith, to tell the truth regarding those things which they will be asked, and shall examine them separately, first concerning the life and honesty of the Parish Priest himself, or another Beneficiary, in this manner.

Namely, whether he is a concubinarian, a fornicator, an adulterer, a drunkard, a gambler, a brawler, a striker, a blasphemer, a usurer, a spendthrift, burdened with debt, obscene in words, gestures, and deeds, or ensnared by another grave crime.

Whether he wears clerical attire and a tonsure appropriate to his order.

Whether divine worship is performed in the Church at the set hours, devoutly, decently, and in an orderly fashion, to the praise of God and the edification of the people.

How often he celebrates during the week, and how often he is obligated to celebrate.

Whether he satisfies pious foundations and other obligations.

Whether on Sundays throughout the whole year he teaches the Catechism or Christian Doctrine.

Whether on those days he also announces from the pulpit the feasts and fasts by commandment of the Church, and also any anniversaries that may occur.

Whether and how often he publishes from the chancel the decree of the Holy Council of Trent concerning clandestine marriage.

Whether he always precedes this with three proclamations, according to the decree of the same Council, before he joins the contracting parties in marriage in the face of the Church.

Whether he has ever joined in marriage those between whom there was a canonical impediment of consanguinity, affinity, compaternity, or public honesty, and how he understands these impediments.

And if the parties have obtained an Apostolic dispensation regarding any canonical impediment, whether the matters narrated therein have been verified by the Vicar General or the Official of Constance.

Whether the bridegroom and bride confess and receive communion before they come together.

Whether he sometimes teaches and examines midwives on how they ought to behave in baptizing infants in time of necessity, and regarding the words which must be used.

Whether, because of the Parish Priest's absence, negligence, or fault, any unbaptized infants have died.

ON THE ELECTION OF THE DEAN, AND THE CELEBRATION OF THE CHAPTER.

First, the *Veni S. Spiritus* <gloss>Come, Holy Spirit</gloss>, etc., is begun.

*HYMN.*

Come, Creator Spirit,
Visit the minds of your people,
Fill with heavenly grace
The hearts that you created.
You who are called the Paraclete,
The gift of the Most High God,
Living fountain, fire, charity,
And spiritual anointing.
You, with your sevenfold gift,
Finger of the Father’s Right Hand,
You, the duly promised of the Father,
Enriching our throats with speech.
Kindle light in our senses,
Infuse love into our hearts,
Confirming the weaknesses of our body
With enduring strength.
Drive the enemy far away,
And grant peace immediately.
With you as our guide,
Let us avoid all that is harmful.
Grant that through you we may know the Father,
And recognize the Son,
pages.62:
<note>Decorative floral ornament surrounding the page number.</note>
<note>Decorative floral ornament at the end of the prayer.</note>

And believe in you, the Spirit of both,
At all times.
To God the Father be Glory,
And to the Son, who from the dead
Rose again, and to the Paraclete,
For ages upon ages. Amen.

*The Dean or Chamberlain finishes with a prayer, etc.*

℣. Send forth your Spirit and they shall be created.
℟. And you shall renew the face of the earth.
℣. O Lord, hear my prayer.
℟. And let my cry come unto you.
℣. The Lord be with you.
℟. And with your Spirit.

*Let us pray.*

O God, who has taught the hearts of the faithful by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, grant us in the same Spirit to perceive what is right, and always to rejoice in His consolation. Through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, God, for ages upon ages. ℟. Amen.

I, N., with firm faith believe and profess all and singular things that are contained in the Symbol of faith <gloss>the Creed</gloss>, which the holy Roman
pages.63:

Church uses; namely: I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God. And born of the Father before all ages. God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God. Begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father: by whom all things were made: Who for us men and for our salvation descended from heaven. And was incarnate by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. And was made Man. He was also crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, suffered and was buried. And He rose again on the third day; according to the Scriptures. And ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. And He is to come again with glory to judge the living and the dead: of whose kingdom there shall be no end. *Let us pray.*

O God, who has taught the hearts of the faithful by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, grant us by the same Spirit to relish what is right, and ever to rejoice in His consolation. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you, in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, God, for ages upon ages. ℟. Amen.

*THE PROFESSION OF FAITH FOLLOWS.*

I, N., with firm faith believe and profess all and singular things that are contained in the Symbol of faith, which the holy Roman Church uses; namely: I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God. And born of the Father before all ages. God of God, Light of Light, true God of true God. Begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father: by whom all things were made: Who for us men, and for our salvation, descended from heaven. And was incarnate by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary. And became Man. He was also crucified for us, under Pontius Pilate, suffered and was buried. And rose again on the third day; according to the Scriptures. And ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father. And he is to come again with glory to judge the living and the dead: of whose kingdom there will be no end. And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son. Who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified together; who has spoken through the Prophets. And one holy Catholic and Apostolic Church. I confess one Baptism, for the remission of Sins. And I look for the resurrection of the dead. And the life of the world to come. Amen.

I, NN., canonically elected as Dean of this Chapter, promise, vow, and swear to God Almighty, to the most Blessed Virgin Mary, and to the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, the patrons of the same, that I will, to the best of my ability, defend and observe the Statutes, Privileges, and customs of the aforementioned Chapter against all people, and will assist my fellow brethren, both present and future, with counsel and aid; and that I will not accept a complaint from anyone against any of them, unless it be under two or three witnesses, according to the Apostle <note>1 Timothy 5:19</note>, who are above all exception. First, this is not our saying, but that of the most holy Martyr of God, Vigilius, formerly Bishop of Trent, as we have already taught in the Colloquy of Poissy (where the Papists were finally defeated and gave us their hands <note>i.e., conceded/surrendered</note>). Next, Osiander ignores this (which is the principal point of this whole dispute) with great craft. For we have never denied that Christ is present in his Supper, brothers, as you rightly remember, nor do we say that his flesh is absent: we only deny the mode of corporal presence, so that the dispute is not about the thing that is present, but only about the mode of presence. Thus, therefore, it should have been said: The Gallic Pastors wish that the body of Christ, by way of corporal presence alone, is as far distant from the very signs of the Supper as the highest heaven is distant from these lands; therefore, they wish the body of Christ to be absent from the Supper of the Lord completely and truly. What follows further, if our position is false, brothers: but that of Osiander is true? That there is clearly no other true reason for the presence of the flesh of Christ with us, or in the Holy Supper, than that which happens by way of corporal presence and its inherence in these lands? Therefore, the sacramental conjunction and the presence of the signified thing with the sign must necessarily be denied, because it is not of this kind. Therefore, let the sacraments be taken away, or let them be posited as modes through which the signified thing is presented to us by way of corporal presence, but not that the things themselves are sealed to us while absent. Therefore, let the flesh of Christ be dragged down from heaven, or be multiplied into different fleshes, therefore

For although the sacramental eating has signs in addition to the spiritual one (which are <term>metonymicē</term> <gloss>metonymically</gloss> called the flesh and blood of Christ because of the signification and, as the Fathers say, the analogy), yet the flesh itself
pages.27:
does not change or lose that nature of Christ which is indeed spiritual, so that it might be eaten in the sacrament itself by any mouth and mode other than a purely spiritual one: and certainly not by a corporal mouth, or (as Osiander wishes) an impious and impure one. And yet this is the Achilles and strongest bastion of Osiander. But he objects against us:

<margin>Pag. 41. Pag. 12.</margin>
The Supper of the Lord was instituted a long time after that sermon of Christ concerning the spiritual eating of his flesh. Therefore, the flesh of Christ itself is eaten in the Supper of the Lord by the mouth of the body. R. Osiander could certainly have just as well concluded: Therefore, the flesh of Christ, which is given in the Supper of the Lord, is not the true food of our souls and the nourishment of eternal life, nor is his blood the drink of our souls, since they are called such before the Supper of the Lord was instituted, and in that same sermon of Christ in John chapter 6, if the eating of the flesh of Christ, spiritual and sacramental, is different. But who does not see how childish these are, and how poorly concluded? Yet he adds: Christ, instituting his Holy Supper, said of the bread, "This is my body," and of the wine, "This is my blood." Therefore, the flesh of Christ itself, and the blood itself, is really consubstantiated with the Bread and Wine of the Holy Supper. R. Christ did not say, "My flesh is under this, In this, and With this bread." Therefore, Osiander departs from the words of Christ and abandons the <term>to rhēton</term> <gloss>the literal word</gloss>. But what of it? If the words and the <term>to rhēton</term> are to be pressed, would not the Papists collect even better from these words: Therefore, the Bread and Wine are transubstantiated into the body and blood of Christ? And yet here he seems to triumph, whereas he concludes so poorly. Thus, on pages 13, 14, 15, and 16, he sings this triumph of his at length, but he does so—unless he is completely dull—before the victory. Paul said,
pages.28:
The bread of the Lord's Supper is a communion of the body of Christ: The Cup is a communion of the blood of Christ. Therefore, Paul consubstantiates the body and blood of Christ with the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper, so that it might coexist at the same time by way of corporal presence, and the flesh of Christ itself might be eaten by the mouth of the body. R. On the contrary, those words of Paul, "communion of the body" and "communion of the blood," contain the proper meaning of those words of Christ, "This is my body, this is my blood," and teach that it is sacramental. For they show that the signs themselves are not the flesh and blood of Christ itself, either transubstantiated or consubstantiated: but that they are tokens, <term>sphragidas</term> <gloss>seals</gloss>, and sacraments of our communion with him. Just as the flesh of the sacrifice, which had once been offered by the sacrificers in the temple of God, was a symbol and pledge of the communion of the sacrificers themselves, both among themselves and with the flesh of Christ itself. 

<margin>Pag. 17.</margin>
This is what Osiander himself writes is true later, when he calls the cup offered by the Lord the confirmation of the New Testament. 

<margin>Pag. 16.</margin>
Irenaeus says in book 4, chapter 34, that the Eucharist consists of two things, the earthly and the heavenly. Therefore, the flesh of Christ itself is really consubstantiated with the signs of the Supper. R. On the contrary, in that very place Irenaeus calls the Bread and Wine (which he says are offered in the Eucharist) signs and arguments. Therefore, he recognizes that they are types and symbols. Which completely overturns this consubstantiation of Osiander. Furthermore, the word "consist" in Irenaeus by no means signifies a mode of presence and corporal coexistence by which a spiritual thing exists with signs in these lands: but it signifies the sacramental conjunction of the signified thing with the signs, since Irenaeus is speaking there not of the signs alone,
pages.29:
but of the whole Sacrament of the Eucharist.

The signs of the Holy Supper are joined with the signified thing because of the signification and the promise of Christ. Therefore, the sign and the signified thing are not separated from one another in place. R. What will Osiander say, brothers, about the water of Baptism and the blood of Christ (which is the other Sacrament instituted for us by Christ himself)? Will he not conclude the same? Therefore, the water by which we are baptized and the blood of Christ, of which it is a sign and signification, are not separated in place there in Baptism, but coexist together in these lands? Which not even the Papists themselves, the authors of both transubstantiation and consubstantiation, have dared to say.

Christ in the Holy Supper presented bread to the disciples, and at the same time gave them his body to be eaten. Therefore, in, under, and with that bread, the body of Christ itself is or was, and it was eaten by the very mouth of the body. R. If this is true, Christ must have clearly had a double flesh. One, which provided the bread itself to the disciples: and another, which entered into the mouth of those same disciples with the bread and perished in their belly.

<margin>Pag. 17.</margin> In the Holy Supper of the Lord, we announce his death in the way that the Apostles announced it in the first Supper of the Lord, and we have the same things that they had. Therefore, in the Supper of the Lord, the body of Christ really coexists and is consubstantiated in, under, and with the bread. R. Neither did the Apostles believe or eat the body of Christ in such a way that it was consubstantiated and joined with the bread: nor is the corporal presence of the flesh of Christ itself necessary for the commemoration of the death of Christ, which we are commanded to perform in the Holy Supper. For a commemoration is made of things that are distant from us in place and far away.
pages.30:
The sheep of Christ hear his voice: Faith does not doubt the truth and power of the divine word. Therefore, it must be believed simply that the bread is consubstantiated with the body of Christ. R. Where, I ask, does Christ speak of the consubstantiation of his body with bread, or is there any word of God regarding it? <margin>Pag. 18.</margin>

God is omnipotent. Therefore, the flesh of Christ is in, under, and with the bread of the Holy Supper. R. Why is it not conceded instead that he who is omnipotent can communicate his flesh to us, although it is in heaven, and bring this about by the power of his spirit? <margin>Pag. 19.</margin>

One must obey and believe God, although our reason (which is blind in divine mysteries) protests. Therefore, it must be believed, because Christ said of the bread, "This is my body," that the Body of Christ coexists with the signs of the Holy Supper in these lands. R. Not our human reason, but the voice of God himself and the Christian faith overturn this conclusion. For since the body of Christ is a true human body, since it has ascended into heaven, and since it will not descend from there until Christ comes to judge the living and the dead, it cannot be believed from the word of God that it is anywhere else than in that heaven. <margin>Pag. 20.</margin> <margin>Ephes. 4. Act. 1. Heb. 7.</margin>

The bread and wine of the Holy Supper are the Sacrament of the New Testament. Therefore, they are not figures and types. R. They are not types and figures of things to be in Christ, as the Sacraments of the Old Testament were of Christ who was to come: but they are sacraments of our Christ, both exhibited and having suffered, and signs and types of the fulfillment of the graces of God and heavenly promises exhibited in his flesh. There is one kind of merely spiritual eating of the flesh of Christ, which is discussed in John chapter 6: there is another which is sacramental, which was instituted in the Supper of the Lord. Therefore, the flesh of Christ itself in the sacramental eating is In, Sub, and With that Bread, and that Wine, by way of corporal presence: and together with the sign itself, it is taken by anyone approaching the Supper, even with an impure mouth. As if, indeed, although the sacramental eating has signs for the sake of teaching and supporting our infirmity, which a merely spiritual eating does not have, the thing of the Sacrament itself—namely, the flesh of Christ (which is one and the same in both, that is, in the spiritual and in the sacramental eating)—is eaten in this sacramental one by a different reason and with a different mouth than in that merely spiritual one.
