The Supper of the Lord was instituted a long time after that sermon of Christ concerning the spiritual eating of His flesh, Therefore the flesh of Christ itself is eaten in the Supper of the Lord with the mouth of the body. R. Osiander could certainly have just as well concluded: Therefore the flesh of Christ, which is given in the Supper of the Lord, is not the true food of our souls and the nourishment of eternal life, nor is His blood the drink of souls, since they are called so before the Supper of the Lord was instituted, and in that same sermon of Christ in John chapter 6, if the eating of the flesh of Christ is different, spiritual and sacramental. But who does not see how childish and poorly concluded these things are? Yet he adds, Christ, instituting His Holy Supper, said of the bread, This is my body, and of the wine, this is my blood. Therefore the flesh of Christ itself and the blood itself is really consubstantiated with the Bread and Wine of the Holy Supper. R. Christ did not say, My flesh is under this, In this, and With this bread, Therefore Osiander departs from the words of Christ and abandons the <term>rhetón</term> <gloss>literal word</gloss>. But what of it? If the words and the <term>rhetón</term> must be pressed, would not the Papists collect from these words even better, Therefore the Bread and Wine are transubstantiated into the body and blood of Christ? And yet here he seems to himself to triumph, because he concludes so poorly. And so, on pages 13, 14, 15, and 16, he sings his triumph at length, but he sees it already, unless he is completely dull, before the victory. Paul said,
pages.28:
The bread of the Lord’s Supper is a communion of the body of Christ: The chalice is a communion of the blood of Christ. Therefore Paul consubstantiates the body and blood of Christ with the bread and wine of the Lord’s Supper, so that it coexists by the mode of corporal presence, and the flesh of Christ itself is eaten by the mouth of the body. R. On the contrary, those words of Paul, communion of the body and communion of the blood, contain the proper meaning of those words of Christ, This is my body, this is my blood, and teach that it is sacramental. For they show that the signs themselves are not the flesh and blood of Christ itself, either transubstantiated or consubstantiated: but are pledges of our communion with Him, <term>sphragídas</term> <gloss>seals</gloss>, and sacraments. Just as the flesh of that victim, which had been offered by the sacrificers of old in the temple of God, was a symbol and pledge of the communion of the sacrificers themselves, both among themselves and with the flesh of Christ Himself.

That which Osiander himself later writes to be true, when he calls the chalice extended by the Lord the confirmation of the New Testament.

Irenaeus says in book 4, chapter 34, that the Eucharist consists of two things, the earthly and the heavenly. Therefore the flesh of Christ itself is really consubstantiated with the signs of the Supper. R. On the contrary, in that very place Irenaeus calls the Bread and Wine (which he says are offered in the Eucharist) signs and arguments. Therefore he also acknowledges them to be types and symbols. Which completely overturns this Consubstantiation of Osiander. Furthermore, the word 'consist' by no means signifies in Irenaeus the mode of corporal presence and coexistence, by which a spiritual thing occurs with signs in these earths: but the sacramental conjunction of the signified thing with the signs, since he does not speak there only of the signs
pages.29:
but speaks there of the whole Sacrament of the Eucharist.

The signs of the Holy Supper are joined with the signified thing because of the signification and promise of Christ. Therefore the sign and the signified thing are not separated from one another in place. R. What will Osiander say, Brothers, concerning the water of Baptism and the blood of Christ (which is the other Sacrament instituted for us by Christ Himself), will he not conclude the same? Therefore, the water by which we are baptized is not separated in place in Baptism from the blood of Christ, whose sign and signification it is: but they coexist together in these earths? This even the Papists themselves, and the authors of transubstantiation and consubstantiation, have not said.

Christ held out bread to the disciples in the Holy Supper, and at the same time gave them His body to be eaten. Therefore it is, or was, in, under, and with that bread, and was eaten by the mouth of the body. R. If this is true, Christ manifestly had a double flesh. One, which provided the bread itself to the disciples: and another, which entered into the mouth of the disciples themselves with the bread, and perished in their belly.

In the Holy Supper of the Lord we announce the death in the way in which the Apostles announced it in the first Supper of the Lord, and we have the same things which they had. Therefore in the Supper of the Lord, the body of Christ really coexists and is consubstantiated in, under, and with the bread. R. Neither did the Apostles believe that they were eating the body of Christ in such a way that it was consubstantiated and joined with the bread, nor is the corporal presence of the flesh of Christ itself necessary for the commemoration of the death of Christ, which we are ordered to perform in the Holy Supper. For commemoration is made of things that are absent in place and far from us.
pages.30:
Christ’s sheep hear His voice: Faith does not doubt the truth and power of the divine word. Therefore it must be simply believed that the bread is consubstantiated with the body of Christ. R. Where, I ask, does Christ treat of the consubstantiation of His body with the bread, or any word of God?

God is omnipotent. Therefore the flesh of Christ is in, under, and with the bread of the Holy Supper. R. Why is it not rather conceded that He who is omnipotent can communicate His flesh to us, although it is in heaven, and effect this by the power of His spirit.

We must obey and believe God, even if our reason (which is blind in divine mysteries) protests. Therefore it must be believed, because Christ said of the bread, This is my body, that the Body of Christ coexists with the signs of the Holy Supper in these earths. R. Not our human reason, but the very voice of God and the Christian faith overturn this conclusion. For since the body of Christ is a true human body, when He has ascended into heaven, and since He will not descend from there until Christ comes to judge the living and the dead, it can be believed from the word of God that it is not now elsewhere than in that heaven.

The bread and wine of the Holy Supper are the Sacrament of the New Testament. Therefore they are not figures and types. R. They are not types and figures of things to be in Christ, just as the sacraments of the Old Testament were for the Christ who was to come: but they are sacraments of our Christ who has been exhibited and who has suffered, and they are signs and types exhibiting the fulfillment of God’s graces and the heavenly promises in His flesh. For Irenaeus excellently teaches that in our sacraments the species is unchanged. Yet the character, signs, and arguments remain. But from this very fact, who will collect Transubstantiation more truly,
pages.31:
than Osiander’s consubstantiation, if there are no types in the sacraments of the New Testament? Finally, it will have to be denied that Baptism is a type of our spiritual regeneration. Indeed, the Apostle himself attributes <term>eikóna</term> <gloss>an image</gloss> to the Gospel and its sacraments: but <term>skiàn</term> <gloss>a shadow</gloss> of <term>mellóntōn agathōn</term> <gloss>future good things</gloss> to the Law and the Old Testament: so that the two testaments do not differ in that they have types, but in that the old had those of future things: but the new has those of exhibited things. Therefore, Osiander, those who acknowledge the sacraments of eternal life even under the New Testament, the Supper and the Baptism of the Lord, are not Judaizing. But they are clearly papizing who force consubstantiation upon us in place of Transubstantiation. But if the sacraments of the New Testament are sacraments and <term>Mystéria</term> <gloss>mysteries</gloss>, therefore they have <term>týpa, é antítýpa, é sýmbola</term> <gloss>types, or antitypes, or symbols</gloss>, namely signs instituted by Christ Himself, just as all pious and learned antiquity has spoken.

Sacraments, that is, signs of the New Testament, exhibit the very things which they promise. Therefore the flesh of Christ is in, under, and with the Bread of the Holy Supper. R. To exhibit is to be a pledge of a promise given and fulfilled by God, and to seal it in us. For otherwise we make the bread and wine themselves the channels and <term>ochémata</term> <gloss>vehicles</gloss> for delivering and communicating to us the body and blood of Christ: and thus we bind or include the promises of God to the signs themselves, or finally, we will have to believe that eternal life itself (which is fully promised to us by these signs) is given and conferred to us entirely here on these earths and in the very moment of celebrating the Holy Supper. Which is most false. But because he confuses many things afterwards

N.text:
the previous saying of Paul, that the Fathers nonetheless ate His flesh before the incarnation of Christ, must be erased. But because these things are true, you perceive, dearest brothers, how inept Osiander’s argument is. Another follows, no less invalid than that one, and yet repeated by him in almost countless places, both here and in his book against Sturmius.

There is one merely spiritual eating of the flesh of Christ, concerning which John chapter 6 treats: there is another sacramental one, which was instituted in the Supper of the Lord. Therefore, the flesh of Christ itself in the sacramental eating is In, Under, and With that Bread and that Wine by the mode of corporal presence: and is taken together with the sign itself by anyone approaching the Supper, even with an impure mouth. R. As if, indeed, although sacramental eating has signs for the sake of teaching and supporting our infirmity, which merely spiritual eating does not have, the thing of the Sacrament itself, namely the flesh of Christ (which is one and the same in both, that is, in spiritual and in sacramental eating), is eaten in this sacramental way by a different reason and with a different mouth than in that merely spiritual one. And that reason, or the mouth suitable for eating the flesh of Christ itself, is faith. What then? Osiander is mistaken, and indeed childishly so, in thinking that the flesh of Christ itself is one thing in spiritual eating, or is eaten as one thing, and another in sacramental eating. But if the flesh of Christ is the same, therefore it is received by the same mouth, with the same teeth, into the same stomach: namely, spiritually, not corporally: by faith, not by the mouth: by the spirit, not by the belly. For although sacramental eating has signs besides the spiritual (which are called the flesh and blood of Christ metonymically for the sake of the signification, and, as the Fathers say, the analogy), yet the flesh itself

pages.32:
<header>TO THE GALLICAN CHURCHES 29</header>
<sig>D3</sig>

Osiander, we shall gather the arguments scattered by him throughout his book.

A creature cannot be above the Creator, nor can it know things equal to the Creator. Therefore, one must simply believe that the body of Christ is consubstantiated with the bread. Answer. Why then is it not also transubstantiated? Yet you deny this.

These words of Christ, "This is my body," are also words of the Testament. Therefore, they are most simple and must be accepted <term>κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν</term> <gloss>according to the letter</gloss>. Answer. These words, "And they shall not teach each his neighbor, and each his brother," are words of the New Testament. Therefore, they must be interpreted <term>κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν</term> <gloss>according to the letter</gloss>, and we must cross over into the camp of the Anabaptists and abolish all Ecclesiastical ministry, because through it we are taught by our neighbor. <margin>Jer. 31. Heb. 8.</margin>

We have the body of Christ in the Holy Supper, not a shadow of the body. Therefore, the flesh of Christ is present corporally in, with, and under the bread of the Holy Supper. Answer. Our soul has the flesh of Christ present through faith, to which it truly and spiritually communicates; our body, eyes, and hands have the signs of a bodily presence which are currently present. Therefore, unless we confuse the thing with the signs, the flesh of Christ is not coexisting with the signs on this earth. Nor does faith require the mode of bodily presence in order to communicate the signified thing to us. Indeed, he who communicates spiritually and truly through faith to the flesh of Christ certainly does not have a shadow of Christ’s body, Osiander; rather, he has the very body of Christ himself and draws life-giving juice from it. But you do not think so, unless it happens on earth. But now, since Osiander could not contain himself, he descended to the omnipresence <note>original: "Ubique praesentiam"</note> of the flesh of Christ. For this had to be unearthed, even though from his own
pages.33:
<header>EPISTLE</header>

hidden and dissimulated [it] broke forth, so that finally the nature of this monster of Ubiquity might appear to you, dearest Brothers. He certainly hides this evil as much as he can with his words, but it is clearly seen from his very discourse. Therefore, he says thus:

*Christ as man received the spirit without measure, John 1. Therefore, the flesh of Christ is present everywhere.* Answer. The gifts which Christ received from the Father without measure as man do not overturn the nature of his human flesh and its essential properties. For otherwise, Christ would no longer have those gifts as man if he ceased to be man. Truly, if the human nature of Christ was present everywhere after receiving those immense gifts, [was] omnipotent, and so forth, as you wish, and equal to God, why does Christ confess that he is ignorant of certain things?

<margin>Matt. 24.</margin>
<margin>Pag. 27.</margin>

All power has been given to Christ as man. Therefore, his flesh is present everywhere. Answer. There is no consequence in created things from the power and authority of a person to their physical location. Nor does it follow that if the most invincible Emperor, who resides in Austria, has the right of imperial power in Speyer and exercises it, he is also at the same time in Speyer on the Rhine while he is in Vienna on the Danube.

The fullness of Deity dwells in Christ bodily. Therefore, Christ can station his flesh everywhere. Answer. The fullness of Deity dwells in Christ, that is, in that person who is called Christ; but the fullness of Deity does not dwell in the flesh itself. For the same one is truly God who is also man; yet humanity itself is neither Deity nor equal to it. For he himself says, "I will not give my glory to another." Therefore, it is neither present everywhere nor omnipotent. Wherefore, what is said truly and properly of the Deity of Christ cannot therefore be truly
pages.34:
<header>TO THE GALLICAN CHURCHES</header>

enunciated of his humanity. We confess that Christ, as he is God, can do all things; but because he can neither lie nor be contrary to himself, he does not wish to destroy his flesh, which he desires to have forever; and he who wishes it to be truly human and bodily flesh does not wish it to be non-human flesh. Yet this must necessarily follow if he were to station this flesh of his everywhere at the same time and at once.

The Son of God accomplishes his actions and operations through his assumed humanity, just as the soul in the human body performs its actions through its body. Therefore, since the Son of God works everywhere, his flesh must be present everywhere. Answer. First, Osiander rehashes the argument of the Apollinarian heretics and directs it against us in this place, [he] who attributes Deity to the flesh of Christ just as a soul [is attributed] to a body. Next, the very likeness of Osiander overturns the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ. For just as the soul, even though hypostatically united to the body, does not exercise all its operations through the body—such as meditating, reasoning, and the like—so too does the Deity of Christ not perform all its actions through his humanity, even after the union. Therefore, it does not conclude that it is present everywhere.

<margin>Pag. 28.</margin> Humanity assumed by Christ is one person with his Deity, and with it is hypostatically united. Therefore, wherever the Deity of Christ is, there also is his flesh or humanity. Answer. First, this man formerly took the presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper not from the hypostatic union, but from these words of Christ: "This is my body." Next, recognizing that this defense of his was weak, he abandons it and takes refuge in the hypostatic union,
pages.35:
<header>EPISTLE</header>
<meta>continues from previous page: or the omnipotence of God, because he sees no safe hiding places for himself. But let us lead him out from these very things, and let us now expose the <term>σοφὸν</term> <gloss>wise/cunning</gloss> <term>φάρμακον</term> <gloss>remedy/drug</gloss> of this man. *Flesh and Deity are hypostatically united in Christ.* Therefore, wherever this is, so is that. By the same method: The head and feet of the same man are hypostatically united to the <term>οὐσίαν</term> <gloss>substance</gloss> of one individual. Therefore, where the head of that man is, there also are the feet. Who would grant this? Furthermore, since the Deity is infinite, but the assumed flesh is finite, it is absolutely impossible that Deity and humanity be coextended in the person of Christ. They complain that we tear apart the one person of Christ, just as Nestorius used to do. But we deny this, unless perhaps they themselves are Eutychians, since we say that this hypostatic union of two natures in one person of Christ was made in such a way that not only did the natures themselves remain unconfused, but their essential properties also remained safe in that union, as the Council of Chalcedon excellently defined.</meta>

<margin>Pag. 29.</margin> *Christ as man can accomplish things that are impossible to any other creature. Therefore, he can station his flesh everywhere.* Answer. Since the power of Christ does not destroy his truth and mercy, and for our salvation he wishes that true human flesh which he assumed to remain united to him forever, he cannot destroy it because he cannot be a liar, because he cannot forget himself and his mercy.

*Christ said, Where two or three are gathered in my name, I am in the midst of them. Therefore, the flesh of Christ is everywhere.* Answer. It is not the flesh of Christ that is in their midst, but Christ by his Spirit and his power. For Christ said this, just as he also said this: "I am
pages.36:
<header>TO THE GALLICAN CHURCHES</header>
<sig>C. j.</sig>

with you even to the end of the age," not concerning the presence of the flesh, but concerning the presence of the Deity, power, and governance, which is done by the virtue of the Spirit of Christ, unless we wish to make Christ contrary to himself. That, however, in no way requires the bodily presence of his flesh. Nor does it follow that, although Christ spoke of his whole self—that is, God and man—*I am in the midst of them*, we must understand this to be of his whole self—that is, of any part or nature of his. For the same Christ says elsewhere, "The poor you will always have with you, but me you will not always have." Likewise, "I go to my Father." Likewise, "He has risen, he is not here." Therefore, it is said truly of the whole Christ—that is, of the person of Christ, who is both God and man—that Christ is with us even today: but not of the whole of Christ, just as Augustine excellently declares this very thing in his Letter to Dardanus; and after him, Damascene in Book 3 of *On the Orthodox Faith*. Yet when we say this, we do not divide, lacerate, or tear apart the person of Christ. For we neither say nor think that Christ is anywhere such that he is not both God and man. However, we certainly deny that his humanity and flesh are spread and diffused as widely or wherever his very Deity extends. For concerning Christ in the concrete, this is truly said: *I am with you even to the end of the age*, because this belongs properly to one of his natures: but concerning each of his natures in the abstract, it is not so; since being everywhere with his Church is a true and essential property of the Deity, which cannot in any way belong to or be communicated in reality to the humanity or flesh of Christ, or to any thing at all that is not God.
pages.37:
<header>EPISTLE</header>

nor can it be communicated in reality. But Osiander submits some other arguments for the ubiquity of the flesh of Christ, certainly no less inept than the former.

<margin>Pag. 31.</margin>
*Christ as man, ascending and exalted above all heavens, fills all things, i.e., all places; therefore with his own flesh.* Answer. Therefore, by your logic, Osiander, he also fills the very underworld and the devils with his flesh, if the word "fills" must be understood of the bodily presence of his flesh itself. And "all things" signifies all places. For you say it is manifest that the Apostle is dealing with the filling of all places, not the filling of Scripture. What more blasphemous thing could have been pronounced? Christ therefore fills all things, since, as Paul says, interpreting himself immediately in the same place, "he gave to his Church Doctors, and Pastors, and all other things which are necessary for the joining together of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ (that is, the Church)." Wherefore both the word "filling" must be understood of the virtue, efficacy, and governance of the Spirit of Christ, and the word "all things" must be understood of the Church of God, especially, and all things necessary for it to attain salvation. For by his powerful word (says the Apostle) he does not sustain all things by his flesh, because, having made purification of our sins, he sits at the right hand of the Father, and all power has been given to him in heaven and on earth.

<margin>Ephef. 4. verf. 12.</margin>
<margin>Heb. 1. Math. 28.</margin>

<margin>Pag. 32.</margin>
<margin>Ier. 23.</margin>
God fills all things, that is, every place (for he said, "Do I not fill heaven and earth?"), therefore the flesh of Christ fills every place.

Even after his ascension, Christ is present to his Church. Therefore, the flesh of Christ is corporally present to the Church.

<margin>Act. 7. & 23.</margin>
Christ, even after his ascension, was seen extraordinarily
pages.38:
<header>TO THE GALLICAN CHURCHES 35</header>
<sig>C. ij.</sig>

by Paul in Jerusalem, and by Stephen. Therefore, the flesh of Christ is truly on this earth. Answer. Who does not pity the stupidity of this man, dearest brothers, when one reads or hears these and such inept foundations of this Osiander's doctrine, which he nevertheless tries to foist upon you, and which, because we do not admit them, we are deemed by him to be neither sincere nor orthodox? But also, what follows, just like the former, is <term>ἀσυλλόγισον</term> <gloss>illogical/non-sequitur</gloss>.

<margin>Pag. 33.</margin> Christ's return on the last day of judgment is to be glorious. Therefore, the flesh of Christ is not in heaven today.
The flesh of Christ after his glorification is full of majesty. Therefore, it is everywhere. Answer. Christ gave glory to his flesh, he did not take away its nature. It would cease to be true flesh if it were everywhere. It would cease to be our mediator unless it remained <term>ὁμοούσιος</term> <gloss>consubstantial/of the same essence</gloss> to us, even in heaven itself, [being] glorious.

<margin>Philipp. 3. vers. 21.</margin>
Christ as man does not sit locally at the right hand of God. Therefore, the flesh of Christ is not in heaven as in a place, but is everywhere. Item: Christ as man sits at the right hand of God; the right hand of God is everywhere. Therefore, Christ's
<margin>Pag. 34.</margin> flesh is everywhere. Answer. As if sitting at the right hand of God and being the right hand of God were one and the same. For in the true sense of this phrase, a legate or general vicar of a King sits at the King's right hand; therefore, the vicar's person is everywhere his vicarious power, which he exercises, is. Who would ever grant this, when from power to the physical location and placement of a person in created things (which Osiander must confess the flesh of Christ to be, unless perhaps he is already a Schwenkfeldian) there is no consequence, as we taught above? And although he does not sit locally
pages.39:
<header>EPISTOLA</header>

Christ as man at the right hand of the Father, who is God and has no place; it does not follow, however, that Christ's flesh is not in heaven as in a place, since it is one thing for Christ's flesh to be in heaven, and another to sit at the right hand of the Father, which two things, however, Osiander confuses here as everywhere.

<margin>Pag. 35.</margin> Christ as man has power over all things. Therefore, the flesh of Christ is corporally present everywhere. Answer. We have sustained you too long, Osiander, [you who are] ignorant of all things. Why then do you judge the Gallican Churches, and the pious who are in them, to whom you write these things, to be stumps or logs, so that they cannot immediately smell these ineptitudes of yours, which reveal themselves openly to even the blind, not to mention those with weak eyes and barbers, by these arguments of yours?

Does the right hand of God not signify the circumference or circumscription of a place? Therefore, the flesh of Christ (which is at the right hand of God) is not to be established in any place by the circumscription of a place. Answer. You would truly say this if the flesh of Christ itself were the very right hand of God; even if there were a true and legitimate consequence from power to location and the "where" of a person. Therefore, you clearly confuse two articles of our faith: "he descended into heaven," which shows the place of Christ's flesh; and "he sits at the right hand of the Father," which declares his right and status in the very heavens.

<margin>Pag. 36.</margin> Christ fills all things in all. Therefore, the flesh is present everywhere. Answer. It is not by the presence of his flesh, but by the power of his Spirit, according to the efficacy of his virtue, that Christ fills all things, as we have already said.

That place of heaven where the flesh of Christ is cannot be demonstrated by fingers or eyes. Therefore, the flesh of Christ is not in heaven. These are the Achilles' arguments of this man

It would cease to be our mediator unless he remained <term>ὁμοούσιος</term> <gloss>consubstantial/of one substance</gloss> to us, glorious even in heaven itself.

*Christ the man does not sit locally at the right hand of God. Therefore the flesh of Christ is not in heaven, as in a place, but is everywhere. Likewise, Christ the man sits at the right hand of God; the right hand of God is everywhere. Therefore, Christ’s flesh is everywhere.* Answer. As if sitting at the right hand of God and being the right hand of God itself were one and the same thing. For from the true sense of this phrase, a legate or vicar-general of the King sits at the King’s right hand; therefore, the vicar’s person is wherever the vicarious power he exercises is. Who would ever concede this, when there is no consequence (as we taught above) from power to the location and placement of a person in created things (unless it happens that Osiander is perhaps a <term>Schwenkfeldian</term> <gloss>follower of Caspar Schwenkfeld, who held that Christ’s humanity was deified</gloss>)? And although he does not sit locally

<margin>Page 35.</margin> *The man Christ has power over all things. Therefore the flesh of Christ is everywhere bodily present.* Answer. We have endured your ignorance of all things for too long now, Osiander. What, then, do you judge the Gallican Churches, and the pious who are in them to whom you write these things, to be logs or stumps, so that they cannot immediately smell your ineptitudes, which betray themselves even to the blind, not to mention the bleary-eyed and the barbers, by these arguments of yours?

*The right hand of God does not signify a circumference or circumscription of place? Therefore, the flesh of Christ (which is at the right hand of God) is not to be established in any place by local circumscription.* Answer. You would say this truly if the flesh of Christ itself were the right hand of God itself! Even if there were a true and legitimate consequence from power to location and the "where" of a person. We confess that Christ, as he is God, can do all things; but because he can neither lie nor be contrary to himself, he does not wish to destroy his own flesh, which he wishes to have forever; and what he wishes to be truly human and bodily flesh, he does not wish to be non-human flesh. Yet this would necessarily follow if he stationed this flesh of his everywhere at the same time and simultaneously.

The Son of God accomplishes his actions and operations through his assumed humanity, just as in the human body the soul performs its actions through its body. Therefore, since the Son of God works everywhere, his flesh must be everywhere present. Answer. First, Osiander re-cooks and retorts against us in this place the argument of the <term>Apollinarian</term> heretics, who attribute the Deity to the flesh of Christ as the soul to the body. Next, Osiander’s very likeness overturns the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ. For just as the soul does not perform all its operations through the body even though it is hypostatically united to the body—such as meditating, reasoning, and the like—so also the Deity of Christ does not perform all its actions through his humanity, even after the union. Therefore, it does not conclude that it is everywhere present.

First, this man formerly took the presence of Christ in the Lord’s Supper not from the hypostatic union, but from these words of Christ, "This is my body." But what of those most robust arguments that we oppose to him regarding the Ascension of Christ into heaven, and the truth of Christ’s flesh even after its glorification? What of the fact that Christ <margin>Pag. 28.</margin> must be contained by heaven until the restoration of all things? He evades all those things with one word, saying that *Christ indeed, by reason of substance*, as he himself speaks—that is, of essence—assumed a flesh similar to ours; yet regarding the essential properties of that very flesh, he answers or concedes nothing. But unless Christ also assumed those properties, Osiander, he did not assume a flesh similar to ours. For it was said long ago, very truly, that he who removes the properties removes the natures. If, therefore, Christ assumed a truly human nature, similar to ours, and in doing so took on its essential properties and retains them in union with himself forever, it is necessary that Christ even now has flesh and bones. And that flesh must have its own certain circumscription, dimension, position, and condition—which is essential to every body and flesh—namely, that it is circumscribed by a certain and defined "where," or place, and cannot be in multiple places at once. For as to what you bring up concerning the glory of Christ’s flesh, we recognize that it resides in Christ’s flesh to a degree that even the celestial angels themselves cannot grasp in heaven, let alone us men on earth. Yet we do not recognize it as something that abolished the nature of flesh and body, but rather as something that adorned it. We recognize <term>ὑπερφυσικὰς</term> <gloss>supernatural</gloss> gifts or immense qualities in Christ’s flesh, but we concede that there are none in it that are <term>ἀνυποστατὰς</term> <gloss>unsubstantial</gloss>, that is, destructive of the nature of flesh, and entirely contrary to it.

And these, most beloved brothers, are all the minor arguments of that monitor who tries to lure you toward a new doctrine. You yourselves see by now, as I hope, how inept, absurd, <term>ἀσυλλόγιστα</term> <gloss>illogical</gloss>, and even blasphemous they are. A word to the wise is sufficient, as the old proverb says. Supper do not take the Lord’s flesh itself, but only those signs of the flesh and blood of Christ (which are called the body and blood of Christ sacramentally). These are not indeed simply bread and wine anymore, but bread and wine as sacraments, and most certain testimonies of God offering his immense gifts to them—gifts which those unworthy ones nevertheless spurn and despise. 

<margin>Pagina 38.</margin> Therefore, to that which Osiander asks, "what do the unworthy take in the Lord’s Holy Supper?" a simple answer is: they take the sacraments, that bread and that wine, the truest signs of the flesh and blood of Christ offered to them by God, but in no way accepted by them. But the unworthy do not take the flesh and blood of Christ itself. He asserts the contrary and teaches that the unworthy take the body of Christ joined together with the signs themselves, and that they eat both with their mouths. For he does not understand that that bread and that wine (which are offered to them as sacraments of the body and blood of Christ) are also called the body and blood by Christ. While he does not understand this, he strips Christ’s flesh itself of its life-giving virtue—that is, he strips the Sun itself of its light. But hear now what the arguments of this man are.

Christ in the Holy Supper offered the same thing to all to be eaten and drunk—that is, the same thing to Judas Iscariot and to John the Evangelist. Therefore Judas Iscariot took the same thing as John the Evangelist, albeit with a different result: Judas, namely, unto destruction; John, however, unto salvation. 

Answer: The sun offers its light to the blind, yet the blind do not see or enjoy that light. For just as the sight of the eyes is the sole instrument for enjoying solar light, so faith is the only mouth

and instrument for eating the true flesh and blood of Christ. For it is not food for the belly, but for the mind; nor is it taken by the mouth, but by faith; and spiritual things require spiritual instruments. Therefore, what is said by this man—that Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, took and ate the body of Christ itself, but unto his own destruction—is false. For the body of Christ is altogether life-giving to anyone who eats it. How, therefore, is the flesh of Christ unto destruction for anyone? When it is despised, not when it is taken and eaten. For it is death when despised, not when taken. Therefore, Judas took the bread of the Lord—that is, the sacrament and sign of the body of the Lord—but not the bread that is the Lord, that is, the true body of Christ himself, because it is always life-giving, as Augustine said excellently.

<margin>Pagina 39.</margin> *Christ called that very thing his body, which he gave to Judas Iscariot, and which Judas took. Therefore Judas took the body of Christ itself.* 

Answer: The bread itself, the sacrament, is called the body of Christ sacramentally, and the essential body of Christ is also called the body of Christ, but not sacramentally; rather, naturally. Therefore, these appellations are not to be confused, and what was said by Christ about the bread sacramentally is not to be understood about the body of Christ itself, which Osiander does here with great error.

*Because of men’s incredulity, the word of Christ does not become vain and ineffective. Therefore, even the unworthy take the body of Christ.* 

What do you say, Osiander? Do you say the word of Christ is ineffective, which, when despised by the unworthy, brings them death and eternal destruction? Therefore it is most effective, as you see, nor does it follow that if Christ always offers his body in the Holy Supper, and offers it to all, that all therefore receive it. Christ through his Gospel offers eternal life to all who hear it and understand the words; yet not all hearers of the Gospel obtain eternal life on that account. For faith is needed so that it may be received, which the unworthy lack; and it is one thing for something to be offered to us by another, and another thing for it to be accepted by us. Therefore, many things are offered to us that are repudiated by us.

*Because of the diversity of the guests, the substance of the food is not changed.* Therefore, even if the worthy and unworthy approach the Supper of the Lord, one and the same food is given to both. 

Answer: That which is not at all set before them is not eaten by the guests, Osiander, even if it is offered and proposed to be set before them. The true flesh of Christ is not set before anyone in the Holy Supper except to faith. Therefore, those guests who do not have faith have nothing but the bread and wine, the sacraments also set in the Supper. But just as the substance of this wine and bread is not the same as the true blood and flesh of Christ, so in the Holy Supper the sign and the thing signified are not truly set before all guests by Christ himself equally; although, so that it could be set before both equally, it was offered equally by Christ. But the worthy eat the thing signified most willingly; many things are often offered to their guests by a host and a feaster that the guests either do not want set before them, or, if set before them, do not touch or eat, but reject.

Paul says that the unworthy who take this bread of the Lord’s Supper eat judgment to themselves. But he who simply eats bread unworthily does not summon eternal destruction upon himself. Therefore, the unworthy in the Lord’s Supper do not simply eat bread, but also the body of Christ itself, joined together with the bread.

Answer: It is one thing to eat any bread unworthily, and another to eat *this* bread. For although every food is a gift of God, which ought to be taken with thanksgiving, yet, as Augustine says, he who eats this bread and this cup, the sacrament, like any other food indiscriminately and negligently, impiously despises the sacraments and the highest benefits of God. For when the sacraments are violated, he to whom they belong is himself violated, says Jerome. Therefore, since those who eat unworthily spurn and mock all the best benefits of God offered to them, it is no wonder if they take eternal destruction upon themselves, and yet eat only the bread—the sacrament—and not the thing of the sacrament, that is, the flesh of Christ itself.

*Good food can be taken by someone, yet it harms his stomach. Therefore, the body of Christ itself can also be taken by the unworthy.* 

Answer: Just as no food at all can be taken by someone who has no mouth, so neither can the true flesh of Christ be eaten by one who lacks faith. For faith is the only mouth for eating the true flesh of Christ, it is the stomach for receiving it, and it is the heat for digesting it.

<margin>Pagina 41.</margin>
*Food can be taken, and yet no substance or nourishment is taken from the food, as with the sick. Therefore, the body of Christ itself can be eaten by the unworthy, yet eternal life itself, which is the nourishment and substance of that flesh, or its other benefits, will not be perceived.* 

Answer: The flesh of Christ is nothing if not life and life-giving. It does not have, like these bodily and earthly foods of ours, one part of itself that is dead, material, and dross, and another that is vivid, vegetating, and life-giving. But it is whole, in whatever part of itself and by whatever touch, because it is the flesh of the only-begotten, and is enlivened by him, and is life-giving. Therefore, just as you could not grasp and hold a burning coal in any part of yourself without feeling its heat, so you could not in any way eat that flesh of Christ and have it within you without it immediately enlivening you. It is a wonder that Osiander, who elsewhere makes the flesh of Christ omnipotent and everywhere present, and full of divine majesty, and finally equal to God himself (except only that what the Godhead has from itself and as its own, the flesh of Christ has communicated and taken from another), would nevertheless, to protect his error, strip the same glorious flesh of Christ of its life and life-giving force, and thus be so self-contradictory. Which, however, can no more be done than stripping the body of the Sun of its light.

The Gospel is heard by some unto destruction. Therefore, the body of Christ itself is also eaten by the unworthy unto their destruction. 

Answer: The body of Christ is not eaten by the bodily mouth in the same way that the voice sounding the Gospel is heard by the bodily ear. For it is taken only by faith, not by the bodily mouth. Therefore, Osiander compares very difficult things here. Rather, that bread and that wine are sacraments of the Holy Supper to be compared with the external sound of the Gospel, which is heard only by the incredulous.

*The unworthy are said by Paul to be guilty of the body of Christ. Therefore, the unworthy receive the body of Christ.* 

Answer: The unworthy are said by Paul to be guilty of the body of Christ because they spurned receiving it, not because they received it. For as we have already said, it is the despised and rejected flesh of Christ—not the taken flesh—that makes us guilty.

Therefore, just as a son who refuses to accept the provisions kindly offered to him by his father, in contempt of the father and so that he may frequent a brothel, is guilty of contempt for the benefit of the father; so the unworthy are guilty of the body of Christ offered to them by Christ himself, but repudiated by them with an ungrateful spirit and through insult and impiety. 

These are the things, most beloved, that that smooth and supposedly benevolent monitor Osiander dared to write in order to suborn you and lead you away from Christ and his sincere doctrine. You all see what and how great an impiety and blasphemy are contained in them.

### ON BAPTISM.

He adds, however, certain other things as well, such as about Baptism, about Predestination, and about Idols. In these matters, because he reproaches both you and your zeal for propagating the kingdom of God, and also holds a doctrine in some points dissenting from the word of the Lord, we must deal briefly with him on these heads as well, so that no one might think that the doctrine of piety (which we have handed down to you from the word of God) is overturned by the arguments of this man. But we will pass over those things in which we clearly agree with him. 

Therefore, regarding Baptism, Osiander holds that which is manifestly erroneous (in which he accuses you, your pastors, of error because we teach otherwise): that he permits women, if extreme necessity demands it and no man is then present, to baptize the infant of Christians. Good food can be taken by someone to whose stomach it is harmful. Therefore the body of Christ itself can also be taken by the unworthy. Food can be taken, and yet no substance or nourishment is taken from the food, as in the case of the sick. Answer: The flesh of Christ is nothing but life and vivifying; it does not have, like these bodily and earthly foods of ours, one part of itself that is dead, material, and refuse, and another part that is vivid, vegetating, and vivifying. ### CONCERNING BAPTISM.

He adds, however, also some other things, such as concerning Baptism, Predestination, and Idols. In these, because he reproves both you and your zeal for propagating the kingdom of God, and also has a doctrine in some matters that dissents from the Lord’s word, we must deal with him briefly concerning these very points, lest anyone think that the doctrine of piety (which we have handed down to you from the word of God) is overturned by the arguments of this man. But what of those most robust arguments that we oppose to them, concerning the Ascension of Christ into heaven, and the truth of the flesh of Christ even after his glorification? What of the fact that Christ must be <margin>Page 28.</margin> contained by heaven until the restoration of all things? He evades all those things with one word: he says that *Christ indeed, by reason of substance* (as he himself speaks), that is, of essence, assumed flesh like ours; but he responds or concedes nothing concerning the essential properties of that flesh. Yet unless Christ also assumed those, Osiander, he did not assume flesh like ours. For it has long been said very truly that he who removes the properties, removes the natures. But if Christ truly assumed a human nature like our own, and in the same way assumed its essential properties, and retains them united to himself forever, it is necessary that even now Christ has flesh and bones, and that that flesh has its certain circumscription of dimension, and its situation and condition (which is essential to every body and flesh), namely that it is circumscribed by a certain and defined "where," or place, and cannot be in several places at the same time. For as to what you bring forward concerning the glory of the flesh of Christ, we acknowledge that there is in the flesh of Christ as much as not even the heavenly angels themselves can grasp in heaven, much less we humans on earth; yet not such that it destroyed the nature of flesh and body, but rather adorned it. For we acknowledge <term>ὑπερφυσικὰς</term> <gloss>supernatural</gloss> gifts or those immense in Christ’s flesh; but we concede that no <term>ἀνυποστατὰς</term> <gloss>unsubstantial, or destroying the nature of flesh</gloss>, and plainly contrary to it, exist in it.

The soul preserves the body through the harmony of qualities proportioned to human operations, and then it vivifies the body while those [qualities] remain; when they are destroyed, the soul withdraws, just as we see in putrefied limbs that must be cut away lest the whole body be infected. However, the soul does not lose any part of itself by the excision of any limbs of the body, but it ceases to vivify that part for the reasons already stated, because the soul is entirely in the whole body and entirely in every part, taking the whole categorically as an integral. Nor can this body, after the soul's departure, be vivified or made alive naturally, even if it were still in the body, unless it returns again to the primary principle of generation, just as it was in the womb through the decision of seed from the generator, and to the body organized through powers cut off from the generator. Although by divine power a soul once removed can be reunited to the same body, as in Lazarus, the young man restored to the widow, and Tabitha, just as the general resurrection will occur on the day of judgment. But someone might say that in many dying people, pain is not apparent, but they seem to die as if sleeping. That is true, because the pain is not seen by those standing around, but we do not know what is happening within, because the heart is the first to live and the last to die. And because the exterior limbs are partly deprived of strength and partly deprived of their operations, as the interior parts to which the blood flows [remain active], therefore the exterior parts remain desolate so that the tongue cannot cry out, the hands cannot palpitate, and the ears cannot hear, but all vital force remains in the heart. And if there were any way that the exterior limbs could be moved, we would see great signs of pain. Therefore the philosopher says: "The death of the aged is sweet," because they arrive at the final deprivation of strength and there is little resistance of nature in them, and as long as that can resist, the soul remains in the body. Therefore young people die more quickly.
pages.12: And those who languish for a long time also die with tranquility. From that I deduce that from a tranquil or heavy resolution, a good or bad state after this life cannot be elicited for the soul from the body, as some ignorant people argue, because death follows the disposition of nature by the law of all. But it is by divine dispensation. Sometimes saints die much more painfully than the reprobate, and sometimes conversely. For we read that Augustine and Bernard departed in heavy pain, and we also read of others who died in such tranquility that their bodies could not be buried, as Gregory narrates of a certain count who was thought to be very holy because, even when he had long rested in the tomb, he was known by the fragrance from his body and the integrity of the corpse. In the Lives of the Fathers, we read also of two spouses, a holy man and a wicked wife, whose husband died with great lack of tranquility and pain, but the woman passed away with great tranquility and peace. And afterwards, it was revealed that the husband was blessed, while the wife was condemned. For God purges the elect here so that they may be secure afterwards. Conversely, He rewards the reprobate here for their goods, so that in the future they have nothing to hope for regarding a reward, as it appears in Luke 16 concerning the rich glutton and the holy Lazarus. However, we believe that the blessed mother of the Lord, Mary, migrated from this age without pain, just as she gave birth to the Savior of the ages without pain. And similarly, John, to whom the Virgin was entrusted under the cross. And we find many of God's elect preserved from the pains of death by a special privilege. Therefore, he who desires to possess a peaceful resolution of his body should strive to keep his life in innocence, for a bad death, even if it is painful, does not follow a good life. But who leads the souls departing from the body, since they are no longer in their own power? It is necessary, therefore, that they be led by others. To this, although we do not find a certain answer in the scriptures, we can estimate that the angels to whom they are entrusted lead them out, or if they are to be damned, [they are led by] tartarean spirits, as the blessed Gregory reports in the fourth book of his Dialogues.
pages.13: As the blessed Gregory refers in the fourth book of his Dialogues concerning a certain rich man, Chrysoreus, who at the end of his life saw a multitude of most cruel demons around him on all sides, who were awaiting the departure of his soul in order to lead it to hell. Similarly, in the Lives of the Fathers, [it is written] of a certain hermit whose soul a certain tartarean spirit pulled out with an ignited trident. Christ expressed the bitterness of the dying when, in his prayer after supper in the garden, his sweat became as drops of blood running down upon the ground, Luke 22. Such is the anxiety in the dying person when he is about to arrive where he will remain perpetually, whether for good or ill, and he is ignorant of the part to which the definitive, irrevocable sentence will decline. But whether demons always show themselves to the dying, we cannot elicit answers from the scriptures. For in the life of Saint Martin, we read that a demon stood by the holy man when he was dying, whom Martin seeing, said: "Why do you stand here, bloodthirsty beast? You will find nothing in me, you fatal one." Gregory also in a certain homily seems to suggest that he was not absent from the dying Christ, upon that verse: "For the prince of this world comes, and in me he has nothing." And Bede seems to want the same, that Satan was not absent from [Christ] hanging on the cross. In other revelations, we also read how demons were seen present around the dying, as the same Gregory refers to the rich Chrysoreus, addicted to a secular and carnal life, who saw them assisting him from all sides and finally snatching his soul to hell. Their appearance is so horrendous, as those who have seen them report, that they would rather be cast into a furnace of burning fire than to look upon or gaze at them for the twinkling of an eye. How harsh it will be for the damned to burn forever with such [beings] in the fire! It seems, therefore, from the perversity of demons by common law, that they leave no one alone and allow no one to die untempted, unless divine clemency has reserved our fragility. They would even force themselves visibly, were they not prohibited by angelic protection.
pages.14:
As Cyril reports, writing to Augustine about Saint Eusebius, the disciple of the blessed Jerome, with what infestation they attacked him while dying, whom they were compelling to despair and deny God. Horrendous things are also read concerning three resurrected [people] at the death of Saint Jerome. Therefore, no remedy against demons around the dying appears more effective than the presence of devout persons in prayers and reading in a clear voice the passions of Christ from the gospels, and the symbols and the litany. Hearing these, the demons flee. As Gregory reports in a homily concerning a certain secular living in a monastery in a secular manner, who, when he had come to the hour of death, saw a dragon coming toward him and absorbing his head into its mouth. And he cried out to the religious brothers present, saying:
> Behold, I am given to the dragon to be devoured. Because of your presence, it cannot devour me. If I am given to it, why should I suffer delays because of you?
To whom the brothers [said]:
> Imprint the sign of the cross upon yourself.
To whom he [replied]:
> I want to, but I cannot, because I am bound by the dragon.
Then the brothers falling to the ground began to pray, so that the dragon retreated. Behold, the prayers of the devout around the dying are of much value. But therefore, after the soul's exit from the bodies, they will soon go to the particular judgment. It can be doubted to what place they are led to be judged. For it is not to be believed that all are led upward to heaven, awaiting the sentence there, especially the reprobate, and that soon after the sentence is received, it is pronounced toward hell. For the dignity of the place and the indignity of a perverse soul do not allow this to happen, but rather right reason. Thus also concerning souls to be purged, that they fall back from heaven to purgatory below. To this, it seems that it must be answered that just as any king in any part of his kingdom can justly claim a place of judgment for himself at his pleasure, so God, who is not encompassed by any place, can exercise the particular judgment of souls in any place whatsoever, unknown to us. Especially because this must be believed to happen in an instant, with consciences opened just as
pages.15:
books in which the hidden things of the heart will be manifest. Whence there will be room neither for excuse nor for interrogation, but only for hearing the sentence. Although the place of the general judgment is believed to be where Christ ascended, namely, in the valley of Jehoshaphat around the Mount of Olives, where Mary was also buried according to Jerome, as Joel 3 says. Yet it must be believed that the souls of the perfect will fly to heaven soon after the exit, according to that of Paul:
> I have a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.
Thus the souls of the infidels are soon snatched into hell without the judgment of discussion, for he who does not believe is already judged, bringing with him the sign of his damnation, his infidelity, as if not pertaining to God nor to his members. It is to be believed that all these things are administered by angels, whether good or bad. Although we read in many revelations how, after the exit of the souls, tribunals were disposed and ordered for the judge to pronounce the sentence against the souls brought [before him], and a great array of armies arrives there. But these visions are believed to have been made for the admonition of the living, who cannot perceive invisible things except through visible signs, as Gregory says in the fourth book of his Dialogues. O what unspeakable terror must then be believed to hang over the souls to be judged, seeing the most just judge and themselves guilty of many sins, and not able to excuse themselves! Where then it will be impossible to flee and intolerable to appear, and no counsel or help will remain for them except to hear the uncertain and irrevocable divine sentence of the most just judge. Then certainly it would have been better for many if they had not been born, or if they had been serpents or frogs. Would that that terror were impressed upon the hearts of mortals! They would not run so to prelacies, to dignities, and to pleasures, which then increase the account to be rendered to the judge. Many pontiffs, kings, and others constituted in dignities would then wish that they had been shepherds and keepers of sheep, or herdsmen, swineherds, and the lowest of all.
pages.16:
Whence Anselm says: "We live in great peril for our souls." And Augustine, in his book of Confessions: "There is still but a little light in Christians." He said this a thousand years ago. What would he say today if he were alive? We read of a certain Anthonian bishop who, brought to the judge, before he approached, said that he was most worthy of hell and begged that he not be presented to the judge. But alas, few heed this most terrible thunderbolt. Whence they not only sleep but are dead, and like drunkards, they do not wake up. Therefore the Church sings: "What am I, a wretch, to say or do, while I offer nothing good before such a judge? I have become trembling and I fear while the discussion approaches and the coming wrath." Therefore everyone should be advised to provide for himself in the time of grace while there is opportunity, according to that of John: "Brood of vipers, who will give you [the power] to flee from the coming wrath?" And let him hear the counsel of the same: "Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of penance," Matthew and Luke 3. O how horrendous it will be to fall into the hands of the living God, Hebrews 10. When the powerful will suffer torments powerfully, Wisdom 6. And a most strict judgment will be made for those who preside. This is concerning those who abuse dignities, namely, the ambitious, saving those who strive devoutly, usefully, and humbly to serve God in their states.

### Regarding the second point, namely, the receptacles of the souls that have departed.

It must be known that, according to the statements of doctors from the fourth book of the Sentences, four receptacles or places of souls are distinguished after this life, namely, three perpetual and one temporal. The first place is the empyrean heaven, which is the receptacle of the blessed, which is called paradise in the scriptures because of its clarity and joyfulness. The second place is hell, believed to be under the earth according to Gregory in the fourth book of his Dialogues, where demons, adult infidels, and perverse Christians dying here in mortal sin without penance are placed. The third is the limbo of children, as much of believers as of infidels, of those departing here without the sacrament of baptism, who are all judged by an equal lot. These indeed are to live there perpetually without sensible pain, but from the face of God
pages.17: they will be deprived, since they are punished for original sin alone with the pain of loss. Nor do they add any other actual sins. Their bodies ought not to be buried in consecrated cemeteries after death. The fourth place is the fire of purgatory, which many Greeks denied, but wrongly, for those who depart here without mortal [sins], or if they committed mortal [sins], they did penance but did not fully satisfy, or [those who died] with venial [sins]. And this has testimony from the holy scriptures. For Paul, 2 Corinthians 3, places three kinds of goods, namely, wood, hay, and stubble, which are consumed by fire sooner or later. Such will be saved, but so as through fire. And Christ says: "He who speaks a blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him in this age nor in the future." Therefore, there are some things to be forgiven in the future age, and not mortal [sins], therefore venial [ones]. Nor does this oppose that statement of Gregory in the fourth book of his Dialogues, and it is had transitionally in the Canon, Dist. 25: "As each one departs from here, such is he presented in judgment." For this [person] earned here that sins be forgiven him in the future. Which are greater or lesser is had in the canon, Distinction 25. The pain of purgatory is the same as the pain of hell, although the former has an end, the latter does not. But it is not doubted that the pain of purgatory is most bitter. Whence Augustine says in the aforesaid canon: "Although the fire, namely purgatory, is not eternal, it is in such a wondrous way afflictive [that] it exceeds every pain that anyone here has ever suffered or could suffer." And in the letter of bishop Cyril to Augustine, he says that he would rather experience any pain [than] suffer all the pain of this world which all men have suffered from Adam until the day of judgment, than to suffer the threat of those pains for one day. Therefore Richard says that a small pain voluntarily assumed here for sins liberates and satisfies for sins more than a great pain in purgatory when it is not simply voluntarily assumed but inflicted. And he alleges Al-Ghazali, 5th of Physics, chapter 4.
pages.18: who says that the pain of purgatory is an unspeakable torture. Concerning this, 4 Sentences, dist. 20. And how difficult it is to evade this purgatory can be pondered from one testimony of Christ. For he says in Matthew 12: "Of every idle word that men have spoken, they shall render an account in the day of judgment." Idle is that which lacks utility or necessity. And that it is difficult to avoid the least and venial [sins] and to perform full penance for mortal [sins] appears sufficiently in human interaction. In the fourth book of Gregory's Dialogues, he enumerates certain venial [sins], namely, constant idle speech, immoderate laughter, the sin of concern for household affairs which a man performs without blame, even by those who know how guilt should be declined, or not [knowing] in what things the error of ignorance [consists]. Whoever, I ask, does penance for these and similar things, or at least considers them to be sins? And yet it is necessary that fire will test such things. We know this magisterial rule: that no sin is dismissed without actual or habitual contrition, in general or in species, even a venial one. Contrition, however, requires pain for what was admitted and a purpose of not admitting [it] and of abstaining in the future. Let everyone consider whether in every venial [sin] these two things are present for him, namely, pain for what was admitted and a firm purpose of abstaining in the future. If these were always present to us, we would not relapse so quickly into what was previously dismissed. Hence it is now clear, the truth of that statement of Augustine: "No venial [sin] is so [minor] that it becomes mortal while it pleases." And it is had in the canon, dist. 25. This authority seems harsh, but yet correctly understood, it is true. And the force is to be placed in this word "pleases." For there is a twofold pleasing of man. One not repugnant to the divine will and pleasure, and Augustine did not intend the statement proposed above to be understood of this. In that way, those things that are of man and of the senses are pleasing, yet subject to reason, which soon yield when reason commands or divine law urges otherwise. And thus venial [sins] are pleasing, such as joking words, laughter, sleep, even immoderate, etc. The other is a pleasing against or above reason, or against the divine.

The powers being destitute, the soul cannot remain in the body for long, just as a harpist cannot play when the strings are destroyed. The body is prepared for another form through elemental qualities, namely putrefaction. The soul maintains the body through the harmony of qualities proportioned to human operations, and then it vivifies the body while those remain; once they are destroyed, the soul withdraws, just as we see in putrefied limbs that must be cut off lest the entire body be infected. Nor does the soul lose a part of itself by the excision of any limbs of the body, even if it loses a part of the body; rather, it ceases to vivify that part for the reasons already stated, because the soul is entirely in the whole body and entirely in each part, taking the whole categorically as a complete entity. Nor can this body, after the soul’s departure, be vivified or become living naturally, even if the soul were in the body, unless it returns again to the first principle of generation, just as it was in the womb through the separation of seed from the generator and to the body organized through virtues separated from the generator. Although, by divine virtue, the departed soul can be reunited to the same body, as in Lazarus and in the widow’s son and Tabitha, just as the resurrection will occur on the day of the general judgment. But someone might say: why does pain not appear in many who are dying, but rather they seem to die as if sleeping? That is true, because the pain is not seen by those surrounding them, but we do not know what is happening inside, because the heart is the first to live and the last to die. And because the exterior limbs are destitute of strength and are deprived of their operations as the interior parts to which the blood flows are, therefore the exterior parts remain desolate so that neither the tongue can shout, nor the hands palpitate, nor the ears hear; but the entire vital force remains in the heart. And if there were any way the exterior limbs could be moved, we would see great signs of pain. Therefore the philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> says: The death of the elderly is sweet, because they arrive at the final destitution of powers and there is little resistance of nature in them, and as long as that can resist, the soul remains in the body. Therefore, the young die with more...

The third is the limbo of children, both of the faithful and of the infidels, who depart here without the sacrament of baptism, who are all judged by an equal lot, who indeed are to live there perpetually without sensible pain, but of the face of God...
