pages.35: nor does it allow a man to remain in terror for long, as is evident in the case of the angel Gabriel to Mary, for he comforted her. The virgin trembled at the light, and Luke says, "Mary was troubled at his speech," and the angel immediately comforted her, saying, "Do not fear, Mary." Thus also Daniel, seeing the angel, was terrified, and immediately he was comforted, Daniel 10. So too Zechariah the priest, Luke 1. But the perverse spirit begins with gentleness and leads to terror, as is evident in Eve, who was not frightened by seeing the serpent speaking to her, but immediately had pleasure and delighted in it. Thus we read in Acts 10 concerning Cornelius the centurion, to whom an angel was sent. <margin>The 29th mode of discernment</margin> The second mode of discernment is by the visible form, according to the properties of visible things, for if it appears as a lion, bear, frog, black serpent, cat, or dog, or a black shadow, it is to be presumed that it is an evil spirit, just as it appeared to Eve in the form of a serpent. And as it is reported of those magicians to whom it appears in a horrible form, because God permits this so that man at first sight might shudder and detest it, whereas it would rather appear in a beautiful form if He allowed it. A good spirit, however, sometimes shows itself in the form of a dove or a human, as to Mary and the holy women on Easter Day and on the day of the Ascension of Christ in white garments, or in the splendor of the sun or light, or as a sheep or a lamb, etc. One must therefore have recourse to the attributes of those appearing things, and also of the sounds and voices that are heard, whether they are gentle, sweet, mild, modest, humble, charitable, pleasant, and sorrowful, such that they are not furious, turbulent, irritable, or otherwise cruel, infectious, or chiding, because charity is patient and kind, does not act in a puffed-up way, etc., as the Apostle says. The opposite properties and attributes befit perverse spirits, because their perversity cannot remain hidden for long, just as the property of a thing demonstrates the quiddity <gloss>essence</gloss> of the thing. And nothing feigned can remain hidden for long, as Tully <note>Cicero</note> says, but like a small flower, it will quickly fall. <margin>The 39th mode of discernment</margin> The third mode of recognizing or discerning is that which is derived from humility, just as Christ said to the Pharisees
pages.36:
tempting him whether it was lawful to pay tax to Caesar or not. "Show me," he said, "the coin of the tax." And they offered him a denarius having upon it the image of Caesar and the inscription with its fixed weight. This is for our proposition: "Whose is this image and inscription?" Certainly Caesar's. It must be noted, therefore, first whether that appearing spirit has the image of Christ, who is the truth, he himself being the witness: "I am the way, the truth, and the life." Which truth excludes all falsehood, vanity, and lies. If, therefore, it is found in this spirit that it mingles no falsehood, vanity, boasting of praise, or arrogance in its showing, it is to be presumed to be of a good spirit. But if in the opposite way, it is held suspect, just as in the temptation of Christ, Matthew 4, he suggested gluttony, vain glory, and avarice. And in the temptation of the first woman, he suggested the appetite for loftiness, saying, "You will be as God," and he swore, saying, "For God knows." For that spirit is a liar and the father of lies, nor did he stand in the truth, but is deceitful and fraudulent, and such things proceed from his heart even if he speaks the truth, as is evident in the Gospel where he is ordered by Christ to be silent even about the truth, because under it he hides deceitfulness.

<margin>The Fourth Mode</margin>
The fourth mode of discernment is if it is according to the superscription on the denarius, that is, apostolic doctrine and a teacher approved by the Church, so that there is nothing in the responses of that spirit or in its deeds that derogates from the faith, or from good morals and the rites of the Church according to canonical laws or the decrees of councils, or against the institutions of the holy Roman Church. And this is against heretics, beguines, <note>a movement of lay religious women, often subject to ecclesiastical suspicion</note> dreamers, augurs, diviners, and enchanters. The vessel of election, Paul, certifies this to us in Galatians 1: "But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel to you other than that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema." And the same says to the Hebrews at the end: "Do not be led away by various and strange doctrines." Concerning these errors and illusions
pages.37:
and the power of demons, I remember that I collected one treatise under that same theme, namely: "Various doctrines," etc. If, however, in dreams parents or known friends appear to someone through visions as if they were in the pains of purgatory, asking for suffrages <gloss>intercessory prayers</gloss>, as I have often heard happen, no harm follows if, with a pious intention, one arranges for some suffrages to be made in masses or alms, with the addition: "If it is a true dream; but if it is something vain, then let them be converted into the bosom of the Church or into the suffrages of other souls through the divine will." The fifth mode of discernment is if there is in its deeds, words, gestures, and morals the weight of humility, just as in the coin the weight is accustomed to be weighed, as if the weeping, groaning, complaint, petition, recognition of sins, or confession of guilt or pains are heard from it, or similar things, such that there is no glorying, boasting, domination, blasphemy, or detraction or cursing. For it must be believed that this spirit behaves in the manner of a beggar, who complains of his own defects, begging for aid and alms from the living, etc. And this is an index of good hope, and one should believe that this was permitted to him by a special grace from God, because perhaps he has no other consolation than the common suffrages of the Church, to whom God mercifully granted that he might also beg for special ones. For the virtue of humility, wherever it appears, cannot be without grace, the Scripture saying, "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." For from the proud, just as water from mountains, it is accustomed to flow down to the valleys of humility. And on the mountains of Gilboa, neither dew nor rain is accustomed to pour itself, 2 Kings 1. Other signs of the discernment of spirits could be found, but these five are sufficient for now. But I wish the pious reader to be warned of this: that those things which were said concerning ceremonies, persons, priests, places, times, or signs, prayers, masses, fasts, etc., I do not define as being always so necessary that never without them can there be a revelation or recognition of spirits, because
<margin></margin>
<note>Handwritten note: "Lintu mon" <gloss>Meaning unclear, possibly related to "lento monito" (slow warning)</gloss></note>
</margin>
pages.38:
and sometimes it can happen without them, as is evident when a departed spirit reveals itself to a living relative, or vice versa, a father to a son or vice versa, a mother to a daughter and vice versa, a brother to a brother, etc., without these aforementioned things. But where no other certainty can be obtained, and the apparition of a spirit is felt, there such a mode is probably believed to be observed. It is necessary, therefore, in this dark matter to proceed under a certain type and exemplarily, as Aristotle teaches in the first book of the Ethics, because demonstrations are not sought here, but from prayers and signs it is necessary to know the truth as much as one can. Nor is it even impossible that that spirit might also sometimes molest some by pulling their clothes, abstracting, slapping, etc., for this reason, that it might imprint belief in itself and make one attentive, so that one does not dissimulate and lightly pass over the vision, just as we read in the fourth book of the Dialogues of Gregory regarding the Bishop of Naruiensis, whose chaplain saw a vision and delayed informing him of it; therefore, he was gravely beaten for the third time until his body was bruised, and then he informed him of it. Thus we have experienced that to those known and to blood relations, and to those having knowledge of particular things, revelations have been made by the spirit concerning the restitution of justly acquired goods, concerning the construction of altars, hospitals, the execution of testaments, pilgrimages to the shrines of the saints for the sake of the fulfillment of vows, all of which were confessed, but not fully fulfilled through satisfaction. Because these and similar things, if they had not been confessed and washed away by previous prayer, there would be nothing to believe except that for mortal sin, punishment would be owed to such as these eternally. And according to Gregory in the Dialogue, it is very incautious to easily believe in the visions of dreams, for this reason, because the causes of them are difficult to know. And he puts there six causes of dreams:
<margin>Six causes of dreams</margin>
Either from the fullness or emptiness of the belly, which we experience daily in waking, or from thought, or from the illusion of demons, or from thought and illusion together, or from revelation, or from thought and revelation together, they are generated.
pages.39: The Scripture says, "Dreams have made many err, and they fell who hoped in them. You shall not use augury, nor shall you observe dreams," and many other cares follow dreams. From the Scriptures it is also evident that dreams were made by divine revelation, as is evident in Matthew 2, how an angel appeared in dreams to Joseph, saying, "Take the boy and his mother." And concerning Joseph the son of Jacob, Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, and Daniel. If anyone, therefore, lacks that grace given freely which is called by the Apostle the discernment of spirits, 1 Corinthians 12, he is often deceived in these revelations. This grace was not lacking to Mary, the mother of the Lord, and to the holy people named previously. But in later ages, such revelations or true visions rarely happen. The reason for which is assigned by the doctors: because God in past centuries, in the rights of the primary institution, namely the natural one, from the doctrines and arts derived from it, sufficiently provided for His faithful in those things which pertain to salvation, according to that saying of Job: "God speaks once, and a second time He does not repeat the same." For God now speaks through the Scriptures and the examples of the saints profusely, He who previously spoke through miracles and revelations. Therefore, He rebukes that official who was asking for a sign from Christ for the healing of his son, saying, "Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe," John 4. And elsewhere in the Gospel of Matthew: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign." And Saint Augustine, concerning the miracles of Holy Scripture, says: "Without necessity, one must not recur to miracles or revelations," bringing forward those of little faith who look to miracles. Therefore, Abraham said to that rich man in hell asking for miracles: "They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them," Luke 16. Nevertheless, sometimes God, ascending to human infirmity, out of the infinite abundance of His pity, reveals as it pleases Him, notwithstanding the aforementioned things. Therefore, in our times, miracles and revelations rarely happen and are precious, nor are they to be sought by
pages.40:
any faithful person where otherwise one can help oneself through the Scriptures and examples, so that the Scriptures do not become cheapened and so that faith may grow and so that we may be studious to revolve the Scriptures, Christ saying, "Search the Scriptures, because you think to have eternal life in them," John 5. One reads in the Lives of the Fathers concerning a certain saint who had the grace of miracles, but by no pact did he wish to use it. One time, the faithful, coming out of devotion to him, sought blessings from him. Among whom, a certain man brought a deceased boy, whom, together with others living, he placed at the feet of the elder not knowing him to be dead. After the elder blessed and prayed, the living rose, with the boy remaining dead lying on the ground. The elder thought he was alive and still seeking a blessing; he said to him, "Rise, son." Immediately the dead man rose and ran to his father. Thus, after the elder found out, moved, he said to the father that he should reveal this to no one, because he would by no means have resurrected him if he had known him to have been dead. ¶ It follows concerning the eighth [point], namely concerning the suffrages by which the souls released can be helped by the living. Since those souls are in that state in which they are not able to exercise penitential works, namely, they are not able to attend to fasts, prayers, alms, and the sacrament of the altar, but they carried with them things to be purged, namely wood, hay, or stubble, that is, venial sins to be purged sooner or later, God provided for them some remedy in the Church militant, since they departed in faith and love. Therefore, through the doctors, four kinds of suffrages are accustomed to be distinguished: namely, first, the immolation of the salutary victim in the sacrament of the altar; second, the distribution of alms; third, the instance of prayers; fourth, the maceration of fasts. To which four, all other things must be reduced, namely, pilgrimage, visitation of churches, the reception of the poor, the augmentation of divine worship. And according to this order, also the efficacy
<note>A red decorative initial 'E' starts the paragraph.</note>
pages.41: and the dignity of them is accustomed to be ordered, such that the oblation of the salutary sacrifice is worth much more than others, as Gregory testifies, 4 Dialogues, concerning a monk who revealed to his brother, by the name of Copiosus, three gold coins acquired from the art of medicine in his final sickness, and he repented. His brother presented them to Saint Gregory, who ordered them to be buried with him, not in the cemetery of the brothers but in the dung heap for the terror of the other brothers. After thirty days, Gregory said to the brother Copiosus, "Go, and study to offer for him for thirty days without interruption the sacrifice of the altar." Which being accomplished, that deceased brother appeared to Copiosus through a vision, and being asked how he was, he replied, "Now I am not badly off, but well, because today I received the absolution." And this was the thirtieth day on which his brother celebrated for his soul. And thus it was known that the deceased escaped the punishment through the salutary host. Nor perhaps was that delay of days a necessity, because I believe that if thirty masses had been celebrated in one day for his soul, it would have been liberated. And from there, the custom grew in the Church that trentals <gloss>a series of thirty masses</gloss> are accustomed to be procured by friends for the dead. Therefore, it seems entirely expedient for the souls of the deceased that testaments, restitutions, masses, alms, and prayers be paid out as quickly as possible for a more swift release from the pains, because the sooner, the better. Whence, in the fourth book of the Sentences, doctors ask whether the deceased feels damage from the delay of testaments or alms instituted by him. And the answer stands in this: as far as the essential reward, which consists in charity, the souls of the deceased feel no damage, but as far as the accidental reward, namely as to the more swift liberation, they feel great damage, namely, the pains by which they are afflicted before the payment. For if they had the whole world in the possession of the soul while existing in punishment, they would most readily give it to the poor so that they could redeem themselves from the pains for even one single hour
pages.42:
and could see their Creator. And therefore their pain is most grievous, as was said, namely both because of the delay of glory and because of the sensation of pain, which most bitterly acts upon the soul separated from the body. In the same place, Gregory puts many other visions in which he proves that the souls of the deceased are helped through the immolation of the salutary sacrifice. And he says that this victim offered for them profits those who, while living here, obtained that good works done here for them by others after death also help them. But he says that those who choose a more healthy and safe path are those who, while they live, do for themselves what they hope will be done for them by others after death. For it is surely more blessed to liberate oneself than to seek freedom after chains. For that which is offered after death is considered as a dead oblation, but that which is given by a living person is as a living oblation and is much more pleasing to God. For we read in the life of Saint Edmund the Bishop that a body of a certain rustic was being carried to the church, and before the bier, one ox was being led, offering it for the soul of the deceased. This being known, the holy bishop said, "If that deceased person had given the yoke in which that ox pulled for the sake of God while he lived, it would have been much more useful to his soul than that he offers the whole ox alive to God after death." Therefore, those executors of testaments, to whom the execution of testaments has been committed, sin greatly if they delay to execute the last will of the testator, who in the meantime always sustains pain, unless the delay was made so that a richer recompense might follow from it. It would be best, therefore, not to delay. But concerning the short or long delay that the souls of the deceased are forced to spend in purgatory, I think no one can know unless it has been revealed by God or by the souls themselves. Nor does this fall under human art, but solely divine. It is not to be doubted, however, that God, who disposes all things in number and weight and regulates by measure, has established a certain time for every soul. We read in the revelations of a man deceased and resurrected, and after the profession dying again, that he had been in purgatory for forty years.

Therefore, in our times, miracles and revelations rarely occur and are precious, nor are they to be sought by any faithful person where one can otherwise help oneself with the Scriptures and examples, so that the Scriptures do not become cheap, and so that faith may grow, and so that we may be studious in revolving the Scriptures, Christ saying: Search the Scriptures, for you think in them to have eternal life, John 5. I read in the Lives of the Fathers concerning a certain saint who had the grace of miracles, but he did not wish to use it under any pact. At a certain time, the faithful, coming out of devotion to him, sought blessings from him. Among them, a certain man brought a deceased boy, whom he placed together with the others living at the feet of the elder, who was ignorant that he was dead. After the elder blessed and prayed, the living rose up, with the dead boy remaining lying on the ground. The elder thought that he was alive and still seeking a blessing, and said to him: Rise, son. Immediately the dead boy rose and ran to his father. Thus, after the elder found out, he was moved and said to the father that he should reveal this to no one, because he would by no means have resurrected him if he had known he had been dead.
pages.40: <note>An ornamental red initial letter E marks the beginning of this paragraph.</note> It follows concerning the eighth point, namely concerning the suffrages by which souls that have departed can be aided by the living. Since those souls are in that state in which they are not able to exercise penitential works, namely to attend to fasts, prayers, alms, and the sacrament of the altar, but have carried with them things to be purged, namely wood, hay, or stubble—that is, venial sins to be purged sooner or later—God provided for them regarding some remedy in the Church militant, since they departed in faith and love. Therefore, through the doctors, four kinds of suffrages are accustomed to be distinguished: namely, first, the immolation of the salutary victim in the sacrament of the altar; second, the distribution of alms; third, the urgency of prayers; fourth, the maceration of fasts. To which four, all other things are reduced, namely pilgrimages, the visitation of churches, the reception of the poor, and the augmentation of divine worship. And according to this order, the efficacy and dignity of them are accustomed to be ordered, such that the offering of the salutary sacrifice is worth much more than the others, as Gregory testifies in the fourth book of the Dialogues concerning a monk who, having acquired three gold pieces from the art of medicine in his final illness, revealed this to his brother in the name of being copiously guilty and repented. His brother presented them to Saint Gregory, who ordered them to be buried with him, not in the cemetery of the brothers, but in the dung heap for the terror of the other brothers.
pages.41: After thirty days, Gregory said to the brother of the deceased: Go, and study to offer without interruption the sacrifice of the altar for him for thirty days. Which being finished, that deceased brother appeared to the one who was guilty through a vision, and being asked how he was now, he replied: Not badly, but now I am well, because today I have received the transition. And this was the thirtieth day on which his brother celebrated for his soul. And thus it was known that the deceased escaped the punishment through the salutary host. And perhaps that delay of days was not of necessity, because I believe that if thirty masses had been celebrated in one day for his soul, it would have been freed. And hence in the Church the custom has grown that trentals are accustomed to be procured by friends for the dead. Therefore, it seems entirely expedient for the souls of the deceased that testaments, restitutions, masses, alms, and prayers be paid out as quickly as possible for a speedier rescue from the pains, because the sooner, the better. Whence, in the fourth book of the Sentences, the doctors ask whether the deceased feels loss from the delay of testaments or alms instituted by him. And the answer stands in this: Regarding the essential reward, which consists in charity, the souls of the deceased feel no loss, but regarding the accidental reward, namely regarding the speedier liberation, they feel a great loss, namely the pains by which they are afflicted before the settlement. For if they had the whole world in their possession, being in the punishment of the soul, they would most readily give it to the poor so that they might redeem themselves from the pains for even one single hour.
pages.42: and could see their Creator. And therefore their pain is most grievous, as was said, namely because of such a delay of glory and because of the sensation of pain which acts most bitterly upon the soul separated from the body. In the same place, Gregory puts forth many other visions in which he proves that the souls of the deceased are aided through the immolation of the salutary sacrifice. And he says that this victim offered for them benefits those who, while living here, obtained that good deeds done here by others for them might aid them even after death. But he says that those choose a healthier and safer way who, while they still live, do for themselves the good they hope will be done for them by others after death. For it is surely more blessed to liberate oneself than to seek liberation after the chains. For what one offers after death is deemed as a dead offering; what is given by a living person is as a living offering and is much more pleasing to God. For we read in the life of Saint Edmund the Bishop that he was carrying the body of a certain rustic to the church, and before the bier, an ox was being led, being offered for the soul of the deceased. Having learned this, the holy Bishop said: If that deceased person had given while he was living the yoke in which that ox pulled for the sake of God, it would have been much more useful to his soul than that he offers the whole living ox to God after death. Therefore, the executors of testaments sin greatly to whom the execution of testaments has been left, if they delay in executing the last will of the testator, who in the meantime always sustains pain, unless the delay was made so that a more abundant compensation might follow from it. It would therefore be best not to delay. But concerning the short or long delay that the souls of the deceased are compelled to spend in purgatory, I think no one can know unless it has been revealed to him by God or by them themselves. Nor does this fall under human art, but only divine. Nevertheless, it is not to be doubted that God, who disposes all things in number, weight, and measure, has most regularly set a certain time for every soul. We read in the revelations of a man deceased and resurrected and dying again after his profession that he had spent forty years in purgatory.

N.text:
and the power of demons, I remember that I collected one treatise under this same theme, namely: Diverse doctrines, etc. If, however, in dreams parents or known friends should appear to someone through visions as if they were in the pains of purgatory asking for suffrages, as I have heard it said occurs often, no inconvenience follows if, with a pious intention, one arranges for some suffrages to be made in masses or alms with the addition: If this is a true dream. If, however, it is something vain, then let them be converted into the bosom of the Church or into the suffrages of other souls through the divine will. The fifth mode of discerning is if there is in its deeds, words, gestures, and morals the weight of humility, just as in a coin the weight is accustomed to be grasped, as if lamentation, groaning, complaint, a petition for the recognition of sins, or a confession of guilt or of pains is heard from it or similar things, such that there is no glorying, boasting, nomination, blasphemy, or detraction or cursing. For one must believe that this spirit behaves in the manner of a beggar, who complains of his own defects while begging for subsidies and alms from the living, etc. And this is a sign of good hope, and one may believe that this was permitted to him by a special grace from God, because perhaps he has no other consolation except the suffrages of the common Church, to whom God has mercifully indulged so that he might also beg for special ones. For the virtue of humility, in whomever it appears, cannot exist without grace, the Scripture saying: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. For just as water is accustomed to flow down from mountains to the valleys of humility, and on the mountains of Gilboa neither dew nor rain is accustomed to pour itself out, 2 Kings 1. Other signs of the discernment of spirits could be found, but these five are sufficient for now. But I wish the pious reader to be informed that those things which were said above concerning ceremonies, persons, priests, places, times, or signs, prayers, masses, fasts, etc., I do not define as being always so necessary that revelation or the knowledge of spirits never occurs without them, because

X.text:
and sometimes it can happen without them, as it is clear that the souls of the deceased reveal themselves to their own living relatives or vice versa, father to son or vice versa, mother to daughter and vice versa, brother to brother, etc., without those aforementioned things. But where no other certainty can be had, and the apparition of a spirit is felt, there such a mode is probably believed to be observed. It is necessary, therefore, in this shadowy matter to proceed under a certain type and exemplarily, as Aristotle teaches in the first book of Ethics, because demonstrations are not sought here, but it is necessary to know the truth as much as one can from conjectures and signs. Nor is it even impossible that that spirit might sometimes molest some by pulling hair, removing clothes, slapping, etc., for this reason, so that he may imprint credibility upon himself and make him attentive, so that he does not dissimulate and pass over the vision lightly, just as we read in the fourth book of Gregory’s Dialogues concerning the Bishop of Narni, whose chaplain saw a vision and delayed in informing him; therefore, he was grievously beaten for the third time until his body was bruised, and then he informed him of it. Thus we have experienced that revelations have been made to acquaintances and blood relatives and those having knowledge of particular matters through a spirit concerning the restitution of justly acquired property, concerning the obstruction of altars, hospitals, and the executions of testaments, and pilgrimages to the thresholds of the saints for the fulfillment of vows, all of which are believed to have been confessed, but not totally fulfilled through satisfaction. For these and similar things, if they had not been confessed and washed away by previous petition, it should not be believed otherwise than that for mortal sin, such a penalty would be due eternally. And according to Gregory in his Dialogue, it is very incautious to believe easily in the visions of dreams, for this reason: because it is difficult to know their causes. And he sets down there six causes of dreams:
<margin>Six causes of dreams</margin>
Either from the fullness or emptiness of the belly, which we experience in daily waking, or from thought, or from the illusion of demons, or from thought and illusion together, or from revelation, or from thought and revelation together, they are generated.

pages.51:
Therefore, descending so that the benevolent reader may find me acceptable, wishing to escape these future punishments, let him learn from the mirror of those who have already gone before what he himself ought to do. And first, let him restore all things unjustly acquired, content with necessities alone according to his station. Then, let him choose such a state of living without great cares, one which is removed from the dignities, riches, and common offices of this world, because these can scarcely or never be administered without sin. Next, let him make himself as alien as possible from the actions of the world, attending only to himself and his own, renouncing the superfluous pomps of this world, associating himself with the company of the righteous, and frequently intent upon the reading of sacred scriptures and preaching. Then, let him frequently recur to the fountain of penance, namely contrition and painful confession, together with satisfaction. For through these, sins are especially blotted out by the virtue of the keys committed to priests, and I say not only the guilt, but also the penalty, as Christ says in John 20: "Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you shall retain, they are retained." For priests do not only show that sins are forgiven to those who confess, as some would have it, which others might also do from the signs of contrition, but they also remit the sins themselves by the virtue of the keys. In which keys the passion of Christ operates. The priest receives these keys in the reception of holy orders. But according to the statements of the doctors in their writings upon the fourth book of the Sentences, distinctions 18, 19, and 20, a threefold key is distinguished, namely the key of authority, which belongs to Christ alone as the principal agent in the sacrament, as God, and this is communicable to no creature, just as the divine essence is not. And through this key, God alone remits sins, just as He alone can confer grace and glory. And this may be called the key in form, as is said in the Apocalypse, which God alone has, and He opens to the sinner who is dead in sins as if in hell, when God grants him grace
<margin>Precepts by which one arrives at those penalties</margin>
pages.52: so that he may arise from sin. He shuts, however, when he withdraws grace from those who exalt themselves by their demerits. There is another key of excellence which Christ has as man, and such a one He could communicate to ministers or priests, who are dispensers of the mysteries of God. And the priests use that key of ministry received from Christ in the administration of the sacraments of the New Testament. And thus the truth is preserved in both; that is, God alone remits sins by the key of authority, and priests by the key of ministry. This is the summary of blessed Thomas in the third part, question 84, article 1 and 4. To which Thomas of Argentina agrees in the fourth book, distinction 18. And he puts forward the example of a prince who has the principal authority of opening and shutting a castle or a city; yet by this he does not exclude the gatekeeper to whom he has entrusted the keys. He puts forward another example: an Emperor grants to his officials the power to punish evildoers, but if they ask for pardon and do this or that, he releases them and sets them free; there the officials have the power of ministry, the prince the power of excellence. So it is with Christ and the priests. Christ has the key of excellence insofar as He uses this key immediately by the merit of His most sacred passion, by this not excluding the ministry of the priests. Therefore He said, "Whatsoever you shall bind upon earth, shall be bound also in heaven." Therefore, in confession, much guilt is remitted, and also penalty. And if it is objected that the entire guilt is remitted in contrition, therefore the priest does not remit any; it is answered that there is no true and sufficient contrition without a firm purpose to show it, according to the definition of contrition, since the commandment of God and the tradition of the Church bind one to confession. Also, if it is said that venial sins are remitted through the sprinkling of holy water and through general confession, etc., it is answered according to Saint Thomas that this is with regard to guilt by reason of the annexed contrition, not with regard to the entire penalty. Because it is necessary always to add something
pages.53:
with regard to the penalty. Let him who suffers also not distance himself from escaping the pains of purgatory through the distribution of alms, and let him not refuse to receive Lazarus begging in his house, whom if that rich man placed in hell had received, he could have been saved. For Tobias says: "Alms deliver from all sin and from death, and will not suffer the soul to go into darkness" (Tobias 4). Also, before all things, let such a one follow the doctrine of Saint Paul to the Romans 12: "I beseech you that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God." Which host is then offered to God when we have studied with pure knowledge to extirpate vices, to restrain passions and concupiscences, refraining the exterior senses from illicit things, exercising ourselves in the roughness of life in fastings, prayers, vigils, hard beds, coarse garments, and other corporal afflictions. Concerning which holy sacrifice of our body, Gregory says in the end of his Dialogues: "Let us burn the hardness of the mind in tears; let us form the grace of kindness for our neighbors." And I say confidently that we shall not need the salutary host, namely the body of Christ, after death if, before death, we shall have been a host to God ourselves. By no means, or rather even in the highest degree, do true indulgences granted by Roman pontiffs and others having authority avail for the pains of purgatory, concerning which I supersede for the present, and they are wont to be treated by theologians upon the fourth book, distinction 20. There follows the <note>Red decorative initial I</note>
exclamation of the author of this treatise, desiring to bring something from the poverty of my meager knowledge to benevolent readers by way of lament and medicine. I seem to say to myself with the Apostle to the Romans 9: "I speak the truth in Christ Jesus our Lord, I lie not, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost, that I have great sadness and continual sorrow in my heart." And he, indeed, was lamenting the turning away of the Jews from the faith of Christ, which they refused
pages.54: while adhering to the legal ceremonies of Moses, which they preferred to Christ. Whence also he says afterwards: "Blindness in part has happened in Israel." In our age of this century, however, a great blindness has happened in an innumerable multitude of Christians who, alas, are found more bestial than the beasts. Yet I do not wish this to be understood of all. For the beasts provide for themselves against the future, preventing losses and pursuing conveniences, as is evident in ants, in cranes, in wild geese, which, with the approaching roughness of winter, either flee cold places or collect food for themselves in caves and caverns; this is by instinct of nature. Rational men, not ignorant of future winter penalties, either eternal or most bitter temporal, with open eyes wish to foresee nothing to prevent them, thinking the name of faith alone suffices them for salvation. Concerning whom Paul says: "They profess that they know God, but in their works they deny Him." We read of Saint Jerome, by his own testimony, that when he was intent upon secular letters and was rapt in his dreams, he was asked who he was; he answered, "I am a Christian." And he heard, "You lie; you are a Ciceronian, not a Christian." And being grievously scourged, he abjured that he would henceforth no longer read such letters. Oh, would that it could now reach many Christians to be asked, and the answer could be given: "You are not a Christian, but a pagan." For many are found whose conversation differs little from the loves of pagans, who worship idols made by hand. But they have exchanged that idolatry for avarice, which according to the Apostle is the service of idols. And they worship as many idols as there are types of avarice, although any pagan might stand intent upon one idol. And I seem to say with probability: if today there were idols giving responses, and relieving poverty, and conferring riches and dignities, we would see how many Christians, having abandoned God, would follow the idols. The name of a true Christian, according to Augustine, is a name of justice, piety, truth, hu
pages.55: mility, meekness, patience, mercy, chastity, and fraternal charity. Where these are not, a feigned name of Christianity is borne. For it is the custom for a name to be imposed on things by the work, such as smith or shoemaker. From previous revelations, many things could be gathered concerning how the judgment of God proceeds differently from that of men; for many are thought to be such before men as they are not before God, whose judgment is true. We can also prove this by this: a most pure revelation is reported, made in the city of Paris, flourishing then as now with solemn study, concerning a certain most famous doctor, and his wondrous fame had spread far and wide, conspicuous in life and doctrine, on the occasion of which the celebrated Carthusian religion took the principles of its first institution under the habit of that man, in the time of Master Bruno. This doctor, therefore, being removed from human affairs, and his body kept for three days on a bier before a multitude of people, on the first day cried out with a terrible voice: "I am accused by the just judgment of God." On the second day: "I am judged by the just judgment of God." On the third day: "I am condemned by the just judgment of God." And who of the living would have believed this of such a celebrated and glorious man, had it not shone forth by a divine voice? Where are now those who say: "It suffices for a Christian to keep the commandments for salvation"? Who could have believed that this such solemn doctor had kept the commandments? But dig into the wall and you will find other things inscribed in the heart than the commandments described on the tablets of Moses. How often does Paul say in his epistles: "They who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God"? It is certain that every mortal sin is against the divine command. And who can enumerate all mortal sins, and especially those concluded with deliberation by the heart alone, even if they never come to light? Once Moses called heaven and earth against those whom he knew would desert God, truly to vengeance and for a testimony
pages.56: because he was setting before them the penalties they were about to suffer for their sins. For He will arm the creatures in vengeance upon His enemies. And who today is of so little experience that he is ignorant of the way of God? The earth is filled with the knowledge of God. And yet all who are called say: one, "I have bought a farm," that is, I am tending toward the master through pride, "have me excused from supper." Another says, "I have bought five yoke of oxen," that is, I insist upon the heats of avarice with all my strength. The third says, "I have married a wife," that is, I am occupied with carnal pleasures; therefore I cannot come. In these three kinds of vices, almost the whole world suffers a precipice, because a thick cloud of carnal desires and earthly solicitudes makes the reason darken so that it cannot see where it is going. We have fallen into times, indeed, in which men flee harsh things, seek delicate things with all their intention, and to obtain these, they do not fear to undergo even hard things; they would be happier, indeed, if they did not fear to undergo these for eternal delights. We certainly see how many storms of wars, even unto the effusion of blood, are raging in different parts of the world for the sake of temporal things alone, either to be acquired or to be preserved, and not for the sake of defending the Catholic faith. In what kingdom or province, I ask, is the tranquility of peace preserved for a long time? All these lead their origins either from pride or from avarice, so much so that the dove sent forth from the ark, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, seeking a place on the earth where it might fix its foot, cannot find it because of the excessive mud and mire of earthly passions, just as once in the time of Noah. Truly, the unhappy times have returned that were before the captivity of the sons of Israel in Babylon, when God sent many prophets to warn them that, having left the idols, they should follow the God of their fathers, through them predicting to them horrible captivities, which they disdained to hear, but rather mocked and turned them into a song of fools in their mockery
pages.57: as is said in Ezekiel 33. Moreover, they even killed them. For as the Psalm says (128), when the holy prophets threatened the sons of Israel with future penalties, they mocked them, saying: "Command, command again, wait, wait again, a little here, a little here." As if they were saying: "Multiply commandments, wait for the execution of penalties, and so a little truth follows." Afterwards, however, through experience they felt the truth, when they were led captive in chains. Thus in our times, when many hear the horrible threats of eternal penalties, they do not see them and take them for a game. If they would wait a little, experience would give understanding to their hearing. Nevertheless, the truth should not be passed over in silence, even if it is not heard gladly by many. For divine speech will find sometime where it may rest. For a certain wise man says that while a wolf is hunting many sheep, he preys upon one. Nor will the reporter of truth lack his reward, by the testimony of Jerome, who says in a certain epistle: "He who invites an Ethiopian to the bath, even if he does not wash the darkness from him, either receives payment for himself, or, even if he does not rejoice in his whiteness, he certainly rejoices in his own gain." So, without doubt, he who warns those disobedient to divine sermons, even if he does not take away the sins of the resister, will acquire a reward for himself from the ministry of charity, by the testimony of Christ who says in Luke 10: "If the son of peace be not there, your peace shall return to you." If the most holy Augustine, this most celebrated theologian, were living, and saw the state of the current time, and contemplated human studies, and especially in the sublimity of those constituted both in spiritual and secular affairs, he would not only say as he said in his lifetime, "As yet there is a little light in Christians," but perhaps he would say, "Almost all the light in the multitude of Christians is extinguished." And a certain holy woman who was frequently rapt in her mind is read to have said: "If the wisest men in the world could see how many souls
pages.58: descend daily into hell, they would be more than the sand of the sea, numbered, and more than the pebbles of the shores along the sea, and infinite souls descend into hell as if they were dead." Who will not tremble hearing this, since no one knows if he is worthy of hatred or love? With whom the poet agrees: "The descent into Avernus is easy." And Seneca: "The sentence of the ancients commanded nothing other than what was to be done and what was to be avoided, and then men were far better. After learned men appeared, good men ceased." For that simple and open truth has been turned into an obscure and cunning science, and we are taught to dispute, not to live. Thus he. How true this is, the daily studies of men declare. And this is affirmed by the apostolic sentence and doctrine, which teaches us to live soberly, justly, and piously in this world, not to expend all our care in this brief space of time on syllogistic disputations, or the tables of Alfonso, or the motions of the planets, but [to consider] how we might be able to render an account to God in a strict examination, since it seems foolish to allege these things then. And when it proceeds to the pains of fire, then all disputation ceases. All those who read of the resurrected, they abandoned the world for vile penance and hid themselves in cloisters, leading an austere life, showing themselves to us as an example, but having few imitators. These things, written in a rude style as much as I was able, not as much as I wished, with certainty of charity and the truth I have estimated, I humbly offer to all benevolent and clearer readers to be amended and limited, ready to yield to clearer truth to which I have not presumed. I set forth in these many revelations read by me, piously believing that the writers of them had not lied, concerning which similar or even greater things, the blessed Pope Gregory did not fear to recount in his Dialogues for the edification of men, asking pardon for prolixity or superfluity, charity instigating me to this. For which may God be blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

pages.35: and it does not permit a person to stand long in terror, as is evident in the case of the angel Gabriel to Mary, for he comforted her. The virgin trembled at the light, and Luke says, "Mary was troubled at his word." And immediately the angel comforted her, saying, "Do not fear, Mary." Thus also Daniel, seeing the angel, was terrified and was comforted by the Lord (Daniel 10). So also Zechariah the priest (Luke 1). But a perverse spirit begins with lightness and leads to terror, as is evident in Eve, who was not frightened by seeing the serpent speaking to her, but immediately felt pleasure and flattered it. Thus we read in Acts 10 about Cornelius the centurion, to whom an angel was sent. <margin>29th mode of discernment</margin> The second mode of discernment is by the visible form, from the properties of visible things; as if it appears as a lion, bear, frog, black serpent, cat, or dog, or a black shadow, it is to be presumed that it is an evil spirit, just as it appeared to Eve in the form of a serpent. And as it is reported of necromancers to whom it appears in a horrible form, because God permits this so that man, at first sight, might shudder and detest it, when it would rather appear in a beautiful form if He permitted it. A good spirit, however, sometimes shows itself in the form of a dove or a human, as to Mary and the holy women on the day of Easter and on the day of the Ascension of Christ in white garments, or in the splendor of the sun or light, or a sheep or a lamb, etc. It is necessary, therefore, to have recourse to the attributes of those appearing things and also the sounds and voices that are heard, whether they are gentle, sweet, mild, modest, humble, charitable, pleasant, and sorrowful, such that they are not furiously turbulent, irritable, or otherwise cruel, infectious, or chiding, because "charity is patient and kind; it is not provoked" etc., as the Apostle says. Opposite properties and attributes belong to perverse spirits, because their perversities cannot be hidden for long, just as the property of a thing demonstrates the essence of the thing. Nor can anything feigned remain hidden for long, as Tully <note>Cicero</note> says, but like a small flower it will soon fall. <margin>39th mode of discernment</margin> The third mode of recognizing or discerning is that which is drawn from humility, just as Christ said to the Pharisees
pages.36:
testing him as to whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not. "Show me," he said, "the coin of the tribute." And they offered him a denarius having upon it the image of Caesar and the inscription with the determined weight. This is to our purpose. "Whose is this image and inscription?" Certainly Caesar's. It is to be noted, therefore, first, whether that appearing spirit has the image of Christ, who is truth, by his own testimony: "I am the way, the truth, and the life." Which truth excludes all falsity, vanity, and lies. If, therefore, it is found in this spirit that it mingles no falsity, vanity, boastful praise, and arrogance in its manifestation, it is to be presumed to be a good spirit. If, however, in the opposite way, it is to be suspected, as in the temptation of Christ (Matthew 4), he suggested gluttony, vain glory, and avarice. And in the temptation of the first woman, he suggested the appetite for greatness, saying, "You will be as God." And he swore, saying, "For God knows." For that spirit is a liar and the father of lies, nor did he stand in the truth, but is deceitful and fraudulent, and such things come out of his heart even if he speaks the truth, as is evident in the Gospel, where he is commanded by Christ to be silent even about the truth, because under it he hides deceitfulness.

<margin>Fourth Mode</margin>
The fourth mode of discernment is if it is according to the inscription on the denarius, that is, apostolic doctrine and a teacher approved by the Church, so that there is nothing in the responses of that spirit or in its actions that derogates from the faith, or from good morals and the rites of the Church according to the canon laws or the decrees of the councils, or against the institutions of the holy Roman Church. And this is against heretics, beguines <note>likely referring to the Beghards or heretical groups of the time</note>, summists, augurs, diviners, and enchanters. The vessel of election, Paul, certifies to us to the Galatians 1: "But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel to you other than that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema." And the same says to the Hebrews at the end: "Do not be led away by various and strange doctrines." Concerning these errors and illusions
pages.37:
and the power of demons, I remember that I collected one treatise under the same theme, namely: "Various doctrines," etc. If, however, in dreams parents or known friends appear to someone as if they were in the pains of purgatory, asking for suffrages, as I have often heard happen, no harm follows if, with a pious intention, one arranges for some suffrages to be made in masses or alms, with the addition: "If this is a true dream." If, however, it is something vain, then let them be converted into the bosom of the Church or into the suffrages of other souls through the divine will. The fifth mode of discernment is if there is in its deeds, words, gestures, and morals the weight of humility, just as in a coin the weight is accustomed to be grasped, such as if weeping, groaning, complaint, petition, recognition of sins, or confession of guilt or pains are heard from it, or similar things, such that there is no glorying, boasting, ominousness, blasphemy, or detraction or cursing. For it must be believed that this spirit behaves in the manner of a beggar, who laments his own defects, begging for subsidies and alms from the living, etc. And this is a sign of good hope, and by some special grace he believes this is permitted to him by God, because perhaps he has no other consolation except the common suffrages of the Church, to whom God has mercifully indulged so that he might also beg for special ones. For the virtue of humility, wherever it appears, cannot be without grace, the Scripture saying, "God resists the proud, but to the humble he gives grace." For it is not from the proud, just as water is not accustomed to flow from mountains to the valleys of humility. And on the mountains of Gilboa, neither dew nor rain is accustomed to pour itself (2 Samuel 1). Other signs of the discernment of spirits could be found, but these five suffice for now. But I wish the pious reader to be cautioned that I do not define those things that I have said concerning ceremonies, persons, priests, places, times, or signs, prayers, masses, fasts, etc., as always being necessary, such that a revelation or knowledge of spirits would never happen without them, because

<margin></margin>
<note>Handwritten marginal note in Latin: "Lintu mon" <gloss>Meaning unclear; potentially a fragment or abbreviated reference.</gloss></note>
</margin>
pages.38:
and sometimes it can happen without them, as it is open that the spirit of a deceased person reveals itself to a living person or vice versa, father to son or vice versa, mother to daughter and vice versa, brother to brother, etc., without these aforementioned things. But where no other certainty can be had, and the apparition of a spirit is perceived, there such a mode is probably believed to be observed. It is necessary, therefore, in this shadowy matter, to proceed under a certain type and exemplarily, as Aristotle teaches in the first book of Ethics, because demonstrations are not sought here, but from occurrences and signs one ought to know the truth as much as one can. Nor is it impossible that that spirit might also sometimes molest some by pulling hair, removing clothes, slapping, etc., for this reason, that it might imprint credibility in itself, and make him attentive, so that he does not dissimulate and lightly pass over the vision, as we read in the fourth book of Gregory’s Dialogues concerning the Bishop of Narbonne, whose chaplain saw a vision and delayed informing him, therefore he was gravely beaten for the third time until the bruising of the body, and then he informed him. Thus we have experienced that to those known and related by blood, and to those having knowledge of particular matters, revelations have been made by the spirit concerning the restitution of justly acquired goods, concerning the obstruction of altars, hospitals, the execution of wills, pilgrimages to the thresholds of the saints for the fulfillment of vows, all of which were confessed but not totally fulfilled by satisfaction. For if these and similar things had not been confessed and washed away by the aforementioned prayer, one would have to believe nothing else than that for mortal sin such a penalty was due to them eternally. And according to Gregory in the Dialogues, it is very incautious to believe easily in the visions of dreams, for this reason, because the causes of them are difficult to know. And he puts there six causes of dreams:
<margin>Six causes of dreams</margin>
Either from the fullness or emptiness of the stomach, which we experience in daily life, or from thought, or from the illusion of demons, or from thought and illusion together, or from revelation, or from thought and revelation together are they generated
pages.39: The Scripture says: "Dreams have made many err, and they failed who hoped in them." "You shall not use augury, nor shall you observe dreams," and many other cares follow dreams. From the Scriptures it is also evident that dreams have been made by divine revelation, as is evident in Matthew 2, how an angel appeared in dreams to Joseph, saying, "Take the child and his mother." And concerning Joseph, the son of Jacob, Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, and Daniel. If anyone, therefore, lacks that grace freely given which is called by the Apostle the "discernment of spirits" (1 Corinthians 12), he is often deceived in these revelations. Which grace was not lacking to Mary, the mother of the Lord, and to the saints previously named. But in later ages such revelations or true visions rarely happen. The reason for which is assigned by the doctors: because God in past ages, in the laws of the primary institution, namely the natural [law] from doctrines and arts deduced from it, sufficiently provided for His faithful in those things which pertain to salvation, according to that of Job: "God speaks once, and does not repeat the same a second time." For God now speaks abundantly through the Scriptures and the examples of the saints, who formerly spoke through miracles and revelations. Therefore, He rebuked that nobleman who asked for a sign from Christ in the healing of his son, saying, "Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe" (John 4). And elsewhere in the Gospel of Matthew: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign." And St. Augustine, in *On the Miracles of the Holy Scripture*, says: "Without necessity, one must not recur to miracles or revelations," bringing [to task] those of little faith who look to miracles. Therefore, Abraham said to that rich man in hell, who was seeking miracles: "They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them" (Luke 16). Nevertheless, sometimes God, condescending to human infirmity, from the infinite abundance of His piety, reveals as it pleases Him, notwithstanding the aforementioned. Therefore, in our times, miracles and revelations rarely happen and are precious; nor are they to be sought by
pages.40:
any faithful person where otherwise one can help oneself by the Scriptures and examples, so that the Scriptures do not become cheap, and so that faith may grow, and so that we may be studious in revolving the Scriptures, Christ saying: "Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life" (John 5). One reads in the *Lives of the Fathers* of a certain saint who had the grace of miracles, but by no means wished to use it. At a certain time, the faithful, coming out of devotion to him, sought blessings from him. Among them, someone brought a deceased boy, whom he placed with the other living ones at the feet of the elder, the elder not knowing him to be dead. After the elder blessed and prayed, the living ones arose, the boy remaining dead lying on the ground. The elder thought that he was alive and still seeking a blessing, and said to him, "Arise, son." Immediately the dead one arose and ran to his father. After the elder found out, he was moved and said to the father that he should reveal this to no one, because by no means would he have resurrected him if he had known him to have been dead. ¶ It follows concerning the eighth point, namely concerning the suffrages by which souls having departed can be helped by the living. Since those souls in that state are in a condition in which they are not able to exercise penitential works, namely fasting, prayers, alms, and to attend to the sacrament of the altar, but have brought with them things to be purged, namely wood, hay, or stubble—that is, venial sins to be purged sooner or later—God provided for them some remedy in the Church Militant, since they departed in faith and love. Therefore, through the doctors, four kinds of suffrages are accustomed to be distinguished: namely, first, the offering of the saving victim in the sacrament of the altar; second, the distribution of alms; third, the urgency of prayers; fourth, the maceration of fasts. To which four all other things must be reduced, namely pilgrimages, the visitation of churches, the reception of the poor, the augmentation of divine worship. And according to this order, also the efficacy

<note>A red decorative initial letter E at the beginning of the paragraph starting "Erquo ille anime..."</note>
pages.41: and dignity of them are accustomed to be ordered, such that the oblation of the saving sacrifice prevails much over others, as Gregory testifies in the fourth book of his *Dialogues* concerning the monk who had hidden three gold coins acquired from the art of medicine in his final illness, and revealed and repented it to his brother, which his brother reported to St. Gregory, who ordered them to be buried with him, not in the cemetery of the brothers, but in the dunghill for the terror of the other brothers. After thirty days, Gregory said to the brother of the deceased: "Go, and study to offer for him the sacrifice of the altar for thirty days without interruption." Which being accomplished, that deceased brother appeared in a vision to his brother, and being asked how he was, he responded: "Not badly, but I am now well, because today I received my liberation." And this thirtieth day was that on which his brother celebrated for his soul. And thus it was known that the deceased escaped punishment through the saving host. Nor perhaps was that delay of days a necessity, because I believe that if thirty masses had been celebrated for his soul on one day, he would have been liberated. And thence in the Church the custom has grown that a trental <note>a series of thirty masses</note> is accustomed to be procured by friends for the dead. Therefore, it seems entirely expedient for the souls of the dead that wills, restitutions, masses, alms, and prayers be paid as quickly as possible for a speedier liberation from pains, because the sooner, the better. Whence in the fourth book of the *Sentences*, the doctors ask whether the deceased feels loss from the delay of wills or alms instituted by himself. And the response stands in this: As far as essential reward is concerned, which consists in charity, the souls of the dead feel no loss; but as regards accidental reward—namely, as regards speedier liberation—they feel a great loss, namely of the pains with which they are afflicted before the payment. For if they had the whole world in their possession, being in punishment, they would most readily give it to the poor so that they could redeem themselves from their pains for even one hour
pages.42:
and could see their Creator. And therefore their pain is most grievous, as has been said, namely as much on account of the delay of glory as on account of the sensation of pain, which acts most bitterly upon the soul separated from the body. In the same place, Gregory puts many other visions in which he proves that the souls of the dead are helped through the oblation of the saving sacrifice. And he says that this victim offered benefits those who, by living here, obtained that good works done here by others for them might also help them after death. But he says that they choose a healthier and safer way who, for the good which they hope to be done for them after death by others, do it themselves while they live. For it is surely more blessed to liberate oneself than to seek liberty after the bonds. For what one offers after death is deemed like a dead oblation, but what is given by a living person is like a living oblation and is much more pleasing to God. For we read in the life of Saint Edmund the Bishop that a body of a certain rustic was being carried to the church, and before the bier one ox was being led, offering it for the soul of the deceased. Having known this, the holy bishop said: "If that deceased person had given for God the yoke in which that ox pulled while he lived, it would have been much more useful to his soul than to offer the whole living ox to God after death." Therefore, the executors of wills, to whom the execution of wills has been left, sin much if they delay executing the last will of the testator, who meanwhile always sustains pain, unless the delay was made so that a richer recompense might be expected to follow from it. It would therefore be best not to delay. But concerning the short or long delay that the souls of the dead are forced to spend in purgatory, I think no one can know unless it has been revealed to him by God or by the souls themselves. Nor does this fall under human art but only divine. Yet it is not to be doubted that God, who disposes all things in number, weight, and measure, has established a certain time for every soul most regularly. We read in the revelations of a deceased and resurrected man, and one dying again after his profession, that he had been in purgatory for forty years.
