Therefore, in descending <note>meaning: in concluding or summarizing my argument</note>, so that the benevolent reader may regard me with favor, let him who wishes to escape these future pains learn what he himself must do by looking into the mirror of those who have suffered them. And first, he must restore all things unjustly acquired, remaining content only with what is necessary according to his station. Then, let him choose a manner of living without great cares, which is remote from the dignities, riches, and common offices of this age; for these are scarcely or never managed without sin. Then, let him make himself as alien as possible from the acts of the world, attending only to himself and his own, renouncing the superfluous pomps of this world, associating himself with the company of the righteous, and being frequently intent upon the reading of the Holy Scriptures and sermons. Then, let him frequently recur to the fountain of penance—namely, contrition and painful confession—with satisfaction. For through these, sins are chiefly blotted out by the virtue of the keys committed to priests, and I say not only the guilt, but also the penalty, Christ saying in John 20: "Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose you shall retain, they are retained." For priests do not only show that sins are forgiven to those who confess, as some wish to argue—which others could also do from the signs of contrition—but they also remit the sins themselves by the virtue of the keys. In these keys, the passion of Christ operates. The priest receives these keys in the reception of holy order. But according to the words of the doctors in their writings upon the fourth book of the Sentences, distinctions 18, 19, and 20, a triple key is distinguished: namely, the key of authority, which belongs to Christ alone as the principal agent in the sacrament, as God, and this is communicable to no creature, just as the divine essence is not. And through this key, God alone remits sins, just as He cannot communicate the power to confer grace and glory to anyone. And this can be called the key of heaven, as it is said in the Apocalypse, which God alone has, and He opens to the sinner who is dead in sins as if in hell, when God grants him grace

<margin>Precepts by which one arrives at those penalties</margin>
pages.52: that he may rise from sin. He shuts, however, when he withdraws grace from those who exalt themselves by their own demerits. Another is the key of excellence, which Christ has as a man, and such a key He could communicate to ministers or priests, who are dispensers of the mysteries of God. And the priests use that key of ministry received from Christ in the administration of the sacraments of the New Testament. And thus the truth is preserved in both: that is, God alone remits sins by the key of authority, while priests do so by the key of ministry. This is the summary of blessed Thomas in the third part, question 84, article 1 and 4. Thomas of Argentina agrees with this in the fourth book, distinction 18. And he places the example of a prince who has the principal authority of opening and shutting a castle or a city; yet by this he does not exclude the porter to whom he has entrusted the keys. He places another example: an Emperor gives his officials the power to punish evildoers; if they seek pardon, and he does this or that, he sets them free. There, the officials have the power of ministry; the prince has the power of excellence. Thus it is regarding Christ and the priests. Christ has the key of excellence insofar as He uses this key immediately by the merit of His most sacred passion, by this not excluding the ministry of the priests. Therefore He said: "Whatsoever you shall bind upon earth, it shall be bound also in heaven." Therefore, in confession, much guilt is forgiven, and also the penalty. And if it is objected that all guilt is forgiven in contrition, therefore the priest does not remit any—it is answered that there is no true and sufficient contrition without a firm purpose to show it, according to the definition of contrition, since the precept of God and the tradition of the Church bind one to confession. Also, if it is said that venial sins are forgiven by the sprinkling of holy water and by general confession, etc., it is answered according to Saint Thomas that this is so regarding the guilt by reason of the annexed contrition, but not regarding the whole penalty. Because it is always necessary to add something
pages.53: regarding the penalty. Let him who grieves to escape the pains of purgatory not distance himself from the giving of alms, and let him not refuse to receive the beggar Lazarus into his house; for if that rich man, placed in hell, had received him, he could have been saved. For Tobias says: "Alms deliver from all sin and from death, and will not suffer the soul to go into darkness" <note>Tobit 4:11</note>. Furthermore, above all, let such a one follow the doctrine of Saint Paul to the Romans, 12: "I beseech you that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God." That sacrifice is then offered to God when we have studied with pure knowledge to extirpate vices, to restrain passions and concupiscences, by refraining the exterior senses from illicit things, and by exercising ourselves in the austerity of life through fasts, prayers, vigils, hard bedding, garments, and other corporal afflictions. Of this holy sacrifice of our body, Gregory says in the end of the <term>Dialogi</term> <gloss>Dialogues</gloss>: "Let us melt the hardness of the mind in tears; let us form the grace of kindness toward our neighbors." And I confidently say that we shall not be in need of the saving sacrifice, namely the body of Christ, after death, if before death we have been a sacrifice to God ourselves. Not at all; indeed, even most especially, true indulgences granted by the Roman pontiffs and others having authority are valid for the pains of purgatory, regarding which I supersede for the present, and they are usually treated by theologians upon the fourth book, distinction 20. There follows the <note>A red decorative initial 'I' appears here.</note> <term>R</term> <note>A red decorative initial 'Q' appears here.</note> Exclamation of the author of this treatise, desiring to bring something to my benevolent readers from the poverty of my own penury by way of lament and medicine. I seem to say to myself with the Apostle to the Romans, 9: "I speak the truth in Christ Jesus our Lord, I lie not, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost, that I have great sadness and continual sorrow in my heart." And he indeed was lamenting the aversion of the Jews from the faith of Christ, which they refused
pages.54: adhering to the legal ceremonies of Moses, which they preferred to Christ. Whence also he says later: "Blindness in part has happened in Israel." In our age, however, a great blindness has happened in an innumerable multitude of Christians who, alas, are found to be more beastly than beasts. I do not wish this to be understood of all, however. For beasts provide for themselves against the future, preventing harms and pursuing benefits, as is evident in ants, in cranes, and in wild geese, which, when the harshness of winter approaches, either flee to warmer places or gather food for themselves in caves and caverns. This is by the instinct of nature. Rational men, not ignorant of the future pains of winter, whether eternal or most bitter temporal ones, with open eyes do not wish to look at anything to prevent them, thinking that the name of faith alone suffices for salvation. Of whom Paul says: "They profess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny him." We read of Saint Jerome, by his own testimony, that when he was intent upon secular letters and was rapt in his dreams, he was asked who he was; he answered, "I am a Christian." And he heard, "You lie; you are a Ciceronian, not a Christian." And being grievously scourged, he swore he would not read such letters henceforth. Oh, would that this inquiry might now touch many Christians; it could be answered, "You are not a Christian, but a pagan." For many are found whose conversation differs little from the loves of pagans, who worship idols made by hand. But they have exchanged that idolatry for avarice, which, according to the Apostle, is the servitude of idols. And they worship as many idols as there are kinds of avarice, although every pagan stands intent upon one idol. And I seem to say with probability: If there were idols today giving responses, relieving poverty, and conferring riches and dignities, we would see how many Christians, having abandoned God, would follow idols. The name of a true Christian, according to Augustine, is the name of justice, piety, truth, hu-
pages.55: mility, meekness, patience, mercy, chastity, and fraternal charity. Where these are not, the name of Christianity is borne falsely. For a name is customarily given to things from their work, such as 'smith' or 'cobbler.' From previous revelations, many things could be gathered concerning how the judgment of God proceeds differently from that of men; for many are thought by men to be such as they are not before God, whose judgment is true. We can also prove this by this event: A most purgative revelation occurred in the city of Paris, flourishing then as now with solemn study, concerning a certain most famous doctor, and his marvelous reputation had spread far and wide, conspicuous in life and doctrine. On the occasion of which, the famous Carthusian religion took the principles of its first institution under his habit—I wish I were worthy to hide beneath it—in the time of Master Bruno. This doctor, therefore, being removed from human affairs, and his body being kept on a bier for three days before a multitude of people, on the first day cried out with a terrible voice: "By the just judgment of God, I am accused." On the second day: "By the just judgment of God, I am judged." On the third day: "By the just judgment of God, I am condemned." And who among the living would have believed this of such a famous and glorious man, unless the divine voice had made it clear? Where are those now who say: "It suffices for a Christian to keep the commandments for salvation"? Who could have believed that this such solemn doctor had kept the commandments? But dig through the wall, and you will find other things inscribed in the heart than the commandments described in the tablets of Moses. How often does Paul say in his epistles: "They who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God." And it is certain that every mortal sin is against the divine precept. And who can enumerate all mortal sins, and especially those concluded with deliberation in the heart alone, even if they never come to light? Once, Moses called heaven and earth against those whom he knew would desert God, certainly for vengeance and as a testimony
pages.56: because he was pointing out the pains they were about to suffer for their sins. For He will arm the creatures in vengeance upon the enemies. And who today is of such small experience that he does not know the way of God? The earth is filled with the knowledge of God. And yet all who are called are as one who says: "I have bought a farm," that is, I am tending toward the Lord through pride, "have me excused from the supper." Another says: "I have bought five yoke of oxen," that is, I insist upon the heats of avarice with all my strength. A third says: "I have taken a wife," that is, I am vacant for carnal pleasures, therefore I cannot come. In these three types of vices, nearly the whole world suffers shipwreck, because a thick cloud of carnal desires and earthly solicitudes makes the reason grow dim so that it cannot see where it is going. We have indeed fallen into the times of women, in which men flee harsh things, seek delicate things with all their intention, and do not fear to undergo even hard things to acquire these; they would surely be happier if they did not fear to undergo these for eternal delights. We see certainly how many storms of wars, even up to the shedding of blood, rage in different parts of the world for the sake of only temporal things, either being acquired or preserved, and not for defending the Catholic faith. In what kingdom or province, I ask, is the tranquility of peace maintained for a long time? All these take their beginnings either from pride or from avarice, so much so that the dove sent forth from the ark, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit seeking a place on earth where it might fix its foot, cannot find one because of the filth and mud of earthly passions, as once in the time of Noah. Truly, the unhappy times have returned that were before the captivity of the children of Israel in Babylon, when God sent many prophets to admonish them that, having left their idols, they should follow the God of their fathers, through them predicting to them the horrendous captivities, which they disdained to hear; nay, they mocked them, and in a song of fools, mocking, they turned the truth
pages.57: as it is said in Ezechiel 33. Moreover, they even killed them. For as it is said in the Prophet, chapter 28 <note>referring to Isaiah 28:10</note>: "When the holy prophets were proclaiming future pains to the children of Israel, they mocked them, saying: 'Command, command back. Expect, expect back. A little there, a little there.'" As if they were saying: "Multiply the precepts, expect the execution of the penalties, and yet so little truth follows there." Afterward, however, they felt the truth by experience when they were led away as captives in chains. Thus in our ages, when many hear the horrendous threats of eternal pains, they do not see them and treat them as a game. If they would wait a little while, experience would give understanding to their hearing. Yet the truth is not to be passed over in silence, even if it is not heard gladly by many. For divine speech will find somewhere to rest. For a certain wise man says: "While the wolf tends to many sheep, he preys on one." Nor will the relator of truth lack his reward, witness Jerome, who says in a certain epistle: "He who invites an Ethiopian to the bath, even if he does not take away his color, still receives his payment for himself; and even if he does not rejoice in the other's whiteness, he certainly rejoices in his own gain." Thus, without doubt, he who warns the disobedient with divine sermons, even if he does not take away the sins of the resister, will acquire a reward for himself from the ministry of charity, witness Christ who says in Luke 10: "If the son of peace be not there, your peace shall return to you." If the most holy Augustine, this most celebrated theologian, were living and saw the state of the current time, and contemplated human studies, and especially in the sublimity of those constituted in both spiritual and secular positions, he would not only say as he said when he was alive: "There is still a little light among Christians," but perhaps he would say: "Almost all light in the multitude of Christians is extinguished." And it is read of a certain saint who was frequently rapt in spirit that she said: "If the most wise in the world could consider how many souls
pages.58: descend daily into hell, they would be more than the sand of the sea, numbered, and more than the pebbles of the banks along the sea, and infinite souls descend as if to death into hell." Who will not tremble hearing this, since no one knows if he is worthy of hatred or love? With whom the poet agrees: "The descent to hell is easy." And Seneca: "The opinion of the ancients taught nothing else than what must be done and what must be avoided, and then men were far better. After the learned appeared, good men ceased." For that simple and open truth has been turned into an obscure and skillful science, and we are taught to dispute, not to live. So he says. How true this is, the daily studies of men declare. And this is affirmed by the apostolic sentence and doctrine, which teaches to live soberly, justly, and piously in this age, not by syllogistic disputes or the tables of Alfonso or the motions of the planets, to spend all one's care in this short space of time, but how we might render an account to God in the strict examination, when to allege these things then seems foolish. And whoever proceeds to the pains of fire, all dispute ceases then. All who read of those who were resurrected have abandoned the world of vile penalties and have hidden themselves in cloisters, leading a strict life of penance, proving themselves to us as an example, but having few imitators. This, written in a rude style as much as I could, not as much as I wanted, with certain charity and, as I estimated, truth, I humbly offer to all benevolent and clearer readers to be corrected and limited, prepared to yield to a clearer truth to which I have not presumed. I present in these many revelations read by me, piously believing that the writers of them did not lie, which, or even greater, the blessed Pope Gregory did not fear to narrate for the edification of men in his Dialogues, asking pardon for prolixity or superfluity, charity instigating me to this. For which may God be blessed for ever. Amen.

N.text: regarding the penalty. Let him who grieves to escape the pains of purgatory not distance himself from the giving of alms, and let him not refuse to receive the beggar Lazarus into his house; for if that rich man, placed in hell, had received him, he could have been saved. For Tobias says: "Alms deliver from all sin and from death, and will not suffer the soul to go into darkness" <note>Tobit 4:11</note>. Furthermore, above all, let such a one follow the doctrine of Saint Paul to the Romans, 12: "I beseech you that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God." That sacrifice is then offered to God when we have studied with pure knowledge to extirpate vices, to restrain passions and concupiscences, by refraining the exterior senses from illicit things, and by exercising ourselves in the austerity of life through fasts, prayers, vigils, hard bedding, garments, and other corporal afflictions. Of this holy sacrifice of our body, Gregory says in the end of the <term>Dialogi</term> <gloss>Dialogues</gloss>: "Let us melt the hardness of the mind in tears; let us form the grace of kindness toward our neighbors." And I confidently say that we shall not be in need of the saving sacrifice, namely the body of Christ, after death, if before death we have been a sacrifice to God ourselves. Not at all; indeed, even most especially, true indulgences granted by the Roman pontiffs and others having authority are valid for the pains of purgatory, regarding which I supersede for the present, and they are usually treated by theologians upon the fourth book, distinction 20. For beasts provide for themselves against the future, preventing harms and pursuing benefits, as is evident in ants, in cranes, and in wild geese, which, when the harshness of winter approaches, either flee to warmer places or gather food for themselves in caves and caverns. Rational men, not ignorant of the future pains of winter, whether eternal or most bitter temporal ones, with open eyes do not wish to look at anything to prevent them, thinking that the name of faith alone suffices for salvation. Of whom Paul says: "They profess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny him." We read of Saint Jerome, by his own testimony, that when he was intent upon secular letters and was rapt in his dreams, he was asked who he was; he answered, "I am a Christian." And he heard, "You lie; you are a Ciceronian, not a Christian." And being grievously scourged, he swore he would not read such letters henceforth. Oh, would that this inquiry might now touch many Christians; it could be answered, "You are not a Christian, but a pagan." And I seem to say with probability: If there were idols today giving responses, relieving poverty, and conferring riches and dignities, we would see how many Christians, having abandoned God, would follow idols. Therefore, descending, so that the benevolent reader may hold me in favor: he who wishes to escape these future punishments should learn in the mirror of those who have suffered what he himself ought to do. And first, let him return everything unjustly acquired, content with only what is necessary according to his own station. Then, let him choose such a way of living without great anxieties, one which is remote from the dignities, riches, and common offices of this age; for these are scarcely or never able to be managed without sin. Then, let him make himself as foreign as he can to the acts of the age, occupying himself only with his own affairs and those of his family, renouncing the superfluous pomps of this world, associating himself with the company of the righteous, and frequently intent upon the reading of sacred scriptures and upon sermons. Then, let him frequently return to the fountain of penance, namely, contrition and painful confession, along with satisfaction; for through these, especially, sins are blotted out by the power of the keys committed to the priests, and I say not only the guilt, but also the penalty, as Christ says in John 20: "Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose you shall retain, they are retained." Nor do priests merely point out that sins are dismissed for those who confess, as some wish to claim, which others might also be able to do from signs of contrition, but they also dismiss the sins themselves by the virtue of the keys. In which keys the passion of Christ operates. The priest receives these keys in the reception of sacred order. But according to the sayings of the doctors in their writings upon the fourth book of the Sentences, distinctions 18, 19, and 20, a threefold key is distinguished, namely the key of authority, which belongs to Christ alone as the principal agent in the sacrament, as God, and this is communicable to no creature, just as the divine essence is not. And through this key God alone remits sins, just as He cannot communicate the power to confer grace and glory to anyone. And this can be called the key in the firmament, as it is said in the Apocalypse, which God alone possesses, and He opens to the sinner who is dead in his sins as if in <term>inferno</term> <gloss>hell</gloss> when God grants him grace.

<margin>Precepts by which one arrives at those penalties</margin>
pages.52: He confers grace so that he may escape from sin. He shuts, however, when He withdraws grace from those who exalt themselves by their own demerits. There is another key of excellence which Christ has as man, and such he was able to communicate to ministers or priests, who are the dispensers of the mysteries of God. And the priests use that key of ministry, not the key of mystery lost by Christ, in the administration of the sacraments of the New Testament. And thus truth is preserved in both: that is, God alone remits sins by the key of authority, the priests by the key of ministry. This is the summary of the blessed <term>Thomas</term> <gloss>Aquinas</gloss> in the third part, question 84, article 1 and 4. With whom <term>Thomas de Argentina</term> agrees in the fourth book, distinction 18. And he puts forward the example of a prince who has the principal authority of opening and shutting a castle or a city; by this, however, he does not exclude the porter to whom he has entrusted the keys. He puts forward another example: an Emperor grants his officials the power of punishing evildoers, provided they seek pardon and do this or that, he releases them free; there, the officials have the power of ministry, the prince the power of excellence. So it is concerning Christ and the priests. Christ has the key of excellence in that, by the merit of his most sacred passion, he uses this key immediately, by this not excluding the ministry of the priests. Therefore he said: "Whatsoever you shall bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven." Therefore, in confession, much guilt is dismissed, and also penalty. And if it is objected that all guilt is dismissed in contrition, therefore the priest does not remit any; the response is that there is no true and sufficient contrition without a firm purpose of manifesting it, according to the definition of contrition, since the precept of God and the tradition of the church bind one to confession. Likewise, if it is said that venial sins are dismissed by the sprinkling of holy water, and by general confession, etc., the response, according to the holy <term>Thomas</term>, is that this is regarding the guilt by reason of the annexed contrition, not regarding the whole penalty. Because it is always necessary to add something.

From previous revelations many things could be gathered concerning how the judgment of God proceeds differently than that of men. Most pure is the revelation made in the city of Paris, flourishing then as now with solemn study, concerning a certain most famous doctor, and great fame had spread far and wide, conspicuous in life and doctrine, on the occasion of which the famous Carthusian order took the principles of its first institution under the habit of that man, in the time of Master <term>Bruno</term>. This doctor, then, being exempt from human affairs, and the body kept in a bier for three days before a multitude of people, on the first day cried out with a terrible voice: "By the just judgment of God I am accused." On the second day: "By the just judgment of God I am judged." On the third day: "By the just judgment of God I am condemned." And who among the living would have believed this concerning so famous and glorious a man, unless the divine voice had made it clear? Where are now those who say: "It is enough for a Christian to keep the commandments for salvation"? Who could have believed that this so solemn a doctor had not kept the commandments? pages.56: because he was pointing out the penalties they were going to suffer for their sins. For He will arm the creatures in the vengeance of His enemies. contend by agreement, so that he might have more power with me than the laws and the custom of the courts. But I do not think that you would demand this of me, given your singular modesty. For it is not the nature of your people, nor of that family, to wish for anything to be obtained in our state by injustice rather than by right. Take care that I do not have to admonish you about the same matter too often, so that when all things are ready for you, you yourself are not judged to have been lacking. Farewell.

If I did not know about what matter and before whom I was acting, I would certainly not dare (at this particular time) to write anything to you. For you know how varied men’s suspicions are, and how ready their tongues are to speak ill. But since the equity of my cause is supreme, and you are the man who can do nothing except what is equitable, I entrust my cause to you with a good spirit. I do not doubt that there are many men who think that I am impelled by some avarice, to wish to remove <insert>r</insert> Fabius from his ancient seat and from his ancestral goods. I, however, am so constituted that I have never sought to be enriched by any man's inconvenience. But to yield one’s right to another on account of the envy of men seems to be the act of a timid or foolish person. For it will be enough that I demonstrate the matter to be not unjust before a most equitable judge. You, however, do not depart from your custom and nature, and I shall require nothing from you except what is worthy of your equity. Farewell.

If your cause does not abhor our laws, I bid you to be of good hope. For I am not the one whom the gossip of the crowd or the opinion of men might promote to common equity, nor am I ignorant that by the ancient institution it is more fitting for a judge to attend to what is established by law than what is established by opinion. But as I have always taken care for myself, never to place rumors before equity, so I think you must take care, lest by some fault of yours this opinion about you might seem certain. Whatever, however, can be provided by my ingenuity or study, so that you are not forced from your right on account of envy,
pages.7:
I promise that I will do all that for you. <insert>¶</insert> That, however, you will consider with your prudence, how you might well reconcile your concerns and your fortunes with my name. Farewell.

An arduous cause compelled me to write to you at this time. For when I heard that you were occupied with most important matters, I would have postponed my own business for another time, had it not been of such a nature that, if neglected by me, it could be corrected by no other man's help or assistance thereafter. You will bear with me, therefore, if I interrupt you while you are agitating the greatest matters. I think you remember what words Tiro used when he met both of us the day before the Kalends of March. For when he himself affirmed with a good spirit that he was returning into grace with me, and said that there were no remainders of hatred left in him, you ordered me not only to be of good spirit but also confident, and to suspect nothing further about you. I, however, placing great faith in his words and your authority, had put aside and banished from my mind all memory of the injuries and insults that had been between us. What followed from that, you will hear better from that man whom I send to you, to whom I gave not only letters but also instructions that he might bring to you regarding this matter. For after you departed from us, matters (as you suspected) being already well-arranged between me and him, Saturninus arrived—that man who is (as you know) the most seditious of all. He disturbed everything and excited such hatred that my fortune has never stood in a worse position. For (as it is wont to be said regarding illness) that evil sometimes breaks out more harshly than it began, which can be healed by no other doctor except by you yourself. Therefore, if you wish me to be safe, if you care for my fortunes, see that you fly back to us; for there is need of speed, lest I be cast into that place from whence, at no time, I do not say help, but not even salvation itself, even if it desires, could extract me. Farewell.

<note>A large decorative drop cap 'Q' in red and brown ink, featuring a central circular geometric motif similar to the initial 'A'.</note>
How great a trouble I received in my soul when I learned of Tiro's fickleness, you can recognize from this,
pages.8:
which, had the republic not openly recalled me from my very journey, I certainly would not only have pursued these letters, but would have also surpassed them by much. If therefore I did not attend to your fortunes as I ought, by no means accuse my duty, for although I desired most greatly to satisfy your spirit, that same love of our homeland, from the midst of the course I was steering toward you, clearly recalled me against my will. I have written to Tiro with such words as were appropriate, and I have also taught him that he ought not to think that the matter should be held between himself and you alone, but between me as well, for I had been the author and guarantor of all the things that were agreed upon between us. I also exhorted him with many arguments to defer the matter as it stood until my arrival, and to yield to that friendship which, as it was first with his patron, so it was afterwards with him for me. I admonished him with many words to let my arguments and the respect for our ancient benevolence weigh more with him than the seditions and hatreds of Saturninus. And if he were to be persuaded by this, I promised that he would receive great thanks from me. But if, contrary to my hope, the bad counsels of seditious men had won, I have remembered that I would omit nothing that would pertain to your defense and my own extraction. I think he will believe me more than Saturninus, and if the matter has deceived my counsel, I will make him repent his deed. I await his letters daily. If anything is done by him in the meantime that happens to your inconvenience, you will make me certain. Farewell.

Not a small or unusual matter is that about which I have now for a long time decided to write to you. For the men to whom in our province you had entrusted the care of your affairs and of those who favor your affairs seem to be day by day more and more alienated from you. Everyone asks, to state the matter in one word: why you made wolves the guardians of the sheep. We who are here with you certainly hoped that your affairs and those of your people could not be ruined by those who had been flattered by your goods, if the agents
pages.9:
had kept watch over them (as they ought). But the danger has been made from that very place from which we were expecting protection. For these good men, first through snares, then openly, not only began to incline toward those who do not wish you well, but even professed themselves to be their leaders. There is need, therefore, of maturation while the matter can still be taken care of, lest that happen to you which is known to happen to those who summon a doctor while dying. Farewell.

Although I was very much in the course and on the very journey of coming to you, on account of those rumors which were reported here concerning my affairs, yet when your messenger happened to encounter me with the letters you had entrusted to him for me, I did not want him to return to you without my own letters, but to come to those things which I have written regarding the perfidy and wickedness of my agents toward my fortunes and those of my people. If I had known beforehand that all things were thus, I would have hastened my departure with greater speed, had I not been detained by the greatest matters. I did not truly wish to answer those things which were reported to me daily, lest perhaps my counsels might be revealed to those to whom I least wished them to be known. Now, however, since I have such faith in your prudence and your supreme goodwill toward me, as I have remembered afterward, I exhort and advise you again and again that you make those who follow my party aware of my arrival, wisely (as is your custom), and persuade them that I will not demand an accounting for my goods until I see them restored to their integrity. To write more to you, I do not hope to be expedient while I am with you, and I shall quickly follow your messenger. Farewell.

What I am writing to you is such that it pertains most greatly to your matter. For although it may seem alien to you, yet it is necessary that, if it is correctly managed, great glory will come to you. For M. Anthonius and Q. Hortensius, most distinguished men, have long since—as you know—been departing toward much hatred
pages.10:
furthermore, because it has hitherto been difficult for our citizens to please them. So, while our state is divided by the study of parties, such contentions arise in the city that the matter already seems to look clearly toward civil war, which, although many deny can happen, I nevertheless judge otherwise. But it has come at an opportune time to remove this danger, for I understand it to be the cause of all these evils, if you (who are worth much in wisdom and industry) should wish to take on this burden. You know how much our citizens trust you. Consider if our state were made certain of your counsels and studies in this matter, a commendable meeting of all good men would occur to you. And they would come into your opinion for the greater part of the city. And I see it will come to pass that M. Anthonius and Q. Hortensius will omit those things for you and will willingly desire to be led by you without all these dissensions of theirs. You will therefore undertake this expedition, honorable for you and necessary for the republic. And you will be judged to be able to do nothing more than to approach your praise, if you should accomplish this matter by your counsel. Farewell.

If by any office of mine the hatred of M. Anthonius and Q. Hortensius can be calmed, I will not cease at any risk and labor of mine: until all things are reconciled and quiet. For I see this whole matter is brought about by the vice of a few men to whom the peace of the state is displeasing. I desire all the citizens to be well to such a degree that I do not desire more to be safe myself than that they be saved. Nothing moves me as much as the respect for Anthonius and Hortensius, whom I hold most dear both for the sake of the republic and from ancient familiarity. Therefore, receive these letters of mine quickly, and whatever can be done by me with any study or care, I will undertake that whole thing willingly. And I shall satisfy the expectation of all those citizens. But I judge that I will have obtained enough reward if, upon my arrival, I learn that such a fire has been extinguished. Farewell.

I do not write to you about a common or negligible matter, but about public commonalities. For I am ashamed of these times, and
pages.11:
I pity our republic, which, while formerly governed by the counsel of those men to whom it had entrusted itself, now arrives into the hands of a few who keep it entirely oppressed. Nothing was brought into the common counsel that did not pertain to the utility of all. There was no one who did not freely say whatever he thought would be profitable for the republic. Nor was it burdensome or troublesome to those who stood within those walls to hear the speech of those who said they were speaking for the common good and had a greater place and reason in speaking for the republic than for private interests. If there are those today to whom those things appear unworthy which are done daily, neither by the custom of our ancestors nor by the laws, they have no place, and no reason in judging. From which it happens that some, who think correctly, do not dare to speak in consultations. Others, however, as if they deem all things to be in their power, do not wish any deliberation to be held unless it agrees with their own private affairs. Therefore, it is no wonder if all things are confused, or if for matters of peace and war nothing has been sufficiently considered or said or done by us these past years. From where, however, such great inconveniences have happened to the republic, I judge it to be nothing else than that there is no one head or prince who thinks well of our republic, and who refers what he thinks to the common utility, and is neither hindered by the favor of anyone, nor broken by fear, so that he does not dare everything that appears to him to be good and honest. But there is no one who wishes to offer himself to labors and dangers for the sake of the fatherland. All allow the republic to be deserted, lest they be urged into some crisis of their own affairs. You, however, although you have departed from the guidance and care of it out of hatred for the wicked, yet you perceive what pertains to your virtue. That, however, I advise and also exhort: that you should prefer, if the republic requires it, to die for it rather than with it to lose all your dignity and reputation. Farewell.

<note>A large decorative red initial Q featuring delicate scrollwork flourishes.</note>
How much I desire our republic to be safe and to see it one day restored to the seats of our ancestors, no one
pages.12: can judge better than you. Nor have I ever departed in spirit or abdicated myself from it if I could have hoped that my counsels could avail more in the preservation of it than the force of certain citizens to the overturning of the public state. But when there were those in whose perfidy more power lay in public counsels than I alone could then resist, and there was no one who would then dare to profess themselves defenders of public utility, I thought it best to yield to this storm for a time and to migrate somewhere where I might live safely. How great was the subsequent license and impunity for sinning, you, who have always been agitated by those waves and storms, can think better for yourself than hear from another. Therefore I do not wonder if I do not find anyone who dares to speak freely in our senate and say those things that he thinks well of the republic. But because you call me back to the guidance of it, I judge that you are doing that more out of an immense study for the republic than that I might be able to free the fatherland from any fear. For when I could accomplish nothing against the force of the wicked, nor help it while it still appeared to stand and held some shadow or likeness of ancient liberty, why did you think that I could help it when I saw it not only expiring but already entirely extinct and dead? I would have wished at least that you had called me to it while some hope of recovering it remained. Now, however, I believe you have invited me to its funeral and to its sepulcher, so that I, to whom it did not happen to die through it, might at least be buried with it. But I do not think it is the act of a wise man, when he can in no way help the fatherland, to prefer to die with it than to live without it. Nor do I judge it to be the intention of one who is a good citizen to throw himself into death or dangers for the sake of those who do not know how to be free, or who do not want to be, as much as to protect his own safety and reserve himself until he can either die more honorably for the fatherland or sees a time when he does not labor and risk himself in vain for his fellow citizens. If therefore chance brings it about that I feel those things can be done by me which conduce to the fatherland, I will do it. You will understand that I am making a greater care of the restitution
pages.13:
of public liberty than of my own safety. In the meantime, I have nothing else that I can offer our republic at this time than tears, which I often shed for its miserable state. Farewell.

What you think of me, you can easily perceive from the turpitude of the man and the infamy of him who wished to alienate your soul from me. For although my cause was not sufficiently perceived by you, yet from the life of that man who accused me to you with false crimes, you can understand that the fame of good men is not usually attacked unless by the wicked. Wherefore, if any fable has been disseminated about me, you ought to be moved, because there is no man's life so watched that some crime cannot be forged. It will be enough for me to live in the eyes of men so that no one can justly accuse me. But why should I write more to you about this matter, when you yourself have experienced in our state that there have always been men who insult the fame of others and think they become more commendable the more they are disparaged by them? But you, by your prudence, will consider not only what anyone says, but also by what man, lest you place faith in the speech of one whose life has been disapproved. Farewell.

contend by agreement, so that he might have more power with me than the laws and the custom of the courts. But I do not think that you would demand this of me on account of your singular modesty. For I do not consider him to be of such a nature, nor of that family, that he would wish anything in our city to be attained by him more through injury than by law. See that I do not have to admonish you often about the same matter, so that when everything is prepared for you, you yourself might not be judged to have been lacking. Farewell.

Unless I knew about what matter and before whom I was acting, I would certainly not dare (at this particular time) to write anything to you. You know, indeed, how varied the suspicions of men are, and how ready their tongues are for slandering. But since the equity of my cause is absolute, and you are that man who can do nothing unless it is fair, I commend my cause to you with a good spirit. I do not doubt that there are many men who think that I am impelled by some avarice to wish to remove Fabius from his ancient seat and from his ancestral goods. I, however, have been so instructed, that I would never desire to be enriched by the inconveniences of any man. But to yield one’s own right to another on account of the envy of men seems to be the act of a timid or foolish person. It will be enough, indeed, that I demonstrate about the matter that it is not unjust before a most fair judge. You, however, do not depart from your custom and nature, and I will require nothing from you except what is worthy of your equity. Farewell.

If your cause does not conflict with our laws, I bid you to be well. For I am not that man whom the rumors of the crowd or the reputation of men might promote to common equity, nor am I ignorant that by the ancient institution a judge ought to attend more to what is established by law than by opinion. But as I have always taken care to ensure that I would never place rumors before equity, so I think you must take care, that by no fault of your own this opinion might seem to be hidden from you. Whatever, however, can be provided by my genius and study, so that you may not yield your right to anyone on account of envy.
pages.7:
I promise that I will do all of that for you. <insert>¶</insert> But you will perceive by your own prudence what things you may well manage regarding your own resources and my name. Farewell.

Bear with me, therefore, if I interrupt you while you are agitating the greatest matters. I think you hold in memory what words Tiro used when we both met before the Kalends of March. And not to suspect anything more about you. For there is need of speed, lest I be cast into that place from which at no time, I do not say any help, but even salvation itself, if it should desire, could extricate me. Farewell.

Now, however, I believe you have invited me to its funeral and to its sepulcher, so that for whom it was not allowed to die for it, I might at least be buried with it. But I do not think it is the act of a wise man, when he can in no way profit the fatherland, to prefer to perish with it rather than to live without it. Nor do I judge it to be the intention of one who is a good citizen to throw himself into death or dangers through those who either do not know how to be free, or do not wish to be, as much as to protect his own safety, and to reserve himself until he can either die more honestly for the fatherland, or sees a time in which he does not labor and risk in vain for his fellow citizens. If therefore chance shall have brought it that I feel those things can be done by me which conduce to the fatherland, I will do it. You will understand that I am concerned about the restitution

of public liberty with more care than I am about my own safety. Meanwhile, I have nothing else that I can offer to our Republic at this time than tears, which I often shed for its miserable state. Farewell.

What you feel about me, you can easily judge from the baseness of the man and the infamy of him who wished to alienate your spirit from me. For although my cause might not have been sufficiently foreseen by you, yet from the life of that man who has accused me before you with false crimes, you can understand that the reputation of good men is not wont to be tempted except by the wicked. Why, therefore, if any fable has been dissipated about me, it behooves you to be moved, especially since there is no man whose life has been so watched that some crime cannot be feigned. That will be enough for me, to live so in the eyes of men, that no one can justly accuse me. But why should I write more to you about this matter, when you yourself have experienced in our city that there have always been men who insult the reputation of others and think they become more commendable the more they have detracted from them? But you, by your prudence, will consider not only what someone says, but also by what man, lest you hold faith in the speech of one whose life has been reproved. Farewell.

How much annoyance I have received in my spirit upon learning of the fickleness of Tiro, you can recognize from this: unless the Republic had recalled me openly from that very journey, I would certainly have pursued not only these letters, but I would also have followed those by much. If, therefore, I was not present at your fortunes as I ought to have been, do not at all accuse my duty, for although I most greatly desired to satisfy your spirit, that very love of our city recalled me quite unwillingly from the midst of the journey which I was making toward you. I wrote, however, to Tiro with what words I could, and I also taught him that he should not think that the matter itself was to be held with you alone, but with me, since I had been the author and sponsor of all things that had been agreed upon between us. I also exhorted him with many arguments to defer the matter entirely until my arrival, and to depart from that sedition which, as it was first with his patron, so later it was with him. I warned him with many words that my arguments and the respect for our ancient friendship should have more value with him than the seditions and hatreds of Saturninus. And if he should be swayed by it, I promised that he would receive great thanks from me. But if, indeed, he had been overcome against my hope by the dishonest counsels of seditious men, I have remembered that I would omit nothing that would pertain to your defense and my own vindication. I think that he will believe me more than Saturninus, for if the matter deceives my counsel, I will see to it that he regrets his action. I expect his letters daily. If anything is done by him in the meantime which happens to you inconveniently, you must make me certain. Farewell.

It is no small or unusual matter about which I have for a long time decided to write to you. For the men to whom you had committed the care of your affairs in our province, and of those who favor your affairs, seem to be alienated from you more and more each day. Everyone asks, to speak the matter in one word: why did you make wolves the guardians of the sheep? We indeed who are here among your friends hoped that your affairs and those of your family could not be crushed, if those who had fawned upon your comforts had acted as curators

Although I was in the midst of the course and on the very journey of coming, on account of those rumors which were spread there about my affairs, nevertheless, when your messenger happened to encounter me with your letters which you had given him to deliver to me, I did not wish him to return to you without my own letters. But in order that I may come to those things which I have written regarding the treacheries and wickedness of my curators against my fortunes and those of my family—if I had known beforehand that all things were so, I would have hastened my departure with greater speed and would not have been delayed by the greatest matters. I truly did not wish to reply to those things which were being reported to me daily, lest perhaps my counsels might be revealed to those to whom I wished them to be least known. For it is not the nature of your people, nor that family, to desire that anything in our state be obtained by injury rather than by right. Take care that I do not have to remind you of the same matter too often, so that when all is ready for you, you yourself are not judged to have been found wanting. Farewell.

If I did not know about what matter and before whom I was acting, I would certainly not dare (at this particular time) to write anything to you. For you know how varied men’s suspicions are, and how ready their tongues are for slander. But since the equity of my cause is of the highest order, and you are the man who can do nothing unless it is just, I entrust my cause to you with a good spirit. I do not doubt that there are many men who think that I am driven by some greed, wishing to remove Fabius from his ancient seat and ancestral property. <insert>r</insert>. But I have been educated in such a way that I would never desire to be enriched by another man’s misfortune. Yet, to yield one’s right to another because of the envy of men seems to be the act of a timid or foolish person. For it will be enough that I demonstrate the matter not unfairly before a most just judge. You, however, do not depart from your custom and nature, and I shall require nothing from you except what is worthy of your equity. Farewell.

If your cause does not abhor our laws, I bid you spare yourself well. For I am not the man whom the talk of rumors or the reputation of men among the commonality would move to equity, nor am I ignorant that by ancient custom it is more fitting for a judge to attend to what is based on law than on opinion. But just as I have always taken care to never place rumors above equity, so I think you must provide that no fault of yours makes this opinion about you seem certain. Whatever, however, can be provided by my intellect and study, so that you do not yield your right because of envy

A difficult matter has compelled me to write to you at this time. For when I heard that you were occupied with the greatest affairs, I would have deferred my own business to another time, had it not been of such a nature that, if neglected by me, it could not afterwards be corrected by any man’s counsel or aid. You will therefore bear with me if I interrupt you while you are agitating the greatest matters. I think you remember what words Tiro <note>Marcus Tullius Tiro, Cicero’s freedman and secretary</note> used when both of us met on the day before the Kalends of March. For when he himself affirmed that he was restoring himself to grace with me with a good spirit, and said that no remainders of hatred remained in him, you ordered me not only to be of good spirit but also to be confident. Nor to suspect anything further about you. I, however, since I held great faith in his words and your authority, had put aside and set out of my mind all memory of the injuries and insults that had existed between us. What followed from that, you will hear better from that man whom I am sending to you, to whom I have not only given letters but also instructions that he should carry to you regarding this matter. For after you departed from us, matters (as you supposed) were already proceeding for me and him, when Saturninus <note>A political agitator</note> arrived, a man (as you know) most prone to sedition. He disturbed everything and stirred up such hatred that my fortunes have never stood in a worse place. For (as is wont to be said of a disease) that evil festers sometimes more harshly than it began, which can be cured by no other physician than by you yourself. Wherefore, if you wish for me to be safe, if you care for my fortunes to be unharmed, fly to us. For there is need of speed, lest I be directed to a place from which at no time—I do not say I could be called back, but even safety itself, even if it desired, could not extract me. Farewell.

beyond that which has been difficult for our citizens to please them. Since, therefore, our state is divided by the study of parties, so many contentions have arisen in the city that the matter already seems to clearly look toward a civil war, which even if many deny that it can happen, I nevertheless judge otherwise. You know how much our citizens believe in you. Consider if our state were made certain of your counsels and studies in this matter, a laudable meeting of all good men will occur to you. Hortensius, whom they will omit for you, will voluntarily wish to be imposed by you without all these dissensions of theirs. If by any duty of mine the hatred of M. Antonius and Q. Hortensius can be settled, I will not cease by any danger and labor of mine until all things are settled and quieted. For I see this whole matter offered by the vice of a few men to whom the peace of the state is displeasing. I truly desire all those citizens to be well, to the extent that I do not desire more to be safe myself than that they be saved. Nothing moves me less than respect for Antonius and Hortensius, whom I hold most dear both for the sake of the republic and from ancient familiarity. Therefore, follow these letters of mine quickly, and whatever can be done by me with any study or care, I will willingly undertake the whole of it. And I shall satisfy the expectation of all those citizens. But I judge that I will have obtained enough reward if, by my arrival, I learn that such a fire has been extinguished. Farewell.

I write to you not about a common or negligible matter, but about public interests. For I am ashamed of these times and

I pity our republic, which, while it was once ruled by the counsel of those men to whom it had entrusted itself, now has arrived into the hands of a few who keep it entirely oppressed. For nothing was brought into the common counsel unless it pertained to the utility of all. There was no one who would not freely say whatever he judged to be conducive to the republic. Nor was it burdensome or annoying to those who stood within those walls to hear the oration of those who said they were speaking for the common good and who had a greater place and rationale for the <term>patria</term> <gloss>fatherland</gloss> in speaking than for private interests. If there are any today to whom those things that are done daily—neither by the custom of ancestors nor by laws—seem unworthy, they have no place, and have no rationale for the <term>patria</term> in judging. From which it happens that some, who think rightly, do not dare to speak in consultations. Others, however, as if they deem everything to be in their power, do not wish for deliberation to be had on any matter unless it agrees with their own private affairs. Wherefore it is no wonder if everything is confused, or if, in matters of peace and war, nothing has been sufficiently considered or said or done by us in these years. From where, however, such great inconveniences have happened to the republic, I judge it to be nothing else than that there is no one head or <term>princeps</term> <gloss>leader/chief</gloss> who feels well about our republic, and who refers what he feels to the common utility, nor is he impeded by anyone’s favor or broken by fear, so that he does not dare all things that seem good and honest to him. But there is no one who wishes to offer himself to labors and dangers for the <term>patria</term>. Everyone allows the republic to be deserted, lest they be urged into some crisis of their own affairs. You, however, although you have departed from the governance and care of it because of the hatred of bad men, nevertheless perceive what pertains to your virtue. That, however, I warn and even exhort: that you would rather wish, if the republic requires it, to perish for it than with it to lose all your dignity and esteem. Farewell.

How much I desire our republic to be safe and to see it one day restored to the seats of our ancestors, no one
pages.12: can judge better than you. Nor have I ever yielded in my spirit, nor would I have abdicated myself from it, if I could have hoped that my counsels were of more value in the preservation of it than the violence of certain citizens was in overturning the public state. But since in those who had more power in public counsels than I alone could then resist, and there were none who would dare to declare themselves defenders of public utility, I judged that it was time to yield to this storm and to migrate somewhere where it might be permitted to live safely for me. How much license and impunity for sinning there has been afterwards, you, who have been agitated by those waves and storms, can think for yourself better than hear from another. Wherefore I do not wonder if none are found who dare to speak freely in our senate, and say those things which they feel well about the republic. But that you recall me to the governance of it, I judge that you do it more out of an immense study for the republic than because you hope for the <term>patria</term> to be liberated by me. For when I could achieve nothing against the power of bad men, nor help it while it still seemed to stand, and still keep some shadow or likeness of ancient liberty, what was it that you thought I could assist, which I saw to be not only expiring but already entirely extinguished and dead? You should have at least called me to it when some hope of recovering this survived. Now, however, you seem to have invited me to its funeral and to its tomb, so that for whom it has not befallen to die for it, I might at least be buried with it. But I do not think it is the act of a wise man, when he can in no way benefit the <term>patria</term>, to prefer to perish with it than to live without it. Nor do I judge it to be the duty of one who is a good citizen to expose himself to death or dangers by those who know not how to be free, or who do not wish to be, as much as to protect his own safety and reserve himself until he can more honestly die for the <term>patria</term>, or sees a time when he may not labor and face dangers for his fellow citizens in vain. If, therefore, chance brings it about that I feel that those things can be done by me which conduce to the <term>patria</term>, I will do it. You will understand me regarding the restoration

the one who desires the welfare of the state should mitigate it. Truly, I seem to myself to divine all future events, which you also fear greatly. I cannot sufficiently admire the madness that drives your citizens into this discord. Perhaps there are some in the city who think they will gain control of affairs if everything falls under the power of the enemy. And it is to be feared that this plague has been set in motion by the cunning of our enemies, so that they may more easily obtain victory. I would prefer to be able to lift this evil from you in this place, or with some aid of mine, than to offer counsel at a time when your affairs can least be helped by counsel. But since matters have come to such a point that what I wished to be done cannot be performed by me, I will not fail to write what I think regarding the salvation of your state. It must be investigated by those themselves who desire the safety of the state, what each man’s mind is. The ancient allies of yours must all be solicited by the wise, so that you may remember the loyalty and friendship of the past. The garrisons of the allies must be secretly received by you into the city, until you see that you can force those who do not think well of your liberty. Nor will this disease be able to be cured, nor will this evil that has already festered be removed from you, unless that part which is diseased is cut away from the body itself. I hope that if your city uses my counsel, you will shortly understand that every danger that abounds in your very bowels has been repelled by you. For just as I sense what you are about to do in your affairs, you will also provide again and again. For I am no less anxious about your salvation than if all things were common between me and you. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'D' starts the text.</note> I will postpone your desire. I will soon satisfy what you most wish to hear from me. You are absolved by the sentences of all the judges, and the lawsuit has been given in your favor. I have never seen a man more learned in advancing causes than the one to whom you had entrusted this case of yours. For he appeared there, as much as legal advocacy could among the judges. He was so vehement and sharp
pages.32:
in exposing the crimes that were being brought against you, so that he made all the judges entirely favorable to you, and made your opponents hateful. Everyone praised the talent of this orator. They approved your cause, and praised the fairness of the judges. When the verdict was finally reached, there was such applause from everyone that they did not rejoice less in the matter than if it were the business of all. I wished to write this to you so that I might relieve your mind of that anxiety which (as I know) you were burdened with. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'H' starts the text.</note> I offer you great thanks, truly, for having liberated me from great anxiety and trouble. But it affected me with no less pleasure that you wrote to me concerning my patron, a most modest and eloquent man. For I am delighted by his vehemence, his praise, and his magnificent service. For even if I never doubted my cause, when the case was to be judged for me, still, because in legal judgments there is often hidden danger, as in sailing, and he who is a skilled helmsman is not the one who waits on the shore. I always feared lest the fairness of the cause or any other fortune might result in something other than what I hoped. I rejoice, therefore, that I have obtained such an orator, in whom neither human eloquence nor diligence was lacking. Shortly (as I hope) I will congratulate him myself. In the meantime, I will signify to him that I hold great gratitude for his studies and services. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'V' starts the text.</note> You desire that it be signified by me what everyone feels about you, both your friends and your citizens. There is one common sentiment: that no one among your peers is greater in talent. But they fear greatly that you do not use it with enough modesty. Wherefore, my Antony, if good fame delights you, if you sustain the opinion of men, which is certainly not small now, see that you do not affect your other virtues, which are great, only with modesty. I understand indeed that you will be the greatest citizen in our city, if you know how to use your talent modestly. That you may do so, I ask you again and again. Farewell.
pages.33:
<note>A red decorative initial Q starts the text.</note> You write that modesty is desired of me. I know whence this comes. If I do, all my citizens and my friends will understand, if there is another virtue in me, that this one is not lacking. It cannot happen that an age like this does not have many things that are reproached by the envious. And often such people are found who, out of envy, twist something and make our faults greater if someone seems to surpass them in talent or study. I know that the whole cause came from there, because since men have praised everything in me, they withdraw from me the reputation of modesty, which does not allow them to be long in that error. I shall strive for one thing, that I am not hindered by the age in which I am, nor by labor, as I will do all things that lead to the betterment of men. You will help me in this matter (as you do), so that just as I have become much more ardent for good arts through your exhortations and counsels, so may I understand through you that I have observed the benevolence of my citizens. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q starts the text.</note> I write to you concerning greater things than those I wrote to you about before, for they are such that they not only invite you to read them, but they also possess great weight. The greatest preparations are being made, such as perhaps have never been heard of in our city. Great fleets of ships are being hired, most instructed squadrons are being readied, they are building new triremes, they are preparing for a huge war on sea and land, against a people that has always been most hostile to us. And the hope of all is that there has never been a time given to us in which victory could be better obtained, and if we have obtained it, there will be eternal peace for our city. For all peoples (this one excepted) who could wage war on us have been defeated by us, both by love and by arms, and their strength is nothing other than what remains of our republic, so that we may also curb this nation, which will not be difficult for us to do, provided that speed is applied to our counsels. We have all things that can easily provide victory to our efforts. The enemy is surprised, we are protected by counsel. He
pages.34:
is impatient, we are most instructed in all necessary things. He is already broken and weakened by domestic and foreign wars, we are whole and never more powerful than now. What more? Many cities have defected from the faith and alliance of our enemies. The strength of our allies increases daily before the cities. There is nothing, therefore, why we should not hold this victory in our hands. We want nothing to be lacking to us. But I also hope well for the timing itself, since we have never used more prudent or stronger men for completing such a matter. I have written this to you; see that you do not divulge anything of these things that would interest the state. But I did not want you to be ignorant of this, so that, as I knew you to be someone who cared most, you might become more learned through me about the greatest things which are being agitated here. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'P' begins the second paragraph.</note> Regarding the fact that you received my letters after everything about which you write to me was already being divulged among us, that was least appropriate to happen if the ancient custom had been preserved in our senate. For nothing was guarded more among our ancestors than silence in deliberations about matters that pertained to public utility. But enough about this to you, as you are not ignorant of these things. That, I judge, pertains more to the matter which is now being agitated: whether it has been deliberated wisely by you regarding the undertaking of war, for which such a great preparation is being readied. You see what to promise regarding the certain victory of your fatherland, and hope for all things well. I, however, since I see nothing more fickle than the outcome of wars, and since everything you are agitating seems to be revealed to your enemies, I fear that your counsels might fail. Wherefore, if a deliberation had been taken by you concerning peace, that matter would have been not only more honorable, but also safer for you. For you could have used the examples of other nations, and seen that many cities often undertook wars when they had everything prepared and instructed, yet they met with an unhappy outcome. Carthage, a most powerful city, for many years
pages.35:
(with Hannibal as leader) waged war with the Romans. And although he had seen the devastation of Italy, and Rome nearly captured, yet the outcome was not victory, as it finally saw itself captive, and subject to Roman laws. Cyrus, also king of the Persians, after he had waged many happy wars for nearly thirty years, rushed into a war with the Scythians, and hoped that once that nation was conquered, he would later be in perpetual peace. But what end did his great efforts abhor? The Scythian queen Tomyris, having captured the king and two hundred Persian soldiers, taught him well enough. And it does not escape me that the wars which are to be waged by you might have a bad outcome, since I advise that you should prefer to lead your mind to peace and harmony rather than war. Nor is there any reason that should dissuade you from this, for the whole matter could be completed with greater glory than that war could be administered, which is not against an impatient enemy. You write that you are undertaking a prudent and powerful war. And it is to be feared that other nations might renew themselves, that cities which are now joined by the fear of your power are still with you, might defect from the faith. It will be, therefore, the wisdom of your people to see all these things, and not to use modesty and humanity in rejecting the mind of those who persuade you toward peace. But if you remain in the counsel you have undertaken, provide that what has been deliberated in your senate does not reach the enemies, as whatever has been begun by you. Nor have I written to you because I have influence in the republic, so that, if it has seemed good, you might have the senate discuss this matter, and deliberate with me more maturely about these things. For I, through my loyalty and benevolence, desire that it might go well for you all. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'P' begins the final paragraph.</note> Never at any time have I written to you about great matters; that is truly the greatest and most significant of all, since such great evils seem to me to be hanging over our affairs that I can easily divine the desolation and ruin of our fatherland. For a most atrocious war, and incredible famine
pages.36:
and plague, the like of which we have neither read nor seen, has already for a long time driven the whole province, nor does the force of such great evil remit even in part, but the evil increases daily, and is becoming worse. Think that we cannot endure such disasters for long, for how far have we already been pushed? Now, however, we are exhausted by suffering, and hope itself, which used to animate us to either repel the evils or endure them with fortitude, or be wise, has been so relaxed that it seems to be gone entirely. Who would not be able to easily divine from this not only the desolation, but also the ultimate extinction of our very city? For there will be a time in which, where the traces of our city were, men will look, and will not draw out any timbers of this once most powerful and flourishing fatherland. Unless God has remitted His anger, and has begun to look upon us, exhausted by such great evils, at last with kindness. And since human resources have abandoned our affairs, we are compelled, as often happens to sailors in a storm, to refer all our counsels, all hope, and thought to God, in following whom you will be a helper and ally to us. Although God may seem to turn His mind and ears away from our prayers, yet we hope that His clemency will be changed for the better, away from the evils by which we are afflicted and nearly undone. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'L' begins the text.</note> Your letters brought such trouble to my mind that at no time have I been in greater sorrow. For since our fortunes and the republic have been led to such a point that now no aid can be expected from men, it is most to be feared that we are even deprived of divine help. If this had happened to us by some other error, I would think that all things should be borne not only with an even but also a strong mind. But since we have always been those who, for the liberty of all, for the faith of allies, have often undertaken the greatest wars with great danger, I know not by what inequity of fortune it has come to pass that we are deprived of human aid, and not far from
pages.37: I see all the evils that you predicted would happen to your city. Perhaps men who come after us will ask where the foundations of such great cities were, and finally that very fame of our fatherland, by which we long flourished in Italy, will perhaps perish, after that which was the cause of our glory and name for a long time will not exist. But we should be consoled by the evils of the past, as we have examples of the most famous cities and kingdoms that once met a similar end, so that nothing except the name itself has reached us. I judge, however, that there were many cities that, in their own times, were famous and excellent for the glory of their deeds, with which the fame was extinguished, due to the lack of poets or orators who might illustrate their deeds with speech or song, and would not allow the memory of those things which were worthy of immortality to perish. Our republic, just as it was eager for glory, so too had acquired men who, by their wisdom and eloquence, were the memorializers of our deeds. I am beginning to understand this, how great the veneration should be among all magnificent cities for those who know how to recount the deeds of war or peace, and I cannot sufficiently admire that the greatest opportunity was lacking to our men, when they could have judged all their efforts and labors to have been undertaken in vain, not providing by what reason they could become immortal. But enough about this. Your counsel, however, is (as they say) the time for appeasing the gods, since necessity makes us suppliants more than our own will. We would have preferred to use this remedy when we had all things intact, and it would have been a sign that it was done by us from a mind that was not compelled, not as I write now, after it can no longer be corrected by us. We are doing what sailors themselves do in a great storm (for I will gladly use your example): now that the mast is broken and the ship is shattered, let us make all our prayers. If our entreaty has been heard, let us not be found ungrateful
pages.38:
against the divine powers. But if the fates cannot be bent by any of our peace, we will enjoy this good, that those who understand in their own adverse affairs that nothing was omitted by them, will be satisfied. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'M' begins the text.</note> Our army followed today with the greatest glory of all, for it stood in the battle line against the enemies so strongly that it took back a most famous victory by dying for the defense of the fatherland. That great fear has been removed from us, and the worry of the whole city has ceased. For since we preferred to hope rather than to be undone by a long siege, we have followed an unhoped-for victory, for it certainly seemed to us in the war that heaven itself and all the divine powers had fought for us. Such was the outcome of this great conflict that hardly any of our soldiers fell in the war. What fortune the other side had, appears from this, that they all stood like cattle for the slaughter. Twenty military standards were captured, the entire camp of the enemies was broken and plundered. Nor was that battle one in which they were not caught on the edge of the sword, and received by our troops. When our victorious army returned to the city, adorned with many and great trophies of the enemies, our whole city was poured out for the spectacle in a wonderful way. There was no one who did not give praises and thanks to God. The others, however, praised not as a human matter, but as a divine one. Truly, the joy and exultation of all was such that it seemed not to be the face of many men, but of one, and the same mind. Truly, no man’s house was not open to all. Everywhere our militia was received with such generosity and such a wealth of all things that never in the mere fertility of the fields had it been greater. I wanted all these things to be known to you, so that you who were an ally in our dangers might also become a participant in the public tranquility, and might congratulate our fortunes. Farewell.
