pages.31:
mitigate that which is intended for the benefit of the republic. Clearly, I seem to myself to divine all future things, which you also greatly fear. I cannot sufficiently admire with what madness your citizens rush into this discord. Perhaps there are some in the city who think they will take possession of power if everything falls into the hands of the enemy. And it is to be feared that this plague has been set in motion by the cunning of our enemies, so that they may the more easily obtain victory. I would prefer at this point to be able to alleviate this evil from you with some help of mine, rather than give counsel at a time when your affairs can least be helped by counsel. But since matters have reached the point where what I preferred to be done cannot be performed by me, I will not omit writing to you what I think regarding the salvation of your republic. It must be investigated by those themselves who desire the salvation of the republic, what each one’s mind is. The wise among your old allies must be solicited so that they may remember your faith and friendship. The reinforcements of the allies must be received secretly by you into the city, until you see that those who do not think well of your liberty can be coerced by force. And as to how this disease can be cured, and this evil which has already infected you can be removed, it cannot be done unless that part which is sick is cut off from the body itself. I hope that if your city makes use of my counsel, you will shortly understand that every danger which abounds in your very vitals has been driven away. For as I feel what you are about to do in your situation, you will provide again and again. For I do not labor less for your salvation than if everything were shared between us. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'D' starts the text.</note> I will postpone your request. I will immediately satisfy you regarding what you most desire to hear from me. You have been absolved by the sentences of all the judges, and the lawsuit has been decided in your favor. Never have I seen a man more learned in presenting a case than he who you entrusted with your own. For he complied as much as the right of speaking could allow before the judges. He was so vehement and sharp in refuting the crimes that were being cast upon you that he rendered all the judges fully favorable and hostile to your flatterers. Everyone praised the talent of this orator. They approved your case and extolled the equity of the judges. When they proceeded to the verdict, it was so much the applause of all that they congratulated the matter no less than if it were their own business. I wanted to write these things to you so that I might relieve your mind of that anxiety which (as I know) you were much troubled by. Farewell.
pages.32:
<note>A red decorative initial 'H' starts the text.</note> I offer you thanks, and great ones indeed, that you have relieved me of my greatest anxiety and trouble. But with no less pleasure did this affect me, which you wrote to me concerning my patron, a most modest and eloquent man. For I am greatly delighted by his praise and the magnificence of his service. For even if I never doubted my case, which was to be given to me in court, yet because in trials, no less than in sailing, danger often threatens, and he who is a skilled pilot avoids it, I was always fearing that neither the equity of the cause nor another fortune would result in what I hoped. Therefore, I rejoice that I have obtained such an orator, in whom neither human eloquence nor study was lacking. Shortly (as I hope), I shall congratulate him myself. Meanwhile, I will signify to him that I am grateful for his studies and services. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'V' starts the text.</note> You desire that it be signified by me what everyone feels regarding you, both your friends and your fellow citizens. Their sentiment is one: that no one among your equals is greater in talent, but they greatly fear that you do not use it with enough modesty. Wherefore, my Anthony, if a good reputation delights you, if the opinion of men—which you certainly hold at no small level now—is important to you, see that you do not allow your other virtues, which are great, to be overshadowed by your lack of modesty alone. I indeed understand that you will be the greatest citizen in our city if you know how to use your talent modestly. That you may do this, I ask again and again. Farewell.
pages.33:
<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' starts the text.</note> Regarding the modesty you write that you desire from me, I know whence this arises. If I do it, all my fellow citizens and friends will understand, even if there is another virtue in me, that this one is not lacking. It cannot be helped, as this age has many things that are reproved and criticized. And often people are found who, almost through envy, criticize something and make our vices appear greater if anyone seems to surpass them either in talent or in study. From there, I know the whole cause has proceeded: because although men have praised everything in me, they withdraw from me the reputation of modesty, because I do not permit them to be long in that error. I shall strive for one thing, so that I am not hindered by the age I am in, nor by labor, as I will do everything that leads to the improvement of men. You will assist me in this matter (as you do), so that just as I have become much more ardent for good arts through your exhortations and counsels, I may also understand through you that I have observed the benevolence of my fellow citizens. Farewell.

A great preparation is being agitated, such as perhaps has never been heard of in our city. Great fleets of ships are commissioned. Highly instructed classes are readied. They are building new triremes <note>original: "triremes"</note> <gloss>three-banked warships</gloss>. They are preparing for a huge war by sea and land against a nation that is in every way most hostile to us. And it is the hope of all that there has never been a time given to us that should be better seized for victory. If we obtain it, there will be eternal peace for our city. For all nations (this one excepted) that could wage war against us have been conquered by us in love, and in arms, and by strength, and there is nothing else that remains for our republic than that we also curb this nation, which will not be difficult for us to do, provided that speed is applied to our councils. We have everything that can easily supply victory to our endeavors. The enemy is surprised, we are fortified by counsel. He
pages.34:
is impatient, we are most instructed in all necessary things. He is already broken and weakened by domestic and foreign wars, we are intact and never more powerful. Why say more? Many cities have defected from the faith and alliance of our enemies. The strength of our allies increases daily before the cities. There is no reason why we should not clearly hold this victory in our hands. We do not want to lack anything. But I also hope well regarding the very maturity of the matter, since we have never used more prudent men and stronger leaders for a task of this kind. I have written this to you, see that you do not divulge anything of these things that is of interest to the republic. But I did not want you to be ignorant of this, so that you might become more learned through me regarding the great things that are being agitated by us, which I knew you wanted most to know. Farewell.

I consider that which pertains more to the matter now being agitated: whether it has been deliberated wisely by you regarding undertaking a war for which such a great preparation is being set up. You see how you promise certain victory to your fatherland and hope for everything to go well. Carthage, a most powerful city, for many years
pages.35:
(under the leadership of Hannibal) waged war with the Romans. And although he had seen the devastation of Italy and Rome almost captured, yet the outcome was not victory, as it finally saw itself captive and subject to Roman laws. Cyrus also, the king of the Persians, after having waged many happy wars for nearly thirty years, rushed into war against the Scythians, and hoped that once that nation was conquered, he would later be in perpetual peace. But what end of his great endeavors did the Scythian queen Thamyris abhor? Having captured the king and two hundred Persians, she taught them well enough. And it does not escape me that the wars which are to be waged by you may have a bad outcome, as I read, and that you should lead your mind rather to peace and concord than to war. Nor is there any reason why you should be dissuaded from this; for the whole matter could be performed with greater glory than that war could be administered, which is not against an unprepared enemy. You write that you are undertaking the war with a prudent and powerful force. And it is to be feared that other nations may rebel, and that cities which are now bound by the fear of your power but are still with you may defect from the faith. It will be, therefore, your wisdom to see all these things, and not to move your mind from the opinion of those who persuade you toward peace. But if you remain in the counsel you have undertaken, provide that what is deliberated in your senate does not reach the enemies, as whatever has been initiated by you is being watched. Nor did I write to you because you have much power in the republic, so that if it seems good to you, you may have the senate deliberate on this matter, and consider it more maturely with me. For I, out of my faith and benevolence, desire that everything turn out well for you all. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'P' begins the paragraph.</note> At no time have I written to you about great matters. That one is truly the greatest and highest of all, as so many evils seem to hang over our affairs that I might ask for some relief from you. I can easily divine the desolation and ruin of our fatherland. For a most atrocious war, and an incredible famine
pages.36:
and plague—such as we have not yet read of, nor have we seen—has already for a long time afflicted almost the entire province, nor does the force of such great evil remit in any part as yet; rather, the evil increases daily and becomes worse. Consider that we cannot bear such great slaughters for long. For how long have we reached this point? Now we are exhausted by suffering, and hope itself, which as long as we could do something was urging us to be strong in repelling evils or wise in bearing them, has so failed that it seems to be nothing at all. Who could not easily divine this, not only the desolation but also the final destruction of our city? For there will be a time in which, where the traces of our city were, men will look for them, nor will they find any remains of this formerly most powerful and flourishing fatherland. Unless God remits His anger and, weary of us in such great evils, at last begins to look upon us with kindness. And since human help has deserted our affairs, we are forced, as often happens to sailors in a storm, to refer all our councils, all our hope and thought, to God, in the pursuing of which you will be a helper and ally to us. Although God may seem to move His mind and ears away from our prayers, yet we hope that His clemency will change for the better the evils by which we are afflicted and almost crushed. Farewell.

<note>A decorative red drop cap 'L' starts the text.</note> Your letters brought such trouble to my mind that at no time have I been in greater sadness. For when our fortunes in the republic have been led to such a point that now nothing of support can be expected from men, it is most to be feared that we are deprived of divine aid also. If this had happened to us through some other error, I would think that everything must be borne not only with an equal but also with a brave mind. But since we have always been those who, for the liberty of all, for the faith of allies, have very often undertaken the greatest wars with great danger, I do not know by what iniquity of fortune it has come to pass that we are deprived of divine as well as human help. And it is not far absent
pages.37: that I see all the evils that you prophesied would happen to your city. Perhaps men who come after us will ask where the foundations of such a great city were, and at last that very fame of our fatherland, which for a long time flourished in Italy, will perhaps perish, after that thing does not exist for the sake of which our glory and name were great for a long time. It is consolation for the evils of the past that we have examples of the most famous cities and kingdoms that at some time had a similar end, so that nothing reaches us except the name itself. I believe there have been more cities that in their own times were famous and renowned for the glory of their deeds, with whom fame has been extinguished together, because of the lack of poets or orators who might illustrate their deeds with speech or poem and not allow the memory of those things which were worthy of immortality to perish. Our republic, as it was greedy for glory, so it had gathered men who, by their eloquence and wisdom, would be the memorialists of our affairs. I begin to understand this, how much veneration there should be among all magnificent cities for those who know how to recount the deeds of things, whether done in peace or war. I cannot sufficiently admire that the greatest opportunity was lacking to our men, since they could judge all their endeavors and labors as having been undertaken by them in vain, not providing by what reason they could become immortal. But enough of this. Your counsel is (as they say) the time for placating the gods, since necessity, more than our will, makes us suppliants. We would have preferred to use this remedy when we had everything intact, and it would have been a sign that it was being done by us from a willing heart. I do not write later what cannot be corrected by us. We do what sailors themselves do in a great storm (for I will gladly use your example): now that the mast is broken and the ship is shattered, let us make all our prayers. If our prayer is heard, let us not be found ungrateful
pages.38:
toward the divine powers. If, however, the fates cannot be bent by any peace of ours, we will enjoy that good which those who understand that nothing was left undone by themselves in their own adverse affairs enjoy. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'M' starts the text.</note> With the greatest praise of all, our army has acquitted itself this day. It stood in battle line against the enemies with such a strong fight that, through persistence for the defense of the fatherland, by dying they brought back a most glorious victory. That great fear and the rumor of the trepidation of the whole city have been removed from us. For when we preferred to hope rather than to be ruined by a long siege, we obtained an unhoped-for victory. For it seemed to us in the war certainly that heaven itself and all the divine powers had fought for us. For such was the outcome of this great conflict that hardly any of our soldiers had fallen in the war. What fortune the other side had, it appears from this, that they all fought like cattle to the death. Twenty military standards were captured. The camps of the enemies were completely broken and plundered. Nor was that battle one where there was not a man taken by the edge of the sword and received by our troops. When our victorious army returned to the city, adorned with many and great trophies of the enemies, our whole city was poured out for the spectacle in a wonderful way. There was no one who did not give praise and thanks to God. The others, however, praised not as a human thing but as a divine one. The joy and exultation of all were so great that it was no longer the faces of many men, but one face and the same mind that was seen. No man's house was not open to all. Everywhere our militia was received with such generosity and abundance of all things that it was never greater in the sole sum of the fertility of the fields. I wanted these things to be known to you, so that as you were an ally in our dangers, you might also be a partaker of the public tranquility and might rejoice in our fortunes. Farewell.

N.text:
<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' starts the text.</note> Regarding the modesty you write that you desire from me, I know whence this arises. If I do it, all my fellow citizens and friends will understand, even if there is another virtue in me, that this one is not lacking. It cannot be helped, as this age has many things that are reproved and criticized. And often people are found who, almost through envy, criticize something and make our vices appear greater if anyone seems to surpass them either in talent or in study. From there, I know the whole cause has proceeded: because although men have praised everything in me, they withdraw from me the reputation of modesty, because I do not permit them to be long in that error. I shall strive for one thing, so that I am not hindered by the age I am in, nor by labor, as I will do everything that leads to the improvement of men. You will assist me in this matter (as you do), so that just as I have become much more ardent for good arts through your exhortations and counsels, I may also understand through you that I have observed the benevolence of my fellow citizens. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' starts the text.</note> I am writing to you about greater things than I wrote previously; for they are such that they not only invite you to read, but also to be very much excited. A great preparation is being agitated, such as perhaps has never been heard of in our city. Great fleets of ships are commissioned. Highly instructed classes are readied. They are building new triremes <note>original: "triremes"</note> <gloss>three-banked warships</gloss>. They are preparing for a huge war by sea and land against a nation that is in every way most hostile to us. And it is the hope of all that there has never been a time given to us that should be better seized for victory. If we obtain it, there will be eternal peace for our city. For all nations (this one excepted) that could wage war against us have been conquered by us in love, and in arms, and by strength, and there is nothing else that remains for our republic than that we also curb this nation, which will not be difficult for us to do, provided that speed is applied to our councils. We have everything that can easily supply victory to our endeavors. The enemy is surprised, we are fortified by counsel. He

X.text:
is impatient, we are most instructed in all necessary things. He is already broken and weakened by domestic and foreign wars, we are intact and never more powerful. Why say more? Many cities have defected from the faith and alliance of our enemies. The strength of our allies increases daily before the cities. There is no reason why we should not clearly hold this victory in our hands. We do not want to lack anything. But I also hope well regarding the very maturity of the matter, since we have never used more prudent men and stronger leaders for a task of this kind. I have written this to you, see that you do not divulge anything of these things that is of interest to the republic. But I did not want you to be ignorant of this, so that you might become more learned through me regarding the great things that are being agitated by us, which I knew you wanted most to know. Farewell.

<note>A large red decorative initial 'P' begins the paragraph.</note> Regarding your previous letters, everything you wrote to me about was already being divulged among us, which ought not to have been done if the ancient custom in our senate had been kept. For nothing among our ancestors was guarded more than silence in deliberations on matters that pertained to public utility. But enough about this to you, as you are not ignorant of these things. I consider that which pertains more to the matter now being agitated: whether it has been deliberated wisely by you regarding undertaking a war for which such a great preparation is being set up. You see how you promise certain victory to your fatherland and hope for everything to go well. But I, since I see nothing closer to me than the outcome of wars, and all that you are agitating seems to be laid open to your enemies, I fear that your councils may fail you. Wherefore, if your deliberation had been taken up for peace instead, that matter would not only be more honorable, but also safer for you. For you could use the examples of other nations and see that often many cities undertook wars when they had everything ready and instructed, yet they met with an unhappy outcome. Carthage, a most powerful city, for many years

pages.31:
the one who wishes for the public good to be preserved, let him mitigate. I truly seem to divine all future things, which you also fear most greatly. I cannot wonder enough at the madness that leads your citizens into this discord. Perhaps there are some in the city who think they will take control of affairs if all things come under the power of the enemy. And it is to be feared that this plague has been devised by the guile of the enemy, so that they may more easily obtain victory. I would rather be able to alleviate the evil from you in this place with some assistance of mine, than to advise you at a time when your affairs can least be aided by counsel. But since matters have reached such a point that what I desired to be done better cannot be done by me, I will not omit to write what I feel concerning the safety of your state. It must be explored by those who desire the state to be safe, what each person’s mind is. All your former allies must be solicited by wise men so that they remember your loyalty and friendship. The reinforcements of the allies must be secretly received by you into the city, until you see that you can force those who do not think well of your liberty. Nor will this disease be able to be cured, nor will this evil that has already festered be taken from you, unless that part which is sick is cut off from the body itself. I hope that if your city uses my counsel, you will shortly understand that all the danger which abounds in its very vitals has been driven away. For just as I feel what you are about to do in your own affairs, you will provide again and again. For I do not labor less for your safety than if all things were common between us. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial D starts the text.</note> I shall postpone your request. I will immediately satisfy you regarding what you most desire to hear from me. You have been absolved by the sentences of all the judges, and the lawsuit has been decided in your favor. Never have I seen a man more learned in increasing the weight of causes than that very man to whom you had entrusted your own. For he complied there as much as the legal profession could before the judges. He was so vehement and sharp
pages.32:
in refuting the crimes that were being brought against you, that he rendered all the judges fully favorable to you and hostile to your accusers. Everyone praised the talent of this orator. They approved your case and held up the fairness of the judges. When the outcome was finally reached, there was such applause from everyone that they congratulated one another no less than if it were a matter concerning them all. I wanted to write these things to you so that I might relieve your mind of that anxiety which (as I know) was troubling you greatly. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial H starts the text.</note> I give you thanks, and great ones indeed, for you have freed me from the greatest anxiety and trouble. But it affected me with no less pleasure that you wrote to me concerning my patron, a most modest and eloquent man. For I am greatly delighted by his praise and his truly magnificent service. For even if I never doubted my case, as far as the law ought to be decided, yet because in trials, no less than in sailing, danger often threatens the one who is skilled as a helmsman before he reaches the shore. I always feared lest the fairness of the cause or another fortune might have had a different outcome from that which I hoped for. Therefore I rejoice that I have obtained such an orator, in whom neither human eloquence nor study was lacking. Shortly (as I hope), I shall congratulate him myself. Meanwhile, I will signify to him that I am grateful for his studies and services. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial V starts the text.</note> You desire it to be signified by me what everyone—both your friends and your fellow citizens—feels about you. There is one common opinion: that no one among your peers is greater in talent. But they fear greatly that you do not use it with enough modesty. Wherefore, my Antony, if good fame delights you, if you sustain the opinion of men which is certainly not small now, see that you do not affect your other virtues, which are great, with a lack of modesty. I understand indeed that you will be the greatest citizen in our city if you know how to use your talent modestly. That you may do so, I ask you again and again. Farewell.

Carthage, a most powerful city for many years,
pages.35:
(under the leadership of Hannibal) waged war with the Romans. And although he had seen the devastation of Italy, and Rome almost captured, yet the outcome was not a victory, for it finally saw itself captured and serving under Roman laws. Cyrus, also king of the Persians, after he had waged many wars happily for nearly thirty years, rushed into war against the Scythians, hoping that after that nation was conquered, he would later be in perpetual peace. But what end did his great efforts abhor from Tomyris, the queen of the Scythians? After the king was captured and two hundred thousand Persians were killed, she taught him enough. And it is not far from me to fear that the wars which are to be waged by you might have a bad outcome, because while you read, you might rather lead your mind toward peace and concord than toward war. Nor is there anything that should dissuade you more, for the whole matter could be managed with greater glory than that war could be administered, which is not against an impatient enemy. You write that you are undertaking the war with a foresighted and powerful spirit. And it is to be feared lest other nations revolt, lest cities that now live under the fear of your power and are still with you, might defect from the faith. It will be, therefore, for your wisdom to see all these things, and not to use your modesty and humanity to turn your mind away from the opinion of those who advise peace to you. But if you remain in the counsel you have undertaken, provide that those things that have been deliberated in your senate do not reach the enemies, and whatever has been begun by you. Nor have I written to you, because you are very powerful in the republic, so that if it seems good to you, you may hold a senate on this matter, and deliberate maturely with me concerning these things. For I, by my loyalty and benevolence, desire that it may turn out well for you all. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial P starts the text.</note> I have never written to you about great things at such a time; that one is indeed the greatest and most important of all, because such great evils seem to be hanging over our affairs that I fear someone might hear of them from us ourselves. I could easily divine the desolation and ruin of our fatherland. For a most atrocious war, and incredible fame
pages.36:
and plague, such as we have neither read of nor seen until now, has almost been driven into the whole province for a long time, and the violence of such a great evil does not yet subside in any part, but the evil increases daily, and behaves for the worse. Think that we cannot bear such great disasters for long, as we have until now. But now we are weary from enduring, and hope itself, which, as long as we were able to do anything, encouraged us to be strong in repelling or wise in enduring the evils themselves, has so departed that it seems to be there not at all. Who could not easily divine from this not only the desolation but also that very final extinction of our city? For there will be a time in which, where the traces of our city were, men will ask, and they will not pull out any timbers of this formerly most powerful and flourishing fatherland. Unless God has remitted His anger, and has begun to look upon us, weary from such great evils, more kindly at last. And since human defenses have abandoned our affairs, we are compelled, as often happens to sailors in a storm, to refer all our councils, all our hope and thought, to God, and in the following of that matter, you will be an assistant and an ally to us. Although God seems to turn His mind and ears from our prayers, yet we hope that His clemency will change into better things the evils by which we are afflicted and almost ruined. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial L starts the text.</note> Your letters have brought such trouble to my mind that at no time have I been in greater sorrow. For since our fortunes have been brought to such a point that now nothing of defense can be expected from men, it is most to be feared that we are also deprived of divine aid. If this had happened to us by some other error, I would think that all things should be borne not only with a steady but also with a brave mind. But since we have always been those who have often undertaken, with great danger, the greatest wars for the liberty of all and for the faith of our allies, I know not by what iniquity of fortune it has come to pass that we have been deprived of divine and human aid. Nor is it far away
pages.37: I see all the evils that you predicted would happen to your city. Perhaps men who come after us will ask where the foundations of such a great city were, and at last that very fame of our fatherland, which flourished for so long in Italy, will perhaps vanish, after nothing remains of that for the sake of which our glory and name were great for a long time. It is permitted to be consoled by the evils of the past, because we have examples of most famous cities and kingdoms that at some time had a similar end, so that nothing came to us but the name itself. But I consider that there have been more cities that in their own times were distinguished and famous for the glory of their deeds, with whom their fame has perished, due to the scarcity of poets or orators who might illustrate their deeds by speech or poem, and not allow the memory of those things which were worthy of immortality to perish. Our republic, just as it was greedy for glory, so it has also acquired men who, by the eloquence of wisdom, would be the chroniclers of our deeds worthy of memory. I begin to understand here how great the veneration should be among all magnificent cities for those who know how to protect, by the reasoning of deeds, things done in peace or war. I cannot wonder enough that the greatest opportunity has been lacking to our men, since they could judge all their efforts and labors to have been undertaken by them in vain, and not provide by what reason they could become immortal. But enough about this. Your counsel, however, is (as they say) a time for appeasing the heavens, since greater necessity than our own will makes us suppliants. We would have preferred to use this remedy when we had everything intact, and it would have been a sign that it was done by us from a heart that truly I do not write later, since it cannot be corrected by us. We do what sailors also do in a great storm (for I shall gladly use your example), since the mast is now broken and the ship is shattered, let us make all our vows. If our prayer has been heard, let us not be found ungrateful
pages.38:
against the divine powers. If, however, the fates cannot be bent by any of our peace, we shall enjoy that good, which those who in their own adverse affairs understand that nothing has been omitted by them. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial M starts the text.</note> Our army has attained the greatest glory of all this day. For it stood in line against the enemy in such a strong fight that, for the defense of the fatherland, they obtained the most famous victory from it by dying with persistence. That great fear has been removed from us, and the agitation of the whole city. For since we preferred to hope rather than to be ruined by a long siege, we obtained an unexpected victory, so that in the war it certainly seemed to us that heaven itself and all the divine powers had fought for us. For such was the outcome of this great conflict that hardly any of our soldiers had fallen in the war. What fortune the other side had, however, appears from this, that they all stood as if they were cattle ready for slaughter. Twenty military standards were captured; the camps of the enemy were completely broken and plundered. And there was not that battle that was not received at the edge of the sword, and intercepted by our forces. When, however, our victorious army returned to the city, adorned with the many and greatest trophies of the enemy, our whole city was poured out to the spectacle in a wonderful manner. There was no one who did not give praise and thanks to God. But they praised not as a human thing, but as a divine one. And there was such joy and exultation of all, that not now did it seem to be the faces of many men, but one face and one mind. Truly, no man's house was not open to all. Everywhere our military was received with such great generosity and abundance of everything, that it had never been greater even in the sole highest fertility of the fields. I wanted all these things to be known to you, so that you who were an ally in our dangers might also become a participant in the public tranquility and might rejoice in our fortunes. Farewell.

pages.39:
<note>A large red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>
Or rather, it was something other than what I had expected from your deliberation. That you write to me about the victory is all the more joyful, and indeed all the more pleasing. I could not be anything but in great pain when I heard that your most loving city was surrounded by a siege. I was also very much saddened that the head of our province had been left to the surrender of the enemy for so long. You have freed me today from the great fear that I was suffering for your safety, and I owe you the thanks that I owe, because you have made me a participant in the events that have turned out so prosperously for you. I understand from these things that you have feared, that it touches upon how much care there is that your safety is a matter for men, since the same has been preserved by the immortal gods even when all hope was lost. I think, however, that you should not judge those names of heaven (as you write) to have fought for you alone, but also to have been victorious. But another thing must be seen by you again and again, that you do not exalt your minds too much in prosperous affairs. And it must be especially provided for (as you are doing) that you refer your victories to the divine rather than to the human. For we are almost all with our minds humbled in our perils, and then we raise and exalt the Lord God. I know that later I will find the ingratitude, when we have reached the sum of our desires. Furthermore, that men judge there to be no perpetual happiness, and they accuse fortune. I, however, judge that there is no other prosperous or adverse fortune than divine providence, which exercises men now by helping, now by correcting them with reason. Furthermore, there is another reason for things, whose instability often happens to us more than fortune. I do not write these things to you because I think they are unknown to you, but so that you might admonish your citizens that at no time is God to be feared more than when we have received greater benefits from him. I hope well for your citizens. Your authority will nonetheless have some weight with them, if you teach them that nothing is more necessary for the <term>res publica</term> <gloss>republic/commonwealth</gloss> than to cultivate religion in peace just as fortitude is cultivated in war. Farewell.
pages.40:
<note>A decorative red initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>
There is nothing that could be done more willingly than to make you better informed about the greatest and most beautiful things that are happening here. For after our city was freed from the enemy's fear and gave itself to leisure and peace, it is incredible how much the state of the <term>res publica</term> <gloss>commonwealth</gloss> began to be reformed and, as it were, renewed day by day. If there were any old discords among our citizens, they have all been lifted and removed. The leaders of the city are entering into new affinities. The fortresses, which had been weakened by the force of wars, are being restored with greater care than before and with greater resources, nor have they ever been held in such high regard. Many ancient laws and old statutes that had become dormant through our insolence and negligence are now being renewed, and almost all of the common offices have been approved, which, if they are obeyed, no one doubts will make us in this city of ours (for such is the state of our city) somewhat happier than we have been, having experienced long calamity and compelled by fortune, which, if it had found the same thing we were long relying on, would have crossed over and always found leisure. Therefore, I gladly do all this for you, so that you, who have been most attentive to our glory, might not be ignorant of our happiness at this time. Farewell.

<note>A decorative red initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>
O you, about what you wrote to me, I have received great pleasure in my mind. For as I was constantly standing in fear, since there was long doubt about your safety, you freed me from great worry when I understood from your previous letters that your city had been freed from the siege that was oppressing it. Your letters filled me with such joy, when you announced to me that you were not only exempt from the most serious danger, but that the <term>res publica</term> <gloss>commonwealth</gloss> itself was daily taking on some new form and a happier state. I rejoice, and more than could be believed, I delight in your happiness. I see indeed that those outstanding foundations of your ancestors' <term>res publica</term> <gloss>commonwealth</gloss> are being stirred up by you with great zeal. For when the laws, in which the safety of your city was placed, had come into your forgetfulness...
pages.41:
and the ancient custom was not being observed in the city, it was no wonder if your homeland was brought to a siege. But now, with the laws restored and every good custom repeated, I hope that your city has now become more ample and opulent. As to what it will be in the future, provided you do not falter in the middle of the course. And where someone perhaps serves power rather than the <term>res publica</term> <gloss>commonwealth</gloss>, it is to be feared that you have rejoiced in this new liberty in vain. Therefore, concord must be retained by you, nor should the ancient laws be weakened, and new institutes should be brought forth, nor should one repent so that more may be able to reach the city. Whence come want and justice. And if it has proceeded from you, I clearly see your <term>res publica</term> <gloss>commonwealth</gloss> (as you write) will be the first in the whole province, and you will govern those nations to whom you once served. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'S' marks the beginning of the text.</note>
I know that you are eager for new things and have often accused me because I never write to you about these matters which are current. I do this on this day so that you might not henceforth be able to blame my negligence. You indicate to me that a war is being prepared with great apparatus by the oriental kings against your common empire, and that nothing is being omitted by you that pertains to pushing away this danger from your cities and those of your allies. I do not see what could be added to this wisdom or your virtue. For if fortune answers to the councils, I do not doubt that you will avert all those movements of wars. If, however, it must be fought by hand, I hope that even if you are inferior in forces, you will be superior in the strength of soldiers and the science of military affairs. For although these Tartar nations have always been worth much in the multitude of horsemen and power, they have nevertheless rarely been victors in their wars. With great
pages.44:
clamor of war, they come against me. They seem strong in the first impetus. They shake their weapons. But when it comes to the swords, with the ranks broken, they all turn their backs. Our soldiers, however, are neither sluggish in undertaking, nor less strong in enduring either dangers or the labors of the camp. As often as they are challenged by the enemy, all things must be attempted first, before the fortune of war is experienced. And if your wisdom does not ask from you whether it must be fought with these barbarians, and it is demanded of you for your glory, and the empire which you received from your ancestors as most ample and illustrious, it must be especially guarded against, lest the enemy strike the unprepared. For while you have sent scouts into all parts, who would report back to you about the counsels of the enemies, about the movements if any are stirred up by them, while envoys are sent to them, the approaches are to be occupied, the arts of how they are to be offended are found, and all things are to be so prepared by you, as if they were already within your borders, and they were raging in the middle of the kingdom. A most divided matter has happened to us these days, nor has it been heard of by any of our citizens before, about which I have thought to make you informed, so that you would not neglect any matter so great and so hidden, which I desire above all for it to be known to you first. I think (unless I am mistaken) that you, while you were among us, understood what we did, that the city sent into exile Sulpicius, a man most loving of the homeland. About which deed I do not write more. For that matter pertains to our city. Our enemies, having invaded the city which
pages.45:
was once advised by the citizen, paid the penalty for their temerity shortly after. When the city was besieged and the supplies were cut off, so that the matter clearly awaited surrender, then Sulpicius, bravely consulting for the first, began to stir up new counsels, by which he might deliver the enemy, already insulting over the members, conquered to his own citizens. He offered himself to the enemy camps, and said that he would speak about the greatest matters before the leader of the enemy, who received him kindly. He said that he was no longer held by any reason by the homeland, which, having never deserved anything bad from him or through any error, had so ill deserved of him. Then he warned our enemy that the city could be taken in only one way, if they obeyed his counsels; it was not doubtful that they would possess the city shortly. For he said that the place was not far from the members, planted with trees, and he persuaded them to simulate a flight with industry, and to occupy the place most suitable for ambushes; he said it would happen that the citizens would be more relaxed in their guard, and that the walls could be easily climbed at night and the whole city taken. When this matter was believed by the enemy, nor was anything done other than what he himself had counseled, then he signified all things to our men, who, with the gates opened, poured out around the second watch, and enclosed the enemies placed in the ambushes. And with few having escaped through the benefit of the night, the rest were oppressed, cut down, or captured. And the matter has not yet been opened, so that we might lead our army to their walls more maturely. You, however, will understand from the letters that time has been given to bring out these secrets. Farewell. But the spirit grows among the enemies, and the hope that had fallen at the first impetus rises greater in them. Furthermore, it happens not sometimes that those who were driven into flight restore the war, and fight more bitterly than if they had not despaired of victory from the beginning. It was expected by me that your deliberation <note>refers to the previous strategic discussions</note> would be concluded. Your writing to me about the victory is all the more joyful, and it is also more gratifying. I could not feel otherwise than in great sorrow, when I heard that your most beloved city was surrounded by a siege. I was grieving, and for a long time I was agitated that such a noble province of ours should have been surrendered to the enemy. Today, however, you have freed me from the greatest fear that I was suffering for your safety, and I owe you the thanks that I owe, for you have made me a participant in the events that have turned out prosperously for you. I understand from these things that have happened to you what anxiety it causes you that your safety should matter to men, when the same has now been preserved by immortal gods even when all had despaired. I do not think that you should judge these names of heaven, as you write, to be such that they have not only fought for you, but also conquered. But you must also see, time and again, that you do not let your spirit become too exalted in successful matters. And that must be provided for above all (as you are doing), that you should attribute your victory rather to divine power than to human effort. For we are almost all prone to let our spirit fail in our dangers, and then we raise and exalt the Lord God. I do not know what iniquity I might find afterward, when we have reached the height of our vows. Then, let men see that no happiness is perpetual, and they accuse fortune. I, for my part, judge that there is no other prosperous or adverse fortune than divine providence, which now exercises men with adversity, now corrects them with reason. Then there is another cause for things, the instability of which is often the cause of what happens to us, not fortune. I do not write these things to you because I think they are unknown to you, but so that you may admonish your fellow citizens that God is to be feared more at this time, when we have received greater benefits from Him. I hope well for your fellow citizens. Your authority among them will nevertheless be of some value, if you teach them that nothing is greater for the republic <term>res publica</term> <gloss>public affairs/commonwealth</gloss> than to cultivate religion in peace just as fortitude in war. When the city was besieged and the supplies were shut off, so that the matter was clearly waiting for a surrender, then Sulpicius, courageously going to the enemy, began to stir up new plans by which he would free the enemy who was already insulting them, having been conquered by his own citizens. He offered himself to the enemy camps and said that he would speak words regarding great matters before the enemy leader, by whom he was received with kindness. He said that he was held by no reason for his fatherland, which never, neither by its own fault nor by any error, had deserved so badly from him. Then he warned our enemy that the city could be taken by them in only one way, if they followed his plans, there was no doubt that they would shortly take the city. For he said that there was a place not far from the walls, planted with trees, and he persuaded them to simulate a flight with industry and to occupy the place most suitable for ambushes; he said it would happen that the citizens would be more relaxed in their guard, and at night they could easily scale the walls and take the whole city. When this matter was believed by the enemy, and things were done other than what he himself had counseled, then he signified all things to our men, who, with the gates opened, having poured out around the second watch, surrounded the enemies who were positioned in the ambushes. And after a few escaped by the benefit of the night, the others were oppressed, slaughtered, or captured. Nor has the result yet been revealed, as we lead our army more maturely to their walls. You will understand, however, that the time was given to me to report these secrets by letter. Farewell. Almost all the cities of this our Cisalpine Gaul are stirring up new things. Some depose their old masters and claim themselves in liberty. Others make new tyrants for themselves. Others, while studying new things, use the talent of others rather than their own. Others follow the examples of the rest. Rome tries to recall old masters whom the wars of the more powerful had displaced from their position. And there is no city in this empire that uses enough counsel in such movements. Citizens conspire, one against another. The peoples have as leaders of their frenzy those who surpass the rest in force and wickedness. Cremona, once a most opulent city, has changed princes within a few years. It is now placed under a most cruel tyrant. Brescia is worn down by the frequent pounding of its factions and already sees its state failing. Men judge it will soon have a new master. Bergamo, a city more oppressed by the discords of civil wars, has admitted other enemies into itself. For it was not only <unclear>that part ruled</unclear>, but also <unclear>what was the</unclear> evil itself, which (as they say) boils much more strongly in the very entrails. For Rome is afflicted under one such prince, and under diverse and many tyrants. Ravenna, since it had once flourished with the great talents and spirits of its citizens, has now been made a colony and filled with a crowd of the most filthy and rustic men, which one could easily judge to be the most miserable and unfortunate in all of Italy. There are innumerable others that have their own unhappy fortune and are placed in a great tempest. But you will understand all things better from him whom I send to you with these letters. If you have any great news in these parts where you are staying, write everything to me, lest I be ignorant of your affairs. Farewell.
pages.48: I have received your letter full of new matters. I pity the state of so many magnificent cities and of the people being provoked. For since I see that in all of Latium there is no genius more illustrious in arms, I see that former glory of Cisalpine Gaul now almost deflowered and reduced to desolation. Oh, this is the greatest fortune of all things, that when it has reached its summit, then we realize it is at its end. Greece itself (if I may repeat the examples of the ancestors a little further back) long conquered Italy not only in disciplines but also in arms. And it was not far from possessing the empire of the whole world under the leader Alexander. This being taken away from human affairs, even their own <unclear>might</unclear> failed. Rome, if I want an example of all the Punic wars and nations, added to the name of the empire that which remained from the kings, under the solar empire which extended to the Parthians, and under the emperors I say not only fame but also its power spread to the borders of the world. Nevertheless, it could not save or even maintain that empire which had once been granted. It heard the end of all its glory through the moans of those in Greece, long since transferred by external kings now to the west, now to the north. It rejoices in and laments this one thing, that there is no one among those to whom the regime of our world passed who does not rejoice to be called a king of the Romans. Gaul, however, had grown to such a point in the fame of its achievements and the excellence of its best men that it seemed to outshine and surpass the splendor of other nations. Now you write to me of its ruin and end. I have no solace by which I can better alleviate your fortune than by these examples, which I also am accustomed to use often, since something happens to me that is too harsh and bitter in my affairs. Nothing is done in this regime that should be wondered at for its novelty or magnificence. I am indeed in such leisure, how much I do not know <unclear>as we were</unclear> otherwise. I fear lest this perhaps harm our virtue itself, away from all our actions. For just as the harshness of fortune is excessive, so is moderate
pages.49:
prosperity often harmful to glory. Farewell.

These things about which I will write to you are not so new or unusual that something of this kind has never happened to men before. Nevertheless, they have excited no small admiration from the opinion that will be held. Vecturius, a man (as you know) once considered a most opulent citizen among his fellow citizens, had his affairs so badly managed that he contracted a great debt to others. And this he did with much necessity, or he would have been found out by those who loved that man. What he did afterward, and whether it was appropriate when his fortune could no longer be aided, the matter might perhaps have been settled in some year. Having collected from everywhere what he could most secretly, he pretended to set out abroad, and he was promised to be present maturely on the first day of August, as he himself had declared on the calends. He encouraged all of us who loved him that we should provide a surety for him, if by chance anyone had summoned him to court. I thought that he was not held by any or only a modest debt. And if he were even held by a large one, we thought he was solvent. What more? I gave surety for him. Then he departed. When the day of the trial had arrived, since this man did not appear (as he ought to have done in good faith), shortly after, we were demanded for satisfaction by the creditors. We begged the judges to extend the day for us, which when I learned was to be exacted from us, it was necessary to pay for him. And that sum of money which he owed to his creditors was paid. Although this event happened very inconveniently for others, it was so heavy for me that I never hope to be able to pay off the debt that was acquired on his account. I never could have thought it possible that that man had come to such poverty that he would attack his own people with such machinations and deceits. Thus the matter stands, that faith is extended to those who have no sense of shame or modesty. Others are very
pages.50:
surprised by this act. If I bear the penalty of my own faith, you, if at any time you must pledge something for another, will become more cautious by my example. For I believe that to be an art that brings less grace and more disadvantage to men than that which teaches one to stand in court for another's debt and to be a guarantor. And it is a known proverb, "He who puts his foot in the snare is excluded by his own peril and labor." But I perceived this late in my own affair. Farewell.

On the second of February, your letters were delivered to me, in which you signaled to me about the betrayal of Vecturius and wisely admonished me that I should be more cautious in my own affairs by your example. You do this out of your benevolence toward me, which is supreme, and I say the greatest thanks to you. But I would have you know that I was not a little disturbed in spirit by this loss of yours, as if the damage had been done to a part of my own fortune. For I have always judged that nothing can happen to you that would not be my own. This, I judge, I have foreseen many times before for your sake. And it is not far from the time when I would repay my spirit to you if the opportunity were present. But since our fatherland has already been worn down and almost ruined by constant wars, and the revenues of the fields do not respond to the masters, and those arts are not practiced in the city by which the citizens previously used to live with great profit and money, all things have indeed deprived us of emoluments. And those who have wealth and money, there is no one who would not prefer to keep their affairs in port than to commit themselves to manifest perils. If there is anything, however, in which I can be of service to you with any zeal or by my own labor, I will do all things with a good spirit, which I understand to be for your benefit. And I do not wish your obligation to be understood in these matters that pertain to you. In other matters, I will use your prudence. I cannot aid you with money. But I will not hesitate to give satisfaction and to provide a guarantor for you and to obligate all my own things, if I understand that such is your will and if it is necessary to pay for you.
pages.51:
And if I learn that you have been unwilling to use my service in any matter out of excessive modesty, you will diminish that opinion which I had formed from the hope in your service to me and our eternal love. Farewell.

That I write to you about unusual things, it seems to me that I can do a pleasing thing for you. For I know that you have always been desirous of this matter. I will tell you of a most beautiful deed, and one not heard of by any of ours for many years. It helped our city, a prince who, having long troubled the public liberty with arms, finally (as we all think) having been brought to the conscience of his own affairs, began to use his counsels for the better. Having called the people to an assembly, he held an oration before that illustrious and noble body, in which, having rendered an account of both his purpose and the administration he had carried out, he taught the citizens with what spirit he was toward the republic. He would yield to them to use the common liberty securely with their fellow citizens. He did many things wisely and magnificently toward this matter, which caused admiration in everyone. After it was announced from that spirit, a great silence remained among us for a long time. Some judged that they had not understood enough, others, in whom more prudence lay, hesitated as to where his speech was going. But when liberty of speech was granted to all, and he plainly urged and exhorted that each one should state his best opinion, there was no one who did not render divine and immortal thanks to him because he had returned the republic to its own seat. And we all promised not only future impunity for the deed, but also that we would defend his safety and immunity even against the health of our own bodies, and that we would give effort so that he might live somewhat more happily as a private citizen than he had previously when he alone ruled the city. When this matter was understood by him, he himself threw down all his fasces to the people, restored to the fatherland the ancient laws and liberty, and omitted nothing from the ancient and good custom of liberty. He now enjoys the right with us. We, however, are in such leisure
pages.52:
that I would never have dared to hope for otherwise. I believe you will admire this happiness of ours because of the most beautiful deed done by him. Therefore, I wanted all things to be signified to you by me. If there is anything that can be done by me in our senate or by the people for your convenience, have me as your supreme friend, and you may freely use me in all your affairs according to your right. Farewell.

It has also happened that your fatherland has been donated its ancient liberty. Whether this happened by chance or by counsel, it cannot be that this did not happen to you by divine favor. But it must be cared for with great zeal by you so that you may enjoy this good of yours for as long as possible. No thing will effect this more than if the fame of the matter is brought to many. Sophocles (as it is in the fables of the Greeks) when he was delivering a certain tragedy to persuade the Athenian people of the same thing, brought in a danger from the enemies, where he urged the Athenians in a long speech not to nourish a lion in the city, or if it were nourished, to bear with an equal spirit the fact that they were being torn apart. The wisest poet inserted this thing into his poem so that he might teach the people, through a noble fiction, not to commit the power of the city to one who surpassed the others in wealth and talent. And if that liberty were committed to him, he urged that servitude should even be preferred, lest the popular state use a stronger master. There was never anything that kept the Roman people, the master of nations, from liberty, because it preferred to have the power that was everyone's be that of a few, and to be human, and rather to serve emperors than to reign. It is incredible how much restored liberty delights, and since one in offering magistrates strives to seem more honorable than another, it easily happens that they cannot all use equal law, since there are many in the city who attract the minds of the multitude to themselves by either wealth or eloquence. If this matter is not beaten back again and again by you, it is to be feared that a new master will be brought
pages.53:
into your republic. <note>original: "in ueram remp. inuetus"</note> By the removing of the yoke from your necks, servitude is lifted. I do not doubt that the same will be accomplished prudently by your wisdom, which is supreme. But if the people have been taught about their own peril, you will see them soon shifting into various studies, and not sufficiently understanding, as if they were regretting their own deeds. But if you desire that I be used for your every service, either in the senate or among the people, you do not affect me with any new pleasure. It is not only usual for you, but also a daily care to take up everything that contributes to the utility of my affairs. There is nothing else that I might desire more from you than that you (as you do) love me maximally, and persuade yourself that there lives no one whose benevolence and truth I value more. Farewell.

I have been liberated from great solicitude and fear. I hope you have understood from many letters and speech that while I was passing through Etruria, intending to go to the city of Rome, I fell in with certain people who were constantly infesting that province with robberies and occupied almost all the approaches of the roads. I thought I had come into the hands of executioners who would torture me in many ways. But when I was preparing my own spirit to bear all the punishments that they might have wished to bring upon me, and no longer asking them anything, I found greater piety among them than I had ever dared to hope for from them. For when they had diligently inquired who I might be, or with what arms or what wealth I was using, and I had answered them about those things which at that time seemed to me to be said for the sake of my fortune, they immediately urged me to hope well. They detained me among them for some days and performed every duty and humanity toward me. When it seemed good to them (having held a council among themselves), they not only dismissed me without any injury, but also provided me with necessary provisions. Having proceeded toward Rome with that purpose (having given many thanks to them), I returned safely to my own people. I write these things to you with great zeal and pleasure
pages.54:
which I know you have always grieved for my adverse cases and especially rejoiced in my successes, due to your singular benevolence toward me. Farewell, and write to me often about your state.

That you have dealt with the most humane people is not to be attributed to your fortune but to their character. For you are the most delightful of all men. I know that your witticisms and that sweetness of yours in all conversation have aided you no less perhaps than the fact that you were never opulent in money. For there is a kind of man, more greedy than cruel. When they saw that you were agreeable and that you did not have anything they could make a profit from, they promised for themselves that you should not be expensive to them, so I judge it happened. As for those things which you narrate were done by them at your departure, that they not only provided you a free departure but also provisions and other offices of humanity, I cannot wonder enough, since such piety is rarely found among those men who wish to be called frugal and good. It is (as I judge) that those who have long been emboldened by their own crimes will sometimes be led to hear honest studies, rather than those who live always under laws and trials. Whatever it may have been, I congratulate you greatly that you have liberated me from the greatest fear and yourself from no small peril. I desire, however, that such fortune should not be experienced again, and you will (as I hope) be more cautious in guarding your own safety henceforth. I give thanks to you that you wrote to me first about your liberation. For you knew that I was no less anguished by your inconveniences than by my own. I urge and beseech you that you come to us. For you will do the thing most pleasing to your friends after your return, and for me, it will be most pleasant, so that you could not affect me with any greater accumulated pleasure. Farewell.

I write a matter not customary to you, which you will have judged to have arisen from your prudence. It will excite (believe me) a certain incredible love in you for great things. Caius Lucius

prosperity often harmful to glory. Farewell.

These things about which I will write to you are not so new or unusual that something of this kind has never happened to men before. Nevertheless, they have excited no small admiration from the opinion that will be held. Vecturius, a man (as you know) once considered a most opulent citizen among his fellow citizens, had his affairs so badly managed that he contracted a great debt to others. And this he did with much necessity, or he would have been found out by those who loved that man. What he did afterward, and whether it was appropriate when his fortune could no longer be aided, the matter might perhaps have been settled in some year. Having collected from everywhere what he could most secretly, he pretended to set out abroad, and he was promised to be present maturely on the first day of August, as he himself had declared on the calends. He encouraged all of us who loved him that we should provide a surety for him, if by chance anyone had summoned him to court. I thought that he was not held by any or only a modest debt. And if he were even held by a large one, we thought he was solvent. What more? I gave surety for him. Then he departed. When the day of the trial had arrived, since this man did not appear (as he ought to have done in good faith), shortly after, we were demanded for satisfaction by the creditors. We begged the judges to extend the day for us, which when I learned was to be exacted from us, it was necessary to pay for him. And that sum of money which he owed to his creditors was paid. Thus the matter stands, that faith is extended to those who have no sense of shame or modesty. Others are very

pages.47: whence I might abundantly satisfy this desire of yours. <term>Tra</term> <gloss>At that time</gloss> there were not as many changes of things from the previous memory as there are today, and which are already happening in our parts. Almost all the cities of this Cisalpine Gaul of ours are agitating for new things. Some are deposing old lords and claiming liberty for themselves. Others are making new tyrants for themselves. Others, while they study new things, are using not their own, but another's genius. Others are following the examples of the rest. They are trying to recall the old lords whom the wars of the more powerful had displaced from their rule. Nor is there any city with an empire that uses enough counsel in such movements. Citizens conspire, one against another. The people have as leaders of their fury those who excel others in violence and wickedness. Cremona, once a most opulent city, has changed princes within a few years; now it is placed under a most savage tyrant. Brescia is worn down by the frequent pounding of factions, and already sees its state collapsing; men judge it will have a new lord shortly. Bergamo, however, a city more oppressed by the discords of civil wars, admitted other enemies into itself; for it was not only fighting from its own power, but also <unclear>from its own situation</unclear>. What is more, the evil itself is (as they say) boiling much more strongly in the very entrails. For it is afflicted not under one such great prince, but under various and many tyrants. For when it had once flourished with the great genius and spirits of its own citizens, it is now made a colony and filled with a most foul and rustic multitude of men, which one could easily judge to be the most miserable and unfortunate of all in all of Italy. Innumerable others there are which have their own unhappy fortune and are placed in a great tempest. But you will understand all things better from him whom I send to you with these letters. If you have any great matter in these parts where you are staying, write all things to me, so that I am not ignorant of any of your affairs. Farewell.
pages.48: I have received your letter full of new things. I pity the sad state of so many magnificent cities and peoples of the provinces. For when I see in all Latium no trace of the ancient glory of our Cisalpine Gaul, I see that the glory which was once almost flourishing has now been reduced to desolation. Oh, this is the greatest fortune of all things, that when it has reached its summit, then we realize it is at its end. Greece itself (if I may repeat the examples of our ancestors a little further back) long conquered Italy not only in disciplines but also in arms; nor was it far from possessing the empire of the whole world under the leader Alexander of Macedon. With this taken away from human things, Greece itself eventually failed. Rome, if I want an example of all the Punic wars and nations, expanded its name and the empire which had remained from the kings, under the solar empire which extended to the Parthians, and under the emperors; I say it not only spread its fame but also its power to the boundaries of the world, yet it could not save or preserve that empire which had once been granted. It heard the end of all its glory through the great <unclear>disturbances</unclear> in Greece, moved long ago from external kings now to the slaughter, now moved to the north. It rejoices in this one thing and is desolate, that there is no one among those to whom the rule of our world came who does not rejoice to be called a king of the Romans. Gaul, however, had grown in both the fame of its deeds and the excellence of its best arts, so that it seemed to conquer and surpass the splendor of the rest of the provinces, and seemed to be our own. Now you write to me of its ruin and end. I have no comfort with which I can better alleviate your fortune than with these examples, which I am also accustomed to use often, whenever something happens to me that is too harsh and bitter in my own affairs. Nothing, however, is being done in this reign that is worth knowing for its novelty or magnificence; for we are all in such leisure as I know not how we have been otherwise. I fear lest this perhaps harms us by keeping us away from all our actions. For just as the harshness of fortune is excessive, so also is moderate prosperity often harmful to glory. Farewell.

And he exhorted us all who loved him to give bail for him if anyone should perhaps summon him to court. We thought, however, that he was held by little or no debt, and if he were held by a large one, we thought him capable of paying. What more? I gave a guarantee for him. Then he departed. Thus the thing turns out, that faith is provided to those who have no sense of shame or modesty. Others are greatly amazed by this act.
