But I perceived this late in my own affair. Farewell.

On the second of February, your letters were delivered to me, in which you signified to me about the guards of Vecturius, and you admonish me wisely that I might be more cautious in my own affairs from your example. You do this out of your benevolence toward me, which is great, and I give you the greatest thanks. But I would like you to know that I am not a little moved in my soul by this loss of yours, as if the damage had been done in part to my own fortunes. For I have always judged of you that nothing could happen to you that was not my own, which I think I have already foreseen for you in many signs through myself. Nor is it far off that I should return my soul to you at this time, if the ability were present. But since our fatherland has already been worn down and almost ruined by constant wars, and the income from fields does not respond to the owners, nor are those arts practiced in the city by which the citizens used to engage in great profit and money, all things have certainly deprived us of gain. And those who are such that they might have wealth and money, there is no one, however, who would not rather keep their affairs in port than commit themselves to manifest dangers. If there is anything, however, in which I can be of service to you with any zeal or my own labor, I shall do all things with a good soul, which I understand would be for your use. Nor do I wish your duty to be understood as being owed in these things which pertain to you. In other matters, however, I shall use your prudence. I cannot help you with my own money. I will not hesitate, however, to provide satisfaction and to act as a guarantor for you, and to obligate all my own things, if I understand what your wish is regarding this matter, and if it is worthwhile to pay for you.
pages.51:
And if I learn that you have not wished to use my service in any matter out of a sense of propriety, you will lessen that opinion which I have made for myself of your service to me and of our eternal love. Farewell.

Because I write to you about unusual things, I seem to myself to be doing a welcome thing for you. For I know that you have always been eager for this matter. I shall do what was done by the leader, a most beautiful thing, and not heard of by anyone of ours for many years. There helps in our city a prince who, although he had long afflicted the public liberty with arms, driven (as we all think) by the conscience of his own deeds, began to use his counsels for the better. Having called the people to an assembly, he held an extraordinary and illustrious oration, in which, having rendered an account of both his intent and the administration which he had carried out, he taught the citizens in what spirit he was toward the republic. He would cede to himself the common liberty to be used securely with his own citizens. He conducted himself wisely and magnificently in this matter, which caused admiration in everyone. After it was announced from that spirit, a great silence persisted among us for a long time, some thinking they had not understood enough, others, in whom more prudence dwelt, doubting what the oration of that man would lead to. But when liberty of speech was given to all, and he clearly encouraged and asked that everyone speak his own opinion as best he could, there was no one who did not give divine and immortal thanks to him because he had brought the republic back to its seat. And we all promised not only future impunity for the deed, but also that we would defend his own body and safety with the opposition of our own, and that we would give effort so that he might live somewhat more happily as a private citizen than he had once when he alone ruled the city. When this matter was understood by him, he cast all his rods of office before the people, restored to the fatherland its ancient laws and liberty, and omitted nothing from the ancient and good custom of liberty. He now enjoys the same right with us. We, however, are in such leisure
pages.52:
that I would never have dared to hope for otherwise. I believe you will admire this happiness of ours as a most beautiful deed. Therefore I wished all things to be signified to you by me. If there is anything, however, that can be done by me for your convenience, either in our senate or among the people, you have me as your greatest friend, and one whom you may freely use in all your affairs according to your right. Farewell.

It has happened that your fatherland has been donated its ancient liberty. Whether this has happened by chance or by counsel, it cannot but have happened to you divinely. But it must be cared for by you with great study so that you may be able to enjoy this good of yours for as long as possible. No matter will effect this more than if the fame of the thing is spread to many. Sophocles (as is in the fables of the Greeks) when he was composing a certain tragedy to persuade the Athenian people of this same thing, introduced a danger from an enemy, in that he exhorted the Athenians with a long oration not to nourish a lion in the city, or if it were nourished, to bear with an equal soul the being torn apart by it. This matter the wisest poet inserted into his poem so that he might teach the people, by the example of the city and a noble fiction, not to commit the power of a city to another who might excel the rest in wealth and genius; and if that liberty were committed to him, he urged that servitude was rather to be preferred than that the multitude should use a lord who might be more serious. Never was there anything that could deprive the Roman people, the lord of nations, of liberty, who when they preferred the power that was of all to be of the few, they were human, and to serve rather under emperors than to rule. It is incredible how restored liberty delights, and when one in offering magistracies strives to seem more honorable than another, it happens easily that they cannot all use equal right, since there are more in the city who attract the spirits of the multitude to themselves either by wealth or by eloquence. Which matter if it has not been struck by you again and again, it is to be feared that you might rather have a new lord
pages.53:
into your republic. Servitude, once lifted from the necks, <unclear>is soon brought back</unclear>. I do not doubt that the same things are being prudently carried out by you according to your wisdom, which is of the highest degree. But if the people should be taught about their own danger, you will see them soon shifting into various studies, and not sufficiently understanding as if they are judging their own deeds.

But if you desire to use me in any duty, whether in the senate or among the people, you do not bring me any new pleasure. It is not only for you a duty, but also a daily one to take up all care that pertains to my own affairs. There is nothing else that I might wish more from you than that you should love me (as you do) greatly, and be persuaded that there lives no one whose benevolence and truth I value more. Farewell.

I have been freed from great solicitude and fear. I hope you have understood from many, both by letter and by speech, that while I was traveling through Etruria, where I was seeking the Roman city, I fell upon certain men who were constantly infesting that province with robberies and occupied almost all the approaches of the roads. I thought I had fallen into the hands of executioners who would torture me in many ways. I, however, when I was preparing my own soul to bear all the punishments which they might wish to inflict upon me, and no longer asking them anything, I found among them greater piety than I had ever dared to hope for from them. For when I had been questioned by them about who I was, or by what arms, or for what search I was traveling, and I had answered them about the things that seemed to me at that time to be spoken for my own fortune, they immediately urged me to hope well. They detained me among themselves for some days, and they fulfilled all duty and humanity toward me. When, however, it seemed to them (a council having been held among them) not only to dismiss me without any injury, but they even provided me with the necessary provisions. Having proceeded from that purpose to Rome (having offered prayers to them), I returned safely to my own. These things I write to you with great study and pleasure
pages.54:
which I know you have always grieved for in my adverse cases, because of your singular benevolence toward me, and have rejoiced in the greatest matters. Farewell, and write to me often about your own state.

It has acted with you in a most humane way, not to be attributed to the fortune of it, but to the manners of it. You are, in fact, the most pleasant of all men. I know that those pleasantries of yours and that sweetness in all your speech were of service to you, perhaps no less than the fact that you have never been opulent in money matters. For there is a kind of men, more greedy than cruel. Since they saw that you were generally agreeable and that you had nothing from which they might make a profit with you, they spared you for themselves so that you would not become expensive to them. Thus I judge the act. Regarding those things which you narrate were done by them at your departure, that not only did they grant you a free departure but also provisions and other offices of humanity, I cannot wonder enough, since such piety is rarely found among those men who wish themselves to be called frugal and good. But (as I think) these men who have been relying on their wickedness for a long time will seek to hear honest studies, just as those who always live among laws and judgments. Whatever it will be, I congratulate you greatly because you freed me from the greatest fear and yourself from no small danger. I desire, however, that such fortune not be tested again, and you will be (as I hope) henceforth more cautious in guarding your own safety. I give thanks to God because you wrote to me primarily about your liberation. For you knew that I was to be tormented no less by your inconveniences than by my own. I urge you, however, and implore you, that you come to us. For you will do a thing after your return most welcome to your friends, and to me most pleasant, so that you could not affect me with any greater accumulated pleasure. Farewell.

I write to you of a matter not unusual, which you will have judged to be born from your own prudence. It will excite (believe me) a certain incredible love in you for great things. Gaius Lucius

This matter, even if it happened quite inconveniently to the others, was nonetheless so heavy that I never hope to be able to pay off the debt which was collected for the sake of that matter. I could never have thought it possible that that man, having come to such poverty, would seek his own people with such machinations and deceits. Thus the thing turns out, that faith is provided to those who have no sense of shame or modesty. Others are greatly amazed by this act. If I bear the penalty of my own faith, you, if ever there is something for you to promise on behalf of another, will become more cautious from my example. For I believe that to be the art of those who bring less <unclear>grace</unclear> and more discomfort to men, which teaches one to stand in court for another's debt and to act as a guarantor. And it is a well-known proverb: "He who puts his hand to the trap is excluded by his own peril and labor." But I perceived this late in my own affair. Farewell.

X.text:
But I perceived this late in my own affair. Farewell.

On the second of February, your letters were delivered to me, in which you signified to me about the guards of Vecturius, and you admonish me wisely that I might be more cautious in my own affairs from your example. You do this out of your benevolence toward me, which is great, and I give you the greatest thanks. But I would like you to know that I am not a little moved in my soul by this loss of yours, as if the damage had been done in part to my own fortunes. For I have always judged of you that nothing could happen to you that was not my own, which I think I have already foreseen for you in many signs through myself. Nor is it far off that I should return my soul to you at this time, if the ability were present. But since our fatherland has already been worn down and almost ruined by constant wars, and the income from fields does not respond to the owners, nor are those arts practiced in the city by which the citizens used to engage in great profit and money, all things have certainly deprived us of gain. And those who are such that they might have wealth and money, there is no one, however, who would not rather keep their affairs in port than commit themselves to manifest dangers. If there is anything, however, in which I can be of service to you with any zeal or my own labor, I shall do all things with a good soul, which I understand would be for your use. Nor do I wish your duty to be understood as being owed in these things which pertain to you. In other matters, however, I shall use your prudence. I cannot help you with my own money. I will not hesitate, however, to provide satisfaction and to act as a guarantor for you, and to obligate all my own things, if I understand what your wish is regarding this matter, and if it is worthwhile to pay for you.

pages.55:
<note>A red decorative initial 'A' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Although because of his age he cannot yet be admitted to the highest magistracies of the republic, he was recently absolved of a great grievance of the city by law, which permits nothing to be done against ancestral custom. For when, because of frequent conflicts, many leaders of ours had been lost through fighting most bravely, and no one else remained for us whom we might send into that danger, the valor of this young man in fighting in previous wars was so spectacular that our soldiers could never hope to be victorious unless he was the leader. Thus, the laws yielded to the common judgment, honesty gave way to utility, and institutions followed necessity. This matter ought to inflame and incite you to such a degree, so that you think of nothing day or night more than how you might also make a way for yourself toward glory of this kind. This will not be difficult for you, if you deem nothing so arduous that it is not easy for a great and noble spirit. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'A' marks the beginning of the text.</note>That Gaius Lucius has been endowed with an outstanding dignity by our republic for his virtue, I judge to have been done for a good example. Nor do I think there is anything better in our city than that each person should be able to achieve as much in our republic as he surpasses others in virtue and deeds performed by himself. But I fear that many, since they trust more in greater glory than in their own virtue, take this very thing badly. You know what evils envy has often brought to our city. For while there are many other plagues that have destroyed many great kingdoms, I do not know if any is more pernicious to the human race than that which I just mentioned. If this could be avoided by modesty alone, it would perhaps be better to lead them to reach honors slowly through laws and character than to use them in timely magistracies with the envy and hatred of many. But since there is no humility (as they say) that can avoid the mode of such men, all things that chance has brought must be borne with a great spirit, and one must use virtue all the more bravely, the more it is attacked by many.
pages.56:
You will soon understand how much these public matters have added to my studies which I undertook for the republic. For the glory of our Gaius often rouses me from sleep. I shall not rest, therefore, until I see those whom I judge to be equal in age and glory to those who came before, having attained the same by greatness of spirit and magnificently performed deeds. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I have signed these letters to you not about private comforts (as often before), but about the safety of our citizens. If there ever was a time when the status of the republic was of concern to you, see that on this very day you are there to assist him, your son, and the state. For a high matter hangs in the balance, which, unless it is attended to by you with the greatest care, will easily break out into a great conflagration. Wherefore, again and again, hasten to us. Nor let any matter be so important that it delays your arrival. Everyone who is affected by your presence believes that the common safety of all is entrusted to you alone. Do not, therefore, delay the great expectation of all. I also persuade you that it is better for a man to be loved by his own citizens than to be of any other status, and for this glory, I would flee no danger or labor for the republic. I would write of the benevolence and hope of all the citizens placed in you, but you, who know all things and love the fatherland supremely, foresee these things better for yourself. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'F' marks the beginning of the text.</note>The ability to be able to assist the evils of the republic is certainly to flee no labor or danger for the common safety. But there are many things that induce in me doubt and despair of this matter. For many of our people would prefer to perturb everything, so that they might appear to be in charge, rather than that we live under equal law. And there are more in the city who do not sufficiently understand what consists in the virtue and liberty of the citizens. If anyone in the city does find what it is to be healthy in the republic, he understands and senses that none of their words have any weight with the multitude. Nor do I see, therefore, what my presence can bring to the fatherland and our citizens, unless I take on many enmities, which are necessary neither for me nor for the republic. But where I am brought to the sentiment that I must entrust my safety to these waves and storms of the republic, I will not refuse to test everything for the love of the fatherland rather than fail the great expectation of our citizens. You have my judgment about the republic. You, as soon as you have determined again concerning the will of our citizens, hasten to write to me. Farewell.
pages.57:
<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>What the status of our city is, you can understand from this, that the foundations of our republic have never been laid with better auspices than on this day. For when once our senate used to assemble to consult about the highest matters, everyone served the times. If anyone divided the sentiments into factions, there was no one who dared to contribute freely what he felt. But now, with minds given to a liberty that is not feigned or shadowy (as before), but such as we have received from our ancestors, we live in a way that we never did, except at this time in which we now are. For those few who were oppressing public liberty having been removed from the city, all use equal law. It is permitted to everyone to say what he feels about our republic, and to feel freely what he says. The efforts that were applied to private matters have all been turned toward the greatness of the republic. And they are most intent on this one thing, as to what is most useful to the city. If, therefore, you desire to be held great among your own, come to this republic of ours, which we hold to be the best and most beautiful. You will be able to accomplish as much in it as you will prepare to labor for others with industry and solicitude. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' marks the beginning of the text.</note>That you are using the best republic is a cause of joy to me even more than for my own sake. For since the greatest part of my life has passed, there can be nothing that I might use for long. Your era, however, which is on a better course, looks toward the future, with many things that it may rightfully promise to itself by appointing magistrates. If there is anything, however, in which I can serve the fatherland, I will not only bravely undertake all labors for it, but I will also bear all annoyances and anxieties with an equal spirit. And I will judge myself to have received sufficient fruit from my labors and studies if I leave your republic, which I consider the best and most ample, to your descendants along with you. If, however, it does not turn out according to my duty, I will rejoice that the greatest and wisest men are found in your city, who can protect the fatherland with the best laws and wisest institutions. I, for my part, desire more leisure than business for my old age. You who are occupied in adorning and enriching it, will consider with your wisdom what is fitting for the republic. For whatever you determine concerning it, I will consider it good. Farewell.
pages.58: <note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I have decided to write to you about the public utility of our citizens and in what way that matter can be better conducted by us, so that I may open to you first the reason for all my plans. I have often perceived in my mind how the revenues and other proceeds of our city can be increased to the greatest extent without any inconvenience to our citizens or allies. To accomplish this matter, I saw that I had need of your counsel and prudence. You do not ignore that for many years before, neither merchants nor publicans (I mean pirates) could safely navigate this sea of ours, whence it happened that our revenues were sold for much less. Since everyone is led by this agreement, that he perishes for himself and not for the republic, it is necessary that the profit of navigation compels them to this measure. It happens that they do not commit themselves to the danger, since the greater part of the comforts arrives to them, from which our treasury sustains no small loss and expenditure. What happens to the merchants in the face of the fear of pirates is understood daily, since
pages.59:
almost all the arts in our city have come to nothing due to a lack of merchandise. The damage reaches not only to private persons, but even to the republic itself. My plan was that the state should equip triremes and enroll men accustomed to maritime wars, who would make the supplies safe. For thus we would strengthen the minds of our allies and recover our revenues as they were before. For the merchants, the sea would be safe, with the pirates not daring to wander the sea for fear of our fleet. We have often mentioned this in our senate, which, although it was approved by many in general, yet partly because of envy or because of the gravity of those who cannot look at me with equal eyes, that matter has not yet been brought into consultation. But when I have you as an assistant for this matter, I hope it will be easy to obtain that all those things be done about which I have written to you. You will not flee (as I trust) this labor, and you will undertake it for the sake of the republic. With your supreme benevolence toward me, this act is both honest and useful to the republic. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Unless the matter about which you write to me can be expedited in some other way than by my presence, I will come to the city. But I wonder greatly that in such a most fitting matter there is no one who agrees with you. For I see what can be added to your son. For if our republic has been long oppressed, we wish necessarily that the sea, which for these years has been vexed by piratical robberies, may finally be open to our revenues and merchants. Otherwise, our republic (which barely stands as yet) will soon be nothing. I have decided, however, to write to the senate about this matter first, and to urge some who have influence in their speeches, so that they might undertake this business for the sake of the republic. For often a certain gravity is had by the greatest men when they speak about the common safety of the republic, which matter, if it is treated by men of a lower order, often effects more envy than the republic
pages.60:
can handle. And because I have known your modesty, I know that you will not bear it badly that what had been wisely perceived by you for the public utility will be completed by another. You will take care, however, that if anything of this matter comes into the consultations, I be informed by your letters. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'S' marks the beginning of the text.</note>That I write to you at this time about our republic, know that I did so as I once did. There is nothing that you ought to admire. Although there was a time when it was necessary to write to you more vehemently for the public utility, for after you exempted yourself from its care, others became more timid. Others, however, have taken on so much license and audacity that they think nothing is forbidden to them in secret speeches. If, therefore, you desire it to be safe, you should approach to govern and rule it after all these things. The foundations that were badly laid, you should rectify with your authority and wisdom, before they confirm themselves and accustom the multitude to serve their own lust. See that if there are any who are not correctly discerning about the common safety, you remove them (if you can) from their secrets. If not, hold the reason of the republic to be greater than that of private friendship. Those, however, whom you see as timid in undertaking these dangers for the citizens, I pray that you will rouse them with your prayer and ignite them to bravely sustain all labors, as often as reason or necessity demands this of them for the republic. You sustain the incredible expectations of all good men. You will do, therefore, what the republic will persuade you is to be done at this time. But one thing I ask of you, do not forget that you are he to whom the republic itself entrusts itself and all its own. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' marks the beginning of the text.</note>When your letters about the status of the republic were brought, not long after others arrived which announced that everything was being done by you out of private hatred and malevolence, and that the state of the city was no different than before, when I left it safe and flourishing. How can it be induced that this was done by you, and those
pages.61:
most grieve that the republic is torn by private dissensions. Whether they say that some malevolence toward you resides in these evils, or (as I think) you could not bear their customs out of a desire to dominate, our republic cannot gain anything from this matter. I rejoiced that I had obtained from them that, in exchange for many labors and for the dangers of the sea, which I had often promised for the public safety, I would finally be granted rest and quiet. It was permitted to me, since I had long been buffeted by waves and storms, to finally rest in the harbor once matters were settled by my labor. But after it has come to this, that either I cannot have my own rest or it cannot be in peace, I will not desert it in the final time, as I have exercised my entire previous life in labors and dangers for its safety. I will sail, therefore, to you as soon as there are winds. I hope, while everything is still new and fresh, that all the rising evils can be removed by me. But if it cannot be done by me, yet neither my effort nor my diligence will ever depart. You, therefore, for your perpetual love for the republic, see to it that the utility of the republic weighs more with you than the hatred or envy of any man. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Do not implicate yourself in any inconvenience in your matters. You believe that everyone is of the same mind toward you as you are toward others. You are deceived, believe me. For of those who appear to be your friends in the present, very few love you from the heart. If, however, you will listen to me, abandon all those whose face is flattering and who immensely praise all the things that are done by you. I suggest that you use the advice of Veturius in all matters to be conducted. He is certainly the wisest of all and he loves you humanely. He will not suffer you to err in a lack of friends. There is no one from the number of our men whose prudence I value more highly, and he can best judge about our nature and the customs of our citizens.
pages.62:
Whatever he will suggest to you, consider it a saying of truthful Apollo, as they say. If you will be willing to attend, you will see that he can neither err because of wisdom, nor would he want to, because of humane benevolence. I desire to understand what you decide, so that when I learn that you have been changed from the opinion in which you have been until now, I might rejoice sufficiently in our friendship. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I use the advice of Gaius Veturius. For I have always valued his wisdom highly. If I may speak with your good leave, you seem to me to think less well of me when you see me dissuaded from using the friendship of those men whose face is flattering. I, however, disagree with you far. But one must live with men in such a way that each has his own custom. I judge it to be the role of a wise man, when others laugh, to weep himself, and not to be too severe when others are in jest. Thus I have instituted my life to accommodate myself to the present matters, nor would I suffer anyone to be angry with me justly. As often as I can, know that I do nothing more willingly than to associate with those from whom I can become wiser by learning. These things I know have not yet been reported by my rivals. These things I thought should be answered by me at this time, not because I am angry at your admonitions, but so that if you had conceived some not good opinion of me, I might purge myself before you. Or if anything else is said of me, that it is according to dignity and the estimation that is held of me, write everything (as you do) in a friendly and free manner. One thing I ask to be obtained from you by your humanity: that you believe nothing rashly about me. For there are many who, moved by some hatred or envy, come to attack the reputation of another, rather than being led by reason or an honest cause. If you will grant me this, I will always be pleased by your admonitions. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'P' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I hope that I have perceived in my mind that your cause can be restored to its integrity by reason, provided that it is not long in coming, only concerning it

<note>A red decorative initial 'A' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Although because of his age he cannot yet be admitted to the highest offices of our republic, he was recently absolved of a great offense by the city and the laws, which allow nothing to be done contrary to ancient custom. For when, because of frequent conflicts, many leaders from our ranks had been lost fighting most bravely, and no one remained whom we could send to that danger, the virtue of this young man in fighting was so evident in previous wars that our soldiers could never hope to win unless he were their leader. Therefore, by common consent, the laws were yielded, honesty gave way to utility, and institutions gave way to necessity. This matter, even if it is nothing to you, ought to inflame and incite you, so that you think of nothing more day and night than how you might also make a path for yourself to such glory. This will not be difficult for you if you think nothing so arduous that it is not easy for a great and noble mind. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'A' marks the beginning of the text.</note>That Gaius Lucius has been endowed with great dignity by our republic for his virtue, I judge to have been done as a good example. Nor do I think there is anything better in our city than that each person should have as much power in our republic as he exceeds others in virtue and deeds performed by himself. But I fear that many, since they rely more on glory than on their own virtue, take this very thing badly. You know what evils envy has often brought to our city. For while there are many other plagues that have overturned many great kingdoms, I do not know if any is more pernicious to the human race than that which I have just mentioned. If this could be avoided by modesty alone, it would perhaps be better to lead men to access honors through the laws and the fatherland than to use the temporary magistrates when there is envy and hatred from many. But since there is no humility, as they say, that can avoid the manner of these men, everything that fortune has brought must be borne with a great mind, and one must use virtue all the more strongly, the more it is attacked by many.
pages.56:
You will soon understand how much more this adds to my studies for the republic which I have undertaken, that this upright action of our city, by which Gaius Lucius was absolved by the laws and established in that dignity which he often earned by fighting most bravely for the fatherland. For the glory of our Gaius often excites me from sleep. I will not rest, therefore, until I see you equal in age and glory to those who preceded you, and having attained the same magnitude of mind and magnificently performed deeds. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I have sealed these letters to you not regarding private conveniences, as often before, but regarding the safety of our citizens. If there ever was a time when the state of the republic was of concern to you, see that on this day you are present with help for them and your son. For a great fire hangs over, which, unless it is most attentively guarded by you, will easily erupt into a great conflagration. Therefore, hasten to us again and again. And let no matter be so great that it delays your arrival. All who desire your presence believe that the common safety of all is placed in you alone. Do not, therefore, delay the great expectation of all. I also persuade you that it is better for a man to be loved by his own citizens than any rule, and with this glory, that he has fled no danger or labor for the republic. I persuade you to write of the benevolence and hope of all the citizens placed in you, and you who know all things and love the fatherland most highly, you will better perceive these things yourself. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'F' marks the beginning of the text.</note>The power to be able to help the evils of the republic means certainly fleeing no labor or danger for the common safety. But there are many things that strike me with doubt and despair of this matter. For many of our people would rather disturb everything so that they themselves might seem to be in charge, than that we should live together under equal law, and there are many in the city who do not sufficiently understand what is in the virtue and liberty of the citizens. If anything is found in the city that truly knows, judges, and feels about the republic, it is of no value against the multitude.
pages.57:
And therefore I do not see what my presence can bring to the fatherland and our citizens, unless I take upon myself many enmities, which are necessary neither to me nor to the republic. But when I come to the decision that I will commit my safety to these waves and storms of the republic, I will not refuse to try everything for the love of the fatherland, rather than deceive the great expectation of our citizens. You have my judgment about the republic. You, when it has been decided again concerning the will of our citizens, hasten to write to me what I am to do. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>What the state of our city is, you can understand from this, that never were the foundations of our republic laid under better auspices than on this day. For when once our senate used to gather to consult about the highest matters, everyone served the times. If anyone divided the opinions, there was no one who dared to contribute freely what he felt. Now, however, we give ourselves to such studies for a liberty that is not feigned or shadowy, as they say, but the same that we received from our fathers, so that we might never live if not for ourselves, except in this time in which we now are. For a few who were oppressing the public liberty have been removed from the city, and all use equal law. It is permitted to everyone to say what he feels about our republic, and to feel freely what he says. The studies that were applied to private matters have all been turned to the amplitude of the republic. And they are especially intent on this one thing, which is most profitable to the city. If, therefore, you desire to be considered great among your own, come to this republic of ours, which we have as the best and most beautiful. You will be able to do as much in it as you will provide in labor, industry, and solicitude for the others. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' marks the beginning of the text.</note>That you use the best republic, I rejoice more than for my own sake. For since the greatest part of my life has been passed, there can be nothing that I might use for long.
pages.58:
But your age, which is in a better course, looks to the future, for which it can rightly promise itself by being given magistrates. If, however, there is anything in which I can serve the fatherland, I will not only bravely undertake all labors for it, but I will also bear all annoyances and anxieties with an equal mind, and I will judge myself to have received enough fruit from my labors and studies if I leave your republic, which I consider best and most ample, to your descendants along with you. But if it does not turn out according to my duty, I will rejoice that the highest and most wise men are found in your city who, with the best laws and most wise institutions, can protect the fatherland. I, for my part, desire more leisure than business for my old age. You who are occupied in adorning and enriching it, consider with your wisdom what is fitting for the republic. For whatever you decide about it, I will consider it good. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I have decided to write to you about what is the public utility of our citizens and in what way that matter can be handled better by us, so that I may first open to you the reason for all my counsels. I have often perceived in my mind how the revenues and other proceeds of our city can be greatly increased without any inconvenience to our citizens or allies. To accomplish this matter, I saw that I had need of your counsel and prudence. You are not unaware that for many years past, neither merchants nor the publicans (I mean the pirates) could safely navigate this sea of ours, whence it happened that our revenues were sold for much less. Since everyone is led by this agreement, so that he perishes for himself and not for the republic, it is necessary that the profit of navigating compels them to this freight. And it happens that they do not commit themselves to the danger, since the greater part of the profits comes to them, from which our treasury sustains no small loss and expense. What happens to the merchants among the pirates is understood daily, since
pages.59:
almost all the arts in our city have come to nothing due to the lack of goods. The damage comes not only to private persons, but also to the republic itself. My counsel was that the republic should equip triremes and enroll men accustomed to maritime wars, who would render the convoys safe. For by this I would strengthen the minds of our allies and recover our revenues as they were before. For the merchants, the sea is safe, since the pirates, fearing our fleet, do not dare to wander by sea. We often mention this in our senate, which, although it was approved by many, yet due to envy or the weight of those who cannot look at me with equal eyes, that matter has not yet been brought to consultation. But when I have you as an assistant for this matter, I hope it will be easy to obtain that all those things about which I wrote to you are done. You will not flee, as I trust, this labor, and you will undertake it for the sake of the republic, for your highest benevolence toward me, this <note>original: "percuratio"</note> is honorable and useful to the republic. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Unless the matter about which you write to me can be expedited by my presence, I will come. But I am very surprised that in a most fitting matter there is no one who agrees with you. For I see what can be added to your son. For if our republic has been oppressed for long, it is necessary that the sea, which has been vexed for these years by piratical thefts, should at length be open to our revenues and merchants. Otherwise our republic (which hardly stands even now) will soon be nothing. I have decided, however, first to write to the senate about this matter and to urge certain men who have influence in their speaking to undertake this business for the sake of the republic. For weight is often given to the highest men when they act for the common safety of the republic, which matter, if handled by men of lower order, often effects more envy than the republic
pages.60:
ratio can. And since I have known your modesty, I know you have not taken it badly that what had been perceived by you wisely for the public utility will be accomplished by another. Take care, however, that if anything of this matter comes into the consultations, I be made aware by your letters. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'S' marks the beginning of the text.</note>If I write to you at this time regarding our republic, know that I do it as I once did. There is nothing that you ought to wonder at. Although there was a time when it was necessary to write more vehemently to you for the public utility. For after you exempted yourself from its care, others became more timid, while others assumed so much license and audacity that they think nothing is forbidden to them in secret speeches. If, therefore, you desire it to be safe, address yourself hereafter to governing and ruling it. The foundations which were badly laid, you change with your authority and wisdom, before they confirm themselves and accustom the multitude to serve their lust. See that if there are any who are not rightly feeling about the common safety, you remove them (if you can) from their secrecy. If not, hold the reason for the republic in greater regard than private friendship. Those who are timid to undertake such dangers for the citizens, I ask that you will excite them and inflame them to bravely sustain all labors, as often as reason or necessity demands this of them for the republic. You sustain the incredible expectations of all good men. You will therefore do what the republic will persuade you is to be done at this time. But one thing I ask of you, do not forget that you are he to whom the republic itself and all its own commend themselves. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' marks the beginning of the text.</note>When your letters about the state of the republic were brought, not long after others arrived which announced that everything was being done by you out of private hatred and malice, and that the state of the city was in no other condition than it was once, when I left it safe and flourishing. How can it be induced that these things were done by you, and those
pages.61:
I grieve most of all that private dissensions are ruining the republic. Whether those who cause such evils say that malice resides in you, or (as I think is sought) you could not bear their manners from the desire to dominate, our republic cannot gain anything from this matter. I rejoiced that I had obtained from the fatherland that, after many labors and after the dangers of the sea, which I had often promised for the public safety, I would at last be gifted with leisure and quiet. It is permitted to me, after I had long been beaten by waves and storms, at last, with matters composed by my labor, to rest in port. But after it has come to this, that I cannot be in my leisure, or it cannot be in peace, I will not desert it in an extreme time, I who have exercised my whole previous life in labors and dangers for its safety. I will sail, therefore, to you as soon as there is wind. I hope, while everything is still new and recent, that all the rising evils can be removed by me. But if it cannot be accomplished by me, yet neither my study nor my diligence will ever be absent. You, therefore, for your perpetual love in the republic, perform this for me, that the utility of the republic may prevail more with you than the hatred or envy of any man. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Do not implicate yourself in your matters in any inconvenience. You believe that each one is of the same mind toward you as you are toward others. You are deceived, believe me. For of those who seem to be your friends in the present, very few love you from the heart. If, however, you will listen to me, abdicate all those from yourself whose face is flattering, and who praise immensely everything you do. I persuade you, in all matters to be handled by you, to use the counsels of <term>Veturium</term> <gloss>a wise advisor/friend</gloss>, certainly the most wise of all, and who loves you humanely, he will not allow you to err in the lack of friends. There is no one from the number of our men whose prudence I value more highly, and who can judge better of our nature and the manners of our citizens.
pages.62:
Whatever he will persuade you of, consider it the saying of the truthful Apollo, as they say. If you are willing to attend, you will see that he can neither err because of wisdom, nor wish to, because of humane benevolence. I desire to understand what you establish, so that when I have known you to be changed in that opinion in which you have been until now, I might sufficiently congratulate our friendship. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I use the counsels of <term>Gaius Veturium</term> <gloss>a wise advisor/friend</gloss>. For I have always valued his wisdom highly. If I may speak with your good leave, you seem to me to feel less well about me, when you see me dissuading the use of the friendship of those men whose face is flattering. I, however, dissent far from you. But one must live with men in such a way that each has his own manner. I judge it the duty of a wise man, while others are smiling to themselves, to laugh, and not to be too severe when others are in jest. For I have instituted my life to accommodate myself to present matters, nor would I allow anyone to be angry with me on account of this. As often as I can, know that I do nothing more willingly than to spend time with those from whom I can become more learned in wisdom. These things, I know, have not yet been reported by my rivals. These things I have thought of writing to you at this time, not because I am angry at your admonitions, but so that if you had conceived any not good opinion of me, I might purge myself before you. Or if anything else is brought against me, which is contrary to my dignity and the estimation that one has of me, write all (as you do) in a friendly and free manner. One thing I ask to be obtained from you for your humanity, that you believe nothing rashly about me. For there are many who, moved by some hatred or envy, come to impugn the reputation of another, than those led by reason or honest cause. If you perform this for me, I will always be most delighted by your admonitions. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'P' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I hope that I have perceived in my mind what can be restored to the whole for your sake, provided that it is not far off, provided that concerning it

N.text:
And therefore I do not see what my presence can bring to the fatherland and our citizens, unless I take upon myself many enmities, which are necessary neither to me nor to the republic. But when I come to the decision that I will commit my safety to these waves and storms of the republic, I will not refuse to try everything for the love of the fatherland, rather than deceive the great expectation of our citizens. You have my judgment about the republic. You, when it has been decided again concerning the will of our citizens, hasten to write to me what I am to do. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>What the state of our city is, you can understand from this, that never were the foundations of our republic laid under better auspices than on this day. For when once our senate used to gather to consult about the highest matters, everyone served the times. If anyone divided the opinions, there was no one who dared to contribute freely what he felt. Now, however, we give ourselves to such studies for a liberty that is not feigned or shadowy, as they say, but the same that we received from our fathers, so that we might never live if not for ourselves, except in this time in which we now are. For a few who were oppressing the public liberty have been removed from the city, and all use equal law. It is permitted to everyone to say what he feels about our republic, and to feel freely what he says. The studies that were applied to private matters have all been turned to the amplitude of the republic. And they are especially intent on this one thing, which is most profitable to the city. If, therefore, you desire to be considered great among your own, come to this republic of ours, which we have as the best and most beautiful. You will be able to do as much in it as you will provide in labor, industry, and solicitude for the others. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' marks the beginning of the text.</note>That you use the best republic, I rejoice more than for my own sake. For since the greatest part of my life has been passed, there can be nothing that I might use for long.

X.text:
But your age, which is in a better course, looks to the future, for which it can rightly promise itself by being given magistrates. If, however, there is anything in which I can serve the fatherland, I will not only bravely undertake all labors for it, but I will also bear all annoyances and anxieties with an equal mind, and I will judge myself to have received enough fruit from my labors and studies if I leave your republic, which I consider best and most ample, to your descendants along with you. But if it does not turn out according to my duty, I will rejoice that the highest and most wise men are found in your city who, with the best laws and most wise institutions, can protect the fatherland. I, for my part, desire more leisure than business for my old age. You who are occupied in adorning and enriching it, consider with your wisdom what is fitting for the republic. For whatever you decide about it, I will consider it good. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I have decided to write to you about what is the public utility of our citizens and in what way that matter can be handled better by us, so that I may first open to you the reason for all my counsels. I have often perceived in my mind how the revenues and other proceeds of our city can be greatly increased without any inconvenience to our citizens or allies. To accomplish this matter, I saw that I had need of your counsel and prudence. You are not unaware that for many years past, neither merchants nor the publicans (I mean the pirates) could safely navigate this sea of ours, whence it happened that our revenues were sold for much less. Since everyone is led by this agreement, so that he perishes for himself and not for the republic, it is necessary that the profit of navigating compels them to this freight. And it happens that they do not commit themselves to the danger, since the greater part of the profits comes to them, from which our treasury sustains no small loss and expense. What happens to the merchants among the pirates is understood daily, since

pages.47: so that I may abundantly satisfy this desire of yours. <term>Things</term> <gloss>at this time</gloss> have not changed so much from the memory of our ancestors as they do today, and indeed are currently happening in our own parts. Almost all the cities of this Cisalpine Gaul of ours are agitating for new things. Some are deposing their ancient lords and declaring themselves in liberty. Others are making new tyrants for themselves. Others, while studying new things, use the nature of another rather than their own. Others follow the examples of the rest. Rome is trying to recall ancient lords whom the wars of more powerful men had displaced from their leadership. Nor is there any city with such command that it uses enough counsel in such upheavals. Citizens conspire against one another. The people have as leaders of their frenzy those who surpass the rest in force and wickedness. Cremona, once an extremely opulent city, has changed princes within a few months; now it is placed under a most savage tyrant. Brescia is worn down by the frequent pounding of factions, and already sees its state failing; men judge that it will soon have a new lord. Bergamo, indeed, a city more oppressed by the discords of civil wars, has admitted other enemies into itself; for it was not only suffering the evil that was commanding, but also the one that was coming. And if the evil itself is (as they say) much stronger, it boils in the midst of the vitals. For Rome is afflicted under one such prince, and here under diverse ones, and in the hands of a tyrant. Rome, although it had once flourished with the great talents and spirits of its citizens, has now been made a colony and filled with a most foul and rustic swarm of men, which one could easily judge to be the most miserable and unfortunate city in all of Italy. There are innumerable others that have their own unhappy fortune and are placed in a great storm. But you will understand all things better from the one whom I send to you with these letters. If you have any great news in those parts in which you are staying, write all things to me, lest I be ignorant of any of your affairs. Farewell.
pages.48: I have received your letter full of new things. I pity the state of so many magnificent cities and peoples being brought into ruin. For since there is no place in all of Latium that is more illustrious in the arts of arms, I see that former glory of Cisalpine Gaul now almost deflowered and reduced to desolation. Oh, this has the greatest fortune of all things, that when it has arrived at the summit, then we realize it is at its end. Greece itself (if I may repeat the examples of our ancestors a little more from above) long conquered Italy not only in disciplines but also in arms; nor was it far from possessing the empire of the whole world under the leader Alexander. With this taken away from human affairs, Greece itself failed. Rome, if I want the example of all the Punic wars and nations, expanded its name and the empire that remained from the kings, under the solar empire that stretched to the Parthians, and under the emperors indeed not only its fame but also its power with the boundaries of the world; yet it could not save or preserve that empire which had once been granted. It heard of all its glory through the custom of the ancestors in Greece, and it was transferred sometimes by external kings, sometimes to the north. It rejoices in this one thing, and is desolate, that there is no one among those to whom the regime of our world has flowed who does not rejoice to be called a king of the Romans. Gallia, however, had grown until then in both the fame of its deeds and the excellence of its best arts, so that it saw itself surpassing and going beyond the splendor of the rest of the Punic wars. Now you write to me of its ruin and end. I have no consolation by which I can better lighten your fortune than by these examples, which I also am accustomed to use often, since something has happened to me that is too harsh and bitter in my own affairs. Nothing, however, is done in this regime that should be known for its novelty or magnificence; for I am, I know not how, in such leisure as we have been at other times. I fear lest this perhaps harms us by keeping us away from all our actions. For just as the harshness of fortune is too much, so is immoderate
pages.49:
prosperity often harmful to glory. Farewell.

As for these things about which I write to you, they are not so new or unusual that something of this kind has never happened to men before. Yet they have excited no small admiration from the opinion that will be held. Vecturius, a man (as you know) once considered the most opulent of his fellow citizens, after his own affairs were badly managed, contracted a great deal of foreign debt. And he had either greatly needed it from someone, or those who loved that man would have learned of the matter. What he did afterward, when it was appropriate, when his fortunes could not be further supported, the matter perhaps would have been placed in some year. Having contracted his debts from everywhere that he could most secretly, he pretended that he was going abroad and promised that he would be present maturely on the first day of August, or on the very calends themselves. He urged all of us who loved him that we should make a pledge on his behalf if anyone happened to summon him to judgment. I thought, however, that he was held by no or very little foreign debt. And even if he were held by a great one, we thought he was solvent. What more? I made a guarantee for him. Then I departed. When the day of the contracted debt had arrived, as that man did not appear (as he ought to have done in good faith), a little later we were called upon by the creditors for satisfaction. When we were questioned about him, we prayed to the judges that they might prolong the day for us; when I learned that payment was going to be demanded of us, it was necessary to pay for him. And that sum of money which he owed his creditors was paid out. This matter, although it happened very uncomfortably to others, was yet so heavy that I never hope I can free myself from the foreign debt that was incurred for the sake of that affair. I could never have thought it possible that such a man had come to such poverty, that he would attack his own people with machinations and deceits of this kind. So the matter turns out, that faith is extended to those who have no sense of shame or modesty. Others are greatly
pages.50:
astonished at this deed. If I suffer the penalty for my faith, you, if ever there is something for you to pledge on behalf of another, will become more cautious by my example. For I consider those arts to be such that they bring less benefit and more inconvenience to men than the one that teaches how to be present in court for another's debt and to be a guarantor. And it is a known proverb: "He who puts his neck into a noose is excluded by his own danger and labor." But I saw it too late in my own affair. Farewell.

On the second of February your letters were returned to me, by which you were signifying to me about the guards of Vecturius, and you admonish me wisely that I might be more cautious in my own affair by your example. You do this out of your benevolence toward me, which is supreme, and I give you the greatest thanks. But I would like you to know that I am little less disturbed in spirit by this loss of yours than if the damage had been done to a part of my own fortunes. For I have always judged of you that nothing could happen to you that was not my own affair, which I think I have foreseen by many signs for you long ago. And it is not far off that I might return my spirit to you at this time, if the faculty were present. But since our fatherland has already been worn down and almost broken by continuous wars, and the revenues of the fields do not respond to the lords, nor do those arts flourish in the city by which the citizens previously used to live with great profit and money, all things have certainly failed to provide profit. And those who are such that they might have wealth and money, there is no one, however, who would not prefer to keep their affairs in port than to commit themselves to manifest dangers. If there is, however, anything in which I can be of service to you with any zeal or my own work, I will do all things with a good spirit which I understand to be useful for your need. Nor do I want your character to be understood to be owed in these matters that pertain to you. In other matters, however, I will use your prudence. I cannot help you with my own money. I will not hesitate, however, to make satisfaction and be a guarantor for you, and to obligate all my belongings, if I understand what your wish is regarding this matter, and if it is necessary to pay on your behalf.
pages.51:
And if I learn that you have not wished to use my service in any matter due to modesty, you will diminish that opinion which I had formed of the hope for me and your service toward me and constant love. Farewell.

Because I write to you about unusual things, I seem to myself to be doing something pleasing to you. For I know that you have always been desirous of this matter. I will do what the prince of our city did, a most beautiful deed, and one not heard of by anyone of ours for many years. There flourishes in our city a prince who, having long troubled the public liberty with arms, acted (as we all think) by the conscience of his own affairs and began to use his counsels for the better. For having called the people to a meeting, he held a speech before that excellent and illustrious gathering, in which, having rendered an account of both his purpose and the administration he had carried out, he taught the citizens in what spirit he was toward the republic. He would yield to them the common liberty so that they might use it securely with their fellow citizens. He brought them to this matter wisely and magnificently, which made for astonishment in all. After it was announced with what spirit he was, there remained a great silence among us for a long time, some judging that they had not understood enough, others in whom greater prudence resides doubting what the speech of that man might portend. But when liberty of speaking was made for all, and he was clearly urging and demanding that each one should state his best opinion, there was no one who did not offer him divine and immortal thanks because he had led the republic back to its seat. And we all promised not only future immunity for the deed, but also that we would defend his own health and safety with the opposition of our own bodies, and would give work so that he might live somewhat more happily as a private citizen than he had previously when he alone had commanded the city. When this matter was understood by him, he himself threw all his fasces to the people, granted the ancient liberty to the fatherland, and restored the ancient laws, nor did he omit anything from the ancient and good custom of liberty. And he now enjoys his rights with us. We, however, are in such leisure
pages.52:
as I would never have dared to hope for at other times. I believe that you will admire this happiness of ours because of the most beautiful deed of that man; therefore I wished all things to be signified to you by me. If, however, there is anything that can be done by me in our senate or by the people for your convenience, you have me as your supreme friend and you may use me freely in all your affairs according to your right. Farewell.

It has happened in a way that your fatherland has been donated its ancient liberty. For whether this happened by chance or by counsel, it cannot but have happened to you divinely. But it must be cared for by you with great study so that you may be able to enjoy this good of yours for as long as possible. No thing will effect this more than if the fame of the matter has been carried to many. Sophocles (as it is in the fables of the Greeks) when he was delivering a certain tragedy to persuade the same thing to the Athenian people, introduced a danger from the enemies, because he was urging the Athenians with a long speech not to rear a lion in the city, or if it were reared, to bear it with an equal mind if it were to be slaughtered. The wisest poet inserted this thing into his poem so that he might teach the people, both by the authors of the city and by a noble fiction, not to commit power over the city to one person who surpassed others in wealth and talent, and if such liberty were committed to him, he was persuading that servitude should even be preferred, lest the people use a lord more grave than the mob. There was never anything that deprived the Roman people, the lord of nations, of their liberty, because they preferred that the power which was of all should be of a few, and that it would be more human, and to serve emperors rather than to reign. It is incredible how much restored liberty delights, and when one strives to seem more honorable than another in offering magistrates, it happens easily that they cannot all use equal law, since there are more in the city who attract the spirits of the multitude to themselves by either wealth or eloquence. Which matter, if it has not been warded off by you again and again, it is to be feared lest you have a new lord
pages.53:
in your republic, after servitude has been taken away from the necks of the people. I do not doubt that these same things are being prudently carried out by you for your wisdom, which is supreme. But if the people were to be taught of their own danger, you will see them shortly after being divided into diverse studies, nor sufficiently understanding that they are struggling against their own deeds. If you desire that I be used in any service, either in the senate or among the people on my behalf, you do not affect me with any new pleasure. For it is not only yours to be useful, but also to take up every daily care that may contribute to the use of my affairs. There is nothing else that I would wish more from you than that you should love me (as you do) greatly, and be persuaded that there is no one living whose benevolence and truth I value more. Farewell.

I have been freed from great solicitude and fear. I hope you have understood from many letters and speech that while I was traveling through Etruria to go to the Roman city, I fell upon certain men who were infesting that province with constant robberies and were occupying almost all the approaches of the roads. I thought I had fallen into the hands of executioners who would torture me in many ways. I, however, when I was preparing my own spirit to bear with fortune all the punishments that they might have wished to inflict upon me, nor indeed asking them anything, found greater piety among them than I had ever dared to hope from them. For when they had diligently inquired who I was, or by what arts or from what quest I was traveling, and I had answered them regarding those things which had seemed to me at that time to be said for my own fortunes, they immediately urged me to hope for the best. They kept me with them for some days and treated me with every service and humanity. When, however, it seemed to them (after holding a council among themselves), not only did they send me away without any injury, but they even provided me with the necessary provisions. Having proceeded with that purpose to Rome (after I had given them the greatest thanks), I returned safely to my own people. I write these things to you with great study and pleasure
pages.54:
because I know that because of your singular benevolence toward me, you have always grieved at my adverse cases and greatly rejoice in favorable things. Farewell and write to me often about your state.

That your most human companion acted with you is not to be attributed to his fortune but to his character. For he is the most pleasant of all men. I know that his witticisms and his sweetness in all conversation were of service to you, perhaps no less than the fact that you were never opulent in pecuniary matters. For there is a kind of man more greedy than cruel. Since you were for the most part polite and did not have what profit they could make with you, they spared themselves from spending, lest you should become too expensive for them; I judge the deed to have been so. As for those things which you narrate were done by them at your departure, that they not only permitted your departure but even provided provisions and other offices of humanity, I cannot admire enough, since such piety is scarcely found among those men who wish to be called frugal and good. For (as I judge) those who have long been relying on the crimes of others will seek to hear honest studies, which those who live by laws and judgments often do. Whatever it was, I greatly congratulate you that you have freed me from the greatest fear and yourself from no small danger. I desire, however, that fortune of such a kind not be experienced again, and you will be (as I hope) more cautious henceforth in guarding your own safety. I give thanks to God that you wrote to me first about your liberation. For you knew that I was to be vexed no less by your inconveniences than by my own. I urge and beseech you, however, to come to us. For you will do a thing most pleasing to your friends after your return, and for me, it will be most pleasant, so that you could not affect me with any greater happiness. Farewell.

I am writing an unusual thing to you, which you will have judged to have been born from your own prudence. It will excite (believe me) an incredible love in you for great things. Gaius Lucius
