pages.55:
<note>A red decorative initial 'A' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Although because of his age he cannot yet be admitted to the highest magistracies of our republic, he was recently absolved of a great offense against the city by the laws, which allow nothing to be done contrary to ancient custom. For since our state had lost many leaders of the most valiant mind in frequent conflicts, and no one else remained whom we might send to such danger, the virtue of this young man in fighting was so evident in previous wars that our soldiers could never hope to be victorious unless he was the leader. Therefore, he yielded to the common opinion of all our laws, and honesty yielded to utility, and institutions yielded to necessity. This matter, insofar as you are concerned, ought to inflame and incite you, so that you think of nothing more, day and night, than how you might also make a path for yourself toward such glory. This will not be difficult for you, if you think nothing so arduous that it is not easy for a great and noble mind. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'A' marks the beginning of the text.</note>That Gaius Lucius has been gifted by our republic with such singular dignity for his virtue, I judge to have been done as a good example. Nor do I think anything is better in our city than that everyone should be able to achieve as much in our republic as they exceed others by virtue and deeds performed by them. But I fear that many, since they trust more in their own reputation than in their own virtue, take this very thing badly. You know what evils envy has often brought to our city. For while there are many other plagues that destroy many great kingdoms, I know not if there is any more pernicious to the human race than that of which I just spoke. If this could be avoided by modesty alone, it would perhaps be better to lead men to honors by laws and prayers, rather than by using envy and the hatred of many during timely magistracies. But since there is no humility (as they say) that can avoid the manner of such men, everything that fortune has brought must be borne with a great mind, and one must use virtue all the more bravely, the more it is attacked by many.
pages.56:
regarding the upright act of our city by which Gaius Lucius was absolved by the laws and established in that dignity which he often earned by fighting most bravely for his fatherland. But you will briefly understand how much that adds to those studies of mine which I have undertaken for the sake of the republic. For the reputation of our Gaius often excites me from sleep. I shall not rest, therefore, until I see that he, equal in age and reputation to his superiors, has attained the same by greatness of mind and by magnificently performed deeds. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I have signed these letters to you not regarding private comforts (as often before) but regarding the safety of our citizens. If there has ever been a time when the status of the republic has been a care to you, see that on this day you are present, for yourself, for your son, and for the help of those who are willing. For a fire hangs over us which, unless it is attended to by you most carefully, will easily erupt into a great conflagration. Wherefore, again and again, hasten to us. And let no thing be so great that it delays your arrival. All who desire your presence believe that the common safety of all is stored in you alone. Do not, therefore, delay the great expectation of all. I urge you, moreover, that it is better for a man to be loved by his own citizens than any principality, and [to obtain] that glory which comes from having fled no danger or labor for the republic. I persuade you to write by the benevolence and hope of all citizens placed in you; you, who know all things and love your country most highly, will better discern these things for yourself. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'F' marks the beginning of the text.</note>The ability to be able to aid the evils of the republic surely requires that one flee no labor or danger for the common safety. But there are many things that strike in me a lack of confidence and desperation regarding this matter. For many of our own prefer rather to disturb everything so that they might appear to lead, than to live among us by equal law; and there are many in the city who do not sufficiently know what is in the virtue and liberty of the citizens. If anyone should find in the city one who understands, judges, and feels well regarding the republic, it is of no avail toward the multitude. Nor do I see, therefore, what my presence can bring to the fatherland and our citizens, unless I take on many enmities, which are necessary neither for me nor for the republic. But where you come to the opinion that I should commit my safety to these waves and storms of the republic, I will not refuse, out of love for the fatherland, to experience everything rather than fail such a great expectation of our citizens. You have my judgment regarding the republic. You, as soon as you have determined again the will of our citizens, hasten to write to me regarding what I am to do. Farewell.
pages.57:
<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>What the status of our city is, from this you can understand, for the foundations of our republic have never been laid under better auspices than on this day. For when once our senate used to gather to consult on the highest matters, everyone served the time. If anyone divided the opinion, there was no one who dared to contribute freely what he felt. Now, however, we have yielded to such desires for a liberty not feigned or shadowy (as it used to be), but such as we have received from our ancestors, that we have never lived in any time as we do now. For the few who were oppressing public liberty having been removed from the city, all use equal law. It is permitted to everyone to say what he feels about our republic, and to feel freely what is said. Studies that were applied to private matters have all been converted to the greatness of the republic. And they are most intent on this one thing: who is most useful to the city. If you desire to be held great among your own, come to this republic of ours, which we hold to be most excellent and beautiful. You will be able to do as much in it as you will provide in labor, industry, and solicitude for the others. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' marks the beginning of the text.</note>That you enjoy an excellent republic, I rejoice more than for my own sake. For since the greatest part of my life has been spent, there can be nothing that I might long enjoy. But your era, which is on a better course, looks to the future for many things which it may rightly promise itself by entrusting the magistracies. If, however, there is anything in which I can serve the fatherland, I will not only take up all labors bravely for it, but I will also bear all annoyances and anxieties with an equal mind, and I will consider myself to have received enough fruit from my labors and studies if I leave your republic, which I hold to be most excellent and most ample, to your descendants along with you. If, however, it does not turn out by my service, I will rejoice that the greatest and most wise men are found in your city, who, by the best laws and most wise institutions, can protect the fatherland. I, however, desire more leisure than business for my old age. You, who are occupied in adorning and enriching it, will consider with your wisdom what is fitting for the republic. For whatever you decide regarding it, I will consider it good. Farewell.
pages.58: <note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I have decided to write to you what I think regarding the public utility of our citizens and in what way that matter can best be conducted by us, so that I might open the reasoning of all my counsels to you first. I have often perceived in my mind how the revenues and other proceeds of our city can be increased to the greatest extent without any inconvenience to our citizens or allies. To accomplish this matter, I saw that I had need of your opinion and prudence. You do not ignore that for many years before, neither merchants nor publicans (I call them pirates) could safely sail this sea of ours, from which it happened that our revenues sold for much less. Since everyone is led by this pact, that they perish for themselves and not for the republic, it is necessary that the profit of sailing impel them to this revenue. It happens that they do not commit themselves to the danger willingly, since the greater part of the comforts arrives to them, from which our treasury sustains no small loss and expenditure. What happens to merchants through fear of pirates is understood daily, since
pages.59:
almost all the arts in our city have come to nothing through a lack of goods. The damage arrives not only to private persons, but even to the republic itself. My counsel was that publicly, triremes should be equipped, and men accustomed to maritime wars should be enrolled who would make the supplies safe. For by this, we would confirm the minds of our allies and recover our revenues, which had perished. And how the merchants are, the sea is safe, with the pirates not daring to roam the sea for fear of our fleet. We often commemorate this in our senate, which, although it was approved by many, still, either through part envy or through the gravity of those who cannot look at me with equal eyes, that matter has not yet been brought into consultation. But where I have you as an assistant for this matter, I hope it is easy to obtain that all those things be done about which I wrote to you. You will not flee (as I trust) this labor, and you will take it up for the sake of the republic, and for your singular benevolence toward me, [I trust you will undertake] this procuration as it is honest and useful to the republic. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Unless the matter about which you write to me can be expedited by something other than my presence, I will come to the city as it is expedited. But I am greatly surprised that in a most fitting matter there is no one who agrees with you. For I see what can be added to your son. For if our republic has been oppressed for a long time, we desire that the sea, which has been vexed for these years by piratical robberies, may eventually be open to our revenues and merchants. Otherwise, our republic (which barely stands as yet) will shortly be nothing. I have decided, however, to write to the senate about this matter first, and to urge certain ones who have influence in their speaking, that they take up this business for the sake of the republic. For a certain gravity is often held by the greatest men when the common safety of the republic is treated by them, which matter, if it is treated by men of a lower order, often effects more envy than the republic
pages.60:
can reason. And because I have known your modesty, I know you will not have taken it badly that those things which had been perceived by you wisely for the public utility will be performed by another. You will take care, however, that if anything of this matter comes into the consultations, I might be informed by your letters. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'S' marks the beginning of the text.</note>If I have written to you at this time about our republic as I once did, there is nothing you ought to admire. Although, for the time in which there was a more vehement need to write to you for public utility, after you removed yourself from the care of it, others have become more timid, while others have assumed such license and audacity that they think nothing is forbidden to them in secret deliberations. If, therefore, you desire it to be safe, you must hereafter approach all to govern and rule it. The foundations which have been poorly laid, you must set right by your authority and wisdom, before they confirm themselves and accustom the multitude to serve their own lust. See that if there are any who are not rightly discerning regarding the common safety, you remove them (if you can) from their secrets. If not, hold the reason of the republic more than private friendship. Those, moreover, who are timid to take up these dangers for the citizens, I pray that you will excite with your exhortation, and inflame them to sustain all labors bravely, as often as reason or necessity demands this of them for the republic. You sustain the incredible expectations of all good men. You will do, therefore, what the republic will persuade you to be done at this time. But I ask one thing of you: do not forget that you are he to whom the republic itself and all its own commend themselves. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' marks the beginning of the text.</note>When your letters regarding the status of the republic were brought, not long after, others followed which announced that all things were being done by you out of private hatred and malevolence, and that the state of the city was in no other condition than it was when I left it safe and flourishing. How can it be led that these things have been effected by you? And I am most grieved by those
pages.61:
who are being destroyed by private dissensions of the republic. Whether those who are envious of you say that the cause of these evils resides in you, or (as I rather think) you could not bear their manners out of a desire for ruling, our republic cannot gain anything from this matter. I rejoiced that I had obtained from them to be granted, at last, leisure and quiet after many labors and after the perils of the sea, which I had often in great number promised for the public safety. Although it was permitted to me, since I had been blown by waves and storms for a long time, at last, with matters composed by my labor, to rest in the harbor. But after it has arrived at the point where either I cannot be in my own leisure, or it cannot be in peace, I will not desert it in the extreme time, I who have exercised my whole previous life often in labors and dangers for its safety. I will sail, therefore, to you as soon as there shall be wind. I hope, while all things are still new and fresh, that all the budding evils can be removed by me. But if it cannot be performed by me, yet neither my study nor my diligence will ever depart. You, however, I wish to provide for me, for your perpetual love in the republic, so that the utility of the republic may prevail more among you than the hatred or envy of any man. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Do not implicate yourself in any inconvenience regarding your own affairs. You believe everyone is of the same mind toward you as you are toward others. You are deceived, believe me. For of those who appear to be your friends in the present, very few love you from the heart. If, however, you will listen to me, abdicate all those from you whose brow is flattering, and who immensely praise all things that are done by you. I urge that in all matters to be conducted by you, you use the counsels of Caius Veturius, certainly the wisest of all and who loves you humanely; he will not suffer you to err in the lack of friends. There is no one from the number of our men whose prudence I value more highly, and [who] can judge better regarding our nature and the manners of our citizens.
pages.62:
Whatever he will suggest to you, consider it to be the word of veracious Apollo, as they say. If you will be willing to attend, you will see that he can neither be able to err, by reason of his wisdom, nor wish to, by reason of his humane benevolence. I desire to understand what you decide, so that when I have known you to be changed in that opinion in which you have been until now, I might sufficiently congratulate our friendship. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I use the counsels of Caius Veturius. For I have always valued his wisdom most highly. If I may speak with your good leave, you seem to me to feel less well of me when you see me dissuading the use of the friendship of those men whose brow is flattering. I, however, disagree with you far. But one must live with men in such a way that each has his own manner. I judge it to be the way of the wise, when others smile to themselves, for him to weep, and to be too severe when others are in jest. Thus, I have instituted my life to accommodate myself to present matters, nor would I suffer anyone to be angry by law. As often as I am able, know that I do nothing more willingly than to associate with those from whom I can become more learned by wisdom. These things, I know, have not yet been reported by my rivals. These things, as I considered them to be mine, I have written to you at this time, not because I am angry at your admonitions, but so that if you had conceived any not good opinion of me, I might purge myself before you. Or if anything is carried about me that is contrary to my dignity and that estimation which one has of me, write all (as you do) in a friendly and free manner. One thing I wish, that you allow yourself to be persuaded by your humanity to believe nothing rashly about me. For there are more who, moved by hatred or envy of some, come to impugn the reputation of another than those led by reason or honest cause. If you will provide this for me, I will always be most delighted by your admonitions. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'P' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I hope that I have perceived in my mind what reason can restore your cause to the whole; it is not far off, provided that [you consult] regarding it.

pages.63:
and you should have counsel with those who desire you to be on the laudable side. For when on the Ides of January I happened to meet Gaius Cornelius, a man most prudent in civil law, and many were present, all of us your friends fell (I know not how) into a conversation about your affairs. There was one who said that he had never heard of anything more iniquitous than the judgment that was rendered against you on the previous day in the criminal court. When everyone had agreed with this matter, there was nothing else to be said, except that everyone was indignant at that particular act. I, truly, when it was already time to depart from there, turned my mind to your case. And when I had examined those things more diligently, I recognized that nothing had been done according to the custom of our ancestors, except that it had been conducted at length. The power of your adversary directed that case more than justice. I advise: appeal to the higher magistrates, who are well-acquainted with sentences of this kind. For the judgment of these men has always been considered most just in our city, and it has never been appealed from their censorship. But see to it that you establish Cornelius <note>the person previously mentioned</note> as your patron, because he knows your case very well, and he is most sharp in malice. If you do this, I see you as the superior. If there is anything, however, in which my work can be of service to you, you will find me not only ready, but also most eager for all things that may come to your advantage. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I do not immediately agree with the unfairness of all those by whom the common sentence was brought against me, as they often have been offended. For it is my way to be moved by the indignity of this fact, although it should not be. Nor can it be that all the good men are moved, when justice has now been openly oppressed. But I not only love you, but I also admire you, because you (with no offense from me toward you) have always loved me like a brother. Nor have you ever allowed my fortunes to be obscured by those who wish for all common right and equity to be yielded to power. It follows that, as in other things, so also in this, I will follow your counsel, for I hold that matter as already almost scattered and abandoned. But as for you exhorting me to seek the patronage
pages.64:
of Gaius Cornelius, you persuade me well. For I have always seen that eloquence prevails most in the causes of orators, and that it dominates in courts as if in its own kingdom. But I do not know how that matter will be transacted well by me. For in this matter, money is needed, and I, from the previous lawsuit, not only was exhausted by pleading (which had been mine), but I am also held by great foreign debt. But I ask and beseech you that if you can apply any remedy to any opportunity through others, do not let any occasion pass. I have determined, indeed, that my friend has deserted me in my hope, so that I might be restored to integrity, and that all patronage might be destroyed. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>My matter is in safety, and you are already sailing in port, as they say. For nothing that could be desired by friends was lacking for the victory of your cause. For it was fought with such zeal and diligence that your matter was led to where it finally arrived. It was God who was concerned about this matter of yours as if it were his own, and perhaps even more so, because in the cause of friends it is fitting that we be more attentive than in our own. You will say what thanks you owe to me and your friends, not because they are ignorant of your mind, but so that your benevolence might be more tenacious among them. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>It is no duty that I would call more necessary than to show gratitude to those by whom we are well received. Nor was there need for your admonition to me, because everything that is said to you not only delights me, but I also regard it greatly. I will write to the friends, nor will I let that type of grace pass. For after my matter, by their zeal, was placed in safety, there is nothing that can be satisfied by me for their duty. But I will make it understood that I will not make an end to living for this great benefit of theirs. To you, however, I give many thanks, who out of benevolence have made me more informed than everyone else regarding these matters which I was most hoping to hear. Farewell.
pages.65:
Having put all things aside, I have accomplished with great zeal all things that I understood pertained to you, and of which I now write to you. I prescribe what things were done by me in order. As soon as I arrived in the province, I immediately asked those men of that region, and I was questioned by them whether the supply for the merchants was still free. Being sufficiently instructed by them regarding this matter, I betook myself to Alexandria. Having expedited your first goods, and whatever I knew pertained to my affairs, I took care lest the time, which was very short for me for the rest of your business, should be left idle. I contracted goods from everywhere, and those that were more ready for sailing, I brought into the port. On the seventeenth of March, when they had already placed everything in the ship, the sailors left the port with them, and since the winds were favorable, almost all at one time began to spread their sails. What followed from there was reported to me not long after: barely two or three ships at most had reached the shore, if any of them were yours. The rest, however, (as it was said) suffered shipwreck. I sense that not yet, through fear of the storm, had they moved themselves from that port, but rather that as soon as the storm abated, they would make the journey to us. I wish that our messages might turn out well. These things I wanted to be known to you first through our triremes, so that you might be more learned about all your affairs, and might put aside all anxiety, if you had perhaps taken any from this shipwreck. In other matters, however, since you are prudent, there is nothing about which I should admonish you. For you yourself can judge sufficiently that the goods are much more expensive, even if there had been no shipwreck. The rest, when the time comes, I will expedite. If you wish me to do anything else in your matter, signify it through your letters. Farewell.

Nothing could be added to this anxiety of yours. You have accomplished it so that if all things had happened adversely, I would still
pages.66:
have had gratitude for you, because your business could not have been conducted with greater zeal than you conducted mine at this time. I rejoice, however, greatly and congratulate you most of all that fortune favored your diligence. For when I had poured out so much money for those goods, such that I had never spent otherwise for the sake of trading, I saw almost all my fortunes having been thrown away. But by divine favor, that ship of ours, among the rest of the ships, arrived safely in port. Your letters were more welcome to me, because I had hoped less for the safety of our things. Already, a little before I received them, a rumor had arisen about this shipwreck. There were those who said that we had not escaped any danger at all. But as you admonish me about the high cost of goods, so that I might become more cautious and prudent in my own affair, you do rightly, as you do everything else. For I will be diligent and attentive, lest when fortune has been of aid to me, I appear to have failed myself. Regarding other matters that pertain to me, there is nothing that I would demand from you, except that as soon as you are able, you sail to us. For I have many things to confer with you, which will bring the greatest utility (as I hope) to both of us. But see that you do not commit yourself to the sea unless you see that all things are safe for sailing. Which opportunity will not be difficult for you to obtain, if you would rather entrust your safety to our triremes than to the beaked ships. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>You ask me to know what approaches closest to living well. For you write to me, as if you were ignorant, of the path I should take. I, truly, have received from the ancients that nothing is better than divine religion, which brings to what we desire in life, which is liberty. And although the greater part of men exists in that opinion, there is no one of them who, from reality and not from opinion, wants to judge, who does not immediately see that their whole life is similar to those who sail in winter. For just as those cannot command the winds and storms, so these cannot command their own affections. From which it is rarely seen
pages.67:
and it is rarely seen that they bring forth a serene mind with a joyful face. There is no one who praises his own sentence, and whoever indulges himself more, is always less pleased. I judge that this happens to them from no other place than because they have departed from the path, and all their counsels were aimed at the peak of it. Those, however, who follow divine worship, everything is tranquil, and nothing happens to them from mental disturbance. Everything is despised among them, they enjoy themselves, they admire nothing except the divine, and nothing concerning the change of fortune pertains to them. In the same place, both favorable and adverse things lie before them. Wherefore, if you will listen to my counsel, there is no thing so great that it is not secondary to the worship of religion and tranquility. Nor let the opinion of men turn you away from this thing, who think that happiness is not placed in anything other than external things. Believe me, they are not your friends, but are ignorant of where true beatitude consists. But if this kind of life is not approved by you, because it has removed itself from humanity, and it pleases you more to use your time with men than to live with God, my opinion is that you should occupy yourself with letters and philosophy. For you will borrow great aid for this civil life, which many follow, from these studies of humanity. But if that splendor of fortune delights you more, see that you do not implicate yourself in a matter from which, when you want, you cannot extract yourself. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'S' marks the beginning of the text.</note>You had satisfied my desire when you wrote that religion has a great advantage for living well, nor did the life of our men who profess it keep me from your counsel. I see things in my own time almost long since, who do not follow those things more in reality than in ambition or avarice. I am ashamed of the good times, and it especially pains me to mention those things which our pontiffs, without any reverence for honesty, do by their own will. It is enough what is said of them by most people, that the heads of the greatest vices (like the sources of huge rivers) were born first in their own house, and afterward, with the corrupted morals of the age, they relapsed to where they had arisen.
pages.68:
I cannot, therefore, commend that life in which I find no leader for morals to whom I might turn, or whom I might follow in that path in which it is most easy to err. But as for what you commend highly after religion, the studies of philosophy, I approve of your son. For the matter is truly worthy of our admiration and praise, in which not only the reason of human things, but also of divine worship, seems to me to be stored. For he takes the causes of the highest things, and instructs me how something well must be done by me, and how to stay chastely with men. I have decided that whether I must trade with the republic or with friends, I should seek both aid and counsel from it. For there is nothing in it that delights me more than that it teaches one to despise those things that most people admire, and it leads the mind away from all mole of sadness and anxiety. Why, therefore, follow more in the middle of the path that is placed in philosophy than that which is other, shadowy and vain, full of error and infamy, which no one professes, except for one whose mind deviates most from honesty? But you, who have been my helper and author for this matter, will often admonish me, nor will you allow me to err in that thing in which you are held by men to be the most prudent of all who live today. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' marks the beginning of the text.</note>When I decided to give my letters to you, no thing appeared in the middle that seemed to me better for your morals or studies, or would be more pleasing to you, than to take care that those things which I received from the wisest men about divine worship be known to you first. Reading, therefore, these days certain writings of the Greeks, I happened upon Basil. In that little book, I found many things about our erudition divinely known and said by that man. It was, however, his opinion that there is such power in divine worship, which the Greeks call <term>latria</term> <gloss>worship</gloss>, that there has never been any race so savage or so barbarous that it denied the gods. Those, however, who were more worth in intellect, established one single principle of all things, and as if a common parent of all divine powers, whom
pages.69:
they called the ruler of men, the father of God. Plato, indeed, wanted to be born so that he might open to the nations many things that were not yet understood about divine things. He felt about God in the same way as men who had written before him, so that he was not far from our philosophers, and what he felt, he committed most accurately to letters. He was the author to me that one should consider divine worship to be lacking in nothing. Wherefore he was inserting that there is no greater augmentation of our faith than that men might have felt something about divinity. Many things, besides, he was adding to these, which you will understand better yourself. I am sending to you the book of Basil. Please, when you have read it, know that you will owe the greatest thanks to that divine man, who opened this path to living well and happily. I desire, however, to understand through your letters what you judge about the sentences, and how much his reading has profited you. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'L' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I read your book of Basil, in which I found no small amount of sweetness and weight of sentences. I would never have thought that there was so much skill in a Greek man, up to our divine worship. And although I always attributed much to other Greek men in those disciplines which pertain to morals, yet in the knowledge of divine things, I was not judging unjustly that our men far surpass them. But the repeated reading of this little book accomplished so much that I judge them almost equal to those of ours. For what more wisely can be said or thought about the highest things than those things which were often discussed by Plato—the god of philosophers, as they say—and by those who followed him afterward, and were not sometimes most prudently written by them? This, indeed, is not unknown to you, to whom not few—all who have flourished in any kind of doctrine among the Greeks, than our Latins—have always been the most known authors and familiars. But what I have profited from reading your Basil, I prefer that you understand from others than from me. Never, however, was I more erect in hoping well
pages.70:
about myself than on this day. There are many things that delight me in that book, but this especially, that that kind of speaking has so much sweetness and modesty that there is nothing beyond it. Never, indeed, has it fallen from my hands. But when I am sufficiently imbued with it and have become more learned, I will take care that I send it to you as soon as possible. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' marks the beginning of the text.</note>What I write to you pertains mostly to divine worship, about which, if you know it as I think, it is well. If, however, you were in another opinion, you will soon know the difference from you. For I judge about religion: all who flee to the mind so that they might give themselves to idleness and languor, not only are these not to be held in the number of the religious, but also of the sacrilegious. Those who serve ambition or pleasure, they have pretended divine worship in such a way that there is no greater plague among men yet. You, however, will see again and again what you know about religion. For I judge thus: it is somewhat better to abstain from religion than to approach it not for the sake of that thing for which it was first intended by our ancestors—not as it ought to be. If you wish your action to be approved by those who were most contrary to you when you wanted to profess religion, there is need of no mediocre virtue. Those, indeed, were not satisfied when he said that this would happen, so that neither constancy nor modesty is held in this matter, when that mind of yours has cooled, which itself was most ardent. All their fear was true, and it will generate a stain on your name, which can never be abolished by you. That which I often thought with you: that constancy is approved in other things, but in religion it is necessary. Which one virtue will not be difficult for you to follow if you do not give yourself to idleness and remission. For since vices in all life are to be shunned, they are especially noted in a religious man. You will see again and again what you seek for yourself. I will love you if you confirm your judgment.

Having put all things aside, I have accomplished with great zeal all things that I understood pertained to you, and of which I now write to you. I prescribe what things were done by me in order. As soon as I arrived in the province, I immediately asked those men of that region, and I was questioned by them whether the supply for the merchants was still free. Being sufficiently instructed by them regarding this matter, I betook myself to Alexandria. Having expedited your first goods, and whatever I knew pertained to my affairs, I took care lest the time, which was very short for me for the rest of your business, should be left idle. I contracted goods from everywhere, and those that were more ready for sailing, I brought into the port. On the seventeenth of March, when they had already placed everything in the ship, the sailors left the port with them, and since the winds were favorable, almost all at one time began to spread their sails. What followed from there was reported to me not long after: barely two or three ships at most had reached the shore, if any of them were yours. The rest, however, (as it was said) suffered shipwreck. I sense that not yet, through fear of the storm, had they moved themselves from that port, but rather that as soon as the storm abated, they would make the journey to us. I wish that our messages might turn out well. These things I wanted to be known to you first through our triremes, so that you might be more learned about all your affairs, and might put aside all anxiety, if you had perhaps taken any from this shipwreck. In other matters, however, since you are prudent, there is nothing about which I should admonish you. For you yourself can judge sufficiently that the goods are much more expensive, even if there had been no shipwreck. The rest, when the time comes, I will expedite. If you wish me to do anything else in your matter, signify it through your letters. Farewell.

Nothing could be added to this anxiety of yours. You have accomplished it so that if all things had happened adversely, I would still

X.text:
have had gratitude for you, because your business could not have been conducted with greater zeal than you conducted mine at this time. I rejoice, however, greatly and congratulate you most of all that fortune favored your diligence. For when I had poured out so much money for those goods, such that I had never spent otherwise for the sake of trading, I saw almost all my fortunes having been thrown away. But by divine favor, that ship of ours, among the rest of the ships, arrived safely in port. Your letters were more welcome to me, because I had hoped less for the safety of our things. Already, a little before I received them, a rumor had arisen about this shipwreck. There were those who said that we had not escaped any danger at all. But as you admonish me about the high cost of goods, so that I might become more cautious and prudent in my own affair, you do rightly, as you do everything else. For I will be diligent and attentive, lest when fortune has been of aid to me, I appear to have failed myself. Regarding other matters that pertain to me, there is nothing that I would demand from you, except that as soon as you are able, you sail to us. For I have many things to confer with you, which will bring the greatest utility (as I hope) to both of us. But see that you do not commit yourself to the sea unless you see that all things are safe for sailing. Which opportunity will not be difficult for you to obtain, if you would rather entrust your safety to our triremes than to the beaked ships. Farewell.

and you have advice with those who desire that you be on their side. For on the Ides of January, I happened to meet Gaius Cornelius, a man very learned in civil law. While many were present, we all, being your close friends, fell (I know not how) into a conversation about your affairs. There was someone who said, or perhaps no one had heard, that the matter which was brought against you the day before in the criminal court had been unfair. When everyone had agreed with this, there was nothing else to be said, except that everyone was too indignant at that fact. But when I was about to depart from there, I applied my mind to your case. And when I had examined those things more diligently, I recognized that nothing had been done according to the custom of our ancestors, except that it had been conducted at such length. The power of your adversary directed that case more than justice. I advise you to appeal to the higher magistrates, who know well how to judge concerning such sentences. For the judgment of these men in our city has always been most weighty, and it has never been appealed from their censorship. But see to it that you appoint Cornelius as your advocate for this matter, for he knows your case best and is very sharp in malice. If you do this, I see you as the victor. But if there is anything in which my work can be of use to you, you will find me not only ready, but also most eager for all things that may be of advantage to you. Farewell.

pages.64:
Gaius Cornelius, you advise me well. For I have always seen that eloquence prevails most in the cases of orators, and that in judgments it dominates as if in its own kingdom. But I know not how that matter will be handled well by me. For in the matter, money is needed, and I am exhausted by the previous litigation, not only by pleading (which had been mine), but I am also held by great debt. But this I ask and beg of you, that if you can apply any remedy for some opportunity through others, do not let any occasion pass. I have determined that if my friend should fail my expectation, I would be restored to integrity, and that all patronage might be cast down. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Your matter is in safety, and you are already (as they say) sailing into harbor. For nothing that could be desired by friends was lacking for the victory of your cause. For it was fought with such zeal and diligence that your matter was brought to the point where it now arrives at these things. It was God who was as solicitous in this matter of yours as if it were his own, and perhaps even more so, because in the causes of friends it behooves us to be somewhat more attentive than in our own. You will say what thanks you owe to me and to your friends, not because they are ignorant of your mind, but so that your benevolence may be more tenacious among them. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>There is no duty which I would say is more necessary than to show gratitude to those by whom we are well received. Nor was there need of your admonition for me, because all things that are said to you not only delight me, but I even magnify them. I will write to my friends, nor will I let that grateful kind of thing pass. For after my affair was placed in safety by their zeal, there is nothing that can be satisfied by me in their duty. But I will make them understand that I will make no end to living up to this great benefit of theirs. But to you, I give much thanks, who, through benevolence, have made me more informed than all others about these things which I most desired to hear. Farewell.

pages.67:
and who carry themselves with a joyful face and a tranquil mind. There is no one who praises his own sentence, and who indulges himself more, is always less pleased; which I judge happens to them from nowhere else but that they have retreated from the path, and all their counsels were without sum. But for those following divine worship, all things are tranquil; nothing happens to them from mental disturbance. They despise all things within themselves, they enjoy themselves, they admire nothing but the divine, nothing regarding the change of fortune pertains to them; in the same place among them lie favorable and adverse things. Wherefore, if you will listen to my counsel, there is no thing so great that it should be preferred to the order and tranquility of religion. Nor let the opinion of men withdraw you from this thing, who think that happiness is not placed except in external things. Believe me, they are not your friends, but are ignorant of where true beatitude consists. But if this kind of life is not approved by you, because it has withdrawn from humanity, and it pleases you more to use your time with men than to live with God, my opinion is that you should occupy yourself with letters and philosophy. For you will borrow great help for this civil life, which many follow, from these studies of humanity. But if this splendor of fortune delights you more, see that you do not entangle yourself in a matter from which, when you wish, you cannot extricate yourself. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'S' marks the beginning of the text.</note>You have satisfied my desire, when you wrote that religion has the greatest support for living well, nor did the life of our men who profess it withdraw me from your counsel. I see things almost as they are in my own time, who do not follow these things so much in reality as in ambition or avarice. I am ashamed of the good times, and it is most burdensome to mention those things which our pontiffs do by their own will, without any reverence for honesty. It is enough that it is said by many concerning them, that the heads of the greatest vices (like the sources of huge rivers) were born first from their own house, and afterwards, by the corrupted morals of the age, returned again to where they had risen.

<summary>The author argues for religion and philosophy as the foundation of tranquility, while lamenting the corruption of contemporary religious leadership.</summary>

I cannot therefore commend that life in which I find no leader for morals to which I might turn myself, or whom I might follow in that path in which it is most easy to err. But what you commend greatly after religion, the studies of philosophy, I approve as your son. For the matter is truly worthy of our admiration and praise, in which not only the reason for human things, but also of divine worship, seems to me to be deposited. For it grasps the causes of the highest things, and instructs me that something well is to be done, and to live chastely with men. I have decided that whether I am to negotiate with the republic or with friends, I will seek both help and counsel from it. For there is nothing in it that delights me more than that it teaches one to despise those things which many admire, and it leads the mind away from all molestation and anxiety. Why, therefore, should one prefer anything other than that kind which is placed in philosophy, rather than something else shadowy and empty, full of error and infamy, which no one professes, unless it be a mind that diverges most from honesty. But you, who have been my helper and author for this matter, will often admonish me, nor will you suffer me to err in that thing, in which you are considered by men as the most prudent of all who live today. Farewell.

pages.73:
<meta>continues from previous page: studies / and as a helper and companion here. I would have been in writing [to you] / of the times. I hope you will be here shortly. Which I beg you vehemently to do. For I hope that we shall deliberate on many things / and have counsel, which will root us out from these cares and troubles, in which we have long been without hope of exiting. Farewell.

<note>A large red decorative initial L begins the paragraph.</note>Your letters have affected me with incredible pleasure. For I have never been inflamed with such great zeal for divine matters as I have been since I read your letter, in which you commend religion and place it in such a position that it ought to be preferred above all things. I, indeed, was not without some moderate sense regarding divine worship, and I praised above all others those who, putting all else behind them, gave themselves entirely to it from the heart. Yet, until now, such admiration for this matter had not possessed me, so that I would profess to desire it. Now, however, I not only desire it, but I am even being led to it in such a way that there can be nothing in life that is able to satisfy me without it. Therefore, I desire to be joined to you as a companion and a student. Formerly, the reason and institution of life was different, while a wife, children, and parents were present. Nor was my mind ever turned toward these things. Nor, if it had been, would it have been permitted while preserving piety. pages.63:
and you have counsel with those who desire you to be on the winning side. For when we happened to meet on the Ides of January, Gaius Cornelius, a man most prudent in civil law, and many others were present, we all fell (I know not how) into a conversation about your affairs. There was one who said, and I never heard anything more unjust, that the decree which was brought against you the day before in the criminal court was valid. When everyone had agreed to this matter, nothing else was discordant, except that each one was indignant at that act. I, indeed, when I was about to depart from there, turned my mind to your case. And when I had examined those things more diligently, I recognized that nothing was done in accordance with the custom of our ancestors, except that it was conducted at great length. The power of your adversary directed that case more than equity. I advise you: appeal to the higher magistrates, who are well acquainted with such sentences. For their judgment has always been held most grave in our city, and it was never appealed from their censure. But see to it that you appoint Cornelius, that pious man, who knows your case best, and is most acerbic in malice. If you do this, I see you as the superior. If there is anything in which my work can be of benefit to you, you will find me not only ready, but even most eager for all things that might conveniently accrue to you. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Not suddenly all the friends of the one who brought that sentence against me have been offended by their iniquity. For it is my way to be moved by the indignity of this fact, although I ought not to be. Nor can it happen, as it touches all good men, when justice has now been openly oppressed. I not only love you, but I also admire you, because you (with no fault of mine toward you) have always loved me as a brother. Nor have you ever suffered my fortunes to be obscured by those who wish all law and equity to be conceded to power. It follows that, as in other matters, so also in this, your counsel is such that I hold that matter now as almost dissipated and abandoned. But as for you exhorting me to use the patronage
pages.64:
of Gaius Cornelius, you advise well. For I have always seen that eloquence in the case of an orator counts for much, and that he dominates in judgments as if in his own kingdom. But I do not know how that matter will be handled well by me. For in the matter of money, there is a need, and I, in the previous litigation, not only by pleading (which had been with me) was exhausted, but I am also held by great debt. But I ask and beseech you that if you can apply any remedy to some opportunity through others, do not let any occasion pass. I have determined that if my friend deserts my hope, I will be restored to integrity, so that all patronage might be cast down. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>My matter is in safety, and now (as they say) you sail into port. For nothing that could be desired by friends was missing for your victory in the case. For it was fought with such zeal and diligence that your matter was led to that point, which finally arrived at the above. It was God who was as solicitous in this case of yours as if it were his own, and perhaps more so, because in the cause of friends it is fitting that we be more attentive than in our own. You will say what thanks you owe to me and your friends, not because they are ignorant of your mind, but so that your benevolence toward them may be more tenacious. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>There is no duty that I would say is more necessary than to be grateful to those by whom we have been well received. Nor was there need for your admonition to me, because everything that is said to you not only delights me, but I even magnify it. I will write to my friends and not let that type of grace pass. For since my matter is placed in safety by their zeal, there is nothing that can be satisfied by their duty from me. But I will make it understood that I will make no end to living up to this great benefit of theirs. To you, indeed, I give many thanks, because through benevolence you have made me more informed than all others about these matters which I most desired to hear. Farewell.
pages.65:
I have, with all things put aside, accomplished with great zeal all things that I understood pertained to you, and of which I now write to you; I write down what was done by me in order. As soon as I arrived in the province, I immediately asked the men of that region, and I inquired from them whether the merchant fleet was still free. When I had been sufficiently informed by them about that matter, I betook myself to Alexandria. And having expedited your first goods, and having learned whatever I could about my own affairs, I took care that I did not allow time, which was very short for the rest of your business, to remain idle. I gathered baggage from everywhere, and those that were more ready for navigating, I brought into the port. But on the seventeenth of March, when all had now been placed in the ship, the sailors left the port with them, and since the winds were favorable, almost all began to set sail at one time. What followed from there was not long after reported to me: that barely two or three ships at most had reached the coast, if any were yours. The others, however (as was said), made shipwreck. I understand that they have not yet moved themselves from that port due to the fear of the storm, but as soon as that storm has subsided, they will make the journey to us; may our messengers turn out well. I wanted these things to be known to you first through our triremes, so that you would be more learned about all your affairs, and would lay aside all anxiety, if perhaps you had conceived any from this shipwreck. In other matters, since you are prudent, there is nothing for which I should admonish you. For you yourself can judge sufficiently that goods are much more expensive, even if there had been no shipwreck. The rest, when the time comes, I will expedite. You, if you wish for anything else to be done by me in your matter, signify it to me through your letters. Farewell.

Nothing could be added to this anxiety of yours. You have caused that, even if all things had turned out adversely, nevertheless I would have owed you thanks, because your business could not have been managed with greater zeal than you have managed mine at this time.
pages.66:
But I rejoice greatly and I most especially congratulate you that fortune has favored your diligence. For when I had poured out so much money for those goods, as I had never before gathered for the sake of trading, I saw almost all my fortunes having been thrown away, had not our ship, by divine favor, reached the port safely among the other ships. Your letters were therefore the more welcome to me, as I was hoping less for the safety of our affairs. Already, a little before receiving them, a rumor had arisen about this shipwreck. There were those who said that no danger at all had been avoided. But that you admonish me about the high cost of goods, so that I might become more cautious and prudent in my own affair, you do rightly, as you do everything else. For I will be diligent and attentive, lest when fortune has been a help to me, I might appear to have been wanting to myself. But concerning other matters that pertain to me, there is nothing I must demand of you, except that as soon as you are able, you sail to us. For I have many things to confer with you, which will bring greatest utility (as I hope) to both of us. But see that you do not entrust yourself to the sea unless you see all things safe for navigating. Which opportunity will not be difficult for you to follow, if you would rather entrust your safety to our triremes than to beaked ships. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I want to know from me what approaches most closely to living well. For you write to me that you are ignorant as to which path you should primarily enter. I, indeed, have received from the ancients that nothing is better than divine religion, which coincides more with the liberty that we desire in life, although the greater part of men exists in the opinion otherwise. But who is there among them, who, if he wished to judge from reality, not from opinion, would not immediately see that their whole life is like that of men who navigate in winter? For just as those cannot command the winds and storms, so these cannot command their own affections. From which it is rarely seen
pages.67:
and they are those who bring forth a joyful brow, or a tranquil soul. There is no one who praises his own sentence, and the more he indulges himself, the less he is pleased, which I judge happens to them from no other cause than that they have departed from the path, and all their counsels were exhausted. But to those following divine worship, all things are tranquil, nothing happens to them from confusion of soul, they despise all things within themselves, they enjoy themselves, they admire nothing except the divine, nothing pertaining to the change of fortune reaches them; in the same place among them lie favorable and adverse things. Therefore, if you will hear my counsel, there is no matter so great that it is not outweighed by religion and tranquility. Nor let the opinion of men turn you away from this matter, who think happiness is placed in nothing other than external things. Believe me, they are not your friends, but ignorant of where true beatitude stands. But if this kind of life is not approved by you, because it has little to do with humanity, and it pleases you more to use your time with men and live with God, my opinion is that you should occupy yourself with letters and philosophy. For you will borrow great help toward this civil life, which many follow, from these studies of humanity. But if this splendor of fortune delights you more, see that you do not entangle yourself in a matter from which, when you wish, you cannot extricate yourself. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'S' marks the beginning of the text.</note>You had satisfied my desire when you wrote that religion has the greatest support for living well, nor did the life of our men who profess it deter me from your counsel. I see many things in my own time that do not pursue these things in reality as much as for ambition, or for the sake of avarice. I am ashamed of the good times, and it especially pains me to commemorate those things which our pontiffs do by their own will, without any reverence for honesty. It is enough that it is said by many concerning them that the heads of the greatest vices (like the origins of huge rivers) were born first from their own house, and afterwards, with the corrupted morals of the age, returned to where they had arisen,
pages.68:
having relapsed again. I cannot, therefore, commend that life, in which I find no leader for morals toward whom I might turn, or whom I might follow in that path in which it is most easy to err. But what you commend greatly after religion, the studies of philosophy, I approve, my son. For it is a matter entirely worthy of our admiration and praise, in which not only the reason of human affairs but also of divine worship seems to me to be stored. For it captures the causes of the highest things, and instructs me how to do something well and to walk chastely with men. I have determined that whether I am to deal with the republic or with friends, I will seek both help and counsel from it. For there is nothing in it that delights me more than that it teaches me to despise those things which many admire, and it draws the soul away from all weight, pain, and anxiety. Why, therefore, should I prefer to live in the middle of a race that is placed in philosophy, rather than another that is shadowy and vain, full of error and infamy, which no one professes, except the soul of someone who most dissents from honesty? But you, who have been an assistant and author for me in this matter, will often admonish me and will not suffer me to err in that matter, in which you are held by men to be the most prudent of all who live today. Farewell.

<note>A large, red decorative initial 'Q' marks the beginning of the text.</note>When I had determined to give my letters to you, no matter appeared in the middle that seemed to me better for your morals or studies, or would be more welcome to you than that I should take care to make known to you in the first place those things which I have received from the most wise men concerning divine worship. Reading, therefore, in these days the writings of certain Greeks, I happened upon Basil. In his little book, I found many things well known and said by that man about our divine erudition. But it was his opinion that there is such force in divine worship, which the Greeks call <term>latria</term> <gloss>worship/adoration</gloss>, that there was never any race so savage or so barbarous that it did not deny gods. Those, indeed, who were more capable in intellect determined that one principle exists above all, and as if the parent of all common numina, whom
pages.69:
they called the ruler of men, the Father God. Plato, indeed, whom he wished to be born, so that he might open to the nations many things that were not yet understood concerning divine things, felt so about God regarding the men who had written before him that he was not far from our own philosophers. What he felt, he committed to letters most accurately. For he was my author that one should consider there is no matter to be preferred to divine worship. Wherefore he inferred that there is no greater increase of our faith than that men should feel something about divinity. Many things he added besides these, which you will understand better yourself through you. I send to you the book of Basil. I ask that when you have read it, know that you will owe the greatest thanks to that divine man, who opened this path to living well and happily. I desire, however, to understand through your letters what you judge about the sentences, and how much his reading has profited you. Farewell.

<note>A large, red decorative initial 'L' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I have read your book of Basil, in which I found no small amount of sweetness and weight of sentences. I would never have thought that there was so much skill in a Greek man, up to this, our divine worship. Although I always attributed much to the Greek men in these disciplines which pertain to morals, yet in the knowledge of divine things, I seemed to myself to judge not unjustly that our men far surpass them. But the repeated reading of this little book has brought it about that I judge them to be almost equal in these things of ours. For what can be said or thought more wisely about the highest matters than those things which were often argued by Plato—the god (as they say) of philosophers—and by those who followed him in succession, and were sometimes written by them most prudently? I do not say this to you, for whom all who have flourished in any kind of doctrine among the Greeks, as well as our Latins, have always been very well-known and familiar authors. But how much I have profited by reading your Basil, I prefer you to understand from others than from me. I have never been more
pages.70:
erect and hopeful about myself than on this day. There are many things that delight me in that book, but this especially, that that type of speaking has so much sweetness and modesty that nothing is superior. For it never falls from my hands. But when I am sufficiently imbued with it and have become more learned, I will take care that I send it to you as soon as possible. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' marks the beginning of the text.</note>What I write to you pertains mostly to divine worship, about which, if you know it as I think, it is well. But if you were of another opinion, you will shortly know the difference from you. For I judge about religion that all who flee to the soul to give themselves to inertia and languor, not only should these not be held in the number of the religious, but also of the sacrilegious. Those who serve ambition or pleasure, they have so constituted divine worship that there is no greater plague among men yet. But you, what you know about religion, you will see again and again. For I judge thus: that it is somewhat better to abstain from religion than to approach it not for the sake of the thing itself, for which it was first established by our ancestors, not as it behooves. If you wish your act to be approved by those who were most contrary when you wished to profess religion, there is need of no mediocre virtue. They were not satisfied by that, when they said that this would happen, so that neither constancy is had in this matter, nor modesty, when that soul of yours has cooled, which itself was most ardent. All of their fear was true, and it would generate a stain on your name, which can never be abolished by you. That which I often thought with you: that constancy is approved in other matters, but in religion, it is necessary. Which one virtue will not be difficult for you to follow, if you do not give yourself to leisure and remission. For when all vices are to be avoided in every life, they are especially noted in a religious man. You, what you seek for yourself, you will see again and again. I will love you if you confirm your judgment.

pages.83:
or by admonishing, you accomplish this. May you render me more learned and better day by day. But it is incredible how these letters of yours have delighted me, which were delivered to me by your messenger. For they smell of ancient wisdom, just as you write to me. Nor am I so consumed by ambition that I do not value your judgment more than the opinion of the crowd. I say that, having set others aside, I am in one mind to follow only that art, and not to occupy my studies with diverse matters at one and the same time. He who does this never makes enough progress for himself. When, however, I have achieved what you see in one thing, then I will give my effort to other studies. Nor will I wander now in one way, now in another, and not before I have drawn enough for myself from those good sources of the art to which I have devoted my labor and intellect. What you write to me regarding the modesty and humanity to be held toward my equals, I perform with such zeal that I seem to depart from them in no novelty of life. And I hope for good in the future. For the more ambitious I shall have been in my studies, the more of grace and benevolence I shall obtain among all men. There is nothing else that I might write to you, unless to remind you of your letters. For as often as I read them, I see myself being with you and speaking. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' begins the text.</note>Everything expects your presence and your service, from which you can imagine that even your enemies desire greatly to return into your favor. If you neglect this matter, you will neither consult your own fame nor satisfy the expectation of all your fellow citizens. For the matter stands thus: even if you did not have the capacity, you could still persuade no one of that. It is necessary, therefore, to work and to apply yourself with all your mind, so that you satisfy the will of your fellow citizens. Nothing can better become your nature, nor be more praiseworthy in industry, than to present yourself to men, and to desire those things which you know are desired by men. For it is clearly said by the <term>Stoics</term> <gloss>ancient philosophers who taught the endurance of pain and avoidance of passions</gloss> that all things on earth were created for the sake of men, and men themselves for the sake of men.

so that they may accommodate their study to one another by mutual service. Nor should labor or danger deter us from that thing. For either there is no other way to immortality, or it is mostly stored in this place: that for the sake of the good, for the sake of friends, we are not broken by any troubles, and that we show ourselves not only placable to those whom we ought to love and protect, but even exorable to our enemies. If you remember how much each of us owes to the fatherland, I rejoice, and I rejoice greatly with you if I learn that my letters have added something to your intellect and virtue, so that you might more quickly achieve all those things which you see are sought of you with great zeal. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' begins the text.</note>If I had thought that enough had been done by me for the state and for friends, I would not have expected you to admonish me in that matter, which, since it is honorable among others, would be necessary for me as well. But since I have grown old in the state at my age, and have never fled any labors or dangers for its sake, I seemed to myself to have offered my leisure, as if it were a port of our life, without injury to the fatherland. And this ought to be granted by all citizens and my associates, so that I, who have sailed the sea for a long time, might finally rest in that port. But it is as in other things, so in friendship and love of the fatherland: there is a certain excessive desire and longing of men, which can never be satisfied. I do not know what the fatherland or friends might want more than that I should repeat old troubles, and when I can still live for myself for some time, seem to have put my hands back into the fray. Do not (if you love me) urge me to that thing which suits neither this age nor my current studies. For our state has enough counsel, if it wants to use the advice of those citizens who are capable. For me, however, quiet should have been earned by my merits in the state. If you, however, defend my cause among the citizens as a friend, I am more grateful to you than if you had
pages.85:
interrupted my leisure. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'V' begins the text.</note>I prefer to have proven myself in holding magistracies by the judgment of others rather than my own. However, I do not hesitate to write this to you: I have never valued anyone's friendship or favor so much that I would prefer it over laws and equity in all private causes. And this I know: no one can live with such considered reason that his service pleases everyone and offends no one. For when we favor one party in settling disputes, it is necessary that we offend the other. Yet this is enough for me: if the laws and rights of the city have been preserved by me. What others may say about me, let them see to it themselves. I shall use my own conscience. You, however, who are wise and have experienced similar things, will see by your wisdom what should be believed of such men. If there is anything that brings any suspicion about me to you, write, and I will (as I hope) remove you from any suspicion. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'A' begins the text.</note>I have never doubted your sense of duty, yet I have received great pleasure from your letters. I rejoice for your sake as much as for others, because you protect your dignity in these letters. For all men see the same thing that I do, and they think of your integrity. And the wills of men are so varied and multiple that even if our life is known to all, it is not yet approved by all. I will not pursue the place where I might judge this. You will understand the cause of this error better than I myself, who am writing to you. I rejoice therefore (to return to where I began) that you have written these things to me, and I urge you greatly that, in all causes which will be to be recognized or judged by you either according to our laws or from equity and good, you be so constant in those things that you understand are drawn to your own fame. For I judge of myself thus, that I think nothing can be done by you contrary to the custom of the ancestors or to equity. Farewell.
pages.86:
<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' begins the text.</note>As often as I write about my duty, it is a thing most incongruous to my ancestors and to fate. But because there are many letters in which I think that this must be done by a wise man, I think you will easily grant me forgiveness if I have had regard for my dignity, and especially against those who cannot be overcome by me through any modesty or humanity, who hope to spread the story of others about me among the people. I hope that you will recognize all my life for your singular prudence. As soon as I arrived in this city of yours, I saw immediately that I must live according to other customs, not my own. I thought and did and said all things that could please these citizens, and offend no one. I admitted minds to me; I excluded no one. My help (if ever there was need) I did not deny even to those who asked, but I even offered it often of my own accord. I hoped, however, that many friends had been made for me through these arts. Nor did that matter deceive me, were it not that envious men could have more power than good men. What happened in this place, what rumors were spread about me, I will not write, except that I learned that through friends, many became my enemies. I will not write fully to you about this matter, except that you should remember your modesty and humanity. Do not suffer that, among you who are the wisest men, envy should have more power than equity, and consider that you are placed in this office by the state to retain good men in the city, and consider more what each man's mind is toward the state and from what ancestors he is born among you. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' begins the text.</note>When your letter was delivered to us during our occupations at sea, we could not write to you immediately. But after it was allowed for us by those, we read them diligently. Our opinion is that we wish those to have the most power in our city who deserve better of our citizens. We will suffer this (the state being safe) to have more power through envy than through equity. If there is anything that you say you have suffered through any need or insult, we advise...

<note>A red decorative initial 'V' begins the text.</note> I preferred to show myself in holding offices, rather according to the judgment of others than my own. But I do not hesitate to write this to you: I have never valued the friendship or favor of anyone so much that I would prefer it to the laws and equality of all. But I know this, that no one can live with such considered reason that his duty pleases everyone and offends no one. For when we favor one party in settling disputes, it is necessary that we offend the other. But that is enough for me, if the laws and rights of the city have been kept by me. What others may say about me, let them see to it themselves. I will use my own conscience. You, however, who are wise and have experienced something similar, will see through your wisdom what should be believed of such men. But if there is anything that brings any suspicion about me to you, write, and I (as I hope) will remove you from all suspicion. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'A' begins the text.</note> I have never doubted your duty, yet I have received great pleasure from your letters. I rejoice for your sake as much as for others, because you defend your dignity in these letters. For everyone thinks the same as I do, concerning your integrity. And the wills of men are so diverse and multiple that even if our life is known to all, it is still not approved by all equally. I will not pursue the place of such error. You will understand the cause of that error better than I myself, who am writing to you. I rejoice therefore (to return to where I began) that you have written those things to me, and I exhort you greatly that, as you understand the desire for your reputation, you may be so constant in all causes, which will be for you to either recognize or judge, either according to our laws or from equity and good. For I judge of myself in such a way that I think nothing can be done by you contrary to the custom of our ancestors or equity. Farewell.
pages.86:
<note>A red decorative initial 'Q' begins the first paragraph.</note> As often as I write about my duty, it is a matter most incongruous with my ancestors by fate. But since there are many epistles by which I think it must be done by a wise man and is necessary, I think you will easily grant me pardon if I have held to the reason of my dignity, and especially against those who cannot be overcome by me by any modesty or humanity, who hope to spread the story of others about me among the people. I hope you will recognize the life of all of me, for your singular prudence. When I first arrived in this city of yours, I immediately saw that I must live from then on by an alien custom, not my own. I thought of friends, I did and said everything that could please these citizens, and offend no one. I admitted minds to myself, I excluded no one. My help (if ever there was a need) I did not deny to those asking, but I even often offered it spontaneously. I hoped, however, that from these arts many friends would have been acquired for me. And that matter did not deceive me, unless envious men could have been more than good men. What happened in this place, what rumors they stirred up about me, I will not write; unless I have understood that for the sake of friends, many enemies were made for me. I will not write more to you about this matter, unless that you may remember your modesty and humanity. Do not suffer that, among you who are most wise, envy should be more than equity, and do not forget that you are placed in this duty by the Republic, so that you may retain good men in the city, and that you should consider more of what sort each person is toward the Republic, and from what ancestors he was born among you. <note>A red decorative initial 'Q' begins the second paragraph.</note> When your letter was delivered to us in our occupations of the sea, we could not immediately write to you.
