or in authority or in virtue. I do not doubt that he can most easily overcome the speeches and malice of these men. I know you will not allow me to be afflicted by this unworthy insult from envious men. Even if I have persuaded myself of this, you will still do a very pleasing thing if you write to me about what you feel regarding this matter. Farewell.

<note>The initial 'A' is rubricated in red.</note>
About your mind toward your parents and relatives and your piety, I have never thought it necessary to doubt. But since your piety is not equally known to all men, it happens easily that some through envy, some through error, and some through the custom of disparaging what should be praised, might invent or believe something about you. But even if the matter has been brought about by no fault of your own, and even if I judge you excellently, it is still a matter that must be considered most carefully. For it could happen that even good men might not form a good opinion of you if you use the money left by your parents poorly. Therefore, it must be ensured again and again that you are not more splendid in your attire, or more extravagant in your servants and other things, than either the custom of your forefathers, or the dignity of your ancestors, or your own means allow. For we see that such rumors are often held by men about these things, who should be praised, and they make more enemies than friends. For there are some in the city whose hearts ache that the goods which were provided for the aid of the republic through the industry and labor of excellent citizens should be consumed by the rashness and intemperance of young men. I do not think these vices are in you, but I mention them to you so that you may be more honorable in all your life, and that you may abhor more deeply all immoderate expense, and all company of those who are the ruin of all wealthy young men. As far as my study or diligence can provide, I will take care of your reputation, if I hear that anything unworthy is reported about you. But you must take care that, while I am commending my own duty, you yourself do not diminish it in the estimation of men by some good deed. Farewell.
pages.99:
<note>A red decorative initial 'Q'</note>
How much I cherish all my relatives from my heart, you will easily understand if you consider my efforts toward them. For everyone is dear to their own, and I do not think there is anyone among them whom I know who pursues his own with greater benevolence than I do mine. I cannot sufficiently admire what some men can think of me, whom neither my previous duties toward my own, nor benefits, can move, and who go about disparaging me. But words, as I see, are suited by them for other things. They wish to be troublesome, and prefer to malign rather than speak well. Yet I have one great relief in this distress and annoyance: that we live in a city where we are sufficiently known to both parties. But I will not be brought to depart from my own custom, and although their eyes may burst with pain, I will always strive to be more dutiful and kind toward my own. Whatever effort can be made by you on my behalf against such men, you will undertake it entirely because of our long-standing benevolence. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'Q'</note>
That I have received great annoyance from your letter, because your duties toward all your relatives were sufficiently evident to all citizens, is true. For I have never been less solicitous for your dignity than for my own. But since there is no one who does not judge excellently of you, I believe it is better to take care of your own dignity from those who wish to lower your good reputation from the minds of men, rather than that you should have to doubt your own fame. If, however, it happens that you hear something about yourself, I will not bear it dispassionately, for I will also act so that those who came prepared to malign others will themselves dare much worse things against themselves. Whatever they may attempt against you, there is nothing that should perturb you greatly. For the opinion that good men have formed of you is stronger than to be able to be violated by such men. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'T'</note>
I have honored the friendship that was founded upon honor above all else, nor have I borne anything else in human affairs with greater...
pages.100: importance than this for me. Now, truly, it would be most shameful to neglect this, whether by reason of virtue or custom, which I have often preferred before many and great things. I will state the reason that has impelled me to this. I have persuaded myself either that there is no good in life, or that it is joined with friendship. If this were done merely by our own study, I would not admire this good so much. But when I see that all men are led and driven by nature itself so that they may live together and love themselves, there is no one who does not judge this thing divine. For not all come to friendship equally, but each one accommodates himself to others more rightly and better according as he is strong in virtue and talent. For we see that the studies of men are varied; some hope for utility in friends, others for honors. Some are excited to these things so that they may have those with whom they may take delight. A wise man, however, places the entire fruit of friendship in honor. I myself, when I had determined not to love except through good men, took care not to follow others, which I understood would please them. I was afterwards attentive in that matter so that I might take care that I was not surpassed by any of my own in duty. I will say what is true; men love so that they may please. I have never loved more than when things are going well for my friends. And if I do not wish them ill, yet that seems to me the highest point of friendship, whether when friends most expect our effort, or when they can love no one from the heart. Those who have some sadness, which can be cured by enduring, made me besides more dutiful in friendship, since I promised myself I could not fail to be loved by them, whom I loved so much, which reason, although it has sometimes deceived me, I will never be tired in the love of my own. I hope, indeed, to be able to reconcile the minds of many men to myself by these reasons. For you yourself have often exhorted me to this matter. You have been of such an opinion, that I valued it more than any other. You will see, therefore, according to your wisdom...
pages.101:
if anyone says something alien about me, that you trust the old friend more than other men. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N</note>
I have never considered any danger or labor to be such that I should avoid it for the comfort of friends. Nor do I judge that there is any other thing so great (virtue excepted) that it should be preferred to friendship. I think you also know this. For you know from the conjecture of our own fate that we had the same teacher, and after we departed from school, our friendship has always remained throughout the years. For whether I was in the republic, whether in private matters, whether in the city or in the country, we have always had a great partnership of advice toward each other, just as the king of all. Yet there has been no time until now in which you might desire my duty in the mutual observance between us. I hope your fortune remains and that you suffer no unworthy insult. But where something might happen to your affairs, you would understand what kind of mind I have toward you. There is one thing that I not only ask but also beseech of you with the greatest intensity: that, since I love you most, you do not allow the envy of men to tear our friendship apart. And may the memory of our friendship, which began from boyhood, prevail with you more than the prayers of those who at this time most strive to destroy our friendship as much as they can. For I strive not only that we remain in friendship, but also that we may be judged as those who are surpassed by no other love and benevolence. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q</note>
That you remind me of our friendship, I receive great pleasure. For it helps to know the memory of our friendship, and of all the studies which we afterwards celebrated in adult age with great effort. But I dare to speak badly of you here, since I do not know what you seem to suspect about our friendship, and to doubt lest it be shaken by envious men. What others judge about this matter, I do not know enough. I, however, think that friendship which is formed from honorable duties has deeper roots...
pages.102:
to have, and firmer foundations. I do not say it ought to. That which is certain is that it cannot be destroyed by any envy or by the withdrawal of some men. Wherefore, if you have admitted any suspicion regarding my mind toward you, I beg you to lay it aside. For since in other matters once undertaken by me I have always wished to seem constant, I have thought this should be maintained most of all in friendship. What is judged about me? You will see, according to your prudence and humanity. As for what pertains to me, I will say: I have certainly cherished you more from the heart today than any other day. With these suspicions of such a kind cast aside, let us do what you write to me about; let us strive vehemently so that we may overcome all men with benevolence and love. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial V</note>
These are the things which I judge should be pursued by me with great study. I give no greater effort to anything than that all who love me might clearly understand that they are not less loved and honored. What may happen to you in experience, I do not know; I conceive well of you, however. But see that you do not disappoint my opinion. For it would be most shameful not to love your own, by whom you are most loved. What kind of thing this is, you will soon learn in that matter of Pomponius, who is your relative and a friend to us. If you desert him, there is no one among your own who would not be alienated from you. But I, especially, since I began to love him openly, think you will not allow us to change our mind, nor to think otherwise of you than formerly. For you will make at one time the loss of almost all your friends, the like of which you have not yet experienced. That this may not happen by your own fault, I ask you again and again. Farewell.

The cause of Pomponius can be defended by right, for there is nothing at all that he would do in his own matter. Neither will it be unjust, nor will his relationship, nor his familiarity (which is common to me with him) be able to weigh more with me than equity and justice. As for the loss of almost all your friends (as you know) that must be made...
pages.103:
by me, unless I comply with his comforts, I do not think I have reached that point of indignity that I should omit what I acquired through virtue and honorable duties in order to do what is right. I will never think (if the opinion of your mind is judged by me) that you will bear that matter; it is for you to judge. For as far as it pertains to me, I judge well of you. Nor do I think that you ask anything on behalf of Pomponius unless it is good and equitable. Concerning this matter, as I am affected in mind toward all, I would have performed it for him even without anyone's prayer. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial O</note>
After I took the toga from my father, I thought there was no matter to be guarded with greater study than that I might seem to act against those from whom I had received many and great benefits. Do not, therefore, trust those who (so that they may remove your mind from me) try to persuade you that I will never have gratitude for your benefits. For I have ordered my life so that I could never be justly accused by those to whom I owe something. But why do they strive so much with you, so that you may have faith in them, since they most wish that I should dispute this matter before you? For unless I refute them so that they repent of their deed, there is nothing in other matters that I would wish to have faith in me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N</note>
That you have been attentive in reporting what you have heard, you do what is worthy of both your ancestors and yourself. Nor is there anyone who has reported anything about you to me yet. I do not know if you have understood it badly from someone else, or what I am ignorant of, you perhaps know better yourself. If, however, you make a conjecture from some sign that I am now going to doubt your gratitude, I would rather hear it from you here in your presence than by letters. If you do this, I will not allow you to be in this error any longer. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial E</note>
That my mind toward your relatives is sufficiently evident to you, I believe, yet I cannot help but write to you concerning my duty toward them. For I rejoice to do all things that have been performed by me with pleasure. B. Appuleius, a man familiar to you, when he was brought to our port by the force of a storm, and was ignorant of our laws and customs...
pages.104:
...of our country, he removed merchandise from the ship in the manner of our merchants. Which, since it had already been seized by the publicans, the matter itself already looked clearly toward confiscation. And there was no doubt but that they were doing it out of subversion. But since I happened to be present there, I began to inquire. After I understood that he was one of your relatives, I immediately approached the praetor, and I alleged the ignorance of a stranger. On that day, I obtained that the confiscation should be suspended. On the following day, however, with my friends, I approached the judges to whom the cognizance of such a cause had been given by the praetor. I taught that it could not be contracted by our laws which was done by ignorance, and thus it could be convicted of being done by deceit. I had many helpers in the cause of your friend. We dismissed that man, therefore, with his goods safe, from whom you will better understand how much study I used in his danger. I write this to you willingly so that you may know that all who are friends to you are also cherished by me. Farewell.

<note>Large red decorative initial 'R'</note>
That your letter was given to me, B. Appuleius explained diligently that you were in all duty and benevolence toward me, and that you would not have rested before you saw him restored to his integrity. I myself, even if I have received the greatest pleasure from these things which he reported to me, yet a great heap of love has been added to my previous benevolence, since I understood that the same was signaled to me afterward by your letters. For I love B. Appuleius greatly, for I used his familiarity. And he is of such virtue and modesty that there is no one to whom he should not be most dear by his own merit. Think, therefore, how much I do, since no duty was missed by you for his defense. I desire something to happen that I would in no way wish to come into your matter with your disadvantage, in which matter...
pages.105:
...I might be able to refer gratitude to you. I hope you will understand there is nothing undertaken by me at any time with greater study than to prove by the thing itself the gratitude which I have for you immortally. If you recognize anything in which my work can be of use to your own, allow that to be most obtained from you, so that, just as you used my duty in the case of Appuleius, you may wish to use me for all your own by your right. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N</note>
It would not have been thought that my study and care which I undertook for your safety could be increased more in you. It is incredible how much every single day adds to my love for you. For after I began to love you, there was no time in which I did not think of you for a long time, and often have discourse about you. If at any time I meet someone familiar to you, with whom I may wish to commemorate what prudence and humanity you have, my love for you is doubled, and my benevolence toward you is increased much more than can be believed. For as often as I consider in my mind your kindnesses toward me, which are greater every day, that thing brings so much to my former love that I now love you more than my own eyes. I make, therefore, no end of loving you, nor is there anything that I think of more than that I may seem sufficiently grateful to you and to men. But your merits are so great in me, such a heap has been added to your benefits, that I do not say for referring gratitude, but not even for speaking of it, (in my judgment) can I be your equal. That, however, you will consider more according to your nature than my merit, with what affection and benevolence, not with what facilities, I am prepared with great mind and study to refer the debt of gratitude to you. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N</note>
You are too dutiful toward me, too grateful in mind, when you attribute more to my benefits toward you than I recognize should be attributed to me. For there is no time in which you have not brought greater gratitude than you have received from me before.

N.text: importance than this for me. Now, truly, it would be most shameful to neglect this, whether by reason of virtue or custom, which I have often preferred before many and great things. I will state the reason that has impelled me to this. I have persuaded myself either that there is no good in life, or that it is joined with friendship. If this were done merely by our own study, I would not admire this good so much. But when I see that all men are led and driven by nature itself so that they may live together and love themselves, there is no one who does not judge this thing divine. For not all come to friendship equally, but each one accommodates himself to others more rightly and better according as he is strong in virtue and talent. For we see that the studies of men are varied; some hope for utility in friends, others for honors. Some are excited to these things so that they may have those with whom they may take delight. A wise man, however, places the entire fruit of friendship in honor. I myself, when I had determined not to love except through good men, took care not to follow others, which I understood would please them. I was afterwards attentive in that matter so that I might take care that I was not surpassed by any of my own in duty. I will say what is true; men love so that they may please. I have never loved more than when things are going well for my friends. And if I do not wish them ill, yet that seems to me the highest point of friendship, whether when friends most expect our effort, or when they can love no one from the heart. Those who have some sadness, which can be cured by enduring, made me besides more dutiful in friendship, since I promised myself I could not fail to be loved by them, whom I loved so much, which reason, although it has sometimes deceived me, I will never be tired in the love of my own. I hope, indeed, to be able to reconcile the minds of many men to myself by these reasons. For you yourself have often exhorted me to this matter. You have been of such an opinion, that I valued it more than any other. You will see, therefore, according to your wisdom...

X.text:
if anyone says something alien about me, that you trust the old friend more than other men. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N</note>
I have never considered any danger or labor to be such that I should avoid it for the comfort of friends. Nor do I judge that there is any other thing so great (virtue excepted) that it should be preferred to friendship. I think you also know this. For you know from the conjecture of our own fate that we had the same teacher, and after we departed from school, our friendship has always remained throughout the years. For whether I was in the republic, whether in private matters, whether in the city or in the country, we have always had a great partnership of advice toward each other, just as the king of all. Yet there has been no time until now in which you might desire my duty in the mutual observance between us. I hope your fortune remains and that you suffer no unworthy insult. But where something might happen to your affairs, you would understand what kind of mind I have toward you. There is one thing that I not only ask but also beseech of you with the greatest intensity: that, since I love you most, you do not allow the envy of men to tear our friendship apart. And may the memory of our friendship, which began from boyhood, prevail with you more than the prayers of those who at this time most strive to destroy our friendship as much as they can. For I strive not only that we remain in friendship, but also that we may be judged as those who are surpassed by no other love and benevolence. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q</note>
That you remind me of our friendship, I receive great pleasure. For it helps to know the memory of our friendship, and of all the studies which we afterwards celebrated in adult age with great effort. But I dare to speak badly of you here, since I do not know what you seem to suspect about our friendship, and to doubt lest it be shaken by envious men. What others judge about this matter, I do not know enough. I, however, think that friendship which is formed from honorable duties has deeper roots...

pages.106:
or you have advanced me by some notable deed or excellent saying of yours. For such is your humanity and your supreme modesty in all things that you magnify the benefits you receive from others, while considering your own as nothing or as belonging to a stranger. As for your love, which I judged to have reached its peak, if it becomes greater every day, I am filled with the greatest pleasure and joy. For what can there be that delights me more in our friendship? I allow myself to do nothing in that matter in which there can never be too much. I allow you to make the judgment that, since you have made me so, this matter becomes one that I would persuade you is the limit to which benevolence must be held in me. Therefore, as much as you are able to believe in your soul, you will love me. This is what I have also proposed to do concerning you, and to give the greatest effort to this one thing, so that you may judge that you are loved no less by me. For I judge that I am loved and observed by you both by many other signs and by these letters. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial O marks the beginning of the text.</note> I would have always loved you dearly, but I never wished to seem obliging in your affairs more than at this very time. Since the state of your business demanded it, I decided that unless I worked with hands and feet so that your affairs might be in a better position, it would have been handled more strongly by your own people. Was I anxious? I decided that I would be so until I had placed all your affairs in safety. I convened friends, I made arrangements for you, I counted the money, I conducted your business, and finally, I led your very adversaries away from all their hope. Many things that had already been disturbed and confused were restored to their proper place and location by my labor and industry. The outcome of the case was such that all your adversaries, with broken spirits and great indignation, withdrew from the very judgment and lawsuit. The sentence which the judges rendered for you, I send to you through this courier, from whom you will learn better than from me what has been done for you in your business. I wanted this to be known, so that my spirit toward you might be better perceived. Farewell.
pages.107:
<note>A red decorative initial S marks the beginning of the text.</note> I praise and admire your solicitude and the zeal which you have used in this matter of mine. I myself use it more. It delights me. For I see nothing that could be added to this benevolence of yours toward me. Would that I could return thanks to you; would that I could eventually repay the matter. If you are pleased by this, I desire it. The memory of your benefits toward me will be a future support. For as much as I will be able to manage in my spirit, I will bring it about so that I think of nothing more often than to always do those things which I understand you want and expect. Otherwise, I will assign it to fortune and imprudence if I do not seem to satisfy you as much as I ought regarding your immortal services to me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial L marks the beginning of the text.</note> I desire that in all matters which I know to pertain to you, you may know all my labor, care, and study to be yours. And I write this to you so that you may not wish to be in debt to me for anything, as you have long since been bound to me by your merit. For you have deserved so much from me that there is nothing so great that I would not undertake and perfect for you. If there is anything in your affairs that can be done by me, you will receive it in advance. Think that there is no task so arduous that I would not consider it very light, provided I understand that some service of mine can be useful to you. Act, therefore, so that you often write to me about all your affairs, and do not permit me to be idle. For then I will think I am loved most by you when you have imposed some great task upon me that is in your affairs. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> It is customary and already ancient for you to write to me about your love. For when was there a time in which you did not value my affairs more than your own? For I truly receive great pleasure whenever I hear anything about your benevolence. And I receive no less joy from your letters than if they were to recount those things to me about which you write. I regret that your presence would bring me much pleasure. If I were not to know
pages.108:
how it happens that my thoughts seem more dull when we are with those whom we love than when we are absent from them, when we think of their studies, conversations, or advice for us ourselves. I think this happens to us because our affection has something greater and more noble than our senses can reach. It promises indeed in the soul, where they are also stored. Therefore, you will do me a very welcome favor if, as often as you have someone to whom you can entrust your letters, you always write something to me. For I seem to be with you as often as I read your letters. Nor let us permit this friendship of ours to be idle; if anything happens in which you can be of use to me with your help, or I to you with mine. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> I do not think anyone is living at this present time who is more unfortunate than I. For such great inconveniences surround me that I see no exit for myself except that which delay has brought to me. I am now so miserable that fortune already has everywhere to strike me. I have lost my country, in which I long flourished with honor and dignity. It has been said to me concerning my paternal goods. The associates whom I had in the republic were taken away by the violence of civil wars. All who had been friends have either perished or are with me in the same calamity. What more remains for me, miserable one, than to put an end to so many evils with death? Believe me, I lack not only counsel, but I even seem to myself to have become mad. I used to relieve my sickness of mind by reading or writing, but now those arts are entirely gone that might delight me. I desire your presence most of all. I hope that by grieving with me or by consoling me, you will bring me some solace in such great mourning. Nothing could happen (since you have always been of such prudence and wisdom) that some counsel would not be provided to me by you so that I might bear all things less bitterly. Since you are able to do so, strive to come here, or if occupations detain you, write something
pages.109:
to me. For I will think, when you have done so, that I have found some remedy for this sickness (if there is anything that can bring it). Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q marks the beginning of the text.</note> How much your letters have affected me with grief, so that I myself am in the greatest need of consolation. Just as our sense used to be accustomed to light things, so afterwards, when those things were disturbed and cast aside, in which your citizens had long flourished, I am not without a disturbed and serious mind, as if all things had been added to my affairs, even though what can be said to be mine is what is yours. You have me as a companion and participant in your hardships rather than as a consoler. But where there is such strength of genius and magnitude, that you are able to be consoled by letters and by my presence, in one certain and the same time I might have brought some help to each of us. But I am not strong enough by myself, nor was I ever a teacher suitable for this matter. What I can easily do, that I will accomplish. In the first days, I will come to you, and if mourning is alleviated by grieving (what kind of consolation might be foreign), I will not omit anything in diminishing your grief. Meanwhile, however, you will borrow some counsel from letters and philosophy, and you will be mindful that you are a man. For since you are considered one of the wisest of almost all men who live in this age of ours, consider how it suits the expectation of those to whom you are known, that you are overcome by grief, when you have always borne prosperous fortune modestly. I do not write this as from myself. But since the eyes of many are cast upon you, I hear men's conversation about you often. I, however, respond to that, that it is impossible for you not to feel such a calamity and loss of things. But still, you bear all things with an equal mind for your wisdom. I do not think counsel is lacking to you, nor a remedy to cure this sickness. You will therefore do what I most desire in this grief of yours. You will stand with an upright mind, and by bearing it, you will conquer the fortune that previously conquered you. If you do this, you will certainly bring back greater glory from your victory than from all
pages.110:
the things you lost. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial U marks the beginning of the text.</note> With such great inconveniences, <unclear>however</unclear>, neither hope nor counsel is provided to me. You who have the means by which you can alleviate this sickness of mine, do so; write to me. Whatever it is that can be provided by you to me in such great evils. For the power of this evil has exceeded all human studies and remedies, and my affairs have reached such a place that what they help, even if salvation itself wishes it, cannot remove me from these evils. You will attempt, however, if there is anything that you can bring to me by some help, omit nothing from those things you might suggest. To tell also in what place it is to be in that state, if grief did not prevent me, and you were such a one who would know my fortune well enough. I cannot write more to you through tears, and you, in your duty and piety, see to me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial A marks the beginning of the text.</note> You say that you can help me with some aid and counsel. Which capacity, if it were present for me, and no matter had impeded your benevolence and piety toward me, and through anything that I most desired in your hardship, could not be done by me, I will write that counsel of yours, which I often used in my own affairs. For when I was in a similar fortune, such that I could not alleviate my grief by the precepts of men, or of philosophers, or by the consolation of friends, I had departed far from the sight of the city and those things of which I was deprived. And this matter is accustomed, when with some citizen, to exacerbate the mind too much and recall the desire for a former fortune. I began, therefore, to lead a life in solicitude. I saw that nature had produced many things, content with these things, and not envying itself. I thought it most shameful for a man who was a participant of reason and divinity not to be able, by counsel and sense, to not believe he could stand among men, to not be adorned with those things, that they do not excel by nature, and further toward the wicked
pages.111:
often than they happen to the good. I truly confirmed my mind with these reasons and examples. And because I could find no remedy for my disturbances by any previous reason, I was relieved of all cares, so that I not only laid aside my mourning, but even judged myself sometimes more fortunate to have been removed from these excessive riches, as if from some impediments to living well. If you wish to judge more attentively with yourself, I do not see why you might not be about to bring some great remedy for your many evils and troubles. For I hope well for you, and if that grief of yours relaxes even a little, I judge that you will use these means all the more easily, as you surpass other men in prudence and wisdom. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial O marks the beginning of the text.</note> My affairs have been brought to such a point that I am already affected by more inconveniences of life than even my enemies dared to hope. I have no one to whom I might seek my life, except to you yourself, whom you have done by loving me dearly, so that you are worth more to me in being cherished than all other friends. There is also no one who, either by prudent wisdom or by defending with steadfastness, could be more powerful than you alone in this city of ours. You will see what the outcome of my fortune will be. My whole hope is placed in you alone. Take, therefore, this care for me, and leave nothing untried. Think, if you can remove me from these evils in which I am endlessly agitated, I will have greater gratitude to you than to my parents, from whom I received life. This matter will be of the greatest glory and honor to you, if you bring the power that has been given to you by fortune to the salvation of your friends. No one can approach closer to God than by being present to these men with counsel and help who, not by their own vice, but by the envy of men, are oppressed by calamity. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial A marks the beginning of the text.</note> I always read your letters attentively; nevertheless, even without them I was warned of your misfortune. But that I did not reach you with my service, it was not my fault, it was the time
pages.112:
I desired to anticipate your letters and to bring it about that you might feel you were being helped in these troubles of your mind by me before you heard it. But since that could not be accomplished by the malice of men, I will take care that you understand you are served by me with no less study than if I were acting for my own safety and for my own fortunes. For it would be shameful and unbearable that I, who have always defended innocent men in their causes, should seem to be without help and protection toward a man who is most attached to me by the greatest familiarity and benevolence. Therefore, be of good spirit and persuade yourself that I would rather endure all inconveniences than abandon your fortunes and the hope you have placed in me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial M marks the beginning of the text.</note> My inconveniences are greater than that anyone can heal them. I have, however, one remedy in these evils, that they are not to be endured by me for long. I hope that death will quickly free me from them. But what is there that might delight me while I live, or for what hope do I reserve myself? For if all men should come together at once, they could scarcely be of help to me. But I enjoy this consolation in these my evils, that I have lived without injury to any man. There is no one who could throw infamy at me, unless they wished to be sons of those whose habits I was most striving to avoid. Perhaps I would not have reached this place. But let the matter be as it will, I will never regret, nor do I grieve, that I have excited the minds of many men against me by doing well. If he considers, he sees that never by reason have so many fortunes gathered to feed their hatreds. I will compose myself, and as long as I must live, I will take care lest I lose virtue (if there was any in me) along with fortune. I feel that I cannot be in conflict with such evils for long. For I have reached the age where, in the prosperity of living, life cannot be much prolonged for me. I wanted you to be ignorant of my hardships, that if I ever had anything pleasant in life

I always had it for myself. Farewell.

I desired nothing less than that at the age you are, you should announce so many evils. I could never have persuaded myself that these things were about to come to you. For when I recall memory, I see that you have never harmed anyone, but you have helped many, either by your counsel or by your resources. I wonder most of all if you can bear this insult of fortune with a sufficiently steadfast mind. For who would not bear it most molestedly, that after many labors at that age, one experiences all things most turbulent, which it was fitting to be a port of all leisure and tranquility. It is indeed a subject of compassion, and I sometimes bear the indignity of this calamity of yours more bitterly than you; it would be more molested to bear if I did not recognize in you that virtue which brings you sufficient protection. But what kind of spirit you are, when I desire your life to demonstrate it, I have nevertheless known this very thing most of all from your letters. For judging rightly, you see that no evil ought to be seen as great that is about to be fleeting. If there is anything that affects you with bitterness of soul, I think it is that the evils which happen to us were not expected. Although by your wisdom I judge that there was no time in which you did not foresee that nothing in these things exists that is firm or stable. Therefore, use these remedies at this time, which you have prepared many years before. What I might bring of my leisure, I do not have, since I myself have used your help in all my affairs. I offer my fortunes, labors, and myself freely to you. And this I wish to be asked of you most of all, that you count all things among your goods.

How heavy it is for me to serve in old age almost in poverty, you can easily make a judgment from yourself and others. But this does not concern me, because you are accustomed to poverty. I, however, since I have always lived in the splendor and abundance of fortune, cannot bear that yoke. To others, the memory of prosperous things is molested; I, however, am not only tortured by this evil, but also when I am in such
