or inferior in authority or virtue. I do not doubt that you can most easily overcome the speeches and slander of these men. I know you will not allow me to be affected by this unworthy disgrace by envious men. Even if I have persuaded myself of this, you will still do a pleasing thing if you write to me about what you feel regarding this matter. Farewell.

<note>The initial 'A' is rubricated in red.</note>
Abo <note>Likely a scribal or OCR error for "Abo" or "Ab eo"</note> regarding your mind and piety toward your parents and relatives, I never thought there was anything to be doubted. But since your piety is not equally known to all men, it easily happens that some, through envy, others through error, and some through the custom of being led to criticize rather than praise, might invent or believe something about you. But even if the matter has turned out to be through no fault of your own, and even if I judge you most excellently, this must still be considered most of all. For it could happen that even good men might not think well of you if you were to use the money left by your parents poorly. Wherefore, it must be provided for again and again, that you are not either in your way of life too splendid, or in your clothes and other things too luxurious, than what either the custom of your fathers, or the dignity of your ancestors, or the wealth itself bears. For we see that men who are talked about in these matters often suffer in reputation, and beget more enemies than friends. For there are some in the city whose hearts ache that the goods which were provided for the aid of the republic, and for the benefit of friends, by the industry and labor of the best citizens, should be consumed by the rashness and intemperance of young men. I do not think such vices are in you. But I remind you of them so that you may be more honorable in your whole life, and abhor more completely all immoderate expense, and all company of those who are the ruin of all wealthy young men. As much as can be done by my study or diligence, I will have regard for your reputation, if I hear that anything unworthy is reported about you. But you must take care that, while I am praising my own service, you yourself do not diminish it in the good estimation of men. Farewell.
pages.99:
<note>A red decorative initial Q.</note> How much I cherish all my relatives from my heart, you will easily understand if you reflect on my efforts on their behalf. For his own are dear to each one, yet I do not think anyone among them whom I know lives who pursues his own with greater benevolence than I do mine. I cannot sufficiently admire what certain men can think of me, whom neither previous services to my own, nor benefits, can move, and who go astray regarding me. But words (as I see) are for them for other matters. They want to be slanderous, and they prefer to speak ill rather than well. I have, however, in this sickness and trouble of mind, one great relief: that we live in this city, in which we are both sufficiently known. But it will not be brought about that I depart from my own custom, and I will always strive to be more dutiful and more kind toward my own, so that their eyes may burst with pain. Whatever effort can be made by you on my behalf against such men, you will undertake it entirely through our old benevolence. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q.</note> That I have received great trouble from your letter, because your services toward all my relatives were sufficiently visible to all citizens. For I was never less anxious for your dignity than for my own. But since there is no one who does not judge most excellently about you, I think that one must rather take care for your dignity against those who desire to diminish your good estimation from the minds of men, rather than that you should have to doubt your own fame. If indeed it happens that you hear otherwise about you, I will not bear it dissemblingly, for I will also act so that those who had come prepared to slander another, may themselves dare much worse regarding themselves. Whatever they may plot against you, there is nothing that ought to disturb you greatly. For the opinion that good men have formed of you is stronger than to be able to be violated by such men. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial T.</note> I have cultivated friendship which is from honesty above all things, and I have endured nothing else in human affairs with greater labor. Now, truly, it would be most shameful to neglect the reason of this, whether of virtue or of custom, which I have often preferred to many great things. I will state the reason that has impelled me to this. For I have persuaded myself thus: that either there is no good in life, or that it is joined with friendship. And if it were brought about by my own study, I would not admire this good so much. But since I see that all men are led and driven by nature itself so that they may live together and love themselves, there is no one who does not judge this thing divine. For not all reach friendship equally; but as much as each one excels in virtue and talent, so much more rightly and better does he accommodate himself to them. We see indeed the varied studies of men, some hoping for utility in friends, others for honors; some are excited to those things so that they may have those with whom they may take pleasure. The wise man, however, places the whole fruit of friendship in honesty. And I, when I had determined not to love except through good men, took care not to follow others, whom I understood did not please me for themselves. I was afterwards so attentive in that matter that I took care of one thing: that I would not be surpassed by any of my own in duty. I will tell what is true: I do not love men more than when things turn out well for my friends. And if I do not wish for things to turn out badly for them, yet that seems to me the greatest time of friendship, whether when friends most expect our effort, or when they can least love from their heart. When there is any sorrow for friends, which can be cured by my acting, it made me besides more dutiful in friendship, because it was promised to me that I could not but be loved by them, whom I loved so much. And although that reason has sometimes deceived me, yet I will never be wearied in the love of my own. For I hope to be able to reconcile the minds of many men to myself by these reasons. For you yourself have also often encouraged me to this matter. You have been of such an opinion that there is none greater. You will see therefore according to your wisdom
pages.101:
<note>A red decorative initial N.</note> I have never thought any danger or labor was to be fled for the convenience of friends. Nor do I judge any other thing so great (virtue excepted) as to be preferred to friendship. I think you also know this. For from the conjecture of my own fate, you know we had the same teacher, and after we departed from the school, our friendship grew with the years. For whether I was in public affairs or in private matters, whether I was in the city or in the country, we always had, as it were, a great partnership of counsels between us. Yet there has been no time until now in which you could desire my duty in that mutual conversation. I wish that your fortune may remain and that you do not suffer any unworthy disgrace. But where anything should happen to your affairs, you would understand what kind of mind I have toward you. There is one thing which I not only ask of you in a greater measure, but also beseech, that since I love you most greatly, you do not allow the tongues of envious men to tear our friendship asunder. And may the memory of our friendship, which began from childhood, have more weight with you than the words of those who at this time most strive to destroy our friendship as much as they can. For I approve that not only should we remain in friendship, but that we should also be judged as those who are surpassed by no other love and benevolence. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q.</note> That you remind me of our friendship, I receive great pleasure. For it is helpful to know the remembrance of our friendship, and of all the studies which we afterwards celebrated in adult age with great effort. But I dare to speak ill to you, because I do not know what you seem to suspect about our friendship, and to doubt, lest it be weakened by envious men. What others judge about this matter, I do not know sufficiently. I, however, think that that friendship which is constructed from honest services has deeper roots
pages.102:
and firmer foundations than I say it ought to have. For that it is certain, and that it cannot be destroyed by any envy or by the detraction of some men. Wherefore, if you have admitted any suspicion into your mind about me, I ask that you put it aside. For since in other matters once undertaken by me I have always wished to appear constant, I have thought this especially to be guarded in friendship. You will perceive, according to your prudence and humanity, what is judged about me. But as far as it concerns me, I will say: that I have certainly cherished you more from the heart than I do today and yesterday. With such suspicions dismissed, let us do what you will write to me about; let us strive vehemently so that we may overcome all men with benevolence and love. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial V.</note> There are those who I judge should be pursued with great study. I give the greatest effort to no thing than that all who love me clearly understand that they are not less loved and cherished. What happens to you in practice, I do not know; I conceive well of you, however. But see that you do not deceive my opinion. For it would be most shameful not to love your own, by whom you are most loved. What this is, you will shortly know in that Pomponius, who is a relative to you and a close friend. If you desert him, there is no one among your own who will not be alienated from you. But I, especially, who began to love him openly, think you will not allow us to change our opinion, nor to think otherwise of you than formerly. For you will make at one time the loss of almost all your friends, such as you have not yet experienced. That this does not happen through your own fault, I ask you again and again. Farewell.

<note>A red paragraph mark.</note> The cause of Pomponius can be rightly defended; there is nothing at all that will be done in his own affair. Neither will it be unjust, nor will his relationship, nor his familiarity (which I have closely with him), be able to have more weight with me than equity and justice. But because the loss of almost all friends (as you know) must be made by
pages.103:
me if I do not comply with his conveniences, I do not think it has reached such a level of indignity that I should omit to do what is right for those whom I have acquired by virtue and honest services. I will never (if the opinion of your mind has been judged by me) be one to bear that matter. It is for you to judge. For as far as it concerns me, I judge well of you. Nor do I think that you ask anything on behalf of Pomponius, except what is good and equitable. This matter, as I am affected toward all in my mind, even without anyone’s plea, I would have granted him. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial O.</note> After I took up the toga from my father, I thought no matter should be guarded with greater study than that I should not seem to be someone who would show ingratitude toward those from whom I received many and great benefits. Do not, therefore, believe those who (so that they may remove your mind from me) try to persuade you that I will never have gratitude for your benefits. For I have ordered my life so that I could never be justly accused by those from whom I might owe anything. But why do they strive so much before you that you should have faith in them, when I desire most of all that you would discuss this matter with me present? For unless I refute them so that they repent of their deed, there is nothing for which I would wish to have faith placed in me in other matters. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N.</note> Not having been sufficiently attentive in reporting what you heard, you act in a way worthy of both your ancestors and yourself. Nor is there anyone who has yet reported anything to me about you. I do not know if you might have understood wrongly from another, or what I am ignorant of, you perhaps may know better than I. If indeed you will make a conjecture from some sign that I am now going to doubt your gratitude, I would rather hear it from you here in person than by letters. If you do this, I will not allow you to be in this error any longer. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial E.</note> That my mind toward your relatives is sufficiently known to you, I believe; yet I cannot refrain from writing to you about my duty regarding another. For I rejoice to do all things which have been done by me with pleasure. B. Appuleius, a man familiar to you, when he was driven into our port by the force of a storm, and ignorant of our laws and custom, brought goods out of his ship in the use of our merchants. Which, when they had already been seized by the publicans, the matter itself was already clearly looking toward confiscation. And there was no doubt that they would succumb. But when I was there by chance, I began to inquire. After I understood that he was one of your relatives, I immediately approached the praetor, and I alleged the ignorance of the foreign man. On that day I obtained that the confiscation be suspended. On the following day, however, I approached the judges with my friends, to whom the examination of this kind of cause had been committed by the praetor. I taught that it could not be held by our laws what was contracted through ignorance, and thus it was proved not to have been done with deceit. I had many of your friends as helpers in the cause. We therefore dismissed that man, with his goods safe, from whom you will better understand how much study I used in his danger. I write this to you willingly so that you may know that all who are friends to you are also cherished by me. Farewell.
pages.104: <note>Large red decorative initial R.</note> Your letters being given to me, B. Appuleius explained to me with diligence that you were in every duty and benevolence toward me, and that you would not have spoken to me before you had seen yourself restored to wholeness. I, however, even if I had received great pleasure from those things which he reported to me, yet a great heap of love was added to my previous benevolence, when I understood later that it was signified to me by your letters. For I love B. Appuleius greatly. For I use him most familiarly. And he is of such virtue and modesty that there is no one to whom he should not be most dear by his own merit. Think, therefore, how much I do, since no duty was missed by you for his defense. I desire something to happen, which in no way I would wish to come to your affair with your inconvenience, in which matter
pages.105:
I might be able to refer gratitude to you. I hope you will understand there is nothing undertaken by me at any time with greater study than to prove by the deed itself the gratitude which I have for you immortally. If, however, you know anything in which my work could be of help to yours, allow that to be most greatly obtained by you, so that as you used my service in the Appuleius affair recently, you may wish to use me for all your own by your same right. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N.</note> It was not to be thought that my study and care which I undertook for your safety could be accumulated more in you. It is incredible how much each day adds to my love toward you. For after I began to love you, there was no time in which I did not think long about you, and often have a conversation about you. If at any time I meet your friends, with whom I wish to mention what prudence and humanity you have, my love toward you is doubled, and my benevolence toward you is increased much more than can be believed. For as often as I consider in my mind your benefits toward me, which are greater every day, that matter brings so much to my former love that I now love you more than my own eyes. I therefore make no end of loving you, nor is there anything I think of more than how I may seem sufficiently grateful to you and to men. But so great are your merits in me, so great is the heap that has been added by your benefits, that I do not say to refer gratitude, but not even to state it (in my judgment) can I be equal to you. That, however, you will consider more according to your nature than my merit: with what affection and benevolence, not with what facilities, I am prepared with a great mind and study to refer to you the due gratitude. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N.</note> You are too dutiful toward me, with too grateful a mind, when you attribute more to my benefits toward you than I know should be attributed to me. For there is no time in which you have not brought greater gratitude than you have received from me before.

X.text:
<note>A red decorative initial N.</note> I have never thought any danger or labor was to be fled for the convenience of friends. Nor do I judge any other thing so great (virtue excepted) as to be preferred to friendship. I think you also know this. For from the conjecture of my own fate, you know we had the same teacher, and after we departed from the school, our friendship grew with the years. For whether I was in public affairs or in private matters, whether I was in the city or in the country, we always had, as it were, a great partnership of counsels between us. Yet there has been no time until now in which you could desire my duty in that mutual conversation. I wish that your fortune may remain and that you do not suffer any unworthy disgrace. But where anything should happen to your affairs, you would understand what kind of mind I have toward you. There is one thing which I not only ask of you in a greater measure, but also beseech, that since I love you most greatly, you do not allow the tongues of envious men to tear our friendship asunder. And may the memory of our friendship, which began from childhood, have more weight with you than the words of those who at this time most strive to destroy our friendship as much as they can. For I approve that not only should we remain in friendship, but that we should also be judged as those who are surpassed by no other love and benevolence. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q.</note> That you remind me of our friendship, I receive great pleasure. For it is helpful to know the remembrance of our friendship, and of all the studies which we afterwards celebrated in adult age with great effort. But I dare to speak ill to you, because I do not know what you seem to suspect about our friendship, and to doubt, lest it be weakened by envious men. What others judge about this matter, I do not know sufficiently. I, however, think that that friendship which is constructed from honest services has deeper roots

pages.106: or by any other distinguished deed of yours, or by some excellent word, you surpass me. Such is your humanity and your supreme modesty in all matters: you magnify the benefits you have received from others, and consider your own as nothing, or as something foreign. But as for your love, which in my judgment had already reached the highest point, that it should grow daily, I am filled with the greatest joy and happiness. For what can there be that pleases me more in our friendship than that you leave no way for me to act in that matter, in which nothing can ever be enough? I allow that you make that judgment, which you have made about me; that the matter is as you have persuaded yourself, that there should be no end to the benevolence in me. As much as you are able to believe in your heart, so much you will love me. And I have also proposed to do the same regarding you, and to give the greatest effort to this one thing, that you may judge yourself to be loved by me no less. For I judge that I am being cherished and observed by you vehemently, both by many other signs and by these letters. Farewell.
pages.107: <note>A red decorative initial O marks the beginning of the text.</note> I have always loved you dearly, but I have never wished as much as at this very time to appear helpful in your affairs. I thought that the state of your business demanded it. For unless I had worked with my feet and hands so that your situation might be in a better place, it would have been acted upon more forcefully by your own people. Was I anxious? Yes, I decided that I would be, until I had placed all your affairs in safety. I gathered friends; I made arrangements for you; I counted the money; I managed your affairs; and finally, I disappointed your very adversaries in all their hopes. And many things that were already disturbed and confused, I restored to their own seat and place through my labor and industry. The outcome of that cause was that all his adversaries, with broken spirits and with great indignation, yielded from that very judgment and lawsuit. The decision which the judges brought for your sake, I am sending to you by this courier, from whom you will learn better than from me what was done in your business by me. I wanted this to be known, so that my spirit toward you might be better perceived. Farewell.
pages.108:
<note>A red decorative initial S marks the beginning of the text.</note> I praise and admire the solicitude and zeal which you have used in this matter of mine. I am more delighted that you yourself use it. For I see nothing that could be added to this benevolence of yours toward me. Would that I could return gratitude to you; that I could one day repay the matter. If you are pleased with this, I would like it. The memory of your benefits toward me will be everlasting. For as much as I can be moved in my heart, so much I will strive that I may think of nothing more often than to always do those things which I understand you wish and expect. Furthermore, you will attribute it to the imprudence of Fortune if I do not seem to satisfy what is appropriate regarding your immortal services toward me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial L marks the beginning of the text.</note> In all business which I know to pertain to you, I place all my labor, care, and study. And I ask that you write to me, so that you may want nothing to be owed to you by me, which is already long since due to you by your merit. For you have deserved so much from me that there is nothing so great that I should not be willing to undertake it and complete it for you. If there is anything in your affairs that can be done by me, take it as yours in advance. Consider that there is nothing so arduous that I would not think it to be very light, provided I understand that some service of mine can be of use to you. Therefore, act so that you write to me often about all your affairs, and do not allow me to be idle. For then I will think that I am loved most by you when you have imposed some great thing that is in your affairs upon me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> That you write to me about your love is customary and already ancient. For when was there a time in which you did not make my business of more importance than your own? I truly receive great pleasure whenever I hear anything about your benevolence. And I receive no less joy from your letters than if they were to treat of these matters which you write to me about. In my business, your presence would bring me much pleasure. If I did not know
pages.109:
how it happens that my thoughts seem more obtuse when we are with those whom we love, than when we are absent from them, and we think for ourselves of their zeal for us, or their conversations, or their counsels. I think this happens to us because our affection has something greater and more noble than our senses can reach. It promises, indeed, in the mind, where they are also stored away. Therefore, you will do a thing very pleasing to me if, as often as you have someone to whom you can entrust your letters, you always write something to me. For I seem to be with you as often as I read your letters. And do not permit our friendship to be idle; if anything happens in which you can be of use to me with your work, or I to you with mine, [let me know]. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> I think no one in the present time lives who is more unfortunate than I. For such great inconveniences surround me that I see no exit, except that which delay might bring me. Now I am so miserable that Fortune has already taken away where she might wound me. I have lost my country, in which I flourished for a long time with honor and dignity. Regarding my paternal property, it has been said to me. The associates whom I had in the republic, the violence of civil wars has taken away. All who had been my friends have either perished or are with me in the same calamity. What else remains for me, a miserable man, but that I should impose an end to such evils with death? Believe me, I not only lack counsel, but I even seem to me to be mad. I used to relieve my sickness of mind by reading something or writing, but now those arts are entirely of no use that used to delight me. I desire your presence most greatly. I hope that by grieving with me, or by consoling me, you will bring me some relief in such great mourning. Nothing could happen (you who have always been of such prudence and wisdom) but that I should have some counsel from you so that I might bear everything less bitterly. Since you can do so, strive to come here, or if occupations detain you, write something
pages.110:
to me. For I will think that when you have done so, you have found some remedy for this disease (if there is any that can bring one). Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q marks the beginning of the text.</note> With how much grief your letters have afflicted me, such that I myself am in need of the greatest consolation. Just as our sense of light used to fail in affairs, so afterward, when those things were disturbed and cast aside, in which you had long flourished among your citizens, I was troubled with no less a mind and spirit, as if everything had happened in my own affairs, although what can be called more mine than what is yours? You have in me a companion and participant in your hardships rather than a consoler. But where there is such strength of genius and greatness, that you can be consoled by letters and by my company, at one and the same time you have brought some aid to both of us. Truly, I am not strong enough for this task, nor was I ever a greater master in this matter. What I can easily do, that I will perform. In the first days, I will come to you, and if mourning is lightened by grieving (which, for the kind of consolation, might be strange), I will not omit anything in diminishing your grief. Meanwhile, however, you will borrow some counsel from letters and philosophy, and you will be mindful that you are a man. For since you are held to be the most wise of almost all men who live in this age of ours, consider how it conforms to the expectation of those to whom you are known, that you should be conquered by grief, you who have always borne prosperous Fortune modestly. I do not write this as a critic, but since the eyes of many are cast upon you, I often hear conversation about you held by men. I, however, respond to that, that it is impossible that you do not feel such a great calamity and loss of affairs, but that nevertheless you bear everything with an even mind for the sake of your wisdom. Nor do I think that counsel is lacking to you, nor a remedy, to heal this sickness. You will therefore do what I most desire in this grief of yours. You will stand with an erect spirit, and by bearing it, you will conquer Fortune, which previously conquered you. If you do this, you will certainly bring back greater glory from your victory than from all
pages.111:
the things that have been lost. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial U marks the beginning of the text.</note> To such great inconveniences, <unclear>however,</unclear> this happens to me, neither hope nor counsel. You who have the means by which you can lighten this sickness of mine, do so; write to me, whatever it may be that can be brought to me by you in such great evils. For the force of this evil has exceeded all human studies and remedies, and my affairs have reached such a place that what might help, not even safety itself, even if it wished, could remove me from these evils. You will try, however, if there is anything that you can bring to me by way of some help, omit nothing from those things that sting. I would tell you what state I am in, if grief did not prevent me, and you were one who knew my fortune well enough. I cannot write more to you through tears, and you, according to your duty and piety, provide for me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial A marks the beginning of the text.</note> You say that you can help me with some aid and counsel. If this faculty were available to me, and nothing had impeded my benevolence and piety toward you, and through that which I most desired in your adversity, it cannot be done by me. I will write to you my counsel, which I have often used in my own affairs when I was in a similar fortune, that I could not lighten my grief by the precepts of men or philosophers or the consolation of friends; I withdrew far from the sight of the city and those things of which I was deprived. And this matter is accustomed to exacerbate the mind too much with some citizen, and to recall the desire for former fortune. I therefore began to live life in solicitude. I saw many things which nature had produced, satisfied with these things, nor did they envy themselves. I thought it to be most shameful for a man who was a participant in reason and divinity, not to be able to [rely] on counsel and sense, and [not] to think he could perform among men, not to be adorned with those things which neither excel by nature, nor [are] further [useful] to the wicked
pages.112:
than they happen to the good. I truly confirmed my mind with these reasons and examples. And since I could previously find no remedy for my disturbances by any reason, I was relieved of all cares, so that I not only laid down my mourning, but I even began to judge myself more happy than those who, by worldly wealth, as if by some impediments, were kept from living well. If you will be willing to judge more attentively with yourself, I do not see why you might not be about to bring some great remedy for so many evils and troubles of yours. For I hope well for you, and if this grief of yours subsides even a little, I judge that you will use these means all the more easily, in the measure that you surpass other men in wisdom and prudence. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial O marks the beginning of the text.</note> My affairs have been brought to such a point that I am now affected by more inconveniences of life than even my enemies themselves dared to hope. I have no one to whom I might seek my life but to you yourself, who, by loving me greatly, have done this: that you alone in favoring me are worth more to me than all other friends together. There is also no one who, by either practicing wisdom or defending through persistence, can do more than you alone in this city of ours. You will see what the outcome of my fortune will be. I confess that my hope is placed in you alone. Take up this care for me, and leave nothing untried. Consider if you can remove me from these evils in which I am being torn apart without end; I will have greater gratitude for you than for my parents from whom I received life. This matter will be of the greatest glory and honor to you, if you bring the power, which has been granted to you most greatly by fortune, to the safety of your friends. No one can approach closer to God than by being present to those men with counsel and aid who, not by their own vice, but by the envy of men, are oppressed by calamity. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial A marks the beginning of the text.</note> I always read your letters attentively; nevertheless, I was admonished of your misfortune even without them. That you did not reach me with your duty is not my fault, but rather the time
pages.113:
which I desired to anticipate with your letters, and to effect that you might feel that you were being helped in these troubles of your mind before you heard of it. But since that could not be achieved by the malignity of men, I will take care that you understand that you are cared for by me with no less zeal than if it were a matter of my own safety and my own fortunes. For it would be shameful and not to be borne that I, who have always defended innocent men in their causes, should allow a man who is joined to me by the greatest familiarity and benevolence to be unsupported by my protection. Therefore, be of good spirit, and persuade yourself that I will endure all inconveniences sooner than I will abandon your fortunes and the hope that you have begun to have in me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial M marks the beginning of the text.</note> My inconveniences are greater than that anyone can remedy them. I have, however, one remedy in these evils: that they are not to be endured by me for long. I hope that death will soon release me from these. But what is there that might delight me while I live, or to what hope do I reserve myself? For if all men were to join together, they could hardly be of aid to me. But I find this consolation in my evils: that I have lived without injury to any man. There is no one who can cast infamy upon me, [or say] that I wished to be the son of those whom I was striving most to be different from. Perhaps I would not have reached this place. But let the matter go as it will, I will never repent, nor do I grieve that by doing good I have excited the minds of many men against me. See, O mind, that no reason has ever provided the hatreds of those for whom so many misfortunes have been gathered for me. I will compose myself, and as long as I must live, I will take care that I do not lose virtue (if there was any in me) along with Fortune. I feel that I cannot be in conflict with such evils for long. For I have reached that age of life that, in living in prosperity, life cannot be prolonged for me much further. I wanted you to be ignorant of my hardships, so that if there was ever anything pleasant in life
pages.114:
that it had always been a gift to me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> I desired nothing less than that you should announce such great evils at that age in which you are. That these things were to come to you, I could never have persuaded myself. For when I recall to memory, you have never harmed anyone, but to many, either by your counsel or by your resources, you have been a help. I admire greatly if you can bear this contumely of Fortune with a sufficiently composed spirit. For who would not bear most molestedly that, after many labors, at that age, he should experience all the most turbulent things, which ought to be a harbor of all rest and tranquility? It is a source of compassion, and I sometimes bear the indignity of this calamity of yours more bitterly than you; [and it is] more molested to bear, if I did not recognize the virtue in you which brings you sufficient protection. For even though your life demonstrates what kind of spirit you have, I have nevertheless learned this very thing most greatly from your letters. You judge rightly that no evil ought to be seen as great that will have an end. If there is anything that affects someone with bitterness of mind, I think it is that the evils which happen to us were not expected. Although, by your wisdom, I judge that there was no time in which you did not foresee that nothing in these fluxed things exists that is firm or stable. Use, therefore, these remedies at this time, which you have prepared many years before. What of my counsel shall I bring? I have none, since I myself have used your hope in all my affairs. I offer you my fortunes, my labors, and myself freely. And I want you to be prayed to most greatly, that you count everything among your own goods.

<note>A red decorative initial Q marks the beginning of the text.</note> How grave it is for me in my old age to serve in near poverty, you can easily make a judgment from yourself and others. But it matters little to me, since you are accustomed to poverty; I, however, since I have always lived in the splendor and abundance of Fortune, cannot bear that yoke. To others, the memory of prosperous things is molesting, but I am not only tortured by this evil, but also [by] the state of [these] things.

N.text:
<note>A red decorative initial S marks the beginning of the text.</note> I praise and admire the solicitude and zeal which you have used in this matter of mine. I am more delighted that you yourself use it. For I see nothing that could be added to this benevolence of yours toward me. Would that I could return gratitude to you; that I could one day repay the matter. If you are pleased with this, I would like it. The memory of your benefits toward me will be everlasting. For as much as I can be moved in my heart, so much I will strive that I may think of nothing more often than to always do those things which I understand you wish and expect. Furthermore, you will attribute it to the imprudence of Fortune if I do not seem to satisfy what is appropriate regarding your immortal services toward me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial L marks the beginning of the text.</note> In all business which I know to pertain to you, I place all my labor, care, and study. And I ask that you write to me, so that you may want nothing to be owed to you by me, which is already long since due to you by your merit. For you have deserved so much from me that there is nothing so great that I should not be willing to undertake it and complete it for you. If there is anything in your affairs that can be done by me, take it as yours in advance. Consider that there is nothing so arduous that I would not think it to be very light, provided I understand that some service of mine can be of use to you. Therefore, act so that you write to me often about all your affairs, and do not allow me to be idle. For then I will think that I am loved most by you when you have imposed some great thing that is in your affairs upon me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> That you write to me about your love is customary and already ancient. For when was there a time in which you did not make my business of more importance than your own? I truly receive great pleasure whenever I hear anything about your benevolence. And I receive no less joy from your letters than if they were to treat of these matters which you write to me about. In my business, your presence would bring me much pleasure. If I did not know

X.text:
how it happens that my thoughts seem more obtuse when we are with those whom we love, than when we are absent from them, and we think for ourselves of their zeal for us, or their conversations, or their counsels. I think this happens to us because our affection has something greater and more noble than our senses can reach. It promises, indeed, in the mind, where they are also stored away. Therefore, you will do a thing very pleasing to me if, as often as you have someone to whom you can entrust your letters, you always write something to me. For I seem to be with you as often as I read your letters. And do not permit our friendship to be idle; if anything happens in which you can be of use to me with your work, or I to you with mine, [let me know]. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> I think no one in the present time lives who is more unfortunate than I. For such great inconveniences surround me that I see no exit, except that which delay might bring me. Now I am so miserable that Fortune has already taken away where she might wound me. I have lost my country, in which I flourished for a long time with honor and dignity. Regarding my paternal property, it has been said to me. The associates whom I had in the republic, the violence of civil wars has taken away. All who had been my friends have either perished or are with me in the same calamity. What else remains for me, a miserable man, but that I should impose an end to such evils with death? Believe me, I not only lack counsel, but I even seem to me to be mad. I used to relieve my sickness of mind by reading something or writing, but now those arts are entirely of no use that used to delight me. I desire your presence most greatly. I hope that by grieving with me, or by consoling me, you will bring me some relief in such great mourning. Nothing could happen (you who have always been of such prudence and wisdom) but that I should have some counsel from you so that I might bear everything less bitterly. Since you can do so, strive to come here, or if occupations detain you, write something

pages.98:
or inferior in authority or virtue. I do not doubt that you can most easily overcome the speeches and slander of these men. I know you will not suffer me to be affected by this unworthy insult from envious men. Even if I had already persuaded myself of this, you would still do a welcome thing if you wrote to me about what you think of this matter. Farewell.

A<note>The initial 'A' is rubricated in red.</note>
As for your attitude and piety toward your parents and relatives, I never thought it was to be doubted. But since your piety is not equally known to all men, it easily happens that some, out of envy, and others out of error, or due to a habit of finding fault where they should be praising, might invent or believe something about you. But even if the matter was brought about through some fault of yours, and even if I judge you most favorably, still this is most especially to be considered. For it could happen that even good men might not have a good opinion of you if you make poor use of the money left by your parents. Therefore, it must be looked to again and again, that you are neither too splendid in dress nor too lavish in banquets and other matters than either the custom of your forebears, or the dignity of your ancestors, or your actual means may bear. For we see that men who are in need of bread often have such speeches about them, and acquire more enemies than friends. For there are some in the city whose hearts ache that the goods which should have been for the aid of the state and the convenience of friends by the industry and labor of good citizens, should be consumed by the rashness and intemperance of young men. I do not think these vices are in you, but I mention them to you so that you may be more honorable in your whole life, and that you may abhor any immoderate expense and any society of those who are the ruin of all wealthy young men. As much as can be done by my zeal or diligence, I will have regard for your reputation if I hear anything unworthy being said about you. But do you take care that, when I have praised my own duty, you yourself do not diminish it by some poor estimation of men. Farewell.
pages.99:
QYou will easily understand how much I cherish all my relatives from my heart if you consider my efforts on their behalf. For everyone holds their own dear, and yet I do not think there is anyone among them whom I know who pursues his own with greater benevolence than I do mine. I cannot sufficiently wonder what some men can think of me, who can be moved by neither my past services to my own kin nor my kindnesses, and who wander away from me. But words, as I see, are suited by them to other matters. They wish to be quarrelsome, and prefer to speak evil rather than to speak well. I have, however, one great relief in this sorrow and annoyance: that we live in this city where we are both sufficiently known. I will not, however, be brought to depart from my own custom, and even if their eyes burst with pain, I will always be more diligent and more kind toward my own. Whatever effort can be made by you on my behalf against such men, you will undertake the whole of it through our long-standing benevolence. Farewell.

QYou have received great annoyance from my letter, although your services to all my relatives were sufficiently known to all citizens. For I was never less solicitous for your dignity than for my own. But since there is no one who does not judge most favorably of you, I think it is rather to be guarded against those who wish to lower your good estimation from the minds of men, than that you should have to doubt about your own fame. If, however, it happens that you hear something else about you, I will not bear it dissimilarly, and I will even ensure that those who come prepared to speak ill of another, themselves dare much worse regarding themselves. Whatever they might contrive against you, there is nothing that should disturb you greatly. For the opinion that good men have formed of you is stronger than to be capable of being violated by such men. Farewell.

TIf I have cultivated friendship which is from virtue, I have held nothing...
pages.100: else in human affairs as of greater importance to me. Now, however, it would be most shameful to neglect this reason of virtue or habit, which I have often preferred before many and great things. I will say what reason has compelled me to this. I have persuaded myself that either there is no good in life, or that it is joined with friendship. And if this were done through our own study, I would not admire this good so much. But since I see that all men are led and driven by nature itself so that they may live together and love themselves, there is no one who does not judge this matter divine. For not all come to friendship equally, but each one accommodates himself to others more rightly and better as he is worthier in virtue and talent. We see that the studies of men are varied; some hope for utility in friends, others for honors, and some are excited to it so that they may have those with whom they may take delight. A wise man, however, places the whole fruit of friendship in honesty. And I, when I had decided not to love except through good men, took care not to follow others, whom I understood did not please for their own sake. I was afterwards so attentive in that matter as to take care of one thing: that I would not be surpassed by any of my own in duty. I will say what is true. I love men so that they may be pleased. I never love more than while things are succeeding for my friends. And although I wish nothing but the best for them, that seems to me the highest point of friendship: either when friends most expect our help, or when they are able to love from the heart. When there is any sorrow of friends, which can be cured by my effort, that also made me more dutiful in friendship, because I promised myself that I could not be unloved by them whom I loved so much. And although I was sometimes deceived by others, I will never be tired in the love of my own. For I hope to be able to reconcile the minds of many men to myself by these reasons. For you yourself have also often encouraged me to this matter. You have valued your own opinion so much that there is none higher. You will see, therefore, according to your wisdom...
pages.101:
If anyone has said something else about me, believe your old friend rather than others. Farewell.

NI have never thought any danger or labor was to be avoided for the advantage of friends. Nor do I judge there is any other thing so great (virtue excepted) as to be preferred to friendship. I think you also know this. For you know by conjecture about my own fate that we have had the same teacher, who, after we departed from school, lived with our friendship for many years. For whether I was in public affairs or private matters, whether in the city or in the country, we always had a great partnership in our councils as well as in all other things. There has not yet, however, been any time in which you could desire my duty in that mutual conversation we have had. I wish that your fortune may remain and that you suffer no unworthy insult. But if anything should happen in your affairs, you would understand what kind of heart I have toward you. There is one thing which I not only ask of you but also beseech you, not only because I cherish you most, but so that you do not allow the friendship between us to be torn away by the words of envious men. And let the memory of our friendship, which began in childhood, prevail more with you than the prayers of those who at this time most strive to destroy our friendship as much as they can. For I approve that we not only remain in friendship, but that we be judged as those who are not surpassed by any other love and benevolence. Farewell.

QThat you remind me of our friendship, I take great pleasure. For it is helpful to know of our friendship, and of all the studies which we afterward celebrated with great effort in adult age. But I hear this evil from you, that I know not what you seem to be suspecting and doubting about our friendship, lest it be undermined by envious men. What others may judge about this matter, I do not know sufficiently. I, however, think that friendship which is concluded from honest services has deeper roots...
pages.102:
and firmer foundations. I do not say it ought to be so. But this, which is certain, is that it cannot be ruined by any envy or by the detraction of some men. Wherefore, if you have admitted any suspicion about my heart toward you, I beseech you, lay it aside. For since I wish to seem constant in other matters once undertaken by me, I have thought this most of all to be maintained in friendship. You will perceive, according to your prudence and humanity, what is judged about me. As for what pertains to me, I will say: I have certainly cherished you more from the heart than I did today or yesterday. With such suspicions dismissed, let us make an end, and as you write to me, let us strive vehemently to conquer all men with benevolence and love. Farewell.

VI consider those things to be pursued by me with great study. I do not give greater effort to anything than that all those who love me may clearly understand they are not less loved and honored. What may happen to you, I do not know. I conceive well, however, of you. But see that you do not fall short of my expectation. For it would be most shameful not to love those by whom you are most loved. What this is like, you will soon know in that matter of Pomponius, who is necessary to you and a close friend. If you abandon him, there is no one among your own who will not be alienated from you. But I, especially, who began to love him openly. I think you will not allow us to change our opinion, nor to think of you otherwise than before. For you will make, at one time, the loss of almost all your friends, which you have not yet experienced. That this may not happen by your own fault, I ask you again and again. Farewell.

The cause of Pomponius can be defended by law, for there is nothing at all that I will not do in his own affair. But neither will his necessity nor his familiarity (which is close to me with him) prevail more with me than equity and justice. But since, as you know, the loss of almost all friends is to be made by...
pages.103:
me if I do not comply with his interests, I do not think it has come to such indignity that I should omit to do what is right for those whom I have acquired by virtue and honest services. I do not know if (if the opinion of your mind is judged by me) you will be the one to endure that matter. It is for you to judge. For as far as it pertains to me, I judge well of you. Nor do I suspect that you ask anything for Pomponius except what is good and equitable. This matter, regarding how I am affected toward all, I would have performed for him even without anyone's prayer. Farewell.

OSince I took up the toga from my father, I have thought no matter to be guarded with greater study than that I should not seem to be someone who has received many and great benefits toward those who appear to be against me. Do not, therefore, believe those who (so that they may remove your mind from me) try to persuade you that I will never have gratitude for your benefits. For I have so ordered my life that I could never be justly accused by those from whom I owe anything. But why do they strive so much before you so that you may have faith in them, while I wish to discuss this matter with you personally? For unless I refute them, so that they may repent of their deed, there is nothing in other matters that I would wish for faith to be had in me. Farewell.

NI know that you have been attentive in repeating everything, and you do what is worthy of you and your ancestors. Nor is there anyone who has yet reported anything to me about you. I do not know if you have understood something bad from another, or what I am ignorant of, which you perhaps know better than I. If, however, you will make a conjecture by some sign that I am now doubting about your gratitude, I would prefer to hear it from you here in your presence rather than by letter. But if you do so, I will not allow you to be in this error any longer. Farewell.

EI believe it is sufficiently perceived by you what heart I have toward your relatives, yet I cannot help but write to you about my duty toward them...
pages.104:
for I rejoice to do everything that has been performed by me with pleasure. B. Appuleius, a man familiar to you, when he was brought to our port by the force of a storm, and was ignorant of our laws and customs, took goods from his ship in use of our merchants. When this was already intercepted by the publicans, the matter itself pointed clearly toward confiscation. And there was no doubt that they would take it for themselves. But when I happened to be there, I began to intercede. After I understood he was one of your relatives, I immediately approached the praetor and alleged the ignorance of the stranger. On that day, I obtained that the confiscation be suspended. On the following day, however, I approached the judges with my friends, to whom the cognition of this kind of case had been mandated by the praetor. I showed that it could not be punished by our laws, because it was contracted through ignorance, and thus could not be convicted as done by deceit. I had many of your friends as helpers in the case. We therefore dismissed that man with his goods safe, from whom you will understand better what study I used in his danger. I write this to you willingly so that you know that all who are friends to you are also cherished by me. Farewell.

RWhen your letter was given to me, B. Appuleius diligently explained to me that you were in every service and benevolence toward him, and that you did not speak before you saw him restored to integrity. As for me, even if I received the greatest pleasure from these things which he reported to me, still a great accumulation of love was added to the former benevolence, when I understood the same was later signified to me by your letters. For I love B. Appuleius greatly. For I am very familiar with him. And he is of such virtue and modesty that there is no one to whom he should not be most dear by his own merit. Think, therefore, how much I do, since no service has been omitted by you for his defense. I desire that something might happen which I would not want to come into your interest in any way with your disadvantage, in which matter...
pages.105:
I might be able to return gratitude to you. I hope you will understand there is nothing undertaken by me at any time with greater study than to prove by the deed itself the gratitude which I hold for you as immortal. If you recognize anything in which my work could be of use to your friends, allow that to be most especially obtained from you, so that as you used service for Appuleius recently, you may wish to use me for all your own by the same right. Farewell.

NI would not have thought that my study and the care which I undertook for your salvation could be accumulated more in you. It is incredible how each day adds to my love for you. For after I began to love you, there was no time in which I did not think about you, and often have conversation about you. If at any time I meet with those familiar to you, among whom I wish to mention how much prudence and humanity you have, my love for you doubles, and my benevolence toward you grows far more than can be believed. For as often as I consider in my heart my benefits toward you, which are greater every day, that matter brings so much to my former love that I now love you more than my own eyes. I therefore make no end to loving you, nor is there anything I think of more than that I may seem sufficiently grateful for you and to men. But your merits in me are so great, and such an accumulation of your benefits has been added, that I do not say for returning gratitude, but not even for speaking about it (in my judgment) could I be equal to you. But you will consider, more according to your nature than my merit, with what affection and benevolence, not by what means, I am prepared with a great heart and study to return the gratitude owed to you. Farewell.

NYou are too dutiful toward me, and of too grateful a heart, when you attribute more to my benefits toward you than I recognize as to be attributed to me in reality. For there is no time in which you have not brought greater gratitude than you have received from me before.
