X.text:
If anyone has said something else about me, believe your old friend rather than others. Farewell.

NI have never thought any danger or labor was to be avoided for the advantage of friends. Nor do I judge there is any other thing so great (virtue excepted) as to be preferred to friendship. I think you also know this. For you know by conjecture about my own fate that we have had the same teacher, who, after we departed from school, lived with our friendship for many years. For whether I was in public affairs or private matters, whether in the city or in the country, we always had a great partnership in our councils as well as in all other things. There has not yet, however, been any time in which you could desire my duty in that mutual conversation we have had. I wish that your fortune may remain and that you suffer no unworthy insult. But if anything should happen in your affairs, you would understand what kind of heart I have toward you. There is one thing which I not only ask of you but also beseech you, not only because I cherish you most, but so that you do not allow the friendship between us to be torn away by the words of envious men. And let the memory of our friendship, which began in childhood, prevail more with you than the prayers of those who at this time most strive to destroy our friendship as much as they can. For I approve that we not only remain in friendship, but that we be judged as those who are not surpassed by any other love and benevolence. Farewell.

QThat you remind me of our friendship, I take great pleasure. For it is helpful to know of our friendship, and of all the studies which we afterward celebrated with great effort in adult age. But I hear this evil from you, that I know not what you seem to be suspecting and doubting about our friendship, lest it be undermined by envious men. What others may judge about this matter, I do not know sufficiently. I, however, think that friendship which is concluded from honest services has deeper roots...

pages.106:
or that you have achieved anything by means of a remarkable deed or an outstanding statement of your own. For such is your humanity and your supreme modesty in all matters, that you magnify the benefits you have received from others while considering your own to be nothing or even foreign. But as for your love, which in my judgment had already reached its summit, that it should grow greater every day is a source of the greatest joy and pleasure to me. For what indeed can there be that delights me more in our friendship than that I find no way to do enough in that matter for which there can never be too much? I allow you to make the judgment that you have made of me, provided the matter is that you have persuaded yourself that there should be no limit to the benevolence I hold for you. So, as much as you are able to believe in your heart, you will love me. This is what I have also proposed to do regarding you, and to devote the greatest effort to this one thing, that you may judge yourself to be loved no less by me. For I judge that you will perceive you are vehemently loved and esteemed by me, both by many other signs and by these letters. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial O marks the beginning of the text.</note> I have always loved you very much, but I have never desired more than at this very time to appear helpful in your affairs. This was required by the state of your business. For unless I had labored with hands and feet so that your affairs might be in a better position, it would have been dealt with more forcefully regarding your property. Was I ever anxious? I resolved that you should not be, until I had settled all your matters in safety. I convened friends, I made arrangements on your behalf, I counted money, I managed your affairs, and finally, I disappointed your very adversaries in all their hopes. And many things that were already disturbed and confused, I restored to their own seat and place by my labor and industry. And what was the outcome of the cause? It resulted in all his adversaries withdrawing from the very judgment and lawsuit, with broken spirit and great indignation. The decision, however, which the judges rendered for you, I am sending to you by this courier; from him you will learn better than from me how your business has been managed by me. I wanted this to be known, so that my spirit toward you might be better perceived. Farewell.
pages.107:
<note>A red decorative initial S marks the beginning of the text.</note> I praise and admire your solicitude and the zeal which you have used in my behalf. I would that I myself could use <unclear>it</unclear> more. It delights me. For I see nothing that could be added to this your benevolence toward me. If I could return thanks, I have thanks for you; if you would ever return it in kind, I would like that. The memory of your benefits toward me will be my future guide; for as much as I shall be able to do in my heart, I will effect it so that I think of no thing more often than that I should always do what I understand you to wish and expect. Furthermore, you will assign to <term>Fortuna</term> <gloss>Fortune/Fate</gloss> and imprudence if I do not seem to satisfy as much as I ought your immortal services to me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial L marks the beginning of the text.</note> In all business which I know pertains to you, I give all my labor, care, and study to the highest degree. And this is written by me so that you may know that nothing is owed by you, as by your merit it has long since been given. For you have deserved so much of me that there is nothing so great that I would not undertake and complete for your sake. If there is anything in your affairs that can be done by me, you will receive it without any request. Consider that there is nothing so arduous that I would not think it to be very light, provided I understand that some service of mine can be useful to you. Act, therefore, so that you write to me often about your affairs, and do not allow me to be idle; for then I will think that I am loved by you most, when you have often imposed upon me some great task that is in your affairs. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> Your writing to me about your love is customary, and already ancient. For when has there been a time in which you did not value my affairs more than your own? For I truly take pleasure whenever I hear something of your benevolence. Nor do I take less pleasure from your letters than if they were to recount those things about which you write to me. I deny that which your presence would bring me much pleasure, if I did not know
pages.108:
how it happens that my thoughts seem more dull when we are with those we love than when we are absent from them, while we ourselves think of their zeal, conversations, or counsels toward us. I think this happens to us because our affection has something greater and more noble than our senses can attain. It promises, indeed, in the mind, where they are also stored. You will do a thing very pleasing to me if, as often as you have someone to whom you can entrust your letters, you write something to me. For I seem to be with you as often as I read your letters. Nor do you allow our friendship to be idle; if anything happens in which you can be helped by my work, or I by yours, do so. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> I think there is no one living at the present time who is more unfortunate than I alone. For such great inconveniences surround me that I see no outcome for them unless that which time has brought me. I am now so miserable that Fortune already has everywhere where she might strike me. I have lost my country, in which I long flourished with honor and dignity. My patrimonial goods have been taken from me. The partners whom I had in the republic, the violence of civil wars has taken away. All who had been friends have either perished or are with me in the same calamity. What more remains for my miserable self than that I should impose an end to so many evils through death? Believe me, I not only lack counsel, but I even seem to myself to have become mad. I used to relieve my sickness of mind by reading or writing, but now those arts are entirely gone which might delight me. I desire your presence greatly. I hope that by grieving with me, or by consoling me, you will bring some solace to me in such great sorrow. Nothing could happen (you who have always been of such prudence and wisdom) but that there would be some counsel from you so that I might bear all things less bitterly. Since you are able, strive so that you may come here, or if occupations detain you, something
pages.109:
write to me. For I will think that when you have done so, you have found some remedy for this sickness (if there is any that can bring one). Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q marks the beginning of the text.</note> How much your letters have affected me with sorrow, that I myself am in need of the greatest consolation! Just as our sense was accustomed to happen in light matters, so after those things were disturbed and cast down, by which you and your fellow citizens had flourished for a long time, I am moved with no less disturbed spirit, as if it had happened to my own affairs, for what can be called more mine than what is yours? You have me more as a companion and participant in your miseries than as a consoler. But where there is such force of character and magnitude, that you are able to be consoled by letters and by my pleading, at one and the same time you have brought some aid to both of us. But I am not powerful enough by myself, nor have I ever been a more suitable master for this matter. What I can easily do, I will accomplish. In the first days I will come to you, and if sorrow is alleviated by grieving (which is foreign to the genre of consolation), I will not omit anything in diminishing your sorrow. Meanwhile, you will borrow some counsel from letters and philosophy, and you will be mindful that you are a man. For since you are held to be the most wise of almost all men who live in this our age, think how it is consistent with the expectation of those to whom you are known that you are overcome by sorrow, you who have always borne prosperous Fortune modestly. I do not write this as from me, but since the eyes of many are cast upon you, I often hear men's conversation held about you. I, indeed, respond to that, that it is impossible that you not feel such great calamity and loss of things, but yet that you bear all things with an even mind for the sake of your wisdom. Nor do I think that counsel or remedy is lacking to you, with which you might heal this sickness. You will therefore do what I most desire in this your sorrow. You will stand with an erect spirit, and by bearing it, you will conquer Fortune which previously conquered you. If you do this, you will surely bring back greater glory from your victory than from all
pages.110:
things from which you have suffered loss. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial U marks the beginning of the text.</note> With such great inconveniences <unclear>nevertheless</unclear> it happens to me that I have neither hope nor counsel. You who have that by which you can alleviate this my sickness, do it, write to me, whatever it is that can be brought to me by you in such great evils. For the force of this evil has exceeded all human studies and remedies, and my affairs have reached such a place that what might help, not even safety itself, if it wished, could remove me from these evils. You will attempt, however, if there is anything that you can bring to me by some work, you will omit nothing of those things that are urging. To recount, also, in what place I am in my state, would not be necessary, for sorrow hinders me, and you are one who knows my fortune sufficiently. But I cannot write more to you through tears, and you will act according to your duty and piety toward me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial A marks the beginning of the text.</note> That you are able to help me by some aid and counsel, this ability if it were present to me, and no thing had hindered my benevolence and piety toward you, and through that which I desired most in your adversity, could be done by me, I will write that counsel of mine which I have often used in my own affairs. For when I had been in a similar fortune, that I could not alleviate my sorrow either by the precepts of men or of philosophers, or by the consolation of friends, I had departed far from the sight of the city and those things of which I was deprived. And this thing is accustomed to exacerbate the mind too much with some citizen, and to recall the desire for former fortune. I therefore began to lead a life in solicitude. I saw many things which nature had produced, contented with these things, nor envying itself. I thought it to be most base for a man who was a participant in reason and divinity not to be able to possess counsel and sense, and that it would be nefarious or not to think that one could excel among men, not to be adorned with these things, I, who neither excel by nature, and to the wicked further
pages.111:
mostly, than happen to the good. I confirmed my spirit with these reasons and examples. And because I could previously find no remedy for my disturbances, I was so relieved of all cares that I not only began to put aside my sorrow, but even to judge myself at times more fortunate than those who, by former riches, were as if by some impediments exempted from living well. If you will wish to judge more attentively with yourself, I do not see why you might not be about to bring some great remedy for your many evils and troubles. For I have good hope of you, and if that sorrow of yours relaxes even a little, I judge that you will use these means the more easily, the more you surpass other men in prudence and wisdom. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial O marks the beginning of the text.</note> My affairs have been brought to such a point that I am already affected by more inconveniences of life than even my enemies themselves dared to hope. I have no one to whom I might seek for life than to you yourself, whom by loving very much you have made it so that you alone have more weight with me in healing than all other friends combined. I even believe that you, whether by exercising prudence or defending by constancy, possess more than one alone in this our city. You will see what the outcome of my fortune will be. My hope is placed in you alone. Take up, therefore, this care for me, and leave nothing unattempted. Consider if you can remove me from these evils in which I am endlessly tortured, I will have greater gratitude to you than to my parents from whom I received life. And that matter will be of greatest glory and honor to you if you bring the power which has been granted to you by Fortune to the safety of your friends. No one can approach closer to God than by being present with counsel and aid to those men who, not by their own vice, but by the envy of men, are pushed into calamity. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial A marks the beginning of the text.</note> I always read your letters attentively; nevertheless, I was admonished of your misfortune even without them. That I did not reach you with my duty is not my fault, but was of the time
pages.112:
I desired to anticipate your letters and to cause you to feel that you were being helped in these troubles of your mind before you heard it. But since that could not be achieved by the malice of men, I will take care that you understand that you are supported by me with no less zeal than if it were a matter of my own safety and my own fortunes. For it would be base and intolerable that I, who have always appeared to defend innocent men in their causes, should leave a man who is joined to me by supreme familiarity and benevolence, in need of my protection and my guardianship. Therefore, be of good spirit, and persuade yourself that I would rather endure all inconveniences than abandon your fortunes and the hope which you have conceived in me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial M marks the beginning of the text.</note> My inconveniences are greater than that anyone can heal them. I have, however, one remedy in these evils: that they are not to be endured by me for long. I hope that death will soon release me from these. But what is there that might delight me while living, or for what hope do I reserve myself? For if all men should attempt it together, there could scarcely be aid for me. But I have this consolation in these my evils: that I have lived without injury to any man. There is no one who could cast infamy upon me, other than that I wished to be a son to those whom I was most eager to be different from. Perhaps I would not have reached this place. But let the matter go as it will, I will never repent, nor do I grieve, that by doing well I have excited the minds of many men against me. May God see that never by reason have so many misfortunes fed their hatreds against me. I will compose myself, and as long as I must live, I will take care that I do not lose Virtue (if there was any in me) along with Fortune. I feel that I cannot be in conflict with such evils for long. For I have arrived at that age so that, in living in prosperity, life cannot be prolonged much for me. I wanted you to be ignorant of my miseries, that if anything was ever pleasant in life
pages.113:
<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note>
<note>A red decorative initial Q marks the beginning of the text.</note>
I have had, it has always been yours for me. Farewell.

I desired nothing less than that at that age in which you are, you would recount so many evils. I could never have persuaded myself that these things were about to come to you. For when I recall to memory that you have never harmed anyone, but have helped many, either by your counsel or by your resources, I admire most if you can bear this contumely of fortune with a sufficiently composed spirit. For who would not bear most molestedly that after many labors, at that age, one experiences all the most turbulent things, which it was fitting should be a port of all leisure and tranquility? It is a great compassion, and I sometimes bear the indignity of this your calamity more bitterly than you; I would bear it more molestedly if I did not recognize in you that virtue which brings you sufficient protection. For even though your life demonstrates what kind of spirit you have, yet I have learned this very thing most from your letters. For you judge rightly that no evil ought to appear great which is about to be good. If there is anything that might bring bitterness to anyone's spirit, I think it is that the evils which happen to us were not expected. Although by your wisdom I judge that there was no time in which you did not foresee that nothing in these fleeting things is firm or stable. You will use, therefore, these remedies at this time which you have practiced for many years. What of my own aid I might bring, I do not have, since I myself have used your hope in all my affairs. I offer my fortunes, labors, and myself freely to you. And this I want you to be most begged, that you count all things among your own goods.

How heavy it is for me to serve in near poverty in old age, you can easily make a judgment from yourself and others. But it matters little to me, since you are accustomed to poverty; I, however, since I have always lived in the splendor and abundance of fortune, cannot endure that yoke. To others, the memory of prosperous things is molesting; I, however, am not only tortured by this evil, but even when in such a condition

N.text:
how it happens that my thoughts seem more dull when we are with those we love than when we are absent from them, while we ourselves think of their zeal, conversations, or counsels toward us. I think this happens to us because our affection has something greater and more noble than our senses can attain. It promises, indeed, in the mind, where they are also stored. You will do a thing very pleasing to me if, as often as you have someone to whom you can entrust your letters, you write something to me. For I seem to be with you as often as I read your letters. Nor do you allow our friendship to be idle; if anything happens in which you can be helped by my work, or I by yours, do so. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> I think there is no one living at the present time who is more unfortunate than I alone. For such great inconveniences surround me that I see no outcome for them unless that which time has brought me. I am now so miserable that Fortune already has everywhere where she might strike me. I have lost my country, in which I long flourished with honor and dignity. My patrimonial goods have been taken from me. The partners whom I had in the republic, the violence of civil wars has taken away. All who had been friends have either perished or are with me in the same calamity. What more remains for my miserable self than that I should impose an end to so many evils through death? Believe me, I not only lack counsel, but I even seem to myself to have become mad. I used to relieve my sickness of mind by reading or writing, but now those arts are entirely gone which might delight me. I desire your presence greatly. I hope that by grieving with me, or by consoling me, you will bring some solace to me in such great sorrow. Nothing could happen (you who have always been of such prudence and wisdom) but that there would be some counsel from you so that I might bear all things less bitterly. Since you are able, strive so that you may come here, or if occupations detain you, something

X.text:
write to me. For I will think that when you have done so, you have found some remedy for this sickness (if there is any that can bring one). Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q marks the beginning of the text.</note> How much your letters have affected me with sorrow, that I myself am in need of the greatest consolation! Just as our sense was accustomed to happen in light matters, so after those things were disturbed and cast down, by which you and your fellow citizens had flourished for a long time, I am moved with no less disturbed spirit, as if it had happened to my own affairs, for what can be called more mine than what is yours? You will stand with an erect spirit, and by bearing it, you will conquer Fortune which previously conquered you. If you do this, you will surely bring back greater glory from your victory than from all

pages.114:
<note>Large red decorative initial 'O'</note>
...you will never find them experienced. Therefore, I can have less patience. No one was born in such misery that they have lived happily, I do not remember. See what inconveniences surround me. Wealth, which I once had, used to be supplied abundantly to me by all my relatives and friends. Now I am forced to seek protection from others. In the sight and before the very eyes of men, I used to walk with great dignity (as you know). Now I cannot bear the gaze of my fellow citizens. I do not believe they are my friends, whom I once entertained splendidly; recently, because of my poverty and need, I do not dare look at them. I am ashamed to confess my calamity to them. To beg among those to whom I myself was accustomed to give much, I blush too much. And since my mind is often seeking unknown lands, where I might hide myself among strangers. And certainly, if there is no other state for my affairs, I shall soon do that. But you, who have considered all my fortune shared with you, if you have any counsel, help me. Farewell.

<note>Large red decorative initial 'O'</note>
Ovid, <note>the author refers to the poet Ovid, who wrote of his exile</note> of your son, I have not enough. To whom, by the duration of my evils, it does not suffice, nor do I seem to be myself. Poverty (as you write to me) is therefore grievous to you, because you are not accustomed to lack. That, however, is too grievous to me, that I have lost that hope which, while the wound was fresh, promised an end to my evils quickly. You, however, are still in that hope from which I have already fallen. But when you say you are more wretched than evils, I will easily concede that, provided you do not deny that I am pressed by a much greater poverty than I can bear. If the society of my misery can alleviate you, you have enough protection. Although I have never approved of the opinion of those who say that evils are less pressing when they have many companions. To me, my evils seem much smaller if I have no companion. But this keeps me in a very bad state, that my friend cannot help me. What you are about to do, you will learn better from those who are in the same state, from a man whom fortune, when it took away his wealth...
pages.115:
at the same time took away his counsel. They can write to you, or what you should attempt by yourself, or from whom you should depart. Farewell.

<note>Red decorative initial 'Q'</note>
In what state I have been, or in what I am placed, I do not think you are ignorant. But it disturbs me most that I have neither mind nor counsel with which I might help myself. For I was not instructed by nature to be able to dissimulate my pain, nor was I educated under these precepts to be able to endure my poverty bravely. You know how softly I was nurtured by my parents. I could never have hoped that I would reach this indignity, to fall from those riches which, gained by great virtue, would have been of use to all good citizens. My counsels, fortune has deceived, and it has dashed my most flourishing state, in which I lived happily for a long time, from what I expected. For I believed that there would be some end to these adversities, and (as is said in the common proverb) that time takes away sickness from men. But I find this to be false. For in the anger of fortune, it always recrudesces, and the longer I am conflicted with these inconveniences and molestations, the worse I see myself to be. Shame, however, stands in my way above all. For if by chance I showed myself to my friends, and confessed my need, much help would come from them. Such confusion holds my mind that I would rather prefer to perish in need than to uncover my poverty. You know how hard it is for a man not ignoble, and who is of noble mind, to supplicate another. I could scarcely have been induced to send this letter to you, who are most familiar to me. But your faith and benevolence have dissolved all my hesitation. You, because of our friendship, will see again and again if there is anything in which you can help me among our friends. For I am prohibited by excessive shyness from doing that. Farewell.
pages.116:
<note>Decorative red initial 'L'</note>
I recently read the letter sent to me by you, from which I truly received great perturbation. But I am angry with you that you wrote to me late about your extreme need. For I judge that if this had been written to me in a timely manner, I would have given effort to our friends so that your poverty would not be so grievous and molesting to you. <note>Decorative red paragraph mark</note> (As I see, and as you write to me) shame was an impediment to you, and it is a vice of all nobility, which is no less than that which is its own, to supplicate for need to another, rather than to lack. You will blame yourself if, with friends unaware, you have been suffering this molestation longer than you ought. What impends, I will take care of, so that in the future you will no longer be in these inconveniences in which you have been so far. And therefore, proceed with such modesty that neither will any shyness hurt you, nor will negligence hurt your friends. I send you a small amount of money, until it will be provided better by me and our friends. Do not, I ask, despair of your friends. I (to speak of myself) promise that in no way (while I am in abundance) will I allow you to labor with any lack of familiar things. All who loved you for yourself, I judge, know this of you. Farewell.

<note>Decorative red initial 'A'</note>
That I am reduced to need (which I see happens to many), I bear my fortune with a mind somewhat more brave. But since all my studies, by doing well to many, have collapsed, I cannot be satisfied enough. I could never bring my mind to be treated badly by those to whom I have always been frugal and liberal. You know well the benefits and services our citizens have exacted from me. How grateful they have been towards me, time has taught me very much. For when the men whom I had made my friends for my own safety turned against me, and had suborned judges, and had instructed false witnesses for me, who defended my right? Or who wished to protect my dignity? But deservedly, I feel that this happens, so that I experience those to be ungrateful, in whom...
pages.117:
in loving them, there was no gratitude toward me. I know and I understand clearly, what is in the old proverb, that all who fall into a trap for the sake of others, absolve themselves at their own risk. But if the matter returned to the beginning, I would certainly do what I would regret at this time. Meanwhile, I suffer pain. But this is nothing to them. I wrote this to you, not that I expect your counsel and protection in a desperate matter, but because I seem to alleviate my pain when I speak with you about my inconveniences. Farewell.

<note>Large red decorative initial 'N'</note>
You do not write to me about a new thing, nor one unknown to me. For how often have I endured such indignity of fortune, and I have judged by myself and through other citizens and guests and eminent men, for the sake of the good and the fair. Although this our calamity is nothing compared to yours, yet it happens (I know not how) that evils which are customary in the city press us less. I would rather you borrow help for this perturbation from your wisdom than from vulgar custom. For I know that this will happen, that no thing will alleviate your sickness more than that nothing of these things happened to you by your merit. And your opinion, in the way you are, will change, if you consider the matter more than the perturbation which is still fresh. To this, in a desperate matter, you do not write to me for the sake of protection or counsel, but because it helps you to talk to me about your inconveniences. You do what is customary for friends. I am accustomed to doing the same, knowing my mind is dissolved. I seem to have laid aside a greater part of my molestations when I opened all my perturbation to my friends. I rejoice greatly at this, and I give you thanks that you chose me from many to whom you might unburden your cares. For you signify with many signs, you also indicate by this, that I am greatly loved by you. The rest which pertains to your consolation, you yourself will better (as I hope) provide for by your virtue than by my letters. Farewell.
pages.118:
<note>Red decorative initial 'N'</note>
I would hope for no end or protection for my need if it were not so hard in this my fortune, which I must bear with a great, unshocked mind. But since no hope holds me at all, what is it that I desire to remain longer in life? I was accustomed to counting my years from my birthday often so that I might understand how much time remained for me according to nature. Then I was most desirous of living, because then there was no reason to accuse life. Now, however, no life seems to be granted. Others fear diseases and death more than becomes a wise man. One weeps in distress, and they desire to escape from shipwreck with lost things. If a pointed weapon is moved to the throat, he begs miserably that one might have mercy on his life. I, however, whom these things horrify, now begin to desire it. And nothing is known to me to be a greater molestation than that I be extinguished quickly. But why do I write this to you, when you, by grieving with me, cannot help me? And in this one thing I am more miserable, that I see you are also miserable. But you love me, and this brings no small consolation to me in these molestations. But before that pain which afflicts you, I also grieve for you as part of my pain. But because of your modesty (which is supreme), you will bear my sickness bravely. Farewell.

<note>Red decorative initial 'Q'</note>
What I should write to you, I do not know, because I am in such a perturbed mind that I have neither reason nor counsel in me. For he can ill advise another who himself is in great need of counsel. That I can easily offer you, this I promise: to grieve with you equally, and to accuse fortune, which adds our adverse affairs to the good. By these remedies, if they are to be called remedies, I can help you, which render the sick mind incurable. I would rather you return to your virtue than use the example of a man of no mind, so that I can borrow from you, who are wiser, the remedy which I see in myself to be none. For no one today lives who could more easily treat this sickness of mine, which has already been from my youth...
pages.119:
<note>Red decorative initial 'N'</note>
<note>Red decorative initial 'A'</note>
be cured of such shame. Which if you do, you will have cured two at once with one and the same remedy. Farewell.

You do not believe I am of sound mind, when I understand that my fortunes are deserted by all friends. This matter so disturbs me that I seem to myself to be changed. I did not expect that I, who helped them by my office, would now be deserted by all of them. But these are the arts of our citizens, when our affairs are prosperous, to promise everything voluntarily, to compete in words about supreme benevolence, about faith, about constancy, with those who truly love us. If, however, they see that our affairs are changed, by reason of their own fortunes, and of their children, rather than of friends, they say it is human. They think nothing of old offices, nothing of accepted benefits. And whom they could protect without danger, they easily allow themselves to be deserted. These things can admonish you, if you are prudent, not to acquire such friends to your own inconvenience (while your affairs are still prosperous). No one can teach you better what should be guarded against at this time than I, who have been made prudent at my own risk. Farewell.

I see that I am warned by the inconveniences of others, and by yours, since you have always loved me greatly. But after this matter is as it is (which I least wished), that you have been deserted by your friends whom you have often defended, I will be more cautious in my affairs. Nor will I have greater regard for friends than for my own conveniences. But if men were in that integrity of life and constancy that they were once, I judge no inconveniences would be to be avoided for the sake of friends. Now, however, since we follow utility, or some pleasure, more than honesty in friendship, everything seems to me to be referred to the times in which I am. That, however, I will guard against, that no friend surpasses me in his benevolence or office. And if it happens to me that I merit in some way...
pages.120:
to understand I am loved, I will make no measure in my offices, or in my love for him. But so that you do not judge that you are deserted by all, I (whom perhaps you did not have in the number of friends) promise you my effort. And (which they did not neglect without wickedness) I am prepared to undertake your defense. You, however, will admonish me of what help you have need, and I will lack neither money nor counsel for you. Farewell.

The happy end of the Letters of Gasparino.

<summary>This page concludes the collection of letters, emphasizing the necessity of loyalty and the exchange of mutual aid in times of fortune's instability.</summary>

pages.114:
<note>A large red decorative initial O begins the text.</note>
You will never experience conveniences. I cannot have less patience for that. No one is born into this world without having lived happily at some point. Do not remind me. See what inconveniences surround me. Wealth, which I once had in abundance for all my family and friends, now forces me to seek support from others. In the presence and before the very eyes of men, I used to go about with great dignity, as you know; now I cannot bear the sight of my own fellow citizens. I do not believe I am the same person. My guests, whom I once received with splendor, I now almost dare not look upon due to my poverty and want. I am ashamed to confess my calamity to them, and I blush far too much to beg from those to whom I myself used to give much. And often my mind longs to seek unknown lands where I might hide myself among strangers. And certainly, since my affairs are in no other state, I shall do this shortly. But you, who have always considered all my fortune to be shared with you, if you have any counsel, help me. Farewell.

That, however, is much more distressing to me: that I have lost that hope which, while the wound was fresh, promised an end to my evils. You, however, are still in that hope from which I have already fallen. But where you say you are more miserable than I am in my evils, I can easily concede this, provided you do not deny that I am pressed by a far greater poverty than I can bear. If the companionship of my misery can relieve you, you have sufficient protection, though I have never approved the opinion of those who say that evils are less pressing when one has many companions in them. To me, my evils seem much less if I have no companion. But this pains me greatly: that my friends cannot help me. You will learn better what you are to do from those who are in the same plight. For when Fortune took away wealth from a man, it
pages.115:
at the same time took away his judgment. They can write to you about what must be attempted by you, and from whom you should depart. Farewell.

For I believed that there would eventually be an end to these adversities and, as is said in the old proverb, that time removes sickness from men. But I find this to be false. For the anger of Fortune is always renewed, and the longer I am afflicted by these inconveniences and troubles, the more I feel myself deteriorating. Shame, above all, stands in my way. But your faith and benevolence have dispelled all my hesitation. You, because of our friendship, will see again and again if there is anything in which you can help me among our friends. For I judge that if this had been written to me in time, I would have given my effort to our friends so that your poverty would not be so grievous and troublesome to you. <note>Decorative red paragraph mark</note> As I see, and as you write to me, shame was a hindrance to you, and that is a vice of all nobility, that one is no less ashamed to beg for what is one's own, due to poverty, than to be in need. You will blame yourself if, with friends unaware, you have been enduring this trouble for longer than was fitting. What is pressing, I will take care of, so that in the future you will no longer be in these inconveniences in which you have been until now, and that you will proceed with such modesty that neither will any shyness hurt you, nor will the negligence of friends. I am sending you a small amount of money until better provision is made by me and our friends. Do not, I ask, despair of your friends. I, to speak of myself, promise that under no circumstances—as I have plenty—will I allow you to labor under any lack of familiar things. I judge that all those who loved you for your own sake know this about you. Farewell.

<note>Decorative red initial A.</note>
Being reduced to poverty (which I see happens to many), I have been bearing my fortune with a somewhat broken spirit. But since all my studies, which were done by doing good to many, have fallen into ruin, I cannot be sufficiently satisfied. I could never bring my mind to be treated badly by those for whom I was always frugal and liberal. You know well enough what benefits and services our citizens have received from me. How grateful they have been to me, time itself has taught. For when men, whom I had made my friends for my own well-being, conspired against me, and had suborned judges and instructed false witnesses against me, who defended my rights? Or who wished to protect my dignity? But I deservedly feel that this happens, so that I experience those to be ungrateful, in whom
pages.117:
there was no thought for me in loving them. For I know and understand that it is true, which is in the old proverb, that all who fall into a trap for the sake of others, absolve themselves at their own risk. And if the matter were to return to its original state, I would certainly regret having done this. Meanwhile, I am suffering the penalty. But this is nothing to them. I wrote this to you, not so that in a desperate matter I expect your counsel and support, but because I seem to relieve my pain when I speak with you about my inconveniences. Farewell.

<note>Large red decorative initial N.</note>
You do not write to me of a new matter, nor one unknown to me. For how often have I, thinking of the indignity of such fortune, endured it myself, and observed other citizens and guests, and excellent men, having suffered for the sake of the good and the just. Although this calamity of ours is nothing compared to yours, yet it happens (I know not how) that evils which are common in the city oppress us less. I would rather that you borrowed help for this perturbation from your own wisdom than from common custom. For I know that nothing will alleviate your sadness more than the fact that none of these things happened to you by your own desert. And you will change your opinion far from the way you are in, if you take into account more of your own virtues than of the perturbation which is still fresh. In this desperate matter, do not write to me for the sake of support or counsel, but because it helps you to speak with me about your inconveniences. You do as I, being accustomed to doing, knowing that I am relieved in my mind. I seem to myself to have laid aside the greater part of my troubles when I opened all my perturbation to my friends. I rejoice in this greatly, and I give thanks to you that you chose me from many to whom you would entrust your cares. By these many signs, and also by this one, I judge that I am greatly loved by you. The rest which pertains to your consolation, you yourself will better foresee, I hope, by your own virtue than by my letters. Farewell.
pages.118:
<note>Red decorative initial N.</note>
<note>Red decorative initial Q.</note>
I would hope that there would be some remedy for my poverty, were it not so hard in this fortune of mine that I could not bear it with a great and unshaken mind. But since no hope possesses me at all, why should I desire to remain longer in life? I used to count my years often from my birthday to understand how much time, according to nature, remained for me. Then I was especially desirous of living, because then there was no reason to accuse life. Now, however, it does not seem so to my weary spirit. Others fear disease and death more than is becoming to a wise man. One weeps in a storm and desires, having lost his belongings, to escape from the shipwreck. If someone has pressed a blade to his throat, he begs miserably that someone might pity his life. I, however, whom you dread, am beginning to desire it. And nothing is better known to me as the cause of my troubles than that I might be quickly extinguished. But why do I write this to you, since you cannot help me by grieving with me? And in this one thing, I am more miserable, because I see that you, too, are miserable. You love me, and it brings no small consolation to me in these troubles. But because of that pain which you suffer, and because you are also part of my pain, I take it too grievously. But due to your modesty, which is supreme, you will bear my sadness bravely. Farewell.

What should I write to you? I do not know, because I am of such a perturbed mind that neither reason nor counsel exists in me. For one can poorly advise another when he himself most needs counsel. That I can easily offer you, I promise: to grieve with you equally and to accuse fortune, which adds to our adversity despite our integrity. With these remedies, if they are to be called remedies, I can help you, which render the sick mind incurable. I would rather you return to your virtue than use the example of a man out of his mind, so that I, who see no remedy from myself, might borrow it from you, who are wiser. For there is no one living today who could more easily heal this disease of mine, which has gone on since the beginning, or more easily
pages.119:
<note>Red decorative initial N.</note>
<note>Red decorative initial A.</note>
remedy it. And if you do this, you will have cured two at once with one and the same remedy. Farewell.

Do you not believe that I am in a state of mind where I realize I have been abandoned by all my friends when I consider my fortunes? This thing so disturbs me that I seem to have become a changed man to myself. I did not expect that I, who had helped them through my duty, would now be abandoned by all of them. But these are the arts of our citizens: when our affairs are pleasant, to promise everything voluntarily, to contend with words about supreme benevolence, faith, and constancy, with those who truly love us. But if they see that our fortunes have changed, they say it is human to consider their own fortunes and those of their children rather than those of their friends. They think nothing of past duties, nothing of benefits received. And those whom they could protect without risk, they easily allow to be deserted by them. These things can warn you, if you are prudent, not to acquire such friends for your own inconvenience while your affairs are still prosperous. No one can teach you better what must be guarded against at this time than I, who have become prudent at my own risk. Farewell.

Better to be warned by the inconveniences of others than by your own, as you have always loved me greatly. But after this matter is as it is—that (which I least wished) you have been deserted by your friends whom you had often defended—I will be more cautious in my affairs, nor will I have greater regard for friends than for my own comforts. But if men were in that integrity of life and constancy that they were once, I judge that no inconveniences would have to be shunned for the sake of friends. Now, however, since in friendship we follow utility, or some property, or pleasure, more than honesty, everything seems to me to be referred to the times in which we are. However, I will take care that no one of my friends outdoes me in their benevolence and duty. And if it happens to me that I merit
pages.120:
that I understand I am loved, I will make no limit to my duties or my love for him. But so that you do not judge yourself to be deserted by all, I (whom perhaps you did not have in the number of your friends) promise you my effort, and (which they did not neglect without sin) I am prepared to undertake your defense. You, however, will advise me of what help you may have need, and I will lack neither money nor counsel for you. Farewell.

The end of the happy letters of Gasparino.

To this, in a desperate matter, neither for the sake of protection nor counsel do you write to me, but because it helps you to speak with me about your inconveniences. You do what is common to friends. I am accustomed to doing the same, knowing that I am released in spirit. I seem to have laid down the greater part of my molestation for myself when I opened all my perturbation to my friends. I rejoice greatly in this, and I give thanks to you, that you chose me from among many, to whom you might entrust your cares. By many other signs, and also by this one, I judge that I am greatly loved by you. The rest which pertains to your consolation, you yourself will foresee better (as I hope) by your own virtue than by my letters. Farewell.

But it is different if he does not lay aside the habit, but hides it under [his clothes] or covers it with another so as not to be recognized, especially if he does so for a good cause, as for instance, because it is summer and he does not wish to be recognized as being of his religion, while he still wears the religious habit. An.</term> <gloss>Johannes Andreae</gloss> says on the word "keeping": coming from outside to the cloister with arms, not with the intention of keeping them, nor keeping them, he does not seem to be bound by the act, and the word [is] with effect. allow</gloss>. ¶ The seventh principal is John XXI, in his Extravagant <term>Sancta Romana</term> <gloss>Holy Roman</gloss>, and it is twofold. ¶ The first sounds thus: The status of all those men who in some places are called Fraticelli or Beguines, or brothers of poor life, or Bizochi, or by other names, and who presume rashly to assume the habit of a new religion, to make congregations and conventicles, to elect superiors for themselves, whom they call ministers or custodians and guardians, or by other names, to receive many into their sect, even to build new places or receive built holy Francis instituted, and pretending to observe it, whereas they do not live under the general or provincial obedience of the ministers of that order, [and] some of whom also assert themselves to be of the Third Order of the blessed Francis, of penitents, in which, however, such a rite is not at all observed: it revokes, permits, and forbids the aforesaid status of them under the veil of such a name, with all things notwithstanding, and they are nevertheless excommunicated <term>ipso facto</term>. ¶ The second: all bishops and other prelates who have observed any rite of living and habit aforesaid without the special mandate of the Apostolic See are excommunicated <term>ipso facto</term>. ¶ The eighth: concerning privileges <note>Refers to Clementines, De privilegiis</note>, contains six cases reserved to the Pope. ¶ The first: religious who, to clerics or laypeople, administer the sacrament of extreme unction—that is the first—or the Eucharist—that is the second. An.</term> <gloss>Johannes Andreae</gloss> notes on the word "from sentences" of the fifth case: I think, he says, that it includes all sentences of excommunication, suspension, or interdict, whose absolution might be necessary. For he does not understand [it] of the excommunicated by a person, which he does not express. From which also appears the seventh case, namely, that all those are excommunicated whom their superior or judge rightly excommunicates by his statutes; thus also are all excommunicated whom their prelates or judges rightly excommunicate. ¶ The ninth principal in the Clementines, concerning penalties <note>Refers to Clementines, De poenis</note>, "Cupientes" <gloss>Desiring</gloss>, is threefold. The first: concerning mendicant religious, that henceforth in no city, castle, village, or place whatsoever, they presume to receive newly, for inhabiting, any houses or places whatsoever, or to change those already received, or to bring them into others by title of sale, exchange, donation, or any alienation, without special license of the Apostolic See. <note>A red paragraph mark appears here in the source.</note> The fifteenth principal is for one who, in the city or diocese of another, while exercising the office of a vicar or prelacy, intrudes himself against the form of the decree <term>De officiis ordinis</term> <gloss>On the offices of the order</gloss> and <term>In plerisque</term> <gloss>In many cases</gloss>. This case happens rarely, whence if someone, without the bishop's invitation, wishes to exercise episcopal functions or carry the cross outside the province, he seems to fall into it.

<note>A red paragraph mark appears here in the source.</note> The sixteenth principal is against those who are summoned to direct nuns in their elections, unless those who are so summoned abstain from this, because discord can arise over the conducting of elections. <note>See the Decretals, On Elections, chapter "Indemnitatibus" (Book VI).</note> And note what <term>Joh. Pa.</term> <gloss>Johannes de Palatio</gloss> says: note that in this case the advocate falls [under censure] who, out of love of gain, strives to appeal against those canonically elected, if he should have advised them well.

<note>A red paragraph mark appears here in the source.</note> The seventeenth principal contains three cases. The first is against those who, regarding the constitutions of Nicholas IV <note>original: "Nicolaus IV"</note>—<term>Exiit qui seminat</term> <gloss>He went out who sows</gloss> (Book VI)—concerning the understanding and exposition of the Rule of the Blessed Francis of the Friars Minor, presume to gloss it by expounding other things grammatically. <term>Joh. An.</term> <gloss>Johannes Andreae</gloss> says: I think it is necessary that an impediment proceed, and [likewise for] many who follow. The second: against doctors or lectors who have taught in public, from certain knowledge and deliberately, things contrary to the understanding of the constitution itself. The third: against those who make any writings or booklets and, from certain knowledge and deliberately, determine in schools or preach things contrary to those which are contained in the aforesaid constitution. It is to be noted also by <term>Joh. XXI</term> <gloss>Pope John XXI</gloss> in the constitution <term>Quia nonnunquam</term> <gloss>Because sometimes</gloss>, that the sentences and penalties laid against the glossators of Nicholas IV's <term>Exiit qui seminat</term> are suspended until the good pleasure of the Apostolic See. Through such suspension, he does not intend to give license to teach, write, determine, preach, or speak privately against the rules of those Friars Minor, publicly or secretly.

<note>A red paragraph mark appears here in the source.</note> The eighteenth principal is in the constitution of <term>Joh. XXI</term>, <term>Suscepti regiminis</term> <gloss>Of the government undertaken</gloss>, as follows: If anyone has taken from the fruits of a benefice, from which the first year's fruits or others are owed to the fabric or church of some person, beyond the portion taxed by the lord Pope John, and has not restored it to him to whom it pertains within a month with effect: if he is a bishop or superior, he is suspended from the entrance of the church and from pontificals. If, however, a single person, whether ecclesiastical or secular, has done this, he incurs a sentence of excommunication <term>ipso facto</term> <gloss>by the act itself</gloss>, from which no one may absolve him, unless the restitution of the aforesaid has been made, except in the article of death.

¶ The nineteenth principal has two parts. The first: if any of those [bishops] as mentioned above has come to the Roman Curia publicly or secretly and has departed from the Curia without the license of the lord Pope, he is excommunicated <term>ipso facto</term>. The second: if anyone has knowingly received bishops lurking at the Apostolic See as mentioned above, or has not cared to manifest to the lord Pope, or to someone through whom the notice might be brought to him, the occurrence and arrival of those who have shown such reception, he is excommunicated <term>ipso facto</term>. These two cases are found in the constitutions of <term>Joh. XXII</term> <gloss>Pope John XXII</gloss> and <term>Platon. R. C.</term> <gloss>Regarding the Clerical Office</gloss>, chapter <term>Si doceat</term> <gloss>If he should teach</gloss>. ¶ The twentieth principal case is confirmed from the Council of Constance by Martin in the same place by the bull <term>Multo</term> <gloss>Much</gloss>, and in these words: We ordain that they are by that very fact suspended. Furthermore, elections, postulations, and confirmations—and whatever petitions concerning churches, monasteries, dignities, personates, offices, and ecclesiastical benefices—made simoniacally in any way, are void by the law itself, and no right is acquired for anyone by them, nor does any promotion, confirmation, or petition produce its fruits. Rather, those receiving them are bound to their restitution as things wrongly given, and both those giving and receiving incur a sentence of excommunication <term>ipso facto</term>, even if they shine with pontifical or cardinal dignity. ¶ The twenty-first: this is from the Council of Basel, chapter 12. Thus it is instructed: those elected simoniacally, or pontiffs, or abbots, and those who were the principals of such a simoniacal election, and those who were electing and confirming, incur the penalty of excommunication <term>ipso facto</term> in such horror. Nor can those elected and confirmed be absolved from such guilt and excommunication unless they freely resign the churches and dignities to which they were shamefully assumed, and render themselves forever unable to obtain those which they attained by a wicked entry. ¶ Regarding cases touching principally upon male and female religious. ¶ Chapter Five.

admitted after the General Council of <term>Innocent</term>, by which also religions were confirmed by the Apostolic See, who after the Council of Lyons of the lord <term>Gregory X</term> admitted some to their profession, or founded a house or acquired any place, or alienated houses or places which they have, without special license of the Apostolic See <note>original: "ex. de reli. domi. c. religionum li. vi."</note>. ¶ The second principal has two orders <note>original: "ex. ne cleri. ut periculosa li. vi."</note>. ¶ First: a religious who in schools or elsewhere rashly puts off the habit of his religion is excommunicated as one apostatizing from the religious life, or rather, as the Pope says: if a religious puts off the habit for a base reason, as for example going at night to a brothel, he incurs it. But it is different if he does not put off the habit, but hides it or covers it with another so he is not recognized, especially if he does so for a good reason, as for example, if he is travelling and does not wish to be recognized for his religious order, provided that he is wearing the religious habit beneath it. But one who puts it off for fear of robbers does not put it off rashly. Nor are they excused who change their habit in schools so they do not appear as religious. Concerning precious cloths and a multitude of candles, when citizens forbid such things, lest they harm themselves with their pomps, others say that it is lawful, provided it is done for the good of all, not wishing by this to harm ecclesiastical liberties. <term>Fourth</term> principal involves two. <term>First</term>, towards those who impede emperors or others recurring to the ecclesiastical forum, regarding causes that pertain to the same forum by law or by some custom, either by themselves or through another, to desist, or to litigate in the secular forum about such questions by the judgment of the churches, or those of the petitioners or the litigants, or those wishing to litigate, or of those same, or of those things; because even capture, or in other ways whatsoever, they have operated, or caused to be compelled, or procured, or by themselves or through others have impeded, so that they might not freely be able to obtain justice before ecclesiastical judges or legates or ordinaries regarding the aforesaid causes. <term>Second</term> is towards those who for doing the aforesaid have given counsel, aid, or favor, as in <term>De emendatione ecclesiae</term>, Book VI, where Petrus de Palude also notes: if anyone counsels his friend to come rather before a lay judge, power, or master of the city where immediately through the possessions of the person or the sequestration of goods he will have his right, than before an official where at length he obtains his right, he does not incur [excommunication], although the other might have wished to litigate before the church. pages.35: The fifth principal concerns the immunity of the church and those who, obtaining temporal dominion by the license of whomsoever, forbid their subjects to sell anything to prelates, clerics, or ecclesiastical persons, or to buy anything from the same, or not to grind grain, bake bread, or show other services to them; the aforesaid is not bound <note>to excommunication</note> by the said Pope, except for dukes and prelates. The sixth principal is against those who, for their own proper things which they do not carry or cause to be carried for the sake of trade, demand or extort tolls <term>pedagia</term> <gloss>tolls/fees</gloss> or suchlike things from churches and ecclesiastical persons by themselves or others in their own name or another's, or compel them to pay such things, contrary custom notwithstanding. And the bishop of the place ought to publish them as excommunicated or have them published by his subjects until they have restored what was thus exacted and have satisfactorily made amends for such transgression, <term>Extra de censibus</term> <gloss>On taxes</gloss>, and the question in book five, <term>§ qui vero</term> <gloss>§ he who indeed</gloss>, not even those are excused by the said Pope at the time from which memory exists, who demand tolls from clerics, which the Pope understands of old tolls, not of new ones. The seventh principal case concerns two. The first: that laymen who formerly by force or by fear compelled prelates or the chapter of churches or other ecclesiastical persons to submit to them immovable goods or rights of the churches without the consent of the chapter and the license of the Pope, unless after repeated admonition he relaxes such submissions. And that henceforth they shall compel prelates or other ecclesiastical persons to do such things. The second: whoever, through a submission duly made up to now, usurps something beyond that which is permitted by a lawful tract, unless being lawfully warned they desist from such usurpation and also by restoring what such things they usurped, <term>Extra de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis</term> <gloss>On not alienating church property</gloss>, and in this newest <term>§ laici</term> <gloss>§ laymen</gloss>, book six. The eighth principal has two. The first is against those who, trying to usurp anew under the title of regalian custody or the guard of their advocacy or defense in churches, monasteries, or other pious places, presume to usurp the goods of the same vacant churches, monasteries, or pious places. The second is against the clerics, monks of monasteries, and persons of the churches of the same places who permit this to be done, <term>Extra de electione</term> <gloss>On election</gloss>.

The second is against those who have demanded reprisals not granted by custom or by use against them, that is, ecclesiastical persons, unless they have revoked such presumption within a month to be counted from the time of the grant or extortion, <term>Extra de iniuriis</term> <gloss>On injuries</gloss>, <term>c. zli pignorationes</term> <gloss>c. and seizures</gloss>, Book VI. ¶ The twelfth principal contains two. This case, as Petrus de Palude says, is rarely omitted; it can be omitted if some judge feigned this, so that he might enter to women living under enclosure, <term>Extra de iudiciis</term>, <term>c. mulieres</term> <gloss>c. women</gloss>, Book VI. The eighteenth principal is: whoever of whatsoever status or grade, even if he shines with pontifical dignity, is an executor, or someone else, has made a human corpse wretched <note>desecrated</note>, or dismembered it to extract bones by boiling for the sake of burial, as in <term>Extravagantes Bonifacii VIII</term>, <term>c. detestandae</term> <gloss>c. to be detested</gloss>. ¶ The nineteenth principal case: when someone has fallen into a deed condemned by a statute of man, made under that form, that whoever does the truth is excommunicated, <term>De sen. ex.</term>, <term>a nobis</term> <gloss>from us</gloss>. Where it is to be known, says Petrus de Palude, that here there is a sentence of law, not papal, special, or synodal or of a council, whence he who is subject to the statutes by reason of his crime incurs it, not another, in the place where the one who makes the statute places the statute or excommunication, because the statute of a council binds well in the diocese of the suffragans. See also above, c. iii, chapter vii, and c. iv, chapter vi. ¶ The twentieth principal is against those who by force or fear have procured absolution from a sentence of excommunication, or any revocation of it, or of suspension or interdict, <term>De his quae vi metusve causa</term> <gloss>On those things which [are done] by reason of force or fear</gloss>, <term>c. finali</term>, <term>absolutionis</term> <gloss>of absolution</gloss>, Book VI. This case, says Petrus de Palude, is to be understood about fear falling upon a constant man, namely, of rape or of the status of beatings and death, or suchlike, by himself or by another, because it does not distinguish. ¶ The twenty-first contains two, <term>De sen. ex.</term>, <term>eos qui</term>, Book VI, and in <term>Clementinae de poenis</term>, <term>c. si quis</term>, <term>§ fi</term> <gloss>§ final</gloss>, and both are sometimes reserved to the Pope. The first: towards those excommunicated by canon or by man, who on account of danger of death or legitimate impediment are absolved from the sentence of the canon by another than him by whom they were to be absolved by law, <term>si quis suadente</term> <gloss>if anyone by persuasion</gloss>, by an ordinary or by another who by law cannot, if, the danger or impediment afterwards ceasing,
pages.39: or such impediment, they have not contemplated themselves to those from whom, these ceasing, they ought to have been absolved by law, as soon as they can conveniently present themselves to receive the mandate of the same concerning those things for which they were excommunicated and to make satisfaction, as justice suggested. And this is a papal case, if the sentence was reserved to the Pope; but an episcopal one, if it was reserved to the bishop. The second is against those to whom, when the benefit of absolution is granted by the Apostolic See or its legates from whatsoever sentences, it is enjoined that they present themselves to their ordinaries, or any others whomsoever, to receive penance from the same, and to show competent satisfaction to those injured or those to whom they are obligated by reason of these things. If he is not able to come to fulfill it when he first conveniently can, both the one and the other fall by the very fact into the sentences of excommunication. And the sense is that those who have been absolved by the Apostolic See or a legate, and it is commanded to them that they make satisfaction, or present themselves to some judge, if he does not do it, in this case he will be absolved by him who can and by the superior, and not by another. ¶ The twenty-second principal contains William of St. Pourçain, <term>De officio legati</term> <gloss>On the office of a legate</gloss>, <term>c. nunc</term> <gloss>c. now</gloss>, whence it is to be given: [regarding] a sentence of his legate or delegate whose jurisdiction has expired, and to whom no one has succeeded in the office enjoined to him, only the Pope absolves, <term>Extra de offi. de le.</term> <gloss>On the office of the legate</gloss>, <term>prudentiam</term> <gloss>prudence</gloss>; if this is true, the same is to be understood, says William in the same place, concerning the constitutions of his legates, [since] the mission is finished, nor does anyone succeed the legate, since in such a case there is no superior except the Pope. ¶ The twenty-third principal: since the Pope before coronation can exercise his office, therefore that on this occasion he might attack the laws, he is excommunicated, as in <term>Extravagantes Benedicti XI</term>, which begins, <term>quoniam nonnulli</term> <gloss>since some</gloss>. ¶ The twenty-fourth principal is in the constitution of John XXII, <term>Fi. fratrum et coepiscoporum</term> <gloss>Faith of the brothers and co-bishops</gloss>, where it holds that if, the empire being vacant, someone by virtue of any commission made to him by the dead emperor, or by any other color, or by authority, has usurped the goods of the empire or exercised jurisdiction or assumed for himself the vicariate or the name of any other office whatsoever, unless by special license of the Pope, both all those and their commissioners in such things obedient, or granting them in this aid, counsel, or favor, are excommunicated by the very fact.

The gloss understands here the lands or places of theirs to be considered not only by reason of property but of jurisdictional superiority, and the places and whatsoever communities and universities subject to an ecclesiastical interdict. ¶ The twenty-fifth, John XXII in the constitution <term>dudum crescente malicia</term> <gloss>lately growing malice</gloss>, the principal thus frames: If anyone in the province of the March of Ancona subject to the Roman Church kills, invades, offends, or otherwise ill-treats a rector or other minister or official deputed by the Apostolic See or any vicar or judge of theirs, or for this gives aid, counsel, or favor directly or indirectly, publicly or secretly, he is unable to hold benefits or offices whatsoever, and is excommunicated by the very fact and reserved absolutely to the Pope; other kinds of punishments are moreover hurled there. ¶ The twenty-sixth principal: all those who falsify the money of the King of France or carry other false money into the Kingdom of France are excommunicated by the very fact and reserved to the Pope for absolution by the constitution of John XXII, <term>pdies qli</term>. ¶ The twenty-seventh principal: if anyone has moved demons or demanded their aid, or made covenants or pacts with demons, or has sacrificed to them or adored them, or in their name has set up images, rings, mirrors, mirrors of a brooch, or any other thing magically for binding the demons themselves, or has asked for answers from them or from those who have heard from the demons themselves, he is excommunicated by the very fact by the constitution of John XXII on that mirror. ¶ The twenty-eighth principal: if anyone has falsified the signet or seal of any cardinal or knowingly has used one falsified by another, he is tied by that very fact in anathema by the constitution of John XXII, <term>impellit nos</term> <gloss>it impels us</gloss>. ¶ The twenty-ninth principal: whoever have presumed to impede legates or even nuncios of the Apostolic See are excommunicated by the very fact, and the kingdoms, lands, and places whatsoever subject to them are for so long subject to ecclesiastical interdict as long as they shall lead to persist in such contumacy, in the constitution of John XXII, <term>Super gentes et regna</term> <gloss>Over nations and kingdoms</gloss>, etc. ¶ The Second Part follows.

How the confessor ought to dispose himself toward him who will confess to him; twelve rules are given above. ¶ Chapter One.

The second part now begins concerning the necessary things accompanying confession, in which, as a confessor performs the office of a physician, he may be able to heal the diseases of the mind more easily in applying the sacrament of penance; it incorporates the seven following chapters. ¶ First, as to how he ought to prepare himself for disposing the penitents well. ¶ Second, what he ought to ask generally from the penitent himself. ¶ Third, what vices of lust, about which there is great force, he may be able to examine specifically from modesty. ¶ Fourth, how he ought to inform concerning the ends of confession, what he should correct, and by what he might expedite to know whether the confessed has been truly penitent or attrite. ¶ Fifth, what kind of penance or satisfaction he ought to duly enjoin. ¶ Sixth, how he may duly absolve from sins and from sentences. ¶ Seventh, how he may cautiously hold himself concerning the sick and the concealment of confession. As to the first, before confession and about it, he should heed the 12 following rules. ¶ First, that he should have authority over the penitent or jurisdiction, if anyone else wishes to hear the confession, for instance, the Pope, the bishop, the parish priest, or that he be a prelate or a bishop duly, if he is a friar of the mendicant order. For a subject can in eight cases confess to another than his own priest or to another than the one who was previously his own priest. First, when the proper priest is entirely indiscreet and ignorant, and license is sought from him, even if not obtained, or at least license ought to be sought from the superior of the proper confessor or priest if it can be had. Second, when a parishioner has moved his domicile, then he is a subject of that priest to whose parish he has moved himself. Third, when someone seeks a domicile to which he may betake himself, because he is without a domicile. Fourth, when someone is a vagabond. Fifth, if he is at a university <note>studio</note> by the license of his prelates. Sixth, if he is a pilgrim who receives a wallet and staff from his own priest or his vicar or license, or if he is a merchant or a traveler, and receives license from his own priest; but otherwise if the pilgrim or merchant or traveler has not done the aforesaid.

N.text: general, Book VI. ¶ The ninth principal is against those who, regarding the election which pertains to them in some churches, monasteries, or other pious places, have presumed to harm clerics or any other ecclesiastical persons, or the kinsmen of the same, or their churches, monasteries, or places, by spoiling them of their goods by themselves or others, or by otherwise unjustly persecuting them, because those asked or otherwise induced did not want to elect the one for whom they were asking or inducing, <term>Extra de electione</term>, <term>sciant cuncti</term> <gloss>let all know</gloss>, Book VI. ¶ The tenth principal contains three cases. The first is against those who have caused some Christians to be killed by other men. The second is against those who have commanded this to be done, even if death does not follow from it. The third is against those who harbor, defend, or hide other men, <term>Extra de homicidio</term> <gloss>On homicide</gloss>, <term>c. per humani</term> <gloss>c. by the human [law]</gloss>, Book VI. ¶ The eleventh principal has two cases. The first is against those who have granted reprisals or seizures where one is burdened for another, against ecclesiastical persons or their goods. The second is against those who have demanded reprisals not granted by custom or by use against them, that is, ecclesiastical persons, unless they have revoked such presumption within a month to be counted from the time of the grant or extortion, <term>Extra de iniuriis</term> <gloss>On injuries</gloss>, <term>c. zli pignorationes</term> <gloss>c. and seizures</gloss>, Book VI. ¶ The twelfth principal contains two. The first is against those who, because in kings, princes, barons, nobles, bailiffs, or ministers whomsoever, or any others, a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict has been promulgated, have given license to others to kill, capture, or otherwise harm them in persons or goods, or those who have brought such sentences, or whose occasion of death they were, or those observing such sentences, or those wishing to excommunicate such excommunicated persons, unless they have revoked the licenses while the matter is intact, or if a process was made for the capture of goods on the occasion of that license, unless they have restored the goods within eight days or have provided satisfaction for them. The second is against those who have dared to use the given license or to omit anything of the aforesaid on their own motion, <term>Extra de sen. ex.</term> <gloss>On the sentence of excommunication</gloss>, <term>c. quicumque</term> <gloss>c. whoever</gloss>, Book VI. And these two cases are reserved to the Pope, if anyone has stood in that excommunication for two months. ¶ The thirteenth

X.text: principal contains two, and both are reserved to the Pope. The first in <term>Clementinae</term>, <term>c. si quis</term> <gloss>c. if anyone</gloss>: if anyone has injuriously or rashly struck the Pontiff, or captured or banished [him], or has commanded it to be done, or has ratified what was done by others, or has been a partner of the doer in these, or has given counsel or favor in these, or knowing [the fact] has defended the same, in those cases of the aforesaid in which excommunicators would not undergo [it] by the edited canons. The gloss on the word "of the aforesaid" as in the one banishing or commanding it, or the partner ratifying it, etc., as follows. The second: the powers, counselors, aldermen, advocates, rectors, consuls, and officials of the same, by whatever name they are called, existing guilty in the premises, all incur excommunications to be absolved by the Popes, except in the article of death, in <term>Clementinae de poenis</term>, <term>c. i.</term> <gloss>c. 1</gloss>. The fourteenth principal is also reserved to the Pope: that temporal lords who compel some to celebrate divine service in an interdicted place, or who through heralds make the people evacuate to hear those [offices], or forbid that the publicly excommunicated or interdicted, upon being warned by those who celebrate masses, should leave the churches, or they themselves being notified do not leave, are excommunicated in <term>Clementinae de sen. ex.</term>, <term>quis</term>. The fifteenth principal is in <term>Clementinae ex gravi</term> <gloss>on the grave</gloss> on usuries, all six cases. Namely, cities and officials making them, behold the first. Dictating them, behold the second. Or writing statutes about usuries to be paid, not to be repeated, or restored, behold the third. Or judging according to them, behold the fourth. Or not deleting them if they could within three months from the books of the city, behold the fifth. Or helping them, behold the sixth: they are excommunicated. Also, they incur sentences, whoever the powers, captains, rectors, consuls, judges, counselors of the cities themselves, or other officials attempting the premises. The sixteenth principal contains six in <term>Clementinae de sanguinitate et affinitate</term> <gloss>on consanguinity and affinity</gloss>, <term>c. unico</term> <gloss>c. only</gloss>, namely: contracting marriage in a degree of consanguinity, behold the first. And of prohibited affinity, behold the second. Or with a nun, behold the third: he is excommunicated. The same is about religious men doing so, and nuns, and also clerics placed in sacred orders, behold again the other three cases. And the gloss that this is established in the expressed aforesaid cases only.
