Concerning those who presume to write in public form <note>that is, legal documents</note> the judged sentences, <term>Ex extra de sententia excommunicationis, cap. Noverit finitatis tuae</term> <gloss>On the sentence of excommunication, ch. May your diligence know</gloss>. Petrus de Palude notes that all are understood there to act against ecclesiastical liberty, such as when rustics decree that no one shall offer except on great feasts, or unless it is for burial, or that there shall not be such a cloth or so many candles over the dead, or that everyone shall contribute to the aiding of the work in a shameful case and suchlike; because the liberty of the church is to be free in oblations and free burials. If, however, those of any one kind order that they should be buried somewhere, and with this there is no statute binding, and if it is a work of one church, it is not seen to fall upon others. Regarding precious cloths and the multitude of candles, when citizens forbid such things, lest they harm themselves with their pomps, others say that it is lawful, provided it is done for the good of all and not by this wishing to harm ecclesiastical liberties. The fourth principal encompasses two. The first is concerning those who, by apostolic letters, emperors, or others recurring to the ecclesiastical forum, regarding causes which belong to that same forum by law or by some custom, either by themselves or by another, [act] to desist or to litigate in the secular forum regarding such questions, instead of by ecclesiastical judgment, or regarding the petitioners themselves or the litigants, or those wishing to litigate, or concerning those same persons or their things; because even [regarding] capture or by other ways whatsoever they operated, or caused to be compelled or procured, or by themselves or by others impeded, so that [the complainants] might not be able to obtain justice freely before ecclesiastical judges, or [before] legates or ordinaries regarding the aforementioned causes. The second is concerning those who gave counsel, aid, or favor to do the aforesaid, as in <term>De emittendis ecclesiae</term> <gloss>On the sending out of the church</gloss>, book six, where Petrus de Palude also notes: if someone counsels his friend to better encounter a layman before a lay judge, power, or master of [the city] where he will immediately have his right through the possessions of the person or by the seizure of goods, than before an official where he finally obtains his right, he does not fall [into excommunication], although the other might have wished to litigate before the church. He by whose counsel someone is forced, unwilling, to desist from litigating in the church, he merits [punishment].
pages.35: The fifth principal concerns the immunity of the church and those who, holding temporal dominion by the license of whomsoever, forbid their subjects to sell anything to prelates, clerics, or ecclesiastical persons, or to buy anything from them, or not to grind grain for them, bake bread, or show them other services. This is not bound by the aforementioned Pope, except for dukes and prelates. The sixth principal is against those who, for their own proper things which they do not carry or cause to be carried for the cause of trade, demand or extort tolls or suchlike things from churches and ecclesiastical persons, by themselves or others in their name or another’s, or compel them to pay such things, notwithstanding a contrary custom. And the bishop of the place ought to publish them as excommunicated, or cause them to be published by his subjects, until they restore what was thus exacted and have made competent satisfaction for such transgression, <term>Extra de censibus et quaestione</term> <gloss>Regarding taxes and questions</gloss>, book five, § <term>Qui vero</term> <gloss>He who truly</gloss>, and the aforementioned Pope, [concerning] the time from which memory exists, [concerning] clerics who pay tolls, which the Pope understands regarding old tolls, not new ones. The seventh principal case concerns two things. First, that laymen who formerly compelled by force or fear the prelates or the chapter of churches or other ecclesiastical persons to submit to them immovable goods or rights of the churches without the consent of the chapter and the license of the Pope, unless after repeated admonition he relaxes such submissions. And that henceforth he shall compel prelates or other ecclesiastical persons to do such things. Second, whosoever through a submission duly made hitherto usurps something beyond that which is permitted by a lawful tract, unless, duly warned, he desists from such usurpation and returns even that which he has usurped, <term>Extra de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis</term> <gloss>On not alienating the goods of the church</gloss>, and this latest § <term>Laici</term> <gloss>Laymen</gloss>, book six. The eighth principal has two. The first is against those who, attempting to usurp anew by royal custody or guardianship of their advocacy or by the title of defense in churches, monasteries, or other pious places, presume to usurp the goods of the same vacant churches, monasteries, or pious places. The second is against the clerics, monks of monasteries, and persons of the churches of the same places who permit this to be done, <term>Extra de electione</term> <gloss>On election</gloss>.

Nunc</term> <gloss>On the office of the legate, ch. Now</gloss>; whence it is to be said that from the sentence of his legate or delegate, whose jurisdiction has expired, and to whom no one has succeeded in the office enjoined upon him, only the Pope absolves, <term>Extra de officio delegati, Prudentiam</term> <gloss>On the office of the delegate, Prudence</gloss>. If this is true, the same is to be understood, says William in the same place, [when] the constitution of his legates is finished by the legate, nor does anyone succeed the legate; because in such a case there is no superior except the Pope. ¶ The twenty-third principal: since the Pope can exercise his office before coronation, therefore [anyone] who would impugn [him] on this occasion is excommunicated, as in <term>Extravagantes Benedicti XI</term> <gloss>Extra-decretals of Benedict XI</gloss>, which begins "Because some." ¶ The twenty-fourth principal is in the constitution of John XXII, <term>Filii fratrum et coepiscoporum</term> <gloss>Sons of brothers and fellow bishops</gloss>, where it has that if, the empire being vacant, by virtue of any commission made to him by the dead emperor, or by any other color, or by authority, he has usurped the goods of the empire or exercised jurisdiction or assumed for himself a vicariate or the name of any other office whatsoever, unless by special license of the Pope, and all those obedient to them and to their commissioners in such things, or providing them aid, counsel, or favor in this, are <term>ipso facto</term> <gloss>by the fact itself</gloss> excommunicated.
pages.40: from their lands. The gloss understands here their lands or places to be reckoned not by reason of property only, but of jurisdictional superiority, and the places and any communities and universities whatsoever subject to the ecclesiastical interdict. ¶ The twenty-fifth, John XXII in the constitution <term>Dudum crescente malitia</term> <gloss>Long since, increasing malice</gloss>, the principal thus sounds: If anyone in the province of the March of Ancona, subject to the Roman Church, has killed, invaded, offended, or otherwise treated badly a rector or other minister or official deputed by the Apostolic See, or any vicar or judge of theirs, or has given aid, counsel, or favor to this directly or indirectly, publicly or secretly, he is disabled for any benefits or offices whatsoever, and he is excommunicated <term>ipso facto</term> <gloss>by the fact itself</gloss>, and it is reserved to the Pope alone to absolve; other types of punishments are also fulminated there. ¶ The twenty-sixth principal: all those who falsify the money of the King of France or carry other false money in the Kingdom of France are excommunicated <term>ipso facto</term> <gloss>by the fact itself</gloss>, and it is reserved to the Pope to absolve, by the constitution of John XXII, <term>Dudum et alii</term> <gloss>Long since and others</gloss>. ¶ The twenty-seventh principal: if anyone has invoked demons or requested their aid, or made treaties or pacts with demons, or has sacrificed to them, or worshipped them, or in their name has constructed images, rings, mirrors, brooches, or other things magically for binding the demons themselves, or has asked for answers from them or from those who have heard from the demons themselves, he is excommunicated <term>ipso facto</term> <gloss>by the fact itself</gloss> by the constitution of John XXII, <term>Super illius speculae</term> <gloss>Upon that watchtower</gloss>. ¶ The twenty-eighth principal: if anyone has falsified the bull or seal of any cardinal or, knowing it to be falsified by another, has used it, by that very fact he is tied in anathema by the constitution of John XXII, <term>Impellit nos</term> <gloss>It impels us</gloss>. ¶ The twenty-ninth principal: whosoever have presumed to impede the legates or even nuncios of the Apostolic See are excommunicated <term>ipso facto</term> <gloss>by the fact itself</gloss>, and the kingdoms, lands, and places whatsoever subject to them are subject to ecclesiastical interdict for as long as they shall lead to persist in such contumacy, in the constitution of John XXII, <term>Super gentes et regna, etc.</term> <gloss>Upon nations and kingdoms, etc.</gloss> ¶ The second part follows.
pages.41: How the confessor ought to dispose himself toward him who will confess to him, twelve rules are given above. ¶ Chap. first. The second part now begins concerning necessary things accompanying confession, in which, as the confessor performs the office of a physician, he may be able to heal the diseases of the soul more easily, in applying the sacrament of penance, [and] incorporates the seven following chapters. ¶ First, how he ought to prepare himself to dispose those confessing well. ¶ Second, what he ought to ask of the confessor generally. ¶ Third, which vices of luxury, of which there is great force, he might be able to search out specially from shame. ¶ Fourth, how he ought to inform [the penitent] around the ends of confession and to correct [him], and through what [means] it is expedient to know if the one confessing is truly contrite or attrite. ¶ Fifth, what [penance] or satisfaction he ought duly to enjoin as penance. ¶ Sixth, how he may duly absolve from sins and from sentences. ¶ Seventh, how he ought to hold himself cautiously around the infirm, and [regarding] the secret of confession. Regarding the first, before confession and around it, he may attend to the following twelve rules. ¶ First, that he may have authority over the one confessing, or jurisdiction, if he, being another, wishes to hear the confession, for instance, the Pope, the bishop, the parish priest, or that he may be a prelate or a bishop, if he is a brother of the mendicant order. For a subject can in eight cases confess to another than his own priest or to another than he who was previously his own priest. First, when his own priest is altogether indiscreet and ignorant, and license is sought from him, though not obtained, or at least license ought to be sought from the superior of his own confessor or priest if it can be had. Second, when a parishioner has moved his domicile, then he is a subject of that priest to whose parish he has moved. Third, when someone seeks a domicile where he may betake himself, because he is without a domicile. Fourth, when someone is a vagabond. Fifth, if he is in study by the license of his prelates. Sixth, if he is a pilgrim who receives a wallet and staff from his own priest or his vicar, or license, or if he is a merchant or traveler, and receives license from his own priest; otherwise, however, if the pilgrim or merchant or traveler has not done the aforesaid.

N.text: <note>continues from previous page: general</note>, book six. ¶ The ninth principal is against those who presume to harm clerics or any other ecclesiastical persons, to whom pertains the election in any churches, monasteries, or other pious places, or their blood-relatives, or their churches, monasteries, or places, by despoiling them of their goods by themselves or others, or by otherwise justly persecuting them, for the reason that those requested or otherwise induced, did not want to elect him for whom they were requested or induced, <term>Extra de electione, cap. Sciant cuncti</term> <gloss>On election, ch. Let all know</gloss>, book six. ¶ The tenth principal contains three cases. The first is against those who have caused some Christians to be killed by other men. The second is against those who have commanded this to be done, even if death does not follow from it. The third is against those who harbor, defend, or hide those other men, <term>Extra de homicidio, cap. Per humani</term> <gloss>On homicide, ch. By human [law]</gloss>, book six. ¶ The eleventh principal has two cases. The first is against those who have granted reprisals or seizures where one is burdened for another, against ecclesiastical persons or their goods. The second is against those who have procured reprisals not allowed by custom or use against those, that is, ecclesiastical persons, unless they have revoked such presumption within a month, to be counted from the time of the granting or the extortion, <term>Extra de iniuriis, cap. Sicut pignorationes</term> <gloss>On injuries, ch. As seizures</gloss>, book six. ¶ The twelfth principal contains two. The first is against those who, for the reason that they have given license to kill, capture, or otherwise harm kings, princes, barons, nobles, bailiffs, or ministers whatsoever, or any others whatsoever against whom a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict has been promulgated, or [against] those who have brought such sentences, or whose occasion [the offense] was, or those observing such sentences, or those wishing to excommunicate such excommunicated persons, unless they have revoked the licenses while the matter is whole, or if a process was made for the seizure of goods by the occasion of that license, unless they have returned those goods or provided satisfaction for them within eight days. The second is against those who have dared to use the given license, or to omit any of the aforementioned on their own motion, <term>Extra de sententia excommunicationis, cap. Quicunque</term> <gloss>On the sentence of excommunication, ch. Whosoever</gloss>, book six. And these two cases are reserved to the Pope, if someone has stood in that excommunication for two months. ¶ The thirteenth.

X.text: principal contains two, and both are reserved to the Pope. The first, in <term>Clementinae, de poenis, cap. Si quis</term> <gloss>Clementines, on punishments, ch. If anyone</gloss>: if anyone has injuriously or rashly struck the pontiff, or captured or banished him, or if he has commanded it to be done, or has ratified it after it was done by others, or has been a partner in these things of the doer, or has given counsel or favor in these things, or knowingly defended the same, in those cases of the aforementioned in which they would not undergo the excommunicators through the published canons. Gloss on the word "of the aforementioned," as in the one banishing or the one commanding it, or the partner holding it ratified, etc., as follows. The second: indeed the powers, councilors, aldermen, advocates, rectors, consuls, and officials of the same, in whatever name they are counted, existing culpable in the premises, all incur excommunications to be absolved by the Pope, except in the article of death, in <term>Clementinae, de poenis, cap. 1</term> <gloss>Clementines, on punishments, ch. 1</gloss>. The fourteenth principal is also reserved to the Pope: that temporal lords who compel some to celebrate divine [offices] in an interdicted place, or who through criers cause the people to be evacuated to hear them, or forbid those publicly excommunicated or interdicted, after they were warned, from leaving the churches while masses are celebrated, or they themselves, having been notified, do not leave, they are excommunicated in <term>Clementinae, de sententia excommunicationis, cap. Quisque</term> <gloss>Clementines, on the sentence of excommunication, ch. Each</gloss>. The fifteenth principal is in <term>Clementinae, Ex gravi, de usuris</term> <gloss>Clementines, Out of serious [offense], on usury</gloss>, all six cases. Namely, cities and officials making [such statutes], behold the first. Dictating them, behold the second. Or writing statutes on usuries to be paid, not to be recovered, or not to be restored, behold the third. Or judging according to them, behold the fourth. Or not deleting them from the city books if they could within three months, behold the fifth. Or aiding them, behold the sixth: they are excommunicated. Also, they incur the same sentences, whoever [they are]: the powers of the cities themselves, captains, rectors, consuls, judges, councilors, or other officials whatsoever attempting the premises. The sixteenth principal contains six in <term>Clementinae, de consanguinitate et affinitate, cap. unico</term> <gloss>Clementines, on consanguinity and affinity, ch. single</gloss>: namely, drawing up a marriage in a degree of consanguinity, behold the first. And of prohibited affinity, behold the second. Or with a nun, behold the third: he is excommunicated. The same is regarding religious so doing, and nuns, and also clerics placed in sacred orders, behold again the other three cases. And the gloss says that this is established in the examples of the aforesaid cases only.

pages.42: Seventh: when, as the holy Saint Thomas says, a subject knows his own priest to be a heretic, or a solicitor to evil, or frail regarding the sin about which one confesses, or likely to reveal the confession, or if he reasonably estimates that the priest is a revealer of confession, or if the sin about which one ought to confess was committed against him. In these cases, and in others where the penitent reasonably fears danger to himself or to the priest from the confession made, he ought to have recourse to the superior and ask for license to confess to another. If he cannot have this, the judgment is the same as for one who does not have access to a confessor; indeed, he ought rather to confess to a layman in this case. And if he has no other priest, let him confess to his own, while remaining silent about that from which the danger arises. Eighth: when one is in danger of death and has a stranger, for then that person is his own in a certain way. ¶ The second rule: let the confessor, who keeps watch to purify souls, strive to be pure. He should place the hope of his labor and of succeeding with others not in his own strength, but in divine beauty, because according to the Apostle, neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase. Therefore, the confessor should pray frequently, as the wise physician also advises, so that God, who heals all infirmities, may direct his work, and may strengthen and increase it through His power. ¶ The third rule: let him be careful not to act precipitously regarding the person confessing. He should not provoke him by merely rushing, but by patience and vigilance, examining and judging everything fully. He should not interrupt, even if the words of the confessor are slow; he should remember what is said, and subsequently ask distinctly. If he cannot trust his memory, he should investigate at least cautiously, cleanly, and individually. He should prompt the confessor <note>The text here refers to the person confessing, though the source text mistakenly uses "ofessor" (confessor) instead of "ofitetis" (the one confessing)</note> to repeat diligently those things that were to be confessed and imposed, and he should take sufficient time for this. For as the Chancellor <note>Johannes Gerson, often referred to as 'Cancellarius' in medieval penitential literature</note> says, it is preferable to hear a few perfectly than many imperfectly, since the scruple of the office is not so much to expedite as to avoid hindering. He asks, therefore, if he is burdened with many, to defer the confessions until after Easter, lest some, like the blind leading the blind, deceive themselves by behaving as if they were absolved when they were not absolved. For what is written in this word of God in Ezekiel: "You, son of man, I have made a watchman to the house of Israel. Hearing therefore the word from my mouth, you shall declare it to them from me. If when I say to the wicked, you shall surely die, you have not spoken so that the wicked might guard himself from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. But if you have announced to the wicked that he should turn from his ways, and he has not turned from his way, he himself shall die in his iniquity, but you have saved your soul."
pages.43: The fourth rule: it is expedient that the confessor obtain from the superior of the subjects, as far as possible, authority in reserved cases, beyond the relaxations. Especially, unless there are public and scandalous cases. For very few, as the Chancellor says, do not fall into some such cases which are reserved. They themselves, the confessors, knowing that they ought not to be sent thereafter to another, reveal everything more freely. The confessor, indeed, presumes to interrogate them more freely, and more fully about each thing, because he trusts to heal them by absolving them at once. For what else is it to send the penitent from judge to judge in hidden things, than to add affliction to the afflicted? Certainly, many existing in filth cause it more casually or occasionally, and become more filthy. Christ did not truly act thus with the Samaritan, about whom Isaiah prophesies thus: "He shall not crush the bruised reed, and he shall not extinguish the smoking flax; he shall bring forth judgment in truth. He shall not be sad, nor turbulent." The fifth rule, according to Hubert in his book on the instruction of officials in the chapter on the audience of confessions: He should provide such a place for sitting that he may be seen by many, especially when he hears women, and so that the confession cannot be heard by anyone. In which, certainly, he aids the reputation of both himself and the one confessing. For the confessor is an angel of the Lord of hosts, as Malachi says. And of the confessor and the one confessing, Christ says: "He who does truth comes to the light, that his works may be manifest, because they are done in God." Thus also blessed Jerome informs Nepotianus: "All suspicions," he says, "and whatever can be probably imagined, let them be avoided by you. Abstain from all evil appearance," the Apostle commands. But those anticipating these rules fall very easily into suspicion regarding women, as Job says: "The eye of the adulterer observes darkness." Therefore, as Hubert says, if any great persons of the male sex wish to confess, of whom the confessor believes they would be ashamed to be seen in the presence of all, he ought to lead them to another place that is more secret and honorable.
pages.44: The sixth rule: the one about to hear women should take care that, while he purges their souls of vices, he himself does not become soiled by voluntary delights. It should not be a cloth that becomes filthy while washing others; if it is to be thus, it should be the hand that shines while wiping others. Therefore, let him not believe himself to be a respecter of persons when he listens to the beautiful or young more freely and quickly than the old in confession, because he should guard himself with good and holy imaginations. First, by considering that he ought to be God's angel and the vicar of God trembling in judgment. Then, from the verse or clause, he should see with the eyes of the body and soul the light of the women, seeing the souls as if they were the leprous or wounded image of God, marked by the dire wounds of demonic mortal sins, or at least wrinkled or scabrous with venial faults, which must be healed through the blood of Christ and the sacraments of penance. The confessor should secretly make the sign of the cross with his thumb upon his own sinner, a little for the sake of protecting purity, and he should invoke at least a brief prayer or short oration to God, and he should avoid, without necessity, sweet words and all useless storytelling of the penitent. And thus, he should firmly apply himself solely to the honor of God and the salvation of another's soul. Nor should he despair if he is tempted while he resists the delight of the flesh, mindful of where Christ said to the disciples: "If they drink anything deadly, it shall not harm them." He removes the appearances, etc. Concerning which, the blessed Gregory says: "Priests, by their good exhortations, remove malice from the hearts of others; they remove the appearances, and while they hear the pestiferous suggestions and pray for those who are tempted, it is deadly what they drink, and it shall not harm them." Let the same be consulted in his Pastoral Care, where he says thus: "It happens frequently that while the rector's soul knows the temptations of another, he is himself struck by hearing the temptations, and these are by no means to be feared by the pastor, who so easily delivers others from their own, and who, with such mercy, is fatigued by the temptation of another." Whose reasons the holy Thomas also manifests in the fourth <note>referring to his Commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, Book IV</note>, saying thus: "The prayer that one gives in the sacrament of penance restores. If any inclination to sin arises from the circumstance—namely, of the necessary speech of carnal things—whether in the confitent or in the confessor." The seventh rule: the confessor should not look at the face of the one confessing, especially a woman, lest the one confessing be ashamed, and lest he be wounded in mind by the woman, as a spiritual surgeon.
pages.45: Because according to that of Habakkuk: "His face is like the burning wind." Whence the gloss upon that in Genesis, "she saw the tree was desirable to the sight," says: "Lest we be tripped up in thought, we ought not to look at what is not permitted to be coveted." For as the pure mind is preserved in thought, the eyes are to be filled by the delight of its pleasure as if they were certain robbers of guilt. For Eve would not have touched the tree if she had not first looked at it incautiously. It must be pondered how much we ought to restrain ourselves from illicit things, because we live mortally if what is alive for others comes to death through the eyes. The eighth rule: let the confessor take the greatest care that, at the beginning of the confession or especially in its progression, he is not sad, austere, or rigid, which is very rare with those confessing, whether timid or simple. For soon the mouth of the sinner will be closed. Rather, he should be kind and mild, in the manner of a prudent physician, and affable. Therefore, before anyone begins to confess, he who is not accustomed to confessing—as is true of many, especially the bashful and the young—he can say something to prompt the confession. And if the situation requires, he can ask about his own father and daughter: "Whoever wishes to confess, let him take the courage to speak." Because certain persons, out of bashfulness at the beginning, lose all memory of what is to be confessed, especially the young and women who confess rarely. Then he may proceed to other doctrines that follow. This is shown by the one whose place the confessor holds, Christ, when he says: "The healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill." Thus he himself acted, who did not abhor the sinner in the city and the publicans, but called them to penance. He says: "The son of man came not to call the just, but sinners." Regarding women, Hubert says he should not delay long, unless the necessity of the confession requires it, and those who call frequently, and those who wish to confess often, he should restrain from such excess and useless frequency. He should assign them a certain time for confessing, so that he may not hear them at other times, nor expose himself in other frequent conversations. He should use harsh and rigid words to them rather than soft ones, because, as the venerable Bonaventure says, such women and those like them, not knowing themselves and the priests, infect them incredibly, and without the loss of time, fall into sins with the priest, losing too much time. Christ taught about the aforementioned rigor of words when he said to his most holy mother: "What is it to me and to you? ... my hour has not yet come." However, the blessed Dionysius, in his letter to Demophilus, persuades with wonderful authorities the aforementioned kindness toward sinners, alleging Moses, the most mild man. Of the most gentle God, who by his nature is most benign, Christ the shepherd, who having left the ninety-nine, carried the lost sheep on his shoulders with joy. The woman sought the tenth drachma solicitously. And the father of the prodigal son, whom he received with gifts most mercifully.
pages.46: The ninth rule is that the confessor should persuade those who confess rarely and those who are bashful that it is an evil, foolish vice to conceal sins knowingly in confession, from which one incurs many new evils. For he incurs a new sin, hypocrisy, which Christ especially persecuted in the Pharisees. He feigns and shows himself innocent when he is guilty. Of pride, because he wants to appear good or less bad than he is. He deceives himself; he does not deceive the priest. He receives no fruit of the confession, because it is null, and he is bound to repeat it entirely. He dishonors the sacrament of penance, which is long and for the sake of second favor. He deceives himself, not the priest. Truly, it would be better not to confess than to feign a confession. Of whom the Psalm says: "The Lord has scattered the bones of those who please men; they are confounded because God has despised them." Which all will have their place on the day of judgment, when all and individual sins will not be known to one man, but will be exposed to the whole world with eternal damnation. Of this, the Truth also says: "Whoever will be ashamed of me, that is, of the truth, before men, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty and the glory of the saints." The tenth rule is that the confessor will be able to tell him who wishes to confess the fruits and the benefits he receives from a pure confession, if he grieves for the past and intends to guard against the future. First, the remission of all sins, according to that of the Psalm: "I said I will confess against myself my injustices to the Lord, and you have forgiven the impiety of my sin." Second, he receives a new sacramental grace and the grace of virtues, or its increase, through the merit of the passion of Christ, which works in the sacraments. Third, he will receive the union of God with the soul, which is new or greater than before, because then God loves him, and he keeps His word, and consequently, to the one confessing, such a union of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is made a dwelling. Fourth, he is adorned with a new soul, or at least a disposition of some good habit is imprinted, because according to the Psalm: "Confession and beauty," then in His sight, when we know the majesty of such a one in the sanctification of God. Fifth, the penalty of hell, which would endure for infinite time for a mortal sin, is changed into a finite penalty, which lasts when one is contrite before the confession.
pages.47: By virtue of the sacrament of confession to be received. And when one actually confesses, the aforementioned finite penalty, by virtue of the sacrament, is proportioned to the strength of the one confessing and is made smaller. Whence in every confession, a certain indulgence is given, known to God, and therefore if anyone is contrite after mortal sins and actually receives the sacrament of penance and dies immediately, he is delivered more quickly from purgatory than one who dies in similar sins, because the one who is contrite receives the sacrament only by desire. Sixth, he is adapted so that he may be able to receive other sacraments worthily and fruitfully, namely the Eucharist, holy oil, and matrimony, which one ought not to receive after mortal sin unless he has confessed first. Seventh, it brings joy to the conscience and is an excellent remedy against sudden death. For one who is confessed and contrite, if he dies in an instant, is entirely saved, although by fire, and thus does not die badly. But one who is not contrite nor confessed dies, and even if he lives a thousand years, such a one dies a bad death and suddenly, because he would depart to be damned. The eleventh rule is that the confessor should avoid the acceptance of persons, which is justice—that one person is preferred to another for an undue cause. Whence he should not honor poverty, deformity, or stupidity, nor, on the contrary, should he accept riches, beauty, or wisdom, unless he ought to hope for greater fruit and honor before God from that wisdom, which he ought to seek principally, as he is the judge of souls, and not favors, gain, or friendship. "Freely," Christ says, "you have received, freely give." So the Lord cries through Moses in Deuteronomy: "Hear the parties, and what is just, judge, whether he be a citizen or a stranger. There will be no difference of persons. You shall hear the small as the great. Nor shall you accept the person of anyone, because it is the judgment of God." And again: "You shall not accept a person nor gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and change the words of the just." Being tempted and observing this rule, it is accustomed to attract the hearts of men to iron, just as a magnet attracts iron. The twelfth rule: if in the confession itself it happens that he hears the enormities of sins of any kind, he should not despise, nor judge the sinner, but hear with patience and compassion, from the example of the blessed Ambrose, who, by hearing similar things, began to weep out of compassion, so that he made the confessors weep with him. Thus also Christ, the most innocent son of the virgin, heard patiently the accusers of the woman taken in adultery for a long time, until one after another departed, saying: "He who is without sin among you, let him be the first to cast a stone at her." For it is the grace of God, as Augustine says in his book On Nature and Grace, to be attributed that you have not done what you could have done through sin.
pages.48: What the confessor has to ask from the one confessing in general, and there are seven things, and how he ought to inform him according to the same, etc., as follows below. ¶ Chapter 2. Second, the confessor should see what he has to ask from the one confessing in general and inform him. For there are seven things, and he should inform him according to the same, fittingly according to the quality of the persons, yet more or less as necessity teaches. ¶ First, let him ask, according to John of Freiburg in his Confessional, how long it has been since he has confessed, if he now wishes to confess and has not confessed to himself before. If he answers that he does not know how long, so that he does not know how to distinguish the sins committed between the last confession and those he has done up to now, then the confessor should order a general confession to be made of all and individual sins. But if he knows how to distinguish those he has perpetrated since the last confession, thus it is not necessary to repeat those previously confessed unless there is a case for which it is necessary to repeat a previous confession. ¶ Second, let him ask whether the one confessing is entangled in any case in which confession is necessarily or probably to be repeated. Of which there are four or five. The first is when the confessor, due to his own fault, could not absolve, as when he was not a priest, or when he could absolve in some things but not in all, and in the same things he did not send to the superior, because thus he is still bound to go to the superior for absolution, unless ignorance would sometimes excuse the one confessing. The second, when the one confessing, due to his own fault, could not be absolved, as for example, because he was excommunicated, and the confessor could not absolve from excommunication, or if he tried to do so, yet he did not have the authority. For no one can be absolved from major excommunication by one who does not have the power of absolution, according to the holy Thomas. The third, when someone, knowingly and out of bashfulness, hypocrisy, or similar cause, concealed a sin that was necessarily to be confessed, unless thereafter he specifically and explicitly confessed his deception to a superior or to the previous confessor, remembering it at least in some way, and confessed those things which he had not confessed even explicitly.
pages.49: And he does not divide other privileged sins in an implicit confession, however, when he asks superiors about greater sins, or when the good faith of the simple or ignorance excuses, or where the confessor or the confitent would be scandalized, as was said in the first rule, in the seventh case of the first chapter. Moreover, if he forgot to do penance or omitted it, and does not remember it, many say that although it is not safer, it is not necessary to confess everything, according to the fourth question of penance <note>Likely referring to the Fourth Book of Sentences</note>, because then it is not necessary to confess all things. Nor even, according to some, is it necessary when the one confessing is only contrite or not contrite, and then he is absolved, for he ought afterwards to confess his contrition. Nevertheless, fiction or feigning in confession occurs, according to the Chancellor, when someone knowingly conceals something or has persisted in the purpose of sinning, or knows and ought to know that he cannot be absolved by such a one. And if there is fiction, he is bound to repeat the confession according to the more probable opinion, and that is the fifth case. For, as will be said later, everyone, even if not contrite, ought to confess all sins for many reasons that follow. Similarly, as the fourth question of penance says, it is not necessary to repeat this confession if he did not think something was a sin, or a venial sin that becomes mortal, and therefore did not confess it, because he did not have it on his conscience. Yet afterwards he has it, although it is safer to repeat it. Furthermore, because he was forgetful of some sin in confession, it is not necessary that he repeat everything later, whether he confesses before or anew. But he is only bound to confess the forgotten things and the forgotten sin. What in the previous case happens is ignorance of the law, and in this case, ignorance of fact. Third, let him ask and labor, especially regarding the young and small, so that he may have the opportunity to make a general confession from them, because, as the Chancellor says, they hardly or never confess completely unless perhaps they are taught by such a confessor as is described here. Indeed, it is useful for those who are old, rural, simple, or women; otherwise they cannot easily be led to this, unless such interrogations are made by them: "Did you have a conscience about such sins, and about such, and about such an age, and about such a company, and were you in the company of such?" And according to the response, the confessor will be able to note if the confession was made fully otherwise, and if not, then he should induce them to complete it. Fourth, if while entering or continuing the confession he perceives that the confessing person is not contrite about some sin, as often happens regarding carnal love, or fraternal hatred, or not wanting to make restitution, or similar things, and because of that...

N.text: The sixth rule: the one about to hear women should take care that, while he purges their souls of vices, he himself does not become soiled by voluntary delights. It should not be a cloth that becomes filthy while washing others; if it is to be thus, it should be the hand that shines while wiping others. Therefore, let him not believe himself to be a respecter of persons when he listens to the beautiful or young more freely and quickly than the old in confession, because he should guard himself with good and holy imaginations. First, by considering that he ought to be God's angel and the vicar of God trembling in judgment. Then, from the verse or clause, he should see with the eyes of the body and soul the light of the women, seeing the souls as if they were the leprous or wounded image of God, marked by the dire wounds of demonic mortal sins, or at least wrinkled or scabrous with venial faults, which must be healed through the blood of Christ and the sacraments of penance. The confessor should secretly make the sign of the cross with his thumb upon his own sinner, a little for the sake of protecting purity, and he should invoke at least a brief prayer or short oration to God, and he should avoid, without necessity, sweet words and all useless storytelling of the penitent. And thus, he should firmly apply himself solely to the honor of God and the salvation of another's soul. Nor should he despair if he is tempted while he resists the delight of the flesh, mindful of where Christ said to the disciples: "If they drink anything deadly, it shall not harm them." He removes the appearances, etc. Concerning which, the blessed Gregory says: "Priests, by their good exhortations, remove malice from the hearts of others; they remove the appearances, and while they hear the pestiferous suggestions and pray for those who are tempted, it is deadly what they drink, and it shall not harm them." Let the same be consulted in his Pastoral Care, where he says thus: "It happens frequently that while the rector's soul knows the temptations of another, he is himself struck by hearing the temptations, and these are by no means to be feared by the pastor, who so easily delivers others from their own, and who, with such mercy, is fatigued by the temptation of another." Whose reasons the holy Thomas also manifests in the fourth <note>referring to his Commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, Book IV</note>, saying thus: "The prayer that one gives in the sacrament of penance restores. If any inclination to sin arises from the circumstance—namely, of the necessary speech of carnal things—whether in the confitent or in the confessor." The seventh rule: the confessor should not look at the face of the one confessing, especially a woman, lest the one confessing be ashamed, and lest he be wounded in mind by the woman, as a spiritual surgeon.

X.text: Because according to that of Habakkuk: "His face is like the burning wind." Whence the gloss upon that in Genesis, "she saw the tree was desirable to the sight," says: "Lest we be tripped up in thought, we ought not to look at what is not permitted to be coveted." For as the pure mind is preserved in thought, the eyes are to be filled by the delight of its pleasure as if they were certain robbers of guilt. For Eve would not have touched the tree if she had not first looked at it incautiously. It must be pondered how much we ought to restrain ourselves from illicit things, because we live mortally if what is alive for others comes to death through the eyes. The eighth rule: let the confessor take the greatest care that, at the beginning of the confession or especially in its progression, he is not sad, austere, or rigid, which is very rare with those confessing, whether timid or simple. For soon the mouth of the sinner will be closed. Rather, he should be kind and mild, in the manner of a prudent physician, and affable. Therefore, before anyone begins to confess, he who is not accustomed to confessing—as is true of many, especially the bashful and the young—he can say something to prompt the confession. And if the situation requires, he can ask about his own father and daughter: "Whoever wishes to confess, let him take the courage to speak." Because certain persons, out of bashfulness at the beginning, lose all memory of what is to be confessed, especially the young and women who confess rarely. Then he may proceed to other doctrines that follow. This is shown by the one whose place the confessor holds, Christ, when he says: "The healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill." Thus he himself acted, who did not abhor the sinner in the city and the publicans, but called them to penance. He says: "The son of man came not to call the just, but sinners." Regarding women, Hubert says he should not delay long, unless the necessity of the confession requires it, and those who call frequently, and those who wish to confess often, he should restrain from such excess and useless frequency. He should assign them a certain time for confessing, so that he may not hear them at other times, nor expose himself in other frequent conversations. He should use harsh and rigid words to them rather than soft ones, because, as the venerable Bonaventure says, such women and those like them, not knowing themselves and the priests, infect them incredibly, and without the loss of time, fall into sins with the priest, losing too much time. Christ taught about the aforementioned rigor of words when he said to his most holy mother: "What is it to me and to you? ... my hour has not yet come." However, the blessed Dionysius, in his letter to Demophilus, persuades with wonderful authorities the aforementioned kindness toward sinners, alleging Moses, the most mild man. Of the most gentle God, who by his nature is most benign, Christ the shepherd, who having left the ninety-nine, carried the lost sheep on his shoulders with joy. The woman sought the tenth drachma solicitously. And the father of the prodigal son, whom he received with gifts most mercifully.

Concerning those who presumed to write those judgments in public form. <note>original: "exē de sen. exē c. nouerit fmitas tua"</note> (concerning sentences of excommunication, in the chapter "Your steadfastness may know"). All these are understood, says Petrus de Palude, where they seem to be works against ecclesiastical liberty, which the rustics established: that no one should offer except on great feasts, or unless they buy, or that there should not be such a cloth or so many candles over a dead body, or that they all distribute all the works of the deceased to help the works themselves in a shameful case, and the like. Because the liberty of the church is free offerings and free burials. If, however, those of any one kind order that they bury somewhere else, and since this is not a binding statute, and if it is the work of one of the churches, it is not seen to fall upon the other. Concerning precious cloths and a multitude of candles, when citizens forbid such things so that they do not harm themselves with their pomps, others say that it is permissible provided it is done for the good of all, not wishing to harm ecclesiastical liberties by this. The fourth principal encompasses two points. The first: concerning those who compel emperors or others recurring to the ecclesiastical forum to desist concerning causes that belong to the same forum by law or by some custom, or [who compel them] to litigate in the secular forum about such questions instead of through the judgment of the churches, or [who compel] the petitioners or litigants themselves, or those wishing to litigate, or those who are their own or their things, because they even by capture or other ways whatsoever have worked [against them], or have caused or procured them to be compelled, or by themselves or others have impeded [the process] so that they cannot freely obtain justice for the aforementioned causes before ecclesiastical judges, or before legates, or [before] ordinaries. The second is concerning those who have given counsel, aid, or favor to do the aforementioned things, as [written] in <term>Eminentium</term> <gloss>a decree concerning ecclesiastical liberty</gloss>, book VI, where Petrus de Palude also notes: if someone counsels his friend to rather encounter a layman before the appointed power, [such as] a master of the guild where he will immediately have his right through the possessions of the person or by the sequestration of goods than before an official, where he eventually follows his right, he does not fall [into excommunication], although the other previously wished to litigate before the church. He whose counsel someone is unwillingly forced to desist from litigating in the church, he mediates.

<summary>This page continues the cataloging of cases resulting in excommunication, focusing on secular interference in ecclesiastical jurisdiction, burial customs, and the use of legal counsel to divert cases from church courts.</summary>
<keywords>Excommunication, ecclesiastical liberty, jurisdiction, burial, Petrus de Palude</keywords>
pages.35:
The fifth principal is concerning the immunity of the church and those who, obtaining temporal dominion by the license of anyone whatsoever, forbid their subjects to sell anything to prelates, clerics, or ecclesiastical persons, or to buy anything from them, or to grind wheat, bake bread, or show them other services; he is not bound by the aforementioned decree, except for dukes and prelates. The sixth principal is against those who, for their own proper goods—which they do not carry or cause to be carried for the sake of trade—demand or extort tolls or such similar things from churches and ecclesiastical persons, either by themselves or others in their name or another's, or compel them to pay such things, contrary custom notwithstanding. And the bishop of the place ought to publish them as excommunicated, or have them published by his subjects, until they have restored what was thus exacted and have properly made satisfaction for such transgression <note>original: "extra de censibus et quaestione libro quinto § qui vero nec exculant"</note> (concerning censuses and question, book five, section "He who indeed," nor do they excuse [them] by the aforementioned decree, from the time of which memory exists). He who tolls clerics—which the Pope understands as concerning old tolls, not new ones. The seventh principal case consists of two parts. First, that laymen who formerly by force or by fear compelled prelates or the chapter of churches or other ecclesiastical persons to submit to them immovable goods or rights of the churches without the consent of the chapter and the license of the Pope, [are excommunicated] unless, after repeated admonition, they relax such submissions. And that they henceforth compel prelates or other ecclesiastical persons to do such things [is also prohibited]. The second: whoever, through a submission duly made thus far, usurps anything beyond that which is permitted by lawful agreement, unless, being lawfully warned, he desists from such usurpation and restores even what he has thus usurped <note>original: "extra de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis et hoc novissimo § laici libro sexto"</note> (concerning things of the church not to be alienated, and in this most recent section "Laymen," book six). The eighth principal has two parts. The first is against those who, under the title of royal custody or the guard of their advocacy or defense, attempting to usurp anew in churches, monasteries, or other pious places, presume to usurp the goods of the same vacant churches, monasteries, or pious places. The second is against the clerics, monks of the monasteries, and persons of the churches of the same places who permit this to be done <note>original: "extra de electione"</note> (concerning election).

<summary>This page details the fifth through eighth principal cases of excommunication, concerning the immunity of church property, the prohibition of tolls on clerics, and the unauthorized usurpation of church goods or rights under the guise of royal guardianship.</summary>
<keywords>Immunity, church property, tolls, excommunication, royal advocacy, monasteries</keywords>

in general, book VI. The ninth principal is against those who presume to harm clerics or any other ecclesiastical persons—to whom election in any churches, monasteries, or other pious places belongs—or their kinsmen, or the churches, monasteries, or places themselves, by spoiling them of their goods themselves or through others, or by otherwise justly persecuting them, for the reason that those requested or otherwise induced did not want to elect him for whom they were requested or induced <note>original: "exē de elec. sciant cūcti li. vi."</note> (concerning election, "Let all know," book VI). The tenth principal contains three cases. The first: against those who have caused some Christians to be killed by other men. The second: against those who have ordered this to be done, even if death does not follow from it. The third: against those who harbor, defend, or hide other men. <note>original: "exē de homicidi. c. p hūani li. vi."</note> (concerning homicide, chapter "By human [law]," book VI). The eleventh principal has two cases. The first: against those who have granted reprisals or attachments where one is burdened for another, against ecclesiastical persons or their goods. The second: against those who have procured reprisals from custom not permitted by use, against those same ecclesiastical ones, unless they have revoked such presumption within a month from the time of the grant or extortion <note>original: "exē de iniurijs. c. zli pignozatōes li. vi."</note> (concerning injuries, chapter "And such attachments," book VI). The twelfth principal contains two. The first is against those who, because of sentences of excommunication, suspension, or interdict promulgated against kings, princes, barons, nobles, bailiffs, or ministers whatsoever, have given license to others to kill, capture, or otherwise harm them in their persons or goods, or those who have brought such sentences, or those who are the cause of them, or those observing such sentences, or those wishing to excommunicate such excommunicated persons, unless they have revoked the licenses while the matter was intact, or if a process was made for the capture of goods on the occasion of that license, unless they have restored the goods within eight days or have made satisfaction for them. The second is against those who have dared to use the given license or to omit any of the aforementioned things by their own motion <note>original: "exē de sen. ex. c. quicūqz li. vi."</note> (concerning sentences of excommunication, chapter "Whoever," book VI). And these two cases are reserved to the Pope, if someone has stood in that excommunication for two months.

<summary>This page covers the ninth through twelfth categories of excommunication, involving retaliation against church electors, homicide, illegal reprisals, and the granting of illicit licenses to harm those acting under ecclesiastical censures.</summary>
<keywords>Excommunication, election, homicide, reprisals, papal reservation</keywords>
pages.37:
The thirteenth principal contains two, and both are reserved to the Pope. The first, from the Clementines <note>original: "in cle. c. si qs"</note>, chapter "If anyone": if anyone has injuriously or rashly struck a pontiff, or captured or banned him, or has ordered it to be done, or has ratified what was done by others, or has been a partner in these things of the doer, or has given counsel or favor in these things, or knowingly has defended the same, in those cases of the aforementioned in which the excommunicators would not undergo [the penalty] by the published canons. The gloss on the word "of the aforementioned" as in the one banning or ordering it, or the partner ratifying it, etc., as follows. The second: the powers, councilors, aldermen, advocates, rectors, consuls, and officials of the same, in whatever name they are called, existing as guilty in the premises, incur the excommunications, to be absolved by the Popes, except in the article of death, in the Clementines <note>original: "in cle. de pe. c. i."</note> (concerning penalties, chapter 1). The fourteenth principal is also reserved to the Pope: that temporal lords who compel some to celebrate divine [offices] in an interdicted place, or who through criers cause the people to be evacuated to hear them, or forbid that publicly excommunicated or interdicted [persons]—upon warning to those celebrating masses—exit the churches, or [those who] do not exit when warned, are excommunicated in the Clementines <note>original: "in cle. de sen. ex. quis"</note> (concerning sentences of excommunication, "Whoever"). The fifteenth principal is in the Clementines, "On usury," all six cases. Namely, cities and officials doing [it]—behold the first. Dictating—behold the second. Or writing statutes about usury being paid, not being reclaimed, or being restored—behold the third. Or judging according to them—behold the fourth. Or not deleting them if they could within three months from the city's books—behold the fifth. Or helping them—behold the sixth, [they] are excommunicated. Likewise, they incur the sentences: whoever of the cities themselves, powers, captains, rectors, consuls, judges, councilors, or other officials attempting the premises. The sixteenth principal contains six in the Clementines, "On consanguinity and affinity," the only chapter; namely, contracting marriage in a degree of consanguinity—behold the first. And of prohibited affinity—behold the second. Or with a nun—behold the third, [he] is excommunicated. The same is for religious so doing, and nuns, and also clerics constituted in sacred orders—behold again the other three cases. And the gloss says that this is constituted in the aforementioned cases only.

<summary>This page outlines the thirteenth through sixteenth cases of excommunication, including physical assault on a pontiff, forcing forbidden religious services, usury, and marriage within prohibited degrees of consanguinity or affinity.</summary>
<keywords>Excommunication, pontiff, usury, marriage, consanguinity, affinity, nun</keywords>

Therefore, if anyone draws [into marriage] with someone having a spouse, or with a Jewess or a pagan, or [someone] related spiritually or legally, or any impediment of public honesty, there is no place for this penalty. The seventeenth principal is against those judges who fraudulently would cause a woman to be named as a witness in a case, so that he might more easily visit or approach her personally, or bring her to the court. This case, as Petrus de Palude says, is rarely omitted. It can be omitted if some judge feigned this, so that he might enter to women living under enclosure <note>original: "ext de iudi. c. mlieres li. vi."</note> (extravagants concerning judges, chapter "Women," book VI). The eighteenth principal is: whoever, of whatever status or degree, even if he shines with pontifical dignity, is an executor, or whoever else has caused a human dead body to be butchered, or divided into limbs, for the sake of carrying the bones for cooking for the sake of burial, as in the Extravagants of Boniface VIII, chapter "Detestable." The nineteenth principal case: when someone has fallen into a fact condemned by a statute of man, made under that form, so that he who does the truth is excommunicated <note>original: "de fen. ex. a nobis"</note> (concerning sentences of excommunication, "From us"). Where it must be known, says Petrus de Palude, that this is a sentence of law, not papal, special, or synodal, or of a council. Whence he who is subject to the statute by reason of his crime falls [into it], not another, in the place where the statute-maker puts it [to be] a statute or to excommunicate, because the statute of a council binds well in the diocese of suffragans. See also above, chapter 3, chapter 7, and chapter 4, chapter 6. The twentieth principal is against those who, by force or fear, have procured absolution from a sentence of excommunication, or any revocation of it, or of suspension or interdict <note>original: "de his q vi met? w. ca. fi. abfolutōis li vi"</note> (concerning these things which [are done] by force or fear, chapter final, "of absolution," book VI). This case, says Petrus de Palude, is to be understood concerning fear falling into a constant person, namely, shame or status, blows, and death, or if so by himself or by another, because it does not distinguish. The twenty-first contains two <note>original: "de fen. ex. eos q li. vi. et in cle. de pe. c. fi qs. § fi."</note> (concerning sentences of excommunication, "Those who," book VI, and in the Clementines concerning penalties, chapter "If anyone," section "final"). And both are sometimes reserved to the Pope. The first: concerning all those excommunicated by canon or by man who, because of danger of death or legitimate impediment, are absolved by someone other than him by whom they were to be absolved, from the canon "If anyone persuading," [are absolved] by an ordinary or by someone else who by law cannot. If, the danger or impediment afterwards ceasing, they have not contemplated those by whom they ought to be absolved by law, as soon as they can conveniently they must present themselves [to receive] the mandate of his concerning those things for which they were excommunicated, to receive and to make satisfaction as justice persuaded. And this is a papal case, if the sentence was reserved to the Pope, or episcopal if it was reserved to the bishop.

<summary>This page covers the seventeenth through twenty-first cases of excommunication, covering topics such as fraudulent judicial practices, desecration of corpses, statutes of man, forced absolutions, and improper absolution in emergencies.</summary>
<keywords>Excommunication, fraud, corpses, statute of man, absolution, papal reservation</keywords>
pages.39:
or such impediment, they have not contemplated those by whom they ought to be absolved by law, [they must] present themselves as soon as they conveniently can to receive the mandate of the same concerning those things for which they were excommunicated and to make satisfaction, as justice persuaded. And this is a papal case, if the sentence was reserved to the Pope; truly episcopal if it was reserved to the bishop. The second is against those who, when they have obtained the benefit of absolution from any sentences whatsoever from the Apostolic See or its legates, [it is] enjoined to them to present themselves to their ordinaries, or to any others whatsoever, to receive penance from the same, and to show proper satisfaction to the injured parties or to those to whom they are obligated by them, if they, when they can first conveniently, have not taken care to fulfill [it]. Both the former and the latter relapse into the sentence of excommunication <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> (by the act itself). And the sense is that those who were absolved by the Apostolic See or a legate, and it is mandated to them that they make satisfaction or present themselves to some judge, if they do not do so, in this case he who can and [who has the power] to do so will absolve, and no one else. The twenty-second principal contains William of Saint-Amour concerning the office of legate, chapter "Now it must be said," section 25: from the sentence of his legate or delegate whose jurisdiction has expired, and to whom no one succeeded in the office enjoined to him, only the Pope absolves <note>original: "exē de offi. de le. prudentiaz"</note> (extravagants concerning the office of legate, "Prudence"). If this is truly the same, it is to be understood, says William there, concerning the constitutions of his legates [whose office] is finished from the legate, nor does anyone succeed the legate, because in such a case there is no superior except the Pope. The twenty-third principal: since the Pope can exercise his office before coronation, therefore, because he would fight the [church's] lands on this occasion, he is excommunicated, as in the Extravagants of Benedict XI, which begins "Because some." The twenty-fourth principal is in the constitution of John XXII, "The son of brothers and fellow bishops," where it is held that if, with the empire vacant, anyone by virtue of any commission whatsoever made to him by a dead emperor, or under any other pretext, has usurped the goods of the empire or exercised jurisdiction or assumed for himself any vicariate or the name of any other office whatsoever, unless by special license of the Pope, all those obedient to them and to their commissaries in such things, or providing them aid, counsel, or favor in this, are excommunicated <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> (by the act itself).

<summary>This page details the twenty-second through twenty-fourth cases of excommunication, focusing on the expiration of legatine jurisdiction, the Pope's authority before coronation, and the unauthorized usurpation of imperial goods or jurisdiction during a vacancy.</summary>
<keywords>Excommunication, legates, papal jurisdiction, coronation, John XXII, empire</keywords>

The gloss understands here their lands or places to be considered not by reason of property alone but of jurisdictional superiority, and the places and whatever communities and universities subjected to the ecclesiastical interdict. The twenty-fifth, John XXII in the constitution "With malice growing," the principal is thus formed: If anyone in the province of the March of Ancona, subject to the Roman Church, has killed, invaded, offended, or otherwise treated badly a rector or other minister or official deputed by the Apostolic See, or any of their vicars or judges, or has given aid, counsel, or favor to this directly or indirectly, publicly or secretly, [he is] made unable for any benefits or offices whatsoever, and is excommunicated <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> (by the act itself) and reserved to the Pope alone. Absolutely other kinds of penalties are furthermore thundered there.

The twenty-sixth principal: all those who falsify the money of the King of France or carry other false money into the Kingdom of France are excommunicated <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> (by the act itself) and [it is] reserved to the Pope for the absolution [of them] by the constitution of John XXII, "The aforementioned," in the same [collection]. The twenty-seventh principal: if anyone has moved demons or demanded their aid or made treaties or pacts with demons, or has sacrificed to them or adored them, or in their name has set up images, rings, mirrors, mirrors of brooches, or any other thing for the sake of binding magic to the demons themselves, or has asked for responses from them or from those who heard [them] from the demons themselves, he is excommunicated <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> (by the act itself) by the constitution of John XXII, "Concerning the mirror." The twenty-eighth principal: if anyone has falsified the seal of any cardinal or, knowing it to be falsified by another, has used it, he is tied by that same anathema by the constitution of John XXII, "It compels us." The twenty-ninth principal: whoever has presumed to impede legates or even nuncios of the Apostolic See are excommunicated <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> (by the act itself), and the kingdoms, lands, and places whatsoever subjected to them are so long subjected to the ecclesiastical interdict as long as they have conducted themselves to persist in such contumacy, in the constitution of John XXII, "Above the peoples and kingdoms," etc.

¶ The Second part follows.

<summary>This page lists the twenty-fifth through twenty-ninth cases of excommunication, encompassing crimes against papal officials in the March of Ancona, counterfeiting, diabolical pacts and magic, forgery of cardinal seals, and obstruction of apostolic legates.</summary>
<keywords>Excommunication, papal officials, counterfeiting, magic, demons, John XXII, cardinal seals, legates</keywords>
pages.41:
How the confessor ought to dispose himself toward him who will confess to him, twelve rules are given above. ¶ Chapter one.

The second part now begins concerning the things necessary concomitantly to confession, in which, as a confessor performs the office of a physician, he may be able to heal the diseases of the mind more easily, he incorporates the seven following chapters in applying the sacrament of penance. ¶ First: concerning how he ought to prepare himself for the penitents to be well disposed. ¶ Second: what he ought to ask of the penitent himself generally. ¶ Third: which vices of luxury, concerning which there is great force, he may be able to specifically pry into from shame. ¶ Fourth: concerning how he ought to inform [the penitent] about the ends of confession, what it is fitting to correct, and by what [signs] he may know it is expedient to know that the confessed [person] is truly contrite or attrite. ¶ Fifth: what penance or satisfaction he ought to duly enjoin. ¶ Sixth: concerning how he may rightly absolve from sins and from sentences. ¶ Seventh: concerning how he ought to hold himself cautiously around the infirm and [concerning] the secrecy of confession. Concerning the first, before confession and about it, he should attend to the following twelve rules. ¶ First: that he may have authority or jurisdiction over the penitent, [if] he is an outsider who wishes to hear the confession, for example, the Pope, the bishop, the parish priest, or [if] he is a prelate, [or] a brother if he is of the mendicant order. For a subject can, in eight cases, confess to another than his own priest or to another than the one who was previously his own priest. First, when his own priest is altogether indiscreet and ignorant, and license is sought from him although not obtained, or at least license ought to be sought from the superior of the own confessor or priest, if it can be had. Second, when the parishioner has moved his domicile; then he is the subject of that priest to whose parish he has moved. Third, when someone seeks a domicile to which he may betake himself, because he is without a domicile. Fourth, when someone is a vagabond. Fifth, if he is in the university with the license of his prelates. Sixth, if he is a pilgrim who receives a wallet and staff from his own priest or his vicar or license, or if he is a merchant or a traveler, and receives license from his own priest; otherwise, however, if the pilgrim or merchant or traveler has not done the aforementioned.

<summary>This page introduces the second part of the manual, detailing the role of the confessor as a physician of the soul and the twelve rules for establishing jurisdiction over a penitent, including exceptions for travelers, pilgrims, and those with incompetent priests.</summary>
<keywords>Confession, penance, confessor, jurisdiction, parishioner, domicile, vagabond, pilgrim</keywords>
