The first is against those who, because of sentences of excommunication, suspension, or interdict promulgated against kings, princes, barons, nobles, bailiffs, or ministers whatsoever, have given license to others to kill, capture, or otherwise harm them in their persons or goods, or those who have brought such sentences, or those who are the cause of them, or those observing such sentences, or those wishing to excommunicate such excommunicated persons, unless they have revoked the licenses while the matter was intact, or if a process was made for the capture of goods on the occasion of that license, unless they have restored the goods within eight days or have made satisfaction for them. The second is against those who have dared to use the given license or to omit any of the aforementioned things by their own motion <note>original: "exē de sen. ex. c. quicūqz li. vi."</note> (concerning sentences of excommunication, chapter "Whoever," book VI). And these two cases are reserved to the Pope, if someone has stood in that excommunication for two months.

<summary>This page covers the ninth through twelfth categories of excommunication, involving retaliation against church electors, homicide, illegal reprisals, and the granting of illicit licenses to harm those acting under ecclesiastical censures.</summary>
<keywords>Excommunication, election, homicide, reprisals, papal reservation</keywords>

X.text:
The thirteenth principal contains two, and both are reserved to the Pope. The first, from the Clementines <note>original: "in cle. c. si qs"</note>, chapter "If anyone": if anyone has injuriously or rashly struck a pontiff, or captured or banned him, or has ordered it to be done, or has ratified what was done by others, or has been a partner in these things of the doer, or has given counsel or favor in these things, or knowingly has defended the same, in those cases of the aforementioned in which the excommunicators would not undergo [the penalty] by the published canons. The gloss on the word "of the aforementioned" as in the one banning or ordering it, or the partner ratifying it, etc., as follows. The second: the powers, councilors, aldermen, advocates, rectors, consuls, and officials of the same, in whatever name they are called, existing as guilty in the premises, incur the excommunications, to be absolved by the Popes, except in the article of death, in the Clementines <note>original: "in cle. de pe. c. i."</note> (concerning penalties, chapter 1). The fourteenth principal is also reserved to the Pope: that temporal lords who compel some to celebrate divine [offices] in an interdicted place, or who through criers cause the people to be evacuated to hear them, or forbid that publicly excommunicated or interdicted [persons]—upon warning to those celebrating masses—exit the churches, or [those who] do not exit when warned, are excommunicated in the Clementines <note>original: "in cle. de sen. ex. quis"</note> (concerning sentences of excommunication, "Whoever"). The fifteenth principal is in the Clementines, "On usury," all six cases. Namely, cities and officials doing [it]—behold the first. Dictating—behold the second. Or writing statutes about usury being paid, not being reclaimed, or being restored—behold the third. Or judging according to them—behold the fourth. Or not deleting them if they could within three months from the city's books—behold the fifth. Or helping them—behold the sixth, [they] are excommunicated. Likewise, they incur the sentences: whoever of the cities themselves, powers, captains, rectors, consuls, judges, councilors, or other officials attempting the premises. The sixteenth principal contains six in the Clementines, "On consanguinity and affinity," the only chapter; namely, contracting marriage in a degree of consanguinity—behold the first. And of prohibited affinity—behold the second. Or with a nun—behold the third, [he] is excommunicated. The same is for religious so doing, and nuns, and also clerics constituted in sacred orders—behold again the other three cases. And the gloss says that this is constituted in the aforementioned cases only.

<summary>This page outlines the thirteenth through sixteenth cases of excommunication, including physical assault on a pontiff, forcing forbidden religious services, usury, and marriage within prohibited degrees of consanguinity or affinity.</summary>
<keywords>Excommunication, pontiff, usury, marriage, consanguinity, affinity, nun</keywords>

pages.42:
Seventh: when, as Saint Thomas says, a subject knows his own priest to be a heretic, or a solicitor to evil, or frail regarding the sin of which one is confessing, or likely to reveal the confession, or if he reasonably estimates that the priest is a revealer of confession, or if the sin about which one ought to confess was committed against that priest. In these cases, and others in which the penitent reasonably fears danger to himself or the priest from the confession made, he ought to recur to a superior and seek license to confess to another. If he cannot have this, the judgment is the same as for one who has no access to a confessor; indeed, in this case, he ought to confess to a layman. And if he has no other priest, let him confess to his own, while remaining silent about that from which the danger arises. Eighth: when he is in danger of death and has another available, for then that one is his own in a certain way. 

¶ The second rule: Let him who watches over the cleansing of souls strive to be clean. He should place the hope of his labor and of profiting others not in his own strength, but in divine assistance, for according to the Apostle, neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase. Let the confessor therefore prepare himself and pray often, just as a wise physician also offers himself, so that God, who heals all infirmities, may direct the work and by His strength bolster and increase it. 

¶ The third rule: Let him beware not to act precipitately regarding the penitent, and let him not be provoked by a mere quick meeting. Let him examine and judge all things fully with careful deliberation, and let him not interrupt even if he can anticipate the words of the penitent. Let him remember what was said, and ask distinctly thereafter, or if he cannot trust his memory, let him at least investigate cautiously and clearly, and individually. Let him repeat with diligent questioning the medicines that should be applied to the sins of the one confessing, and let him take sufficient time for these things, for as <term>Cancellarius</term> <gloss>Chancellor Gerson</gloss> says, it is preferable in the audience of confessions to hear a few things completely than many things imperfectly, since the scruple of the office is not so much to expedite as to avoid rushing. He says, therefore, that if one could, it would be better to defer the confessions of many until after Easter, than to see some return like the blind leading the blind, since they might behave as if absolved when they were not truly absolved. For what is written in that word of God from Ezekiel? God says: "Son of man, I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel. Hearing the word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me. If, while I am saying to the wicked man, 'You shall die the death,' you have not spoken so that the wicked man might be guarded from his way, that same wicked man will die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand. But if you have announced it to the wicked man, so that he might turn from his ways and he has not turned from his way, he himself will die in his iniquity; furthermore, you have freed your own soul."
pages.43:
"The fourth" rule: It is expedient that the confessor obtain, as far as he is able, power from the prelate regarding his subjects in reserved cases, beyond those that are relaxed, especially if there are no public and scandalous cases. For very few are found, as the Chancellor says, who have not fallen into some such case that is not reserved. They themselves, the confessors, knowing that they ought not to be sent back to another, more freely and quickly reveal everything. The confessor, likewise, presumes to interrogate them more freely and fully one by one, and trusts in healing them by absolving them at once. For what else is it to send the penitent from judge to judge in hidden matters, but to add affliction to the afflicted? Certainly, many existing in filth, by making their confession causal or occasional, become even dirtier. Christ did not act thus toward the Samaritan, of whom Isaiah prophesied: "A bruised reed he shall not break, and a smoking flax he shall not extinguish. In truth he will bring forth judgment. He will not be sad nor turbulent." 

<term>The fifth</term> rule, according to <term>Hubertus</term> <gloss>Hubert of Romans</gloss> in his book on the instructions of officials in the chapter on the audience of confessions: He should choose such a place for sitting that he can be seen by many, especially when he hears women, and so that the confession can be heard by no one, in which he certainly provides for the fame both of himself and the penitent. For the confessor is the angel of the Lord of hosts, as Malachi says; and Christ says of the confessor and the one confessing: "He who does truth comes to the light, that his works may be manifested, which have been done in God." Thus also blessed <term>Jerome</term> informs Nepotianus: "Avoid all suspicions," he says, "and whatever can be probably imagined, do not let it be imagined by you. Abstain from every evil appearance," the Apostle commands. But those who allow these rules are easily subject to suspicion regarding women, as Job says: "The eye of the adulterer watches for darkness." Thus, as Hubertus says: If some great persons of the male sex wish to confess, of whom the confessor believes that they would be ashamed to be seen in the general assembly of confessions, he ought to lead them to another more secret and honorable place.
pages.44:
The sixth rule: One who is about to hear women should take care that, while he cleanses their souls from vices, he himself does not become soiled with voluntary delights. Let there not be a cloth that becomes filthy while washing another; if it be thus, let it be a hand that shines while wiping another. And so let him not believe himself a respecter of persons when he listens more freely and quickly to beautiful or young women than to old women in confession, so that he may protect himself with good and holy imaginations. First, by considering that he ought to be an angel of God and the vicar of God trembling in judgment. Then, from the verse or closing, let him see with the eyes of the body and the eyes of the soul that the woman's soul is, by the images of God, leprous or wounded by the dire wounds of mortal sins of demons, or at least wrinkled or scabby with venial faults, which must be healed by the blood of Christ and the sacraments of penance. Let the confessor secretly mark the cross with his thumb upon his own heart to protect his purity, and invoke God with at least a brief prayer or short petition; and let him avoid sweet words without necessity and all useless chatter with the penitent, and thus let him firmly and only seek the honor of God and the salvation of the soul of the other. Nor let him despair if he is tempted while he resists the delight of the flesh, mindful of what Christ said to the disciples: "If they shall drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them." The appearances remove, etc. Upon which blessed Gregory says: "Priests, through their good exhortations, remove malice from the hearts of others; they take away the appearances, and while they hear the pestiferous temptations, and then turn to prayers against the depraved, it is a deadly thing that they drink and it shall not hurt them." Let the same be consulted in his Pastoral Care, where he says thus: "It happens frequently that while the rector's soul knows the temptations of another, by hearing the temptations, he himself is also struck; and these are by no means to be feared by the pastor, who so easily snatches his own soul away, and who mercifully endures the fatigue of another's temptation, whose reasons Saint Thomas also makes manifest in his fourth book, saying: The prayer which he gives in the sacrament of penance restores. If any inclination to sin should necessarily proceed from the circumstantial thought, namely of carnal things, either in the penitent or in the confessor." 

The seventh rule: The confessor should not look at the face of the penitent, especially a woman, lest the penitent be ashamed and lest he be wounded in spirit by a woman, the spiritual surgeon.
pages.45:
For according to that saying of Habakkuk: "His face is like the burning wind." Whence the gloss upon that in Genesis, "She saw the tree was desirable to the sight," says: "Lest we be used to slippery thoughts, we ought not to look upon that which it is not permitted to desire." For, as the pure mind should be established in thought and not filled with the lascivious pleasure of its own, the eyes should be held as if they were robbers of guilt. For Eve would not have touched the tree if she had not first looked upon it incautiously. It must be weighed how much we ought to restrain ourselves from illicit things, since we live as mortals; if the matter of the living comes to death through the eyes. 

The eighth rule: Let the confessor strive with great effort, especially at the beginning of the confession and in its continuation, not to be sad, austere, or rigid, but very rarely to the penitent, whether timid or simple. For soon he will close the mouth of the sinner. Rather, let him be benign and mild after the manner of a prudent physician, and affable. Therefore, before anyone begins to confess, who is not accustomed to confessing, especially for the bashful and children, he may say things pertaining to confession, and if the situation demands it, ask about his parents and children, "Whoever wishes to confess, let him take the courage to speak." For certain persons, out of bashfulness, at the beginning lose all memory of things to be confessed, especially youths and women who rarely confess. Then let him proceed to the other doctrines that follow. This is shown by Him whose place the confessor holds, Christ, when He says: "There is no need of a physician for the healthy, but for those who are ill." Thus He did the same, who did not abhor the sinner in the city and the publicans, but called them to penance, saying: "The Son of Man did not come to call the just, but sinners." Concerning women, Hubert says: Let him not linger long, unless the necessity of confession demands it. Those who are truly penitent, and those who wish to confess frequently, let him stop from such excessive and useless frequency, and let him assign them a certain time for confessing, so that he does not hear them at other times and does not expose himself in other frequent conversations. And let him use harsh and rigid words to them rather than soft ones, because, as the venerable Bonaventure says, such women, and those like them, not knowing how to infect even themselves and the priests incredibly, without the waste of time which they incur, since they waste too much time with the priest. Christ taught regarding the aforementioned rigor when He said to His most holy mother: "What is it to me and to you? My hour has not yet come." Yet, with the aforementioned benignity, he persuades sinners toward goodness.
pages.46:
By wonderful authorities, blessed Dionysius persuades in his epistle to Demophilus, alleging Moses, the meekest of men, concerning the most meek God who is benign by His own nature, Christ the Shepherd who, having left the ninety-nine, joyfully carried the lost sheep on his shoulders, sought the tenth drachma solicitously, and most clemently received the prodigal son with gifts. 

¶ The ninth rule is that the confessor should persuade those who rarely confess and the bashful that it is an evil and foolish vice to hide sins knowingly in confession, from which one incurs many new evils. For he incurs a new sin of hypocrisy, which Christ most persecuted in the Pharisees. He shows himself to be innocent when he is guilty; of pride, because he wants to appear good or less evil where he is not. He deceives himself, not the priest; he receives no fruit of confession, since it is null and he must repeat it entirely; he dishonors the sacrament of penance which he long desired and needs to seek again. He deceives himself, not the priest. It would be better not to confess than to feign a confession, of which the Psalm says: "The Lord has dissipated the bones of those who please men; they are confounded because God has despised them," all of which will have a place on the day of judgment, when all and individual sins will be exposed not to one man but to the whole world with perpetual damnation. Of this also the Truth says: "He who will have been ashamed of me—that is, the Truth—before men, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty and the glory of the saints." 

¶ The tenth rule is that the confessor will be able to tell him who wants to confess the fruits and the utilities which he receives from a pure confession, if he grieves for the past and intends to beware of the future. First, the remission of all sins, according to that Psalm: "I said, I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord, and You have remitted the impiety of my heart." Second, he receives new sacramental grace and the graces of virtue or its increase through the merit of the passion of Christ, which works in the sacraments. Third, he will receive the union of God with the soul, or it is newer or greater than before, because then God loves him and he keeps His word, and thus, subsequently, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit will make a dwelling with such a penitent. Fourth, a new adornment of the soul, or at least a disposition of some good habit, is imprinted, because according to the Psalm: "Confession and beauty are in His presence," then when we know the beauty and magnificence of such a one in the sanctification of God. Fifth, the pain of hell, which was going to last for an infinite time for a mortal sin, is changed into a finite pain when one is contrite before confession.
pages.47:
By the power of the sacrament of confession to be received. When one actually confesses, the aforementioned finite pain is made lesser by the power of the sacrament, proportionate to the strength of the penitent. Whence in every confession a certain indulgence is given, known to God. And therefore, if anyone is contrite after mortal sins and actually receives the sacrament of penance and dies immediately, he is freed from purgatory sooner than if he had died in similar sins; for he who is contrite receives the sacrament by the mere desire. Sixth, it fits so that one may be able to receive other sacraments worthily and fruitfully—namely, the Eucharist, the holy oil, and matrimony—even those which one ought not to receive after a mortal sin unless one has confessed first. Seventh, it brings joy to the conscience and is the best remedy against sudden death. For he who has confessed and is contrite, if he dies in an instant, is entirely saved, although perhaps he might be in purgatory, and thus he does not die badly. But he who is neither contrite nor confessed, if he lived for a thousand years, such a one dies badly and suddenly, because he would depart to be damned. 

The eleventh rule is that the confessor should avoid the acceptance of persons, which is justice, because he prefers one person over another for an undue cause. Whence he should not fear poverty, deformity, or ignorance, nor, conversely, accept riches, beauty, or wisdom, unless one ought to hope for greater fruit and honor before God from that wisdom, which this one, who is the judge of souls, ought to seek principally, and not favors, profit, or friendship. "Freely," Christ says to the confessors, "you have received, freely give." Thus the Lord cries out through Moses in Deuteronomy: "Hear them and judge what is just, whether he is a citizen or a pilgrim; there shall be no distinction of persons. So you shall hear the small as the great, nor shall you accept the person of anyone, because the judgment is God's." And again: "Do not accept a person nor gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and change the words of the just." Temptation and observation of this rule is accustomed to draw men to the heart, just as a magnet draws iron. 

The twelfth rule: If in the confession itself it happens that he hears the enormous sins of sinners, let him not despise them, nor judge them too harshly, but let him hear them with passion, from the example of blessed Ambrose who, by hearing such things, began to weep out of compassion, so that he made the confessors weep with him. Thus also Christ, the most innocent son of the virgin, heard the accusations of the woman caught in adultery patiently, until one after the other went out, saying: "He who is without sin among you, let him cast the first stone at her." For the grace of God is, according to Augustine in his book on the dignity and gift of God, to be attributed to whatever you did not do that you could have done by sinning.

What the confessor generally has to ask of the penitent, and there are seven [things], and how he ought to inform him according to the same, etc., as below. ¶ Chapter 2. 

Secondly, the confessor should see what he has to ask of the penitent himself generally, and he ought to inform him according to the same. There are seven, and he ought to inform him according to them, some fitly according to the quality of the persons, yet more or less as necessity teaches. ¶ First, let him ask, according to <term>Johannes Friburgensis</term> <gloss>John of Freiburg</gloss> in his confessional, how long it has been since he confessed, who now wishes to confess, and if it has not been confessed to him before. If he answers that it has been a long time, so that he does not know how to distinguish whether he sinned between the last confession and those things he did previously, then the confessor should order a general confession to be made of all and individual sins. But if he knows how to distinguish between those things perpetrated since the last confession, then it is not necessary to repeat what was previously confessed, unless there is a case because of which it is necessary to repeat the confession. ¶ Second, let him ask whether the penitent is entangled in any case in which the confession is necessarily or probably to be repeated, of which there are four or five. The first is when the confessor could not absolve because of his own fault, as one who was not a priest or who could [absolve] in some things but not in all, and in those same ones did not send him to a superior; for thus he is still bound to go to the superior for absolution, unless ignorance would sometimes excuse the penitent. Second, when the penitent could not be absolved because of his own fault, as for instance because he was excommunicated and the confessor could not absolve from excommunication, or if he tried to do so but did not have the authority; for no one, according to Saint Thomas, can be absolved from major excommunication by one who cannot absolve. The third is when someone, knowing and out of bashfulness, hypocrisy, or a similar cause, concealed a sin that necessarily had to be confessed, unless he later told the priest—at least by remembering the fiction—that he had confessed his deception, and what he did not confess explicitly.
pages.49: And other privileged things by implicit confession, yet he does not divide [the confession] when he seeks superiors with greater sins, or when the good faith of the simple or ignorance excuses, or where the confessor or penitent would be scandalized, as was said in the first rule in the seventh case of the first chapter. But what if he neglected to do penance or omitted it, and does not remember it? Many say that, although it is not safer, it is not necessary to confess everything, and also, according to some, not when the penitent is only contrite or not contrite, and then he is absolved, he ought afterwards to confess his contrition. Nevertheless, fiction in confession happens, according to the Chancellor, when someone knowingly conceals something, or persists in the purpose of sinning, or knows and ought to know that he cannot be absolved by such a one. And such a fiction, he is bound to repeat the confession according to the more probable opinion, and that is the fifth case. For it ought to be, as will be said later, that everyone, even if not contrite, confesses all sins because of the many things that follow. Similarly, as was said before, it is not necessary to repeat this confession if he did not think something was a sin, or a venial [sin] became a mortal one, and therefore he did not confess it, because he did not have the conscience of it, yet afterwards he has [it]; although it is safer to repeat it. Furthermore, because he forgot some sin in confession, it is not necessary that he repeat everything afterwards, whether he confesses it before or anew, but he is only bound to confess the forgotten thing. In the preceding case, there is ignorance of law, and in this case, ignorance of fact. Third, let him ask and labor, especially regarding youths and children, so that he may have the opportunity to make them make a general confession, because, as the Chancellor says, they hardly or never confess entirely, unless perhaps they are instructed by such a confessor as is described here; indeed, it is also useful for the elderly, rural, simple [people], and women; otherwise, one cannot easily be induced. Toward this, let such interrogations be made by him of them: "Is your conscience made aware of such sins, and of such and such, and of such an age, and of such a society, and of having associated with such?" And according to the answer, the confessor will be able to perceive if a full confession was made previously; and if not, then let him induce them to complete it. Fourth, if while questioning or continuing the confession, he perceives the penitent is not contrite about some sin, as happens often regarding carnal love, regarding hatred of a brother, regarding not wishing to make restitution, or similar things, and because of this...

pages.74:
Deceitful laborers who work uselessly or accept too much in price, such as physicians, notaries, scribes, chancellors, surgeons, and apothecaries, omitting <term>simony</term> <gloss>the buying or selling of ecclesiastical offices</gloss>—concerning all of whom you have in the <term>summae</term> <gloss>summaries of theology</gloss> more distinctly where restitution must be made or not. It is declared, or the aforementioned verses according to <note>Thomas Aquinas, or alternatively, Duns Scotus</note>: 

*Command*: that is, when someone probably believes that the removal of a thing followed from his command, or he ratified it as done in his name, such a person is held liable *in solidum* <gloss>for the whole amount</gloss>; otherwise, he is not. 
*Counsel*: as when an abstraction, damage, or what is probably believed to have followed, results from counsel, one is held liable *in solidum*; otherwise, not. 
*Consent*: that is, where the effect is shown in the work of cooperation; such a person, if he cooperated such that without him the damage could not have been done, is held liable *in solidum*. If, however, it would have been done without him, let him restore as much as he harmed, whether by himself or through his household or through his own, or as much as he had or spent of those things. Whence Petrus de Palude says that an advocate is held liable even if he was ignorant of the injustice of the case due to an error of law. 
*Flattery*: that is, a flatterer praising, let us say, a robber as if he were vigorous, and the like; if damage resulted from this, he is held liable *in solidum*; otherwise, not. Understand the opposite regarding a detractor or reviler. 
*Recourse or Receiving*: that is, when someone is a receiver of thieves, robbers, or plunderers, and he holds them so that they are not compelled to restore, or he maliciously hides the robbed or stolen thing so that restitution is impeded by this, he is held liable *in solidum*. 
*Participating*: that is, in the crime of robbery; that is, one who associates himself with such evildoers to plunder. If the robbery or theft would not have been done without such association, he is held liable *in solidum*. If, however, he participates in the crime by associating with the robbers to plunder, and it is held that the plunder would have been done without him, such a person is not held liable except for what reached him or how much he harmed casually or occasionally. If, however, he participated in the robbed thing by knowingly buying the stolen good or receiving it, he is held to restore; otherwise, if he bought or received it ignorantly. 
*Silence*: that is, one who sees a theft being committed and deceitfully keeps silent when he could have impeded it with a single word without his own peril, and does not do so when he is held to do so by his office.
pages.75:
to forbid it, he is held liable *in solidum*; otherwise, if he is not held by office to oppose or impede, and he does not impede, he is not. 
*Not Obstructing*: that is, one who has the power to resist without his own peril and does not do so when he is held by office to obstruct, as is the case with princes who are held by their office to observe justice, because the revenues they have are established for this, they are held to restore; otherwise, those who are not held by office to observe [justice], because they are not held to restitution. 
*Not Manifesting*: that is, one who knows where a robbed or stolen thing is and does not indicate it when it is requested, and when he is held by office to do so, he is held to restitution; otherwise, if he only knows where it is and does not indicate it even when he is asked about it, because then one sins, but one is not held to restitution. Whence a judge who ought to pronounce on the matter of which he has knowledge, and thus manifest the law through himself, if he does not do so, is held to restitution. 
From the premises it is also clear that any heir, whether a son or a stranger, without distinguishing the truth of the robber or another, is held by canon law to pay all debts of the deceased, whether they were from a contract or quasi-contract, or from a crime, or otherwise; whether that thing for which the debt was contracted came to him or not, whether the lawsuit was contested with the deceased or not. 
A contract is such as buying, selling, leasing, hiring, a loan, and similar things. A quasi-contract is such as guardianship or the management of another's business. A crime is such as theft, robbery, or another crime, such as when a judge judges out of ignorance, or when something is thrown or poured from another's house which harmed passersby. <note>A red paragraph mark indicates the start of a section where the author demonstrates who is held to restitution in special cases, especially regarding robbers, plunderers, those causing damage to fruits in war, or those causing damage in benefices and the like.</note> Chapter Three. 
As to what and how much one is held to restore, certain degrees or differences are to be noted from the premises, especially regarding robbery and theft. The first: if some go with robbers and do not cooperate with them in doing any damage, nor have they received anything from the stolen things, such persons are held to restore nothing. But the second, who
pages.76:
neither help nor in anything consent, yet something is given to them from the robbery or theft, and they knowingly accept or eat from it, or wear it, or put it to other uses, they are held to restitution. Concerning such, however, who had received something as a gift and consumed it before they understood the truth of the matter, they are not held to restore. 
Similarly, it is excepted when someone acts in the cause of plunderers by admonishing and inducing the robber by his power to make restitution, especially if he has a probable hope for the correction of the plunderers, and when it is effected by such corruption that the plunderer is made unable to restore in whole or in large part. Those admonishers, therefore, who insist constantly at opportune hours so that the plunderer may restore the stolen goods, are not held to restore. 
Under the second case, also, those who know or probably believe that by reason of their following or association with the robbers, or other inducement or detraction, the robbers themselves did no more than they would have done otherwise, and yet they had and spent something from the robbed goods, such persons are held to restore from the goods held or spent, and also for all damage that they or any of their family did, directly or occasionally. 
The third: when several do damage together, and yet one would have done it without the other, or several without this one, such a person is held to pay *pro rata* <gloss>proportionally</gloss>, that is, for his portion, that is, how much it reduces him from the universal damage, if the damage that he himself inflicted cannot be distinguished from that which the others inflicted. In this, however, an estimation must be had so that whoever is more vigorous and who struck greater fear and terror into the enemies is also held more. Similarly, also in the case when some are associated with robbers and believe that the robbers would have done the damage even without their aid or instigation, but they are only held to that which they probably believe them to have done by reason of their instigation or aid. 
The fourth: if some associate with robbers and do not cooperate with them to do any damage, but are in their mind prepared to defend if perhaps those to be plundered had wished to defend their things from the plunderers, and by reason of their presence and that of their associates they dared not resist those plundering
pages.77:

Whence it is the same as if they helped them; according to whether they emboldened the adversaries, because then it is seen to be in the first case. 
The fifth: he who was the cause of all the damage is held *in solidum*, that is, for the whole damage. This is the case where there were several robbers, none of whom induced the other to go, nor did any lord command another, but each says for himself "I am going," and almost as if it were an army, each is held *in solidum*, because in such a case each helped the others and made them stronger, and all are cooperators. Otherwise, if they did not go together but each was doing damage separately by himself, each is held for that which he did; understand, however, beyond what has already been said, because one would not dare or be able to do the damage without the other, otherwise each is held even for the part of the damage which he inflicted. 
Note also that a stolen or robbed thing ought to be restored with all the fruits and profits which it produced, because they could have been received, because they are held for interest and for all damages. Nor is one excused if the thing perishes in his possession, because he was in delay of returning it. If, however, the owner, being provoked, did not want to accept it, he is excused. Furthermore, regarding any damage where restitution is to be made, because the one damaging unjustly is held, not, however, to restore the thing if he is also held for interest, that is, for the compensation of the damage and to the fruit perceived from the thing if the thing was fruit-bearing; not, however, to the fruit which comes from the industry of the one who uses that thing. Where a usurer or another damaging another by providing usury, and the poor man is forced to sell his grain for less, or someone has lost the profit of trade by which he lived, when he was a laborer, he is held to the expenses of physicians, damages to work, and the like, to the interest, unless the one damaged, at the request of the one who damaged him, voluntarily remits it. Not, however, is the usurer held to restore money or [things] acquired through usurious money, or the usury or the money which he had through that usury; whence also the learned say that

Therefore, he is held, according to the same learned men, to the restitution of this, who hinders someone from the obtaining of any reward which he would honestly receive from another. 
Item, the same Thomas: whoever hinders someone from the obtaining of a benefice unjustly, or out of hatred or vengeance or any such thing, if he hinders it so that the reward is not given to the worthy, counseling that it not be given before it is confirmed, he is held to give him not what he would have had, because that was not obtained and could have been hindered in many ways, but he is held to some recompense, the conditions of the persons and the matters being weighed according to the judgment of a wise man. If, however, it is already confirmed that it is to be given to another, he is held to equal restitution. 
To this his faculty, Scotus adds that if someone was only intending to provide for his own utility by hindering directly or indirectly another in a reward or similar thing, and thus procures for himself without the intention of damaging the other or out of envy, although the other is damaged beyond his intention, such a one is held to restore nothing. 
When, however, in war some things are robbed by the subjects of lords, how is restitution to be made there? It is to be noted that for a war to be just, five things are required: 
1. The person: that is, secular, not ecclesiastical. 
2. The cause: that is, because of necessity, and so that peace may be had, let him fight. 
3. The spirit: so that it is not done out of hatred, envy, vengeance, or greed, but because of charity, justice, and obedience. 
4. The authority: of the church or the prince. 
5. The thing: that is, so that it is done for recovering things or for the defense of the fatherland. 
Although, therefore, says Wilhelm in the gloss, war is thus unjust in the first four, if indeed the thing is satisfied, because it is done for recovering things, he who moves the war is not held to restore what he took there, unless he took or damaged his adversary beyond what he had
pages.79:

Here it is shown when someone is held to restore immediately and in which five cases the restitution to be made can be deferred. Chapter Four. 
When, indeed, or at what time, and who is held to restore immediately? Three rules are to be noted. 
The first: it is not permitted at any time to detain another's [property] against the owner's will, that is, [while he is] unwilling, and according to right reason, [one] ought not to be [unwilling]; and consequently, regularly, restitution is to be made immediately, for the same reason that one must cease immediately from the act of mortal sin, not only the exterior act, therefore it is light. Leviticus 19 says: "The work of a hireling shall not abide with thee until the morning." Item, for another reason, because if I detain your thing, I hinder you in the use of it more than if I frequently took it away. 
The second rule: whoever detains or accepts another's thing against the owner's will, is held by affection to restore immediately, that is, he is held to have the purpose, if he wishes to be contrite, of restoring as much as possible with opportune circumstances. 
The third rule: in many cases it is permitted to defer exterior restitution, the interior will to restore having been placed, namely, when opportune circumstances occur. Those cases, however, contain this universal maxim: it is permitted to detain another's thing when he ought to reasonably want it to be detained by the other, in fact, the will to restore having been placed with opportune circumstances. And this happens in five cases: 
The first: when the one who detains cannot restore because of poverty, because then he is not held, but when he has come to a fatter fortune, he ought, however, to seek in the meantime a delay from the owner of the thing, if it can be had. 
The second: when restitution made immediately would be believed to be to the prejudice of the community or even of him to whom it should be made, as a sword ought not to be restored to a madman, because he would harm either himself or the community, or the owner of the thing. 
The third: when restitution made immediately would lead to the infamy of the restorer because of hidden gifts; for he does not then immediately damage himself, he is held to give it to the injured [party] through another for the place and time of restitution

The fourth: when restitution made immediately would yield no or meager comfort to him to whom it is owed, but [would result] in the loss or notable damage of the debtor. Whence it is clear when someone acts in remote parts to whom restitution should be made, then no greater expense ought to be put forward in the transmission than that which is worth what is sent, but the penitence of the person is to be awaited, if it is believed that it can be had, or if it is not believed that it can be had, and a messenger does not supervene without excessive expenses, it is to be given to the parents, who if they are not present, it is to be given to the poor. 
Similarly, if it is not known where they are, nor is it hoped that they can easily be known, it should be given to the poor. If, however, it is known that, the aforementioned not obstructing, it may be sent to him faithfully and securely. Which understand to be done when it can be done conveniently, because in such a case the circumstances are to be weighed, namely, the quantity of the owed thing, the expenses of the place removed which would be made by promising, and the poverty or riches of him to whom restitution is to be made; because the sum of the thing to be restored could be so meager, and the expenses that would be made in sending it so great, and he to whom restitution is to be made so rich, that he should in no way want his neighbor to be burdened so much for so meager a thing, and then it is not necessary that he send it; in such things one must recur to the arbitration of a good man. 
The fifth case is according to Henry of Ghent, in book 6, quolibet 23, where he says: when someone awaits a greater opportunity for restoring, then it is permitted not to restore immediately, as if he to whom restitution is to be made is ignorant of the debt. Scotus also says: when someone has the will to restore at an opportune time, from then on he holds with the owner being willing, and if not in the elicited act, yet in the owed act, because the owner ought to want that he who has his own hold it until he can render it opportunely. Regarding the opportune time of restoring for manifest usurers and public robbers, there are two special things, says Petrus de Palude: manifest usurers ought to restore or sufficiently guarantee restitution before confession and the charity of the offering at the altar, because for usurers

Seventh, when, as the blessed Thomas says, the subject knows his own priest to be a heretic, or a solicitor to evil, or fragile regarding the sin about which one confesses, or likely to reveal the confession, or if he reasonably estimates that the confessor is a revealer of confessions, or if the sin about which one ought to confess was committed against him. For in these cases, and others in which the penitent reasonably fears danger to himself or to the priest from the confession made, he ought to have recourse to the superior and seek license to confess to another. If he cannot have this, the judgment is the same as for one who has no access to a confessor; indeed, in this case, he should rather confess to a layman. And if he has no other priest to whom to confess, let him confess to his own, while remaining silent about that from which the danger arises. Eighth, when he is in danger of death and has another available, for then that one is in a way his own. ¶ The second rule: Let the confessor, who keeps watch to purify souls, strive to be pure himself, and let him place the hope of his labor and of profiting others not in his own power, but in the divine power. For according to the Apostle, neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase. Therefore, the confessor should pray frequently and piously, just as the wise physician also offers prayers, that God, who heals all infirmities, may direct his work and strengthen and increase it with His power. ¶ The third rule: Let him take care not to act precipitously regarding the person confessing, nor to be provoked by the mere flow of words, but with patient vigilance, fully examining and judging, he should not interrupt, even if he hears the words of the person confessing, but should remember what is said and ask distinctly afterward. Or if he cannot commit it to memory, he should at least investigate carefully and clearly into each point. He should urge the one confessing to store up what is to be said and imposed with diligent repetition, and he should take sufficient time for these things. For it is preferable, as the Chancellor says, that a confessor in the hearing of confessions should hear a few fully rather than many imperfectly, since the burden of the office is not so much to expedite as to avoid impeding. He says, therefore, that if one is busy, he ought to defer the confessions of many until after Easter, lest some, like the blind leading the blind, seduce others, or while they believe themselves absolved, they conduct themselves as if they were not absolved. For what is written in that word of God in Ezekiel? He says: "If, O son of man, I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel, and you hear a word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me. If, while I speak to the wicked, you have not spoken to the wicked man so that he might guard himself from his way, that wicked man himself will die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. If, however, you have warned the wicked man so that he might turn from his ways, and he has not turned from his way, he himself will die in his iniquity; but you have delivered your soul."

you have delivered your soul." <term>The fourth</term> rule: It is expedient that the confessor obtain from the prelate, as far as he is able, the power to absolve his subjects in reserved cases, beyond those that are relaxed, especially if the cases are not public and scandalous. For, as the Chancellor says, very few are found who have not fallen into some such cases that are reserved. Those who have confessed, knowing that they do not need to be sent again to another, confess all things more freely and clearly. The confessor, indeed, presumes to interrogate them more freely and to heal them more fully, trusting in himself to absolve them all at once. For what else is it to send the penitent from judge to judge in hidden matters, but to add affliction to the afflicted? Certainly, many existing in filth are made to sin more causally or occasionally, and they become filthier for the worse. Christ did not do this to the Samaritan, of whom Isaiah prophesies thus: "A bruised reed he shall not break, and smoking flax he shall not quench; he shall bring forth judgment in truth. He will not be sad nor turbulent." <term>The fifth</term> rule: According to Hubert in his book *On the Instruction of Officials*, in the chapter on the hearing of confessions, he should choose such a place for sitting that he can be seen by many, especially when he hears women, and yet the confession cannot be heard by anyone, for in this, certainly, both his reputation and that of the penitent are helped. For the confessor is the angel of the Lord of hosts, as Malachi says. And of the confessor and the one confessing, Christ says: "He who does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be manifest, because they were done in God." Likewise, the blessed <term>Jerome</term> informs Nepotian: "Avoid all suspicions," he says, "and avoid anything that can be reasonably feigned by you. Abstain from every evil appearance," as the Apostle commands. Yet, those who disregard these rules regarding suspicions regarding women very easily succumb, as Job says: "The eye of the adulterer observes darkness." And as Hubert says: "If any great persons of the male sex wish to confess, of whom the confessor believes they might be ashamed to be seen in the presence of all during confessions, he ought to lead them to another place that is more secret and honest."

<term>The sixth</term> rule: He who is about to hear women should take care that, while he purges their souls of vices, he himself does not become defiled by voluntary delectations. Let him not be a vessel that becomes filthy while washing others; if he is such a hand that shines while cleansing others, let him not consider himself a respecter of persons. When he listens to the beautiful or the young, he should not do so more freely and quickly than he does to old women in confession. He should arm himself with good and holy imaginations. First, by considering that he ought to be an angel of God and a vicar of the God who trembles in judgment. Then, with the eyes of the body and of the soul, he should turn away from women and turn his lights toward the soul, so that he may see it as a leprous or wounded thing, or as an image of God scarred by the dire wounds of mortal sins, or at least wrinkled or scabious with venial sins, which must be healed through the blood of Christ and the sacraments of penance. The confessor should secretly make the sign of the cross with his thumb upon his own sinner <note>meaning: his own heart/body</note> for the sake of protecting purity, and he should at least invoke a brief prayer or small petition to God. And he should avoid without necessity all sweet words and all useless conversation with the penitent. And so, he should firmly apply himself to the honor of God and the salvation of a foreign soul. Nor should he despair if he is tempted while renouncing the delectation of the flesh, mindful of Christ saying to the disciples: "If they drink any deadly thing, it shall not harm them." He removes the temptations, etc. Regarding which the blessed <term>Gregory</term> says: "Priests remove malice from foreign hearts through their own good exhortations, and they remove temptations, and while they hear of pestiferous inclinations, they turn to prayers against the wicked; it is a deadly thing that they drink, but it shall not harm them." The same is advised in his *Pastoral*, where he says: "It happens frequently that while the soul of the rector learns of the temptations of others, he is himself struck by the heard temptations; and these things are by no means to be feared by the pastor, since he easily tears his own soul away from them and compassionately fatigues himself with the temptation of another." Whose reasons the holy <term>Thomas</term> also manifests in the fourth <note>referring to his Commentary on the Sentences, Book IV</note>, saying: "The prayer which he gives in the sacrament of penance restores. If any inclination to sin should necessarily come from a circumstantial thought, namely of carnal things, either in the penitent or in the confessor." <term>The seventh</term> rule: The confessor should not look at the face of the one confessing, especially a woman, so that the one confessing might not blush and so that he might not be wounded in his soul by a woman, as a spiritual surgeon.

<summary>The sixth and seventh rules focus on maintaining purity of mind and sight during the confession of women, emphasizing the confessor's role as a spiritual physician and the protection afforded by prayer and meditation.</summary>

Whence the gloss upon that in Genesis: "She saw that the tree was delectable to the sight," says: "Lest we be used to slippery thoughts, we ought not to look at what is not permitted to be coveted. For as the clean mind is used to being in thought, the eyes are to be filled by the lascivious pleasure of the same, as if they were robbers of guilt. For Eve would not have touched the tree if she had not first looked at it incautiously." One must weigh how much we ought to restrain ourselves from illicit things, since we live in a mortal state; if the matter of the living comes to death through the eyes, one must be cautious. <term>The eighth</term> rule: The confessor should take the utmost care that at the beginning of the confession, and especially in its progress, he is not sad, austere, or rigid, particularly to those who are rarely confessing, or to the timid, or to the simple. For soon the mouth of the sinner will close. Rather, let him be benign and mild in the manner of a prudent physician, and affable. Whence, before anyone begins to confess, who is not accustomed to confessing—many, for instance, the ashamed and the young—he can say: "The beginning of confessions is necessary." And if the matter so requires, asking of his own daughter <note>referring to a spiritual daughter</note>, "Whoever wishes to confess, let him take the boldness to speak," because some persons out of shame at the beginning lose all memory of what is to be confessed, especially the young and women who rarely confess. Then he should proceed to the other doctrines that follow. Those who confess frequently should be warned against such excessive and useless frequentation, and a certain time should be assigned to them for confessing, so that he does not hear them at other times, nor expose himself to other frequent conversations. And the father who received the prodigal son with most clement gifts. <term>The ninth</term> rule: The confessor should warn those who confess rarely and those who are ashamed what an evil and foolish vice it is to hide sins, knowing that in confession one incurs many new evils. Namely, that one incurs the new sin of hypocrisy, which Christ especially persecuted in the Pharisees; he shows himself innocent when he is guilty, and of pride, since he wants to appear good or less evil where he is not. He deceives himself; he does not deceive the priest. Since he receives no fruit of the confession, which is null, he is forced to repeat the sacrament of penance entirely, which he long delayed and secondly neglected. He deceives himself, he does not deceive the priest. It would be better not to confess than to feign a confession, of which the Psalm says: "The Lord has scattered the bones of those who please men; they are confounded because God has scorned them," all of which will have a place on the day of judgment, when all and individual sins will be exposed not to one man but to the whole world with perpetual damnation. Of which the Truth also says: "He who denies me, that is, the Truth, before men, the Son of Man will deny him when He comes in His majesty and the glory of the saints." <term>The tenth</term> rule: The confessor will be able to tell him who wishes to confess the fruits and the benefits that he receives from a pure confession if he grieves for the past and intends to beware of the future. First, the remission of all sins, according to that Psalm: "I said I will confess against myself my injustice, and you have forgiven the impiety of my heart." Second, he receives new sacramental grace and the graces of virtue or its increase through the merit of the passion of Christ, which works in the sacraments. Third, he will receive the union of God with his soul, which is new or greater than before, because then God loves him and he keeps His word, and consequently for the one confessing, such a union is made, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit making their dwelling [in him]. Fourth, a new ornament of the soul, or at least a disposition for some good habit, is imprinted, because according to the Psalm: "Confession and beauty," at that time in His sight, when we know all things and His magnificence is in the sanctification of God. Fifth, the punishment of the inferno, which would last for an infinite time for a mortal sin, becomes a finished punishment when one is contrite before confession.

<summary>The ninth and tenth rules emphasize the danger of hypocrisy in confession and the spiritual benefits of a sincere, full confession, including the remission of sins, sacramental grace, union with God, and the reduction of eternal punishment.</summary>

For when one confesses in act, the aforementioned finished punishment, by the power of the sacrament, is proportioned to the strength of the one confessing and is made smaller. Whence in every confession a certain indulgence is given, known to God. And therefore, if anyone is contrite after mortal sins and receives the sacrament of penance in act, and immediately dies, he is liberated more quickly from purgatory than one who dies in similar sins, since he who is contrite but not confessed receives the sacrament [only by desire]. Sixth, it adapts him so that he can rightly and fruitfully receive other sacraments, namely the Eucharist, the holy oil, and marriage, which even after mortal sin one ought not to receive unless one has confessed. Seventh, it brings forth the joy of the conscience and is the best remedy against sudden death. For he who has confessed and is contrite, if he dies in an instant, is entirely saved, even if through fire, and thus he does not die badly. But he who dies neither contrite nor confessed, even if he lives for a thousand years, such a one who dies, dies badly and suddenly, because he will depart to be damned. <term>The eleventh</term> rule: The confessor should avoid the acceptance of persons, which is an injustice, in which a person is preferred to another for an undue reason. Whence he should not abhor poverty, deformity, or ignorance, nor, on the contrary, should he accept riches, beauty, or wisdom, unless [one hopes for] greater fruit and honor before God, which he ought to seek principally, as he who is the judge of souls, and not favors, gain, or friendship. "Freely," says Christ to the confessors, "you have received, freely give." Thus the Lord cries through Moses in Deuteronomy: "Hear them and judge what is just, whether he is a citizen or a pilgrim; there shall be no distance of persons. You shall hear the small as well as the great; you shall not accept the person of anyone, because it is the judgment of God." And again: "Do not accept a person nor gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and change the words of the just." The fear and observation of this rule is accustomed to draw men to the heart, just as the magnet draws iron. <term>The twelfth</term> rule: If during the confession itself it happens that he must hear the enormities of sinners, he should not despise them, nor judge them too harshly, but hear them with compassion, from the example of the blessed <term>Ambrose</term>, who by hearing similar things, began to weep out of compassion so that he made the confessors weep with him. For the grace of God is, according to <term>Augustine</term> in his book *On Nature and Grace*, to be assigned as a gift: whatever you did not do, which you could have done through sin.

<summary>This page concludes the twelve rules for confessors, covering the benefits of confession, the importance of impartiality (avoiding the acceptance of persons), and the necessity of hearing sins with patience and compassion rather than judgment.</summary>

Whatever the confessor generally has to ask of the one confessing, and there are seven, and how he ought to inform him according to the same, etc., as below. ¶ Chapter the second.

Secondly, the confessor should see what he has to ask of the one confessing in general and inform him according to the same. There are seven, and he should inform him according to them, some fittingly according to the quality of the persons, yet more or less as necessity teaches. ¶ First, ask, according to <term>John of Freiburg</term> in his *Confessional*, how long it has been since he was confessed, if he now wishes to confess and was not previously confessed to him. If he answers that he does not know, so that he does not know how to distinguish the sins committed between the last confession and those he committed previously, then the confessor should order a general confession to be made of all and individual sins. If, however, he knows how to distinguish those he perpetrated since the last confession, thus it is not necessary to repeat those previously confessed, unless there is a case on account of which it is necessary to repeat the whole confession. ¶ Secondly, inquire whether the one confessing is entangled in any case in which the confession is necessarily or probably to be repeated. Of which there are four or five. The first is when the confessor, on account of his own fault, could not absolve, as he who was not a priest, or because he could [absolve] in some but not in all, and in the same he did not send to the superior; for thus he is still bound to go to the superior for absolution, unless ignorance would sometimes excuse the one confessing. Second, when the one confessing, on account of his own fault, could not be absolved, as for instance because he was excommunicated, and the confessor could not absolve from excommunication, or if he tried to do things but did not have the authority; for no one, according to the holy <term>Thomas</term>, can be absolved from major excommunication by one who does not have the power to absolve. Third, when someone, knowing and out of shame, hypocrisy, or a similar cause, concealed a sin that was necessarily to be confessed, unless afterward he confessed his fiction notably to a better confessor, at least remembering what he had previously confessed, and what he did not confess even explicitly.

<term>The sixth</term> rule: He who is about to hear women should take care that, while he purges their souls of vices, he himself does not become defiled by voluntary delectations. Let him not be a vessel that becomes filthy while washing others; if he is such a hand that shines while cleansing others, let him not consider himself a respecter of persons. When he listens to the beautiful or the young, he should not do so more freely and quickly than he does to old women in confession. He should arm himself with good and holy imaginations. First, by considering that he ought to be an angel of God and a vicar of the God who trembles in judgment. Then, with the eyes of the body and of the soul, he should turn away from women and turn his lights toward the soul, so that he may see it as a leprous or wounded thing, or as an image of God scarred by the dire wounds of mortal sins, or at least wrinkled or scabious with venial sins, which must be healed through the blood of Christ and the sacraments of penance. The confessor should secretly make the sign of the cross with his thumb upon his own sinner <note>meaning: his own heart/body</note> for the sake of protecting purity, and he should at least invoke a brief prayer or small petition to God. And he should avoid without necessity all sweet words and all useless conversation with the penitent. And so, he should firmly apply himself to the honor of God and the salvation of a foreign soul. Nor should he despair if he is tempted while renouncing the delectation of the flesh, mindful of Christ saying to the disciples: "If they drink any deadly thing, it shall not harm them." He removes the temptations, etc. Regarding which the blessed <term>Gregory</term> says: "Priests remove malice from foreign hearts through their own good exhortations, and they remove temptations, and while they hear of pestiferous inclinations, they turn to prayers against the wicked; it is a deadly thing that they drink, but it shall not harm them." The same is advised in his *Pastoral*, where he says: "It happens frequently that while the soul of the rector learns of the temptations of others, he is himself struck by the heard temptations; and these things are by no means to be feared by the pastor, since he easily tears his own soul away from them and compassionately fatigues himself with the temptation of another." Whose reasons the holy <term>Thomas</term> also manifests in the fourth <note>referring to his Commentary on the Sentences, Book IV</note>, saying: "The prayer which he gives in the sacrament of penance restores. If any inclination to sin should necessarily come from a circumstantial thought, namely of carnal things, either in the penitent or in the confessor." <term>The seventh</term> rule: The confessor should not look at the face of the one confessing, especially a woman, so that the one confessing might not blush and so that he might not be wounded in his soul by a woman, as a spiritual surgeon.

<summary>The sixth and seventh rules focus on maintaining purity of mind and sight during the confession of women, emphasizing the confessor's role as a spiritual physician and the protection afforded by prayer and meditation.</summary>
<keywords>confessor, purity, temptation, penance, spiritual physician, Gregory, Thomas Aquinas, rules</keywords>

Concerning all these, you have in the *Summae* <note>refers to the *Summa Theologiae* or similar canonical works</note> more distinct information where restitution ought to be made or not. This is declared, or the aforementioned verses according to Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, in the last article of the second part, thus: order, that is, when someone reasonably believes that a theft of a thing followed from his order, or he ratified it having been done in his name, such a person is held liable for the whole; otherwise, no. Counsel, as when from counsel a theft or damage follows, or is reasonably believed to have followed, he is held liable for the whole; otherwise, no. Consent, that is, where the effect is shown in the work of cooperation; such a person, if he cooperates so that without him the damage could not have occurred, is held liable for the whole. If, however, it would have been done without him, let him restore as much as he harmed, whether by himself or by his household or by his own, or as much as he had or spent of those things. Whence Peter de Palude says that an advocate is held liable even if he was ignorant of the injustice of the case on account of an error of law. Flatterer, that is, a sycophant praising, namely, a robber as if he were energetic, and such like; if damage followed from this, he is held liable for the whole; otherwise, no. Understand the opposite regarding a detractor or reviler. Recourse or recipients, that is, when someone is a receiver of robbers or thieves or plunderers, and he holds them so that they are not forced to restore, or with evil intent conceals the robbed or stolen thing so that restitution is hindered by this, he is held liable for the whole. Participant, namely, in the crime of robbery, that is, one who associates himself with such evildoers to plunder; such a person, if the robbery or theft would not have been committed without such association, is held liable for the whole. If, however, he participates in the crime by associating with robbers to plunder, and yet the robbery would have been committed without him, such a person is not held liable except for what reached him or as much as he harmed accidentally or occasionally. If, however, he participated in the robbed thing by knowingly buying the stolen good or receiving it, he is bound to restore; otherwise, if he bought or received it ignorantly. Mute, that is, one who sees a theft being committed and deceitfully stays silent when he could have hindered it with a word without personal danger and does not do so when he is held by duty to this.

Not opposing, that is, one who has the power to resist without his own danger and does not do so when he is held by duty to oppose, as are princes who by their office are held to observe justice, because the revenues they have are instituted for this; they are held to restore. Otherwise those who are not held by duty to observe, because they are not held to restitution. Not manifesting, that is, one who knows where a robbed or stolen thing is and does not indicate it when he is asked, and when he is held to this by office, he is held to restitution; otherwise, if he only knows where it is and does not indicate it even when he is asked about this, although one sins in this, he is not held to restitution. Whence a judge who ought to pronounce on the matter of which he has knowledge and thus manifest the law, if he does not do so, he is held to restitution. From the aforesaid it is also clear that any heir, whether a son or a stranger, not distinguishing the true nature of the robber or another, is held by canon law to pay all debts of the deceased, whether they were from a contract or quasi-contract, or from a crime or something else, whether the thing for which the debt was contracted reached him or not, or whether the lawsuit was contested with the deceased or not. For there is a contract, such as purchase, sale, renting, hiring, loans, and similar. A quasi-contract is such as guardianship or the management of another's business. A crime is such as theft, robbery; another crime is when a judge judges out of inexperience, or when something is thrown or poured from another's house which harmed passersby. <note>A red paragraph mark indicates the start of a section showing who is held to restitution in particular, especially regarding robbers, plunderers, those causing damage to fruits in war, or those causing damage to benefices and similar. Chapter Three.</note> What and how much one is held to restore are to be noted from the aforesaid, certain degrees or differences, especially regarding robbery and theft. First, if some go with robbers and do not cooperate with them to do any damage, nor have they received anything from the taken things, such people are held to restore nothing. Second, those who
pages.76: neither help nor in anything consent, but something is given to them from the robbery or theft and they knowingly accept or eat from it, or wear it, or put it to other uses, they are held to restitution. Concerning such people, however, who had accepted something as a gift and consumed it before they understood the truth of the matter, they are not held to restore. Similarly, it is excepted when someone acts in the cause of the plunderers by warning and inducing the robber by his power to make restitution, especially if he has a probable hope of the correction of the plunderers, and when it is effected by such corruption that the plunderer is rendered unable to restore in whole or in large part. Therefore, the monitors who urge continuously at opportune hours so that the plunderer makes restitution are not held to restore the plundered goods. Under the second case also, those who know or probably believe that because of their following or association with the robbers, or other abduction or detraction, the robbers themselves did not do more than they would have otherwise done, and yet they had and spent something of the robbed goods, such people are held to restore regarding those things had or spent, and also for all damage which they or any of their family did directly or occasionally. Third, when several do damage together and even if one without the other, or several without this one, would have done it, such a person is held to pay pro rata, that is, for his portion, this is as much as he lessened the whole damage if the damage he inflicted cannot be distinguished from that which the others inflicted. In this, however, an estimation is to be had so that he who is more energetic and who struck greater fears and terrors into the enemies also be held to more. Similarly also in the case when some associate themselves with robbers and believe that even without their aid or instigation the robbers would have done damage, but they are held only for that which they probably believe they did because of their instigation or aid. Fourth, if some associate themselves with robbers and do not cooperate with them to do any damage, but are nevertheless in mind prepared to defend [the robbers] if perhaps those to be plundered had wanted to defend their things from the brigands, and because of their presence and the presence of his associates [the victims] did not dare to resist the plunderers
pages.77: or those burning their houses, and if anyone has associated [with them], he cannot be free from restitution. Indeed, if some go with robbers with the intention of pacifying, they are not excused unless they signify this to the adversaries, who otherwise, for fear of them, would not have dared to defend their things; whence it is as if they helped them; similarly, if they encouraged the adversaries, who then seem to be in the first case. Fifth: he who was the cause of all the damage is held in solidum, that is, for all the damage, even in the case where there were several robbers, none of whom induced another to come, nor did any lord buy from another, but each says for himself, "If they go, it is nothing." As if it were one army, each is held in solidum, because in such a case each helped the others and made them stronger, and all are cooperators. Otherwise, if they did not go together but each was doing damage separately, each is held for that which he did, understanding, however, beyond what has already been said, that one would not dare or be able to do damage without the other; otherwise, each is held for the part of the damage which he inflicted. Note also that the stolen or robbed thing ought to be restored with all the fruits and profits which were produced, or which could have been produced, because they are held for interest and for all damages. Nor is it excused if the thing perishes in his possession because he was in delay of restoring. If, however, the owner refused to accept it, he is excused. Furthermore, concerning any damage-doing where restitution ought to be made, because the damage-doer is unjust, he is not, however, held to restore the thing if he is also held for interest, that is, for the reparation of the damage, and for the fruit perceived from the thing if the thing was fruit-bearing, yet not for the fruit which comes from the industry of him who uses that thing where a usurer or another damage-doer harms another by providing usury, and the poor man was forced to sell his grain for less, or someone lost profit or merchant's gain by which he lived when he was a laborer, he is held for the expenses of doctors, damages, labor, and interest, unless the injured party, having been asked, voluntarily remits it. However, a usurer is not held to restore the money or what was acquired through the loan, nor the interest or money which he had through the usury itself. Whence also he says that
pages.78: he who digs up someone's field, or who inflicts damage on another by not paying his debt at the proper time, is held to restore the whole damage. Since it is doubtful in these how the fruits of the field could have been sold in that doubt, or for how much the merchant would have sold his profit in that doubt, he is held, therefore, according to the same, to restitution, [and] he who hinders someone from the attainment of any reward which he would honestly receive from another. Also, Thomas says: whoever hinders someone from the attainment of a benefice unjustly, either because of hatred or vengeance, or some such thing, if he hinders it so that the reward is not given to the worthy, advising that it not be given before it is confirmed, he is held to give him not what he did not attain, because he could have been hindered in many ways, but he is held to some recompense, weighing the conditions of the persons and businesses according to the judgment of a wise man. If, however, it is already confirmed that it is given to another, he is held to the restitution of an equal amount. However, Scotus adds to his faculty that if someone only intended to provide for his own utility by hindering directly or indirectly another in a reward or similar, and thus procures for himself without the intention of harming another or out of envy, although the other is harmed beyond the intention, such a one is held to restore nothing. When, however, in war some things are robbed from the subjects of lords, how is it to be restored there? It is to be noted that for war to be just, five things are required: Person, namely, secular, not ecclesiastical. Cause, that is, because of necessity, and so that peace may be had, let him fight. Mind, so that it is not done out of hatred, envy, vengeance, or greed, but because of charity, justice, and obedience. Authority of the church or prince. And Thing, that is, so that it is done for recovering things or for the defense of the fatherland. Although, therefore, William says in his gloss, war is thus unjust in the first four, if the thing is secondary, because it is done for recovering things, he who moves the war is not held to restore what he took there, unless he took or damaged his adversary beyond what he had

Here he shows when someone is held to restore immediately and in which five cases the restitution to be made can be deferred. Chapter Four. When, however, or at what time, and when someone is held to restore immediately, three rules are to be noted. First, it is not permitted at any time to detain another's property against the owner's will, that is, when he is unwilling and, according to right reason, ought not to be willing, and consequently, as a rule, restitution must be made immediately, for the same reason that one must immediately cease from the act of mortal sin, not only the exterior act, therefore, Leviticus 19 says: "The wage of the worker shall not remain with you until morning." Also for another reason, because if I detain your thing, I hinder you in the use of it more than if I frequently withdrew it. Second rule: whoever detains or accepts another's thing against the owner's will is held to retain the desire to restore immediately, that is, he is held to have the intention if he wants to be contrite, to restore as much as he can with opportune circumstances. Furthermore, concerning whatever damnification where restitution is to be made, because the one damnifying unjustly is not, however, held to restore the thing if he is also held for interest, that is, for the vacation <note>loss of opportunity</note> of damage and for the fruit perceived from the thing if the thing was fruit-bearing; however, not for the fruit which comes from the industry of the one who uses that thing. Where a usurer or another damnifying another by lending usury, and the poor man is forced to sell his grain for less, or someone lost the profit or trade from which he lived when he was a laborer, he is held for expenses of physicians, damages, works, and daughters, as interest, unless the one damnified, asked, voluntarily remits it.
